01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.name: *The Aqueduct in the Forest of Belgrade, Istanbul*
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.short_description: This painting by an anonymous Ottoman artist shows the aqueduct of Belgrade Forest outside Istanbul. Istanbul’s water was stored in the reservoirs of Belgrade Forest and conveyed to the city across a number of aqueducts like this one. Established in early Ottoman times, the Istanbul water supply system was expanded and improved throughout the Ottoman period, incorporating complex systems of reservoirs, aqueducts and supply pipes endling in fountains and waterspouts.

021ca6c1-9f8d-5f9a-87db-f4c9193cbe1f.name: Saint John the Baptist from a Deesis Tier
021ca6c1-9f8d-5f9a-87db-f4c9193cbe1f.description: John the Baptist was the cousin of Jesus Christ and preached in the Judean desert. He lived a life of self-denial by wearing camel hair clothing and eating only locusts and wild honey. The people of the region came to him to be baptized in the Jordan River. When Jesus asked to be baptized, John proclaimed that he was not worthy of such a task and that Christ should baptize him instead. Christ insisted, however, and during the baptism the Holy Spirit descended and a voice from heaven proclaimed, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). John got into trouble when he criticized King Herod’s marriage to Herodias, who had a child from her previous marriage to Herod’s brother. Herod’s stepdaughter, Salome, convinced him to arrest John and demanded his head on a silver platter. Granting her wish, Herod ordered John beheaded. In this icon, John the Baptist stands in three-quarter profile and faces left. This icon was once part of a Deesis tier of an iconostasis and would have hung to the right of an icon of Christ in Majesty.
021ca6c1-9f8d-5f9a-87db-f4c9193cbe1f.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Sotheby's Auction in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

026c87e2-b1b2-5050-b96e-a327d8e94473.short_description: Mughal emperors stressed on recording their achievements, they commissioned miniature paintings of their ancestors and invited artists to accompany them on expeditions. This miniature painting dated circa 1605 depicted prince rides out with a hunting party.

03306ff5-668c-5706-a70c-d5ed5a3886c1.name: The Arrival of the Mahmal
03306ff5-668c-5706-a70c-d5ed5a3886c1.description: The painting is after is after Konstantin Makovsky’s 1876 work, ‘The Arrival of the Holy Carpet in Cairo’ (during this period the mahmal was often referred to as ‘the holy carpet’, or ‘le tapis sacré’ in French). It is not clear whether de Mango had seen Makovsky’s work or if he had access to the original photograph from which the painting was made. However, we do know that de Mango spent time in Cairo and was greatly inspired by life in the Middle East. An engraving of Makovsky’s work by R. Brendamour also appeared in a German periodical of 1893, and de Mango may have been aware of that version as well.

03769685-706c-53a4-99dd-0ddabeddce9c.name: *The Attack of Smârdan*
03769685-706c-53a4-99dd-0ddabeddce9c.short_description: Romania, that in the second half of the 19th century was still under Ottoman sovereignty, participated in the Russian-Ottoman of 1877-1878 war on Russia’s side. In May 1877 the Parliament declared Romania’s independence, which was recognized by the Ottoman Empire and the Great Powers at the peace congress organized in Berlin after the conflict (June – July 1878). When Romania entered the war, Nicolae Grigorescu was one of the painters hired to accompany the Romanian army. One of his best known works depicts the victory that the Romanian soldiers won against the Ottomans at Smârdan (24 January 1878). The painting, which has several variants, was based on others’ accounts because Grigorescu was sick and could not be present on the front when the battle took place.

037e2e8a-4c21-57dd-b0a6-532274d43a0d.name: Baalbec : engineers removing the Kaiser's commemoration stone from the Temple of Apollo
037e2e8a-4c21-57dd-b0a6-532274d43a0d.description: British Royal Engineers at work on an ancient stone temple. Three engineers stand on the ground at the foot of a tall ladder, which leads up to a stone platform where three other engineers are removing a more recent German commemorative stone. They have attached a pulley to the top of the platform in readiness to move the stone. The composition is framed by two enormous pillars that are part of the temple.

051a1449-1c86-578a-b00f-63151a22996d.name: Shapur besieges a fortress of the Ghassanid king Ta’ir
051a1449-1c86-578a-b00f-63151a22996d.short_description:
This folio from the dispersed copy of the “Second Small” *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) illustrates an episode concerning the historical Sasanian king, Shapur II (r. 304–79). In fact, for the historical section of the “Second” Small *Shahnameh*, this particular painting seems to be the first recorded picture, of a series of only eight.\[1\]  
The “actors” in this episode are the Ghassanid Arab king, Ta’ir; his daughter Malika (born of his liaison with a Sasanian princess, Naubahar); and the Sasanian Shapur II (r. 309–79). Ta’ir, “that ravening lion,” had captured Naubahar, daughter of Shah Narsi, in a campaign extending as far as the Sasanian capital city of Ctesiphon and taken her by force into his household. Their daughter was so nobly beautiful that her father named her Malika, meaning “Queen,” and her mother did not leave her ignorant of her lineage and circumstances. In due course, Sasanian Persian forces under the leadership of Shapur Shah, grandson of Narsi (and thus cousin to Malika), embarked on a retaliatory campaign into Ta’ir’s lands and the populace fled, some as far as the Yemen. Among those who found refuge in an abandoned fortress was Ta’ir’s daughter, Malika; but Shapur and his troops pursued them. The Sasanian army’s arrival is shown in this painting.

056dead0-e9f9-5694-939a-2d3d5752e145.name: "Jonah and the Whale"
056dead0-e9f9-5694-939a-2d3d5752e145.alternate_name: Folio Probably from a Jami al-Tavarikh (Compendium of Chronicles)
056dead0-e9f9-5694-939a-2d3d5752e145.description: The story of Jonah and the Whale, mentioned in the Qur'an (37:139), was popular in the Muslim world and frequently illustrated in manuscripts of world history. This large-scale painting, however, never formed part of a manuscript. Rather, it may have been used during oral recitation or storytelling. Scholars have also suggested that with its strong palette, monumental figures, and spare composition, this work may reflect a now-lost wall painting tradition. Here, we see Jonah after his release from the belly of the fish. Above him, a gourd vine grows—sent by God to protect him from the elements—and, gliding across the top of the painting, a spirited angel with colorful spreading wings offers Jonah a garment.

056fab85-863d-5746-9108-31105c02bedc.name: *The Judgement of Solomon*
056fab85-863d-5746-9108-31105c02bedc.description:
The Biblical episode tells the story of two prostitutes who give birth in the same house, but one of the newborns dies. Both claim to be the mother of the surviving baby and call on King Solomon to adjudicate. When he decides to split the newborn child in two with his sword, in tears the real mother renounces the child in order to save it, an astute strategy used by the wise king to identify her. This shows the capacity the Lord gave Solomon to distinguish Good from Evil, not as a gift, but as a readiness to listen through which the wisdom of God can be found. It is also a celebration of the wisdom of those who reign in the name of God.  
Over the centuries in the absence of any documents to verify the actual artist, the work has been variously attributed. One of the most notable theories is that an unknown follower of Caravaggio known as the Master of the Judgement of Solomon, on account of his strong personality (Longhi, 1943) painted it.  
The strong affinities to a non-Italian follower of Caravaggio have led some to attribute the painting to the Roman period of the young Jusepe de Ribera, when he had not fully assimilated the naturalism of his master although this is present in his later paintings (Papi, 2005).  
The essence of the painting is its compositional structure. The source of light outside the painting makes the scene a truly theatrical event. The rhythm is marked by the gestures of the figures in the scene arranged in a rigidly orthogonal progression.  
The king sits on a chair that rests on a step decorated with an ancient bas­‑relief, in front of a column acting as a perspective wing.  
The exasperation of the drama is not only evoked by the light and style, but by the atmosphere, a real stage on which the main player, Solomon, stands; the dark tones adding to the dramatic effect. These elements are consistent, notwithstanding the peculiarities of each artist, in what is known as the baroque language.
056fab85-863d-5746-9108-31105c02bedc.short_description: The biblical subject matter of this work is expressed through the dramatic use of gesture and light. Believed to be by an unknown follower of Caravaggio called the Master of the Judgement of Solomon, it is in a style similar to van Baburen and Neapolitan artists. Some scholars have identified the painter as the young Jusepe de Ribera.

0577e30a-dd75-503a-92c2-461ccdfb426d.name: A forest conflict
0577e30a-dd75-503a-92c2-461ccdfb426d.short_description: This slightly tinted drawing has been described as “noisy,” \[1\] and indeed, it depicts a chaotic match between life and death. Such decorative drawings come from a long tradition in Iranian art, beginning in the second half of the 14th century with the Jalairid dynasty (1335–1432). Such drawings of lively animal hunts and combats, with Chinese-inspired elements such as curling clouds, were prepared in the royal Timurid workshops or ateliers (*ketabkhaneh*) as design models for other craftsmen. This drawing appears to be a pattern or a model to be copied in other media, such as bookbinding, and is evidence of the variety of pieces produced by the workshop. The unrelated frame of alternating text panels, *mathnawi* verse in *taliq* script, would have been pasted on at a later date. Their source is the poem “*Halnameh*” (also famous as “*Guy u Chaugan*”) by the late 14th-century poet “Arifi.”

06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.name: *The Holy Family and Relatives*
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.description:
This small, sketch-like picture represents the Holy Family with the Virgin Mary and child Jesus in the centre. St. Elizabeth presents young St. John the Baptist, who is handing Jesus an apple, symbol of rule over the world. St. Anne kneels before Jesus. Male family members occupy the background: St. Joseph with a palm branch absorbed in a book, and Zachariah and Joachim, Anne’s husband and Mary’s father.  
The scene is not derived from the Bible but is a story from the Pseudo-Bonaventura. about the Holy Family. The story relates that on their return from Egypt the Holy Family visited a relative, Elizabeth, whose small son, John, we are told, showed great respect for Jesus. Sadler approaches the story in genre fashion, exploiting the individual gestures of all the characters and the evening atmosphere. The painter fully exploits the effects of light and colour, using chiaroscuro to accentuate the family group that spans three generations: Anne, Mary and Jesus. Green, blue, yellow and red tones merge into an almost monochromatic background. The mode of painting on a non-absorbent copper base demonstrates Sadler’s brushwork, along with his trademark facial expressions for the figures.  
The devotional subject, a symbolic triangular composition, and the emotional effects of the scene indicate that the piece may have been designed for private worship. It is worthy of note that in the final phase of his studies at the Academia di St. Luca in Rome, Sadler took part in a painting competition which he won with a picture of the Holy Family. The painting corresponds with the Academia’s style, applying approaches associated with Pietro da Cortona, Corrado Giaquinto and Carlo Marrati.  
Sadler’s work, influenced by his studies in Rome, was unique in Moravia. His oeuvre, comprising ceiling and easel paintings, was chiefly associated with central and north Moravia. He was a son of the Olomouc sculptor Filip Sattler and son-in-law of the painter Jan Kryštof Handke.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.short_description: The devotional subject, symbolic triangular composition, and emotional effects of the scene indicate that the piece might have been designed for private worship. The painting is typical of Sadler, a leading Olomouc artist influenced by studying at the Rome Academy.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.method_for_datation: The picture was previously considered the work of Paul Troger. However, the figure types and brushwork confirm that Josef Ignaz Sadler, a prominent Olomouc artist, is author of the work as determined by Vlasta Kratinová.

070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.name: *The Assumption of the Virgin*
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.description: This altarpiece was made for the chapel of the Bonasoni family in the church of San Francesco in Bologna. In 1798, following the Napoleonic suppression of the Franciscan convent, the painting became the property of the Italian State. The date “1592” is inscribed in the lower middle of the sarcophagus. Therefore, it is believed the picture was created in the early stage of Annibale Carracci's career. At that stage the painter was working in Bologna and was strongly influenced by Venetian models, especially Tintoretto. The figures of the Apostles are inspired by Raphael's *Transfiguration*, which is now in the Pinacoteca Vaticana. Great sixteenth-century models are combined with a detailed realism, thus making miraculous events credible because of their tangible appearance. There is an emphasis on the wonder of the Apostles, the naturalism of their bodies, including the Virgin and the absence of complex symbolic structures typical of sixteenth-century art. This becomes an efficacious religious teaching which involves people of every social and cultural status. The solid mass of the clouds under the Virgin and the angels as well as the landscape underneath are significant stylistic elements and anticipate the Baroque style to come.
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.short_description: This painting, dated 1592, was made for the chapel of the Bonasoni family in the church of San Francesco in Bologna. It became part of the Pinacoteca collections after the Napoleonic suppressions (1798). It is one of the masterpieces of Annibale's youth, influenced by Tintoretto and Raphael as well as real life experiences.
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.method_for_datation: The date is inscribed on the sarcophagus. The painting is mentioned in the Bonasoni chapel in San Frencesco by all the local guide books starting from Francesco Cavazzoni's manuscript *Pitture et Sculture* (1603).

07ac9ce1-f5e9-5c45-8c0c-b25875e68e94.name: *Six Episodes from the Life of Luigi Ferdinando Marsili*
07ac9ce1-f5e9-5c45-8c0c-b25875e68e94.description:
The peace of Carlowitz between the Habsburg Empire, Venice, Poland and Russia on one side and Turkey on the other was negotiated in 1698–99. Bolognese Count Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, a representative of Emperor Leopold I of Austria, was among the diplomats involved. After his return to Bologna he founded the Istituto delle Scienze (Institute of Sciences) (1711). This series is composed of six paintings: five depicting military camps, travelling armies and trains and one representing the discussion about the borders of the Habsburg empire. The paintings describe the negotiations and the following operations in order to define the borders of Venice, the Empire and Turkey in Bosnia and Dalmatia. All paintings are described in the *Instrumentum Donationis*, housed in the Istituto delle Scienze (first half XVIII century). Each painting originally bore a wooden caption explaining the scene depicted in it, today only one survives. This sort of documentary painting was new for Bolognese culture, and has been connected with the astronomical scenes commissioned from Donato Creti in 1711 by Marsili himself (now in the Pinacoteca Vaticana).  
In scene n. 291, painted with a rich brushstroke showing the influence of Giuseppe Maria Crespi, is depicted an episode of the negotiations for the peace: under a camp tent three diplomats sit next to their respective generals. In the foreground we are able to identify, thanks to the sealed letters they are holding in their hands, from the left the representative of Austria (Leopold Slink von Wischkirken or maybe Marsili himself, even if he was not the head of the diplomatic expedition), the representatives of Turkey (Reys Mohamed Effendi) and Venice (Carlo Ruzzini). We cannot say which exact moment of the negotiations is depicted here because the caption has been lost. The persons depicted are each identified with a letter which was further explained in a caption beneath the painting. However, the caption is now lost. It is a sort of birds-eye view of the military camp where the meeting took place, with a tent housing the diplomats and their respective armies. The paintings, dating to Marsili's most significant period of cultural and scientific zeal, employ a precise topographical description. They are a thorough representation of people, rather than focused on the epic and rhetorical meaning of the episodes.
07ac9ce1-f5e9-5c45-8c0c-b25875e68e94.short_description:
In n. 291 is depicted a scene of the peace negotiations: under a camp tent three diplomats sit next to their respective generals.  
The persons depicted are identified with a letter which was explained in a caption beneath the painting. However, the caption is now lost. Note the birds-eye view of the military camp where the meeting took place, with the tents housing the diplomats and their respective armies.

08086d2e-5ac6-53f2-810f-71dc4434785f.name: Portrait of the young dervish Nur 'Ali Shah (ca. 1748-1798)
08086d2e-5ac6-53f2-810f-71dc4434785f.short_description:
Half a century after his death, the dervish Nur ʿAli Shah (Hegira ca. 1161-1212 / AD ca. 1748-1798) enjoyed great popularity in Persia. Countless carpets from Kerman as well as various miniatures and oil portraits bear witness to this. It seems that this popularity was closely connected with the revival of Sufi traditions in the 19th century. All the portraits known so far can be traced back to two portraits painted by Ismaʿil Jalayer (d. Hegira 1284-1289 / AD 1868-1873) around 1865.  
  
The leaf originally belonged to an album made for Dr. Joseph Désiré Tholozon (Hegira 1235-1315 / AD 1820-1897) who was Nasir al-Din Shahʼs (r. Hegira 1264-1313 / AD 1848-1896) personal physician. He might have received the album from the shah in 1889 when he retired. This folio bears the number 50 and must have been the last leaf of his album, which itself was taken apart and probably sold in the early 20th century. Individual leaves formerly belonged to the collection of Jean Pozzi and are now in the Musée dʼArt et dʼHistoire in Geneva (Switzerland).

0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.name: *St. Francis Xavier Preaching in Goa*
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.description:
The set of 20 paintings portraying the life of St. Francis Xavier (1506–1552) form the back-piece to a large chest-of-drawers in the sacristy of the 16th-century Church of St. Roque, and are the work of the Portuguese proto-Baroque painter André Reinoso and collaborators. Installed in 1619, three years before the official canonisation of St. Francis Xavier on the 12th March 1622, the set of paintings form part of a religious “propaganda” exercise to highlight the life and work of the great Jesuit missionary, which it was hoped, would speed up the process of his canonisation by the Catholic Church. The paintings were inspired by the first Portuguese biography of the saint written by Father João de Lucena (*Histórica da Vida do Padre Francisco Xavier, e do que fizerão na Índia os mais religiosos da Companhia de Jesus*) published in Lisbon in 1600.  
The scene featured here shows the saint ardently preaching in the cosmopolitan city of Goa shortly after his arrival there in 1542. The picture has particular interest from an ethnographic viewpoint in that it shows the variety of oriental customs as well as recording different social classes. In the picture a crowd of new converts: men, women and children, as well as Portuguese noblemen watching on horseback, surround the saint. The background scene features a landscape fashioned in the Italian style.
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.short_description: This oil on canvas painting, part of a set of 20, is attributed to the Portuguese proto-Baroque painter André Reinoso (c. 1590-1641). Commissioned by the Society of Jesus for the sacristy of the Jesuit Church of St. Roque, this and other paintings of the set form the back-piece to a large chest-of-drawers installed in 1619, three years before the canonisation of the great missionary of the Far-East, St. Francis Xavier.

0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.method_for_datation: This painting, as well as the other ones that make up the painted cycle dedicated to the life of St. Francis Xavier, was attributed to André Reinoso by the Art Historian, Prof. Vitor Serrão, after a thorough research on Reinoso’s life and his works, in the decade of 1990.

08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.name: *Thronus Pietatis*
08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.description:
The crucified Christ is at the centre of the painting; the Holy Father hovers in the clouds holding up the cross, supported in the lower part by two *putti*. Above His head the Holy Ghost – a dove radiating light – is surrounded by cherubs.  
*Thronus Pietatis* is by the Bavarian painter, Johann Michael Rottmayr, who later moved to Austria and made his name working for the Austrian Monarchy. His first works in Vienna were frescoes in Lichtenstein Palace. He then worked in Melk Abbey and in the Viennese Church of St Charles, Borromeo.  
One of the best-known painters of late Austrian Baroque, his work is characterised by voluptuous figures, strong colours and Baroque gesture. His later works stand apart with calmer movement and paler colours.  
The painting was a commission for the chapel at Valpovo Castle owned by the Hilleprand-Prandau family, by origin from Tyrol. The Prandaus were one of the four most important foreign aristocratic families in Slavonia. The Habsburg Crown granted estates to foreign nobles in Slavonia after the retreat of the Ottoman Turks.

0add5409-b394-5bfa-bd30-f8a38dd5179f.name: *The Martyrdom of St. Ursula*
0add5409-b394-5bfa-bd30-f8a38dd5179f.description: The altarpiece is hanging on the main altar of the church San Nicola e San Domenico, in Imola. It was originally painted for the left side chapel, patronised by the Vendini family. The painting survived many attempts of confiscation, including the Napoleonic suppression at the end of the eighteenth-century, thanks to the determination of the Vendini family. It is an example of Ludovico's full mature style, painted after his exposure to Venetian influence. This work testifies to the adoption of a new expressive language, a baroque rhetoric, which melds Venetian colour and mannerist composition. The chaotic bundle of victims and villains, theatrically exhibited, stand in contrast with the hieratic figure of the saint who is absorbed in prayer and clearly deriving from the *St. Cecilia* by Raphael. The colours are mostly dark, emphasised by a cloudy dawn; the background is the colour of blood, the same shade as Ursula's dress. This painting was a turning point for painting in Imola, not only in a positive way: patrons turned completely to Bologna and the local school of painting was blocked and made sterile by the impossible competition with the Carraccis Academy.
0add5409-b394-5bfa-bd30-f8a38dd5179f.short_description: The painting was commissioned by the Vandini family for the church where it hangs today. It is a great altarpiece which ties together Baroque language and Counter-reformation liturgy: Venetian colours combine with the rhetoric of gestures and feelings in a strongly emotional painting.

0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.name: *Seated Moor*
0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.description: This small oil painting was painted in Valencia in a very early date (1880–1884) and is an example of Sorolla’s early works, when he still painted small pieces that follow the taste of the time. This Orientalist topic was very popular in Europe at the end of the century and the paintings sold very well. The inspiration was not from travel or cultural knowledge, but instead was the result of studying engravings, watercolours, and other paintings of the time. The production of this type of topic in Sorolla is very short and almost all of it dates to his early years.
0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.author: Covadonga Pitarch
keywords: Orientalist painting; Spain; Formation of painters

0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.name: *Raft Conveying Winged Bull to Baghdad*
0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.short_description: Layard describes the removal of the winged bulls from the site of the mound of Nimrud in Nineveh and its remains, 1849, from where they had lain for approximately the last 2,730 years. They were carefully loaded on to rafts, made in the traditional way of using hundreds of inflated goat and sheep-skins supporting a wooden superstructure. Layard (who had learnt Arabic and Persian) recruited the crew locally, as he had done with his workforce. In April 1847, he sent them floating with the current, off on a six hundred mile journey down the river Tigris to Basra, where ships of the British Navy were waiting to take them the next 12,000 miles to England. Although the artist Cooper was not present on this occasion, he subsequently witnessed similar events, and would have been able to reconstruct the scene.
0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: Engineering

0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.name: *Boy with a Basket of Fruit*
0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.description:
The canvas is one of the first works Merisi undertook in Rome, having joined the workshops of Giuseppe Cesari, known as the Cavalièr d'Arpino, shortly after his arrival in the city in 1592. He stayed there for several months, exercising his abilities as a painter of still-life. In this painting, the artist represents different qualities of fruit, some of which are very ripe, with extreme realism. The extraordinary realism of the boy showing us the basket, illuminated by a source of light behind his back, can be attributed to the young painter's Lombard influence, his sensitivity so similar to that of the Flemish school.  
The Borghese painting should be compared to the famous *Basket* from the same period in the Pinacoteca Ambrosiana in Milan, belonging to Cardinal Federico Borromeo and executed in Rome on recovered canvas in the mid-1590s. At the time, Caravaggio, unknown and in financial straits, used second-hand canvases to save money.  
This work was one of the pieces that Scipione Borghese had confiscated from the Cavalièr d'Arpino in 1607. The famous painter personally owned a valuable collection of paintings, which ended up in the hands of the greedy cardinal. They became the core of the splendid Borghese Collection.  
The technical ability that Caravaggio shows in the work exemplifies the artist's idea that the same method is required to paint people and objects.  
The subject has been interpreted in different ways. Fruit is used as an allegory for abundance, but on account of its natural tendency to perish, is also a metaphor for the transience of life.
0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.short_description: This painting dates from the first Caravaggio period in Rome. The canvas is painted with a strong realism that gives the still-life the same importance as the figure. The Lombard, Venetian, and Flemish influences do not prevent the painting from representing a new artistic expression.
0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

0e6e6bac-3e5d-5bc0-b143-7f8c186c37a6.name: A Portrait of a European, after Jacques de Gheyn's print 'Terra'
0e6e6bac-3e5d-5bc0-b143-7f8c186c37a6.short_description: This miniature painting depicted an image of a European soldier made by Mughal artist around 17th century. The original image is based on a European print by Dutch printmaker Jacques de Gheyn (1565–1629). This painting which is made with gouache on paper technique showing a European with fair skin colour in European style of clothes holding a long object, probably a weapon such as a spear or gun. At the margin of the painting inscribed the word ‘awwal’, possibly indicating the grade of the painting and at the back with Mughal seals impressions. The fondness to European prints was common in Mughal court. Emperors such as Akbar and later Jahangir were among the collectors of European prints.

0f8914a6-32b8-5c6c-8562-d748aa45552b.name: *Fountain of Sultan Ahmed III*
0f8914a6-32b8-5c6c-8562-d748aa45552b.short_description: Although essentially a realist painter, Şevket Dağ worked with free brush stokes in the style of Corot. He is celebrated for his paintings of the interiors of mosques. He took lessons from Osman Hamdi Bey, and followed his master in painting genre pictures reflecting various aspects of Ottoman life. In addition to mosque interiors he would also paint scenes in market places, still-life compositions and the interiors of houses. Over time, Şevket Dağ's work began to be appreciated abroad following exhibitions in European art centres such as Munich and Paris, and he was awarded a gold medal in the Munich International Exhibition of 1909. He later came under the influence of the impressionists.
0f8914a6-32b8-5c6c-8562-d748aa45552b.dates: Late 19th century – beginning of the 20th century
keywords: Painting; Şevket Dağ; orientalist painters

0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.name: *Discovery of the Holy Cross*
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.description:
The scene depicts the discovery of the cross upon which Jesus died and the verification of its authenticity. The search for the cross was initiated in 324 by St. Helen, mother of the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, who legalised the Christian faith by an edict in 313. These figures are not represented in this sketch executed for part of a ceiling painting in the Provost Church of St. Hyppolith in Hradisko near Znojmo, owned by the Order of the Knights of the Red Star.  
The discovery, erection and celebration of the cross are arranged in chronological order along the perimeter of the church cupola. In the ancient Roman empire, the cross, tool of the most degrading capital punishment, was designated for slaves and rebels. For Christians, it became the epitome of the redemption of mankind through Christ. The scene is set on Golgotha, where three identical crosses have been excavated. The crosses were laid on dead bodies, and when the genuine cross was applied, the dead person miraculously came to life. In the picture, this is the reclining figure on the left. Maulbertsch's masterly use of light, dramatic chiaroscuro, expressive exaggeration of shapes and rhetorical gesture, is particularly marked in the lifting of the cross. Accents of red and dark blue lend mystery to the picture.  
The final fresco differs from Maulbertsch's sketch only in the decorative detail and colour scheme, which appears less contrasted when seen in large format and makes allowance for the white-green-yellow Rococo stucco decoration of the interior. Josef Winterhalder Jr., later Maulbertsch's most faithful disciple, created his first independent paintings, side altar altarpieces, in this church. The cupola murals are also associated with a sketch by Josef Winterhalder Jr., Maulbertsch's associate and pupil for the *Celebration of the Holy Cross* and the drawings for the cupola paintings (Vienna, Albertina).
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.short_description: This sketch for the mural in the cupola of the Church of St. Hyppolith in Hradisko near Znojmo depicts the discovery of the cross upon which Jesus died and the verification of its authenticity. It exemplifies Maulbertsch’s masterly use of light effects, expressive exaggeration of shapes and rendering of rhetoric gestures.
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.method_for_datation: The Provost of the Order of the Knights of the Red Star signed a contract with Franz Anton Maulbertsch for the decoration of the Church of St. Hyppolith on 9 October 1765. The painter was to start work the following spring. He received 900 gold pieces and was provided board and lodging by the order for himself and his two assistants. The sketch or *modello* was a template for the artist's associates.
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.obtention: Acquired in 1960 from the Mojmír Helcelet Collection, Brno.

1024af4a-05a4-55d4-9f91-818959c2b7ed.name: Rustam Slaying Alkus
1024af4a-05a4-55d4-9f91-818959c2b7ed.alternate_name: Page from the *Shahnama* for Shah Ismaʿil II (r. 1576-78)
1024af4a-05a4-55d4-9f91-818959c2b7ed.short_description:
The illustration depicts the battle between the Iranian hero Rustam, recognisable by his helmet with a leopard crest and tiger-skin jerkin, and his Turanian adversary Alkus. In this paarticular scene, Rustam has struck the decisive blow, indicating an imminent victory for the Iranians. Nevertheless, the artist Siyavush depicts the battle so dynamically that its course is not yet foreseeable. The two princes, who are observing the carnage from behind the rocks and bite the back of their hands or their fingers in astonishment, are still feverishly following their respective troops, seemingly unsure of victory.  
  
The leaf comes from a dispersed *Shahnama*, a Book of Kings made for Shah Ismaʿil II (r. Hegira 985-986/ AD 1576-1577). The orginal manuscript has been preserved only in a fragmentory state, with just 52 illustrations having been identified to date. Thirteen illustrations alone are the work of the highly esteemed court painter Siyavush, whose signature can be seen on one of the rocks.

113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.name: The Ghetto of Florence
113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.short_description: Telemaco Signorini was part of the group of artists known as The Macchiaioli Movement, a group drawn to colour and nature. After his studies at the Academy of Florence, he started painting from real life and spent some time in Paris, where he met Corot and the painters from the School of Barbizon. Back in Italy the artist went to Tuscany and Liguria. He also travelled frequently to France, England and Scotland, where he was well known. Signorini liked painting urban scenes and cityscapes. The artist developed urban themes with a unique emphasis, matching together vivid descriptions, social and humanitarian features and cultural issues.

1203d512-7e1e-58c1-b5ee-087144132528.name: The Miracle of Saint George and the Dragon
1203d512-7e1e-58c1-b5ee-087144132528.description: Saint George was born to Christian parents in the 3rd century. He joined the Roman army and became a high-ranking officer at a young age, earning the respect of Emperor Diocletian. At that time, Diocletian persecuted Christians and required that all soldiers offer sacrifices to the pagan gods. Saint George publicly denounced the emperor and confessed to being Christian. He was subjected to brutal punishments but refused to renounce his faith. Eventually, he was beheaded and became a popular martyr saint. In one story of his life, he rescued a town besieged by a dragon. The townspeople had been sacrificing children, who were randomly chosen by casting lots, to the dragon. Saint George rode in just as the town’s princess was to be sacrificed. He killed the dragon, a symbol of paganism, and converted the townspeople to Christianity. In this icon, Saint George rides a white horse and slays the dragon with a spear while Christ, seen in the upper right corner, bestows a blessing.
1203d512-7e1e-58c1-b5ee-087144132528.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2003. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography

140738ee-bca0-54e2-80dc-fdbd56b1dd67.name:
A blood-measuring device  
*Kitab al-Hiyal al-naficah* (The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices)
140738ee-bca0-54e2-80dc-fdbd56b1dd67.short_description: This painting comes from a popular treatise on mechanical devices and automata written in 1206 and copied continuously in the following centuries. Al-Jazari, the author of *Kitab al-Hiyal al-naficah* (The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices), included descriptions of more than a hundred devices in his treatise, one of which can be seen here. This fascinating device builds on two scientific ideas: bloodletting as a medical treatment and the use of simple machines to create complex automata. The treatment of various ailments through bloodletting was common until the nineteenth century, and it clearly did not need such a complex device. Here, the patient puts a cut finger into a hole in the basin and blood falls through channels into a lower chamber, displacing a float. The float is attached to one end of a rod that, on its other end, attaches to the pen in the hand of the scribe on the upper left. As the level of the blood in the basin rises, it pushes the float up, moving the scribe’s pen and indicating marks on his writing board.
140738ee-bca0-54e2-80dc-fdbd56b1dd67.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Painting; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; science; learning; science-and-learning
materials: Opaque watercolour, ink, and silver on paper

1526ad94-18c0-5a77-9a29-be3d308e0e29.name: *The Abduction*
1526ad94-18c0-5a77-9a29-be3d308e0e29.alternate_name: *Liberation of a Maid; Scene from the Legend of St. Ladislav; The Rape of Proserpina*
1526ad94-18c0-5a77-9a29-be3d308e0e29.description:
As the subject of the painting is unknown, it is referred to here as *The Abduction*, which may be interpreted in this case as both rape and liberation. On the left emerges the sketched figure of a defeated man, his head severed. It is worthy of note that the artist paid attention to the position of the sword; no warrior ever allowed his sword to remain on the ground in combat. As is obvious from the central section, the sword does not belong to the horseman. The “abduction” of a young woman, dressed in a fine white robe with gold ornaments and a pearl clasp in her hair, whose eyes are fixed on the viewer, seems not to be the result of a fight between the two men. The armour of the horseman with a red cloak, flag, and a helmet with flying-bat ornamentation, along with the harness of his white horse, indicate that the scene was derived from a history scene or a heroic epic (possibly Alexander or Troya?).  
Despite the difficulty in deciphering the theme, this does not diminish the spectacular nature of the picture. The artist's virtuoso brushwork does much to absorb the viewer. Maulbertsch depicts the dramatic situation in lighter tones and impasto accents underlined by the intense light he introduces. Red, blue and yellow, spreading from the centre, supplements the diagonal composition.  
The artist was clearly inspired by Rembrandt's use of chiaroscuro, and by the work of Peter Paul Rubens, especially *Oreithia* *Seized by Boreas* and the Marie de' Medici cycle. Maulbertsch would have studied the work of both these painters at the Vienna Academy. A white horse foaming at the mouth was among Maulbertsch's favourite motifs, as was the “action” scene of a kidnapped woman. Prominent during the Habsburg monarchy in the mid-18th century, this small, sketch-like picture is typical of Maulbertsch's original style.
1526ad94-18c0-5a77-9a29-be3d308e0e29.short_description: The impossibility of deciphering the theme represented here makes the picture all the more attractive. The artist’s virtuoso brushwork along with his use of light, enhance the picture. Prominent during the Habsburg monarchy in the mid-18th century, this work is a typical of Maulbertsch’s original style.
1526ad94-18c0-5a77-9a29-be3d308e0e29.method_for_datation: The motifs and the rendering employed correspond with Maulbertsch’s original style of the 1750s. This style is typified by an expressive exaggeration sometimes resulting in deformed shapes and energetic impasto brushwork.
1526ad94-18c0-5a77-9a29-be3d308e0e29.obtention: The picture was acquired from a private owner in 1946.

16779f12-bb0c-53b2-8168-9ebb33d19221.name:
Bahram entertained by Arezu, daughter of Mahyar the jeweller  
Folio from a dispersed copy of Firdausi’s *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
16779f12-bb0c-53b2-8168-9ebb33d19221.short_description:
This folio from the dispersed copy of the “Second Small” *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) illustrates an episode concerning the historical Sasanian king, Bahram (or Vaharam) V (r. 420–38). It shows the visit paid by Bahram Gur to the home of one of his subjects.  
Bahram Gur, “that great hunter,” had performed another of many feats with his great bow, this time killing a pair of savage lions who would have preyed on the great flock of Mahyar’s sheep; and the head shepherd, not recognizing Bahram, addresses him, wishing to thank the brave archer and also praising the justice of the Shah’s rule. Bahram—still incognito—decides to visit the jeweller’s house where, says the shepherd, he will hear toasts and the sound of a harp. Indeed, Mahyar has “just one daughter, who plays the harp” and she does so, seated before both her white-bearded father and the Shah.

keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; hunting; battle; animal; Shahnama; Shahnameh

179f9d9d-6b5a-52fc-8dea-c159da198fd5.name: *La Reine de Saba: 14 costume sketches*
179f9d9d-6b5a-52fc-8dea-c159da198fd5.short_description: Charles Gounod turned to the librettists Jules Barbier and Michel Carré for advice when he was writing his great opera, and so they recommended him the legend of Hiram, the great tale narrated by Gérard de Nervale in his *Voyage en Orient*. The opera was put on in Paris in 1862. As this costume from the court of Suleiman shows, the models and costumes responded above all to the Orientalist stereotypes in vogue at the time.
keywords: Opera; Orientalism

17a114d9-989f-52a9-85d5-689485ba21f6.name: Icon *The Holy Seven Slav Teachers*
17a114d9-989f-52a9-85d5-689485ba21f6.short_description: This icon represents icon-painting in Macedonia in the 19th century. This painted variant of the motif of the seven Slav teachers was enriched by Dimitar Dicho Zograf with the romantic awareness of the Macedonian Revival. The style of the most popular and most productive Macedonian painter in the 19th century follows the experience of the painters from that period. It was commissioned by the Robev family for the church of St. Nicholas Gerakomia in Ohrid. It was painted on wood with oil. It represents the Slav missionaries Ss. Cyril and Methodius and their most prominent disciples Clement, Nahum, Gorazd, Sabbas and Angelariy, in a sole composition entitled as “Sedmochislenitzi” (The Seven Holy Teachers). The saints' names are inscribed in the Old Church Slavonic language.
17a114d9-989f-52a9-85d5-689485ba21f6.author: Viktorija Popovska Korobar, art historian
keywords: Icon; iconography

183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.name: *Adoration of the Painting of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo*
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.description:
The image within, praised by angels, is a painted reproduction of an adoration picture of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo which originated in the 1630s. Its subject is the miraculous transportation of the picture which, according to legend, was brought to its new location by angels. The gloomy landscape in the bottom section of the painting has, beyond doubt, an allegorical meaning, while the illuminated adoration image presents a reality higher than the earthly life, here represented by thistles, military fortresses and rocks. The artist accentuated the difference between the miraculous picture and mundane reality through quaint, rustic elements in the picture of the Virgin Mary, in terms appropriate to chronology and the taste of the period. On the other hand, the figures of the angels and the landscape are rendered in Herdt’s trademark warm red-brown and golden tones, revealing his Flemish training.  
This sizeable painting is an example of the then popular picture-within-a-picture type. The intention of such paintings was to visually enhance, or “update”, well-known and already worshipped miracle-inspiring pictures. These “miraculous” pictures were displayed on altars, like relics, and as such were to be venerated. At the same time, pictures-within-pictures were employed, by Counter-Reformation and missionary orders in particular, for more striking presentations of “miraculous” pictures among ordinary town and country people.  
The origination of the painting marks a key moment in the history of the worship of the miraculous Znojmo picture, since the burgeoning importance of the Znojmo Dominicans in South Moravia involved the cult of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo. One of the first mentions of a Marian brotherhood of the Holy Rosary, active in one of the chapels of the monastery complex, date to the same period. In 1734 the “miraculous picture” was festively crowned and placed on a new altar in the monastery church.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.short_description: The canvas is typical of the picture-within-a-picture approach of the time, intended to visually “update” miracle-inspiring pictures. Rustic elements used in the painting within the painting contrast the sacred with the mundane; the warmly rendered angels and landscape reveal the artist’s Flemish training.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and dated 1678. The Dominican monastery, established in Znojmo around the mid-13th century, suffered serious damage during the Thirty Years' War and was not substantially restored until several decades later. At that time, *The Invention of the Holy Cross*, a painting by Jan Daniel (de) Herdt a Dutch artist formerly active in Brescia, Italy, was obtained for the main altar. A year later, Herdt painted another canvas for the monastery, its subject being the adoration of a picture of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.obtention: The painting was probably found in one of the chapels of the Dominican monastery church in Znojmo which was pulled down in the late 19th century. The picture was transferred to Znojmo Castle chapel, administered by the Museum of Znojmo since the early 20th century.

18ce1dd3-9c8e-520a-add7-46441936d12f.name: *The impalement of heads of two trapped Austrian soldiers during the combat at Jaice, August 7th 1878*
18ce1dd3-9c8e-520a-add7-46441936d12f.short_description: This painting depicts a brutal war crime that occurred during the Austro-Hungarian Army's occupation campaign in 1878. On the reverse side of the painting there is a contemporary inscription, which sheds light on the situation: “During the battle at Jaice, Master Corporal Grilec and Private Matko, members of the 53rd Infantry Regiment have been trapped and beheaded. Their heads have been impaled in front of the gate to the river Pliva.” This treatment of prisoners of war was unfortunately not rare during the first weeks of the campaign; it provided a glimpse into a difference in approaches to warfare that would be borne out during the upcoming wars in the Balkans, 1912–13.

keywords: Bosnia; Austrian army; war; warfare

This miniature painting depicted a Northern Goshawk, a type of bird used for hunting. This painting is attributed to Mihr Chand, one of important artist during the second half of 18th century.

1947528b-a97f-56af-b6c4-fe8372c9bdd5.name: *The Western Wall*
1947528b-a97f-56af-b6c4-fe8372c9bdd5.short_description: The Western Wall of the Haram es-Sharif in Jerusalem, as depicted for the readers of the Illustrated London News by William ‘Crimea’ Simpson. Simpson’s sketches were turned into engravings for publication in the ILN, and were among the most important graphic depictions which helped to introduce western readers to the present-day appearance of Jerusalem and Jerusalemites.
keywords: archaeology

19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.name: *Susanna and the Old Men*
19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.description:
According to historical sources, Rubens was one of the artists patronised by Scipione Borghese, who was a great admirer. This painting was probably done expressly for Cardinal Borghese, given that in 1622 it was fitted with a frame, now unfortunately lost. The commission, which lacks documentary support, could be understood to be a sign of recognition for the assistance that Borghese gave to the painter, who was already committed to Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, in asking him to consent to a longer stay in Rome.  
The painting relates to Rubens' second stay in Rome (1606–1608), when he was working on the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella – where Caravaggio had worked – in which he was decorating the high altar.  
The work depicts the story of Susanna as told in the Old Testament (Daniel 13, 1–64). This is a biblical theme that is particularly dear to the culture of the Counter Reformation, which saw in the heroine an example of truth and virtue as against lying, symbolised here by two old men who are trying in vain to seduce the maiden. To render the protagonist, Rubens, a passionate devotee of ancient art, drew on the famous bronze sculpture *Spinario* on the Capitoline Hill. It is an extremely harmonious figure in which the classical combines perfectly with the voluptuous and abundant forms, typical of the artist. There are also references to the great Venetians of the 16th century, especially Titian in his later style, Paolo Veronese and Tintoretto. These are evident in the use of a particular colour palette based on browns and golds, entirely different from the choices made by contemporary Caravaggesque painters, who focused on strong contrasts between light and shadow.
19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.short_description: Rubens probably executed this work during his second stay in Rome (1606–1608). The pose of the central female nude shows knowledge of antique art (the *Spinario*) and appears from the darkness with the contrasting light of Caravaggio's tenebrism.
19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.obtention: Acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.name: *Adoration of the Shepherds*
19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.description:
The New Testament account of the shepherds' adoration of the infant Jesus is rendered as a genre picture. The landscape setting is not typical of Kremser-Schmidt's oeuvre which predominantly comprised sizeable altarpieces. The artist reduced the scene to primary figures and their attributes and based the picture on atmospheric use of colour and light. A contrasting motif of a forked tree receding into a dark cloud separates the main scene from the background. The light appears to emanate from within the picture itself, from the infant Jesus, and is reflected on the hay in the barn and tools in the foreground. These motifs are reminiscent of 17th-century Dutch painting, something that Kremser-Schmidt focused upon unlike his contemporaries. His interest in chiaroscuro and the relaxed brushstrokes pay tribute to Rembrandt's painting style. The colour scheme is, however, original. The scale of brown tones illuminated with various hues of golden ochre are offset by Mary's blue robe and accents of vermilion in the detail. The palette is complemented by a grey-blue background with light effects.  
The picture is one of only a few known examples of the artist's early work, that often appears to be inspired by northern Italian painting, and which he probably saw either during a journey to Venice in 1746 or through prints brought back from there for him. He later settled in Stein near Krems, and sent his paintings to Lower Austria, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia. In the last quarter of the 18th century his paintings were distributed in Moravia (Vranov, Bratrušov). His student, Franz Oesterreicher, worked in Jihlava. Schmidt's oeuvre spanned changes in style from the late baroque to classicism and this was accompanied by an extension of thematic scale: portrait, genre painting and ancient mythology.
19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.short_description: The shepherds’ adoration of the infant Jesus is rendered as a genre picture. The landscape setting is not typical of Kremser-Schmidt, whose work largely comprised altarpieces for the Habsburgian lands. The painter reduced the scene to primary figures and based the picture on the atmospheric use of colour and light.
19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.method_for_datation: The picture was determined as a work by Kremser-Schmidt on the basis of a style analysis by Ivo Krsek.

1a291f62-97b6-5628-b0d7-aa7f8c26f74e.name: *Abgar of Edessa admiring a picture of Christ*
1a291f62-97b6-5628-b0d7-aa7f8c26f74e.short_description: This painting conflates two versions of the legend of King Abgar V of Edessa dating from late Antiquity. He is said to have written to Christ to deliver him from an illness. In his history of the church Eusebius of Caesaria (AD 260/64– c. 339/40) says he discovered Abgar’s letter and Christ’s reply in an archive in Edessa; the painting’s Latin inscription conforms to his report of the letter. Eusebius says Christ sent a Disciple to Edessa, but the painting features a more famous version of the legend: Abgarg received a miraculous portrait of Christ that healed him. Venerated as the Mandylion (or the image of Edessa), it was said to be a mechanical reproduction of Christ’s features. In accordance with baroque ideas, the artist has softened the formality of Christ’s head typical of early copies of the now-lost original. The king’s turban is a reference to the Oriental origins of the legend and its protagonists.

1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.name: *The Beggar*
1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.description:
This painting has only recently (2002) been attributed to Jusepe de Ribera, despite the fact that it was ascribed to him in an old inventory of the Scipione Borghese collection.  
The painting is considered to be a reference point in the Roman phase of the Spanish painter (1612–1616), which some scholars identify with the work of another artist known as the Master of the Judgement of Solomon.  
The work is recognised as one of the first completed by a young de Ribera, when his style was still strongly dependent on Caravaggesque naturalism. With this painting, the composition and voluminous construction of his early career begins to blend with the more compact and tangible brushstrokes for which he is renowned in his successive Neapolitan phase.  
Also, the innovative nature of the canvas is evident in the choice of subject: the beggar, despite being poor and dressed in rags, is treated with the same dignity as an eminent figure, launching a trend for the depiction of paupers that evolved extensively in Rome in the following decades.  
The fragmented brushstrokes, the threads of colour that freely define the dense highlights, the shadows that add drama to the scene: it is the chromatic elements that emphasise the heightened humanity of the character. Through his close attention to reality, even on the very margins of society, de Ribera focuses on the profound and human gaze of the beggar, the results of an effort to transform the idea of Christian compassion into a tangible expression of pathetic suffering.
1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.short_description: The painting has recently been attributed to Ribera from a Borghese inventory from 1615–1630. Ribera stayed in Rome from 1612 to 1616 and this work probably dates from this first period of Caravaggio's influence. The work initiates the “*pittura pauperistica*” that developed in later years.
1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

1b32d683-31be-5270-b83f-6a9d2a5fc3b7.name: *Rustam Slays the White Div*. Folio from an album
1b32d683-31be-5270-b83f-6a9d2a5fc3b7.short_description:
Rustam is the ancient Iranian legendary hero, one of the main characters of *Shahnama* (Book of Kings) by Ferdowi. More than one third of the epic poem is devoted to Rustam's deeds and other adventures. His last - the seventh - heroic action was the murder of the White Div, a powerful chief of demons and sorcerers who captured and blinded Iranian king Kay Kavus. Rustam released the king, but only the blood from the White Div's liver could return sight to the ruler. Thus, Rustam entered into a fierce battle with a monster. The miniature shows a moment of Rustam's victory. Having cut off the demon's leg, Rustam thrust his dagger into the right side of the monster's body in order to get his liver. The Persian warrior is depicted according to the iconographic canon established in the 14th century: a beard (maturity of a man) and a cape made of tiger skin (highest military strength). The big object pictured to the right of Div is probably a Rustam's mace.  
The vertical composition of the scene and the absence of minor details (like depiction of the demon's cave where the battle took place or other landscape elements) indicate that the folio was intended for an album.  
In the upper left of the composition there is an inscription in Persian: "Behzad's work, no doubt." However, the miniature is hardly the work of the glorious painter Kamaleddin Behzad. Apparently, the caption was added to the miniature later.
1b32d683-31be-5270-b83f-6a9d2a5fc3b7.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (1926, date, origin); A. Ivanov (1966, specified date).
1b32d683-31be-5270-b83f-6a9d2a5fc3b7.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927). Old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

1b6254e3-cc23-516a-85ce-ff122e61f5e2.name: *Saliha sultan fountain and sabil*
1b6254e3-cc23-516a-85ce-ff122e61f5e2.description:
This work was exhibited in the “Miniatures and Fountains” exhibition held within the scope of Istanbul’s 2010 European Capital of Culture program.  
  
This miniature illustrates a well-known Ottoman story about Saliha Sultan, whose life changed through a moment of honesty at a neighborhood fountain.  
In the district of Azapkapı in Karaköy lived a young girl named Saliha. At that time, homes in Istanbul had no running water, and people fetched water from communal fountains. One day, while filling her clay pitcher, Saliha accidentally broke it and began to cry in grief. Coincidentally, Emetullah Gülnuş Sultan, the wife of the reigning sultan, was passing by in her imperial carriage. Seeing the weeping girl, she asked her attendants to offer the child some money to comfort her. Saliha, however, refused the gift, saying:  
"I am not crying because I lost the pitcher or its value. I am crying because I failed to complete the task entrusted to me."  
Impressed by her sincerity and sense of responsibility, palace officials conveyed the incident to Gülnuş Sultan. Soon after, Saliha was invited to be educated and raised in the imperial palace. When Gülnuş Sultan’s son, Prince Mustafa, came of age, he married Saliha. Mustafa later ascended the throne as Sultan Mustafa II, making her Saliha Sultan.  
Their son, Mahmud, became Sultan Mahmud I upon his father’s death, and thus Saliha Sultan rose to the rank of Valide Sultan, the Queen Mother—one of the most influential positions in the Ottoman court.  
  
Wishing to commission a charitable fountain, Saliha Sultan began preparations, but she passed away before its completion. Her son, Sultan Mahmud I, fulfilled her wish by constructing the Saliha Sultan Fountain and Sebil, the structure depicted in this miniature.  
According to popular tradition, the incident of the broken pitcher inspired an Anatolian custom: during weddings, clay pitchers are broken so that the bride’s fortune may be open and the household blessed.

1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.name: *Annunciation*
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.description:
This painting was made for the altar of the church of the Santissima Annunziata (Blessed Annunciate) in Pieve di Cento, a small town near Bologna. The church was part of a recently built college held by the Scolopian Fathers, whose mission was the free education of poor children.  
The simple and clear structure of the painting is perfect for religious instruction. It follows the tenets of religious and profane painting as described in a 1582 book by Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti the Bishop of Bologna.  
Guercino depicts God the Father explaining his mission to the archangel Gabriel rather than depicting the Annunciation. The beautiful angel is a set on a diagonal cutting the picture in two, thus separating heaven from earth. In the lower half of the painting the kneeling Virgin is reading in a bare room, unaware of what is happening above her.  
Thanks to the Scolopian father Giacomo Bottini the painting “Intangible Dowry for the Instruction of the Poor” was saved from the French requisitions, in 1798.
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.short_description: The simple and clear structure of the painting is perfect for religious teaching. Guercino depicts God the Father explaining his mission to the archangel Gabriel rather than representing the Annunciation. The beautiful angel is placed on a diagonal cutting the picture in two, separating heaven from earth. In the lower half of the painting the kneeling Virgin is reading in a bare room, unaware of what is happening above her.
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.method_for_datation: The commission of the painting for the Church of the Santissima Annunziata (Blessed Annunciate) in Pieve di Cento as well as a series of payments were registered by Paolo Antonio Barbieri, Guercino's brother in the painter's Account Book in 1646.

1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.obtention: The painting was moved to the council room of the City Hall Municipal Palace of Pieve di Cento in 1924. At that time the church was closed, deconsecrated and converted into a store. Later the painting was moved along with its altar to the church of Santa Maria Maggiore.

1c205c93-bc85-56c7-bb96-3f280389af94.name: *Comares Courtyard at the Alhambra*
1c205c93-bc85-56c7-bb96-3f280389af94.description: The monument of the Alhambra, the last palace of the kingdom of Granada, fascinated travellers to Spain during the nineteenth century. Sorolla saw it for the first time in 1902 and in his successive trips to Granada during 1909, 1910 and 1917 he painted it, away from the Orientalist clichés, focusing on its corners, and especially in its gardens and fountains. In this view of the Patio de Comares, he highlights the reflection of the arches over the pond and a set of mirrors that is repeated in successive rooms of the palace.
1c205c93-bc85-56c7-bb96-3f280389af94.author: Covadonga Pitarch
keywords: The Alhambra; Painting development

1c45a682-1820-5eee-b604-862620e6fcea.name: *The Tunisian post service*
1c45a682-1820-5eee-b604-862620e6fcea.short_description: This oil on canvas painting shows a scene from daily life at the Tunis post and telegraph office, built on the Rue d'Italie (now Rue Charles-de-Gaulle). One of the busiest rooms, the revenue office's great hall is, with its tremendously high ceilings, an impressive example of neo-classical architecture. Featuring elements of carved plaster and a map of Tunisia on a central marble panel, this painting faithfully reproduces the opulence of this historic building.

1c78b924-ed6f-5a33-8922-4aa69a219c71.name: Portraits of Jahangir and Shah Jahan
1c78b924-ed6f-5a33-8922-4aa69a219c71.short_description: This album painting shows portraits of two Mughal emperors; the upper portrait shows Jahangir (r. 1605–27) in a *jharoka* window-scene, while the lower, larger portrait depicts his son, Shah Jahan (r. 1627–58) in greater dimensions, a golden nimbus or halo encircling his head. Most famous today for commissioning the Taj Mahal, Shah Jahan was also a connoisseur of gemstones. In this portrait, he is richly adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and pendants of pearls, emeralds, rubies, and other jewels. He wears an orange turban decorated with strings of pearls, rubies, and emeralds and a sapphire turban-ornament (*sarpech*) of black aigrette feathers. His gold belt glitters with diamonds and a large opal. In his sash is tucked a dagger or *katar*, and his right arm leans on a sword. He is holding his imperial seal on his left hand, a sign of his sovereignty.
1c78b924-ed6f-5a33-8922-4aa69a219c71.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

1ca4ae5b-e753-59d1-a5de-423460efb5d1.name: Iconostasis in the Church of the Holy Saviour
1ca4ae5b-e753-59d1-a5de-423460efb5d1.short_description: This iconostasis was created by one of the greatest Macedonian masters of woodcarving, Petre Filipovski Garka, who formed his own group of artisans and developed his outstanding style of wood-carving, which was widely recognizable in the Balkans in the early 19th century. This exquisite piece of wood-carving was made from walnut in the technique of high relief. The iconostasis depicts scenes from the Old and the New Testament in which biblical figures are rendered wearing traditional costumes worn in Macedonia. The detail shows the self-portraits of Petre Filipovski and his associate artisans.

1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.name: *Glorification of Emperor Charles VI*
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.description:
Sitting in his ceremonial tent on the right, the ruler is receiving a report. Surrounded by angels and wearing a crown, the Virgin Mary – in a cloud over the tent – reaches out towards the Emperor with an olive branch. To the right of the tent there is a column decorated with portraits of Habsburg rulers in roundels: emperors Ferdinand III, Leopold I, Joseph I and Charles VI. The dates inscribed on the column, 1740 and 1745, may refer to the emperorship of Charles Albert Elector of Bavaria and the Peace of Dresden Treaty, which resulted in the election of Maria Theresia's husband, Francis of Lorraine, as emperor. This is why it is likely that Francis of Lorraine commissioned the picture as a monument to his father-in-law's Ottoman campaigns. In the foreground on the left, a battle scene probably depicts the Siege of Belgrade, displaying the recognisable figure of Prince Eugene von Savoy.  
The fresco and altarpiece painter, Joseph Adam Mölck, studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and records mention that he was there in 1733. Mölck worked for 15 years in Bavaria and Tyrol. In 1764, he painted frescos and altarpieces for churches in Steiermark. He worked in Lower Austria for the final 12 years of his career. His oeuvre was extensive and he worked with collaborators to achieve large commissions. The art and theory of the Italian architect and painter, Andrea Pozzo, influenced Mölck's frescos.  
Mölck visited Vienna in 1754, but why he did so remains a mystery; there is possibly a connection between the commission of this painting and Mölck's appointment as Tyrolean court painter in 1755.
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.short_description: An allegorical composition of an emperor's military deeds is a special subject and this is a unique example of it. The dates on the column (1740 and 1745) may refer to the Peace of Dresden Treaty, which resulted in the election of Maria Theresia's husband, Francis of Lorraine, as emperor. It is likely that Francis of Lorraine commissioned the picture to commemorate his father-in-law's Ottoman campaigns.
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and dated.
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.provenance: Probably commissioned by Emperor Francis of Lorraine
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.obtention: From the old collection of the Hungarian National Museum.

1de5d379-77f2-53f5-8b74-1effd8f999f9.name: Saint Mary Magdalene renouncing worldly vanities
1de5d379-77f2-53f5-8b74-1effd8f999f9.description:
Under the cover of a daily feminine toilette scene depicting a lady magnificently dressed taking off her jewellery in a luxuriously furnished room, this oil-on-copper allegory has both moral and apologetic purposes in line with the Counter Reformation. The painting records the first steps of St. Mary Magdalene towards her religious conversion, to renounce worldly belongings, retreat to the desert and her penitence, meditation and mystic encounter with Christ. St. Mary Magdalene was the embodiment of one who had abandoned a life of riches and ephemeral pleasures, and replaced it with a frugal contemplative way of life, thereby disdaining all worldly vanities.  
Several details in the painting carefully describe the circumstances of her retreat: the characterisation of St. Mary, and the room in which we see her, enhance the contrast between the luxury she is about to leave behind and the redemption she will achieve through a simple life and penitence in the desert.  
Within these details one can point out the furniture, the richness of the fabrics, and the detail of the lute on the arch – music is included within the worldly pleasures – and even the cat under the table, a symbol of domestic comfort. Yet the central topic of the action, vanitas, is represented by the gold, pearls and precious gems and jewels, which she is gradually scattering on the table, supreme emblems of vanity, beauty and worldly matters.  
In fact, therefore, this oil-on-copper painting is a precious iconographic document of the epoch, depicting both furnishing and sartorial fashion, but most importantly recording the jewellery in vogue at the time.  
Lastly it is also worth mentioning that this image was not painted by a professional painter. Sister Joana Baptista's biography is almost unknown; she was a nun from the Maltesas Convent of S. João of Estremoz, a small town in Alentejo. Her charming and naïve painting style is a fine example among other similar works made in Franciscan and Benedictine convents, painted by nuns to be seen by nuns, it presents St. Mary Magdalene as an example of good behaviour and devotion.
1de5d379-77f2-53f5-8b74-1effd8f999f9.short_description: Mary Magdalene strips off her jewels as symbols of vanity, thereby renouncing worldly luxury before embracing a life of penitence in the desert. As an iconographic document, the painting is a good example of the religious and moral ethics of the Counter-Reformation, while offering a window onto the daily life of the aristocracy.

1e902b54-02bc-52d4-a41f-4b3abe60ea34.name: *Sybil*
1e902b54-02bc-52d4-a41f-4b3abe60ea34.description:
The work was obtained by Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1617, and may originally have been commissioned from Domenichino by Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, although this is not certain. It is the first known piece having this subject (there is another original from 1622 in Rome at the Pinacoteca Capitolina).  
It shows one of the famous 'ideal figures' created by the painter through a progressive selection of forms until a studied, classical equilibrium between nature and perfection, beauty and expression of emotion is achieved: the representation of moods that is a central theme in the language of the Baroque.  
The figure assumes a singing pose. Numerous details refer to the musical background of the artist, who was a frequent visitor to the *Kapellmeisters* of Bologna. In this context Domenichino started to research a musical form that was entirely new at the time and that would become the style of instrumental Baroque music par excellence: the *trio sonata*. The maiden sits beside a beautifully carved viol and is holding a musical score in her hands. The laurel bushes allude allegorically to Apollo, to whom the sibyls were devoted, while the vine refers to the god, Bacchus, who is associated with poetic inspiration.  
The 11 pagan sibyls communicate the responses of the god Apollo through the oracles. Christian doctrine interpreted these maidens, who were dedicated to divinity, as forerunners of Christianity, attributing them the role of prophets of the coming of Christ. The female figure with her head bound in a turban alludes to the martyr Cecilia, whose body was miraculously found intact at the beginning of the 17th century, and whose story was painted as a fresco by Domenichino in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi. The painting shows an extraordinary synthesis between the colours of Bolognese painting and the drawing of Raphael and Leonardo's theories on aerial perspective, established at around the same time.
1e902b54-02bc-52d4-a41f-4b3abe60ea34.short_description:
The Sybil, holding a musical score in her hand, is portrayed as the revelator of the Divine Word. The figure is connected to the discovery of the body of Saint Cecilia, patron saint of music, in Trastevere, from whom it borrows the image of the turban as worn by the martyr, who was found near to the basilica of the same name in Trastevere.  
Through a selection of forms the painter reaches a refined and classical balance between nature and perfection; between beauty and the expression of feelings.

1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.name: *Saint Michael Archangel with Four Saints*
1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.alternate_name: *Saint Michael Archangel with the Saints John the Baptist, Benedict, Francis and Jerome*
1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.description: This painting once on the high altar of the church of San Michele, St. Michael is described by the Bolognese art historian Malvasia as “of peculiar invention and of such a pictorial good taste”. The five saints, rarely associated, are crowded in the narrow space without being in emotional contact with each other: Benedict, Francis and Jerome are absorbed in their meditations, only the Baptist seems to notice the presence of the archangel. He points to the scale that will be used on the day of the Last Judgement to weigh merits and sins. The painting can be dated around the half of the second decade of the seventeenth-century based on the pictorial language maturity clearly visible in the monumental scale of the figures and the skilled brilliant use of colour.
1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.short_description: The five saints, rarely associated, are crowded in the narrow space without seeming to be in emotional contact with each other.

20abb534-7f0e-5447-96ad-59b7c1f4354d.name: Pendant with The Miracle of Saint George and the Dragon
20abb534-7f0e-5447-96ad-59b7c1f4354d.description: Saint George was born to Christian parents in the 3rd century. He joined the Roman army and became a high-ranking officer at a young age, earning the respect of Emperor Diocletian. At that time, Diocletian persecuted Christians and required that all soldiers sacrifice to the pagan gods. Saint George publicly denounced the emperor and confessed to being Christian. He was subjected to brutal punishments, but refused to renounce his faith. Saint George was beheaded and became a popular martyr saint. In one story of his life, he rescued a town besieged by a dragon. The townspeople had been sacrificing children, who were randomly chosen by casting lots, to the dragon. Saint George rode in just as the town’s princess was to be sacrificed. He killed the dragon, a symbol of paganism, and converted the townspeople to Christianity. In this miniature icon, Saint George is seen atop a white horse slaying the dragon with a spear. The princess stands nearby with the town in the background. The icon has a beautiful enameled *oklad* (frame) with a silver loop at the top. It may have been worn around the neck and was probably commissioned for a military officer from a wealthy family since Saint George is a patron saint of soldiers.
20abb534-7f0e-5447-96ad-59b7c1f4354d.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Christie's Auction, London, in 2007. Gifted by Gordon Lankton to the Museum of Russian Icons in 2008.
keywords: Saints; Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography
materials: Egg tempera on wood with silver oklad, gems, enamel

20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.name: *Still-Life*
20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.description:
Baltazar Gomes Figueira was born and worked in Óbidos, although he studied in Seville where he worked with the great 17th-century Spanish painters Francisco Herrera, Zurbaran and Juan de Castillo. There he probably learned how to paint *bodegones*, a Spanish term given to both still-life and domestic interiors, and sometimes featuring kitchen scenes. This type of still-life painting was very much appreciated in the 16th century as a result of the growing artistic interest in scenes from daily life as well as an increased curiosity in the natural sciences. In the framework of the Baroque aesthetic, the still-life genre conveys transcendental values through the depiction of inanimate objects.  
The painting is composed of three elemental groups: on the left-hand side the fish lying on the bare table represent the four cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, strength and temperance. The fish, separated from the other parts of the painting, are immersed in an intense penumbra and illuminated with a luminous white.  
Lying on a light-green tablecloth are the other two groups: four dead birds – a sparrow, green woodpecker, duck and partridge – represent disrespect, human fragility and vice, lust and temptation. The grapes lying within this ensemble represent redemption of all these sins through the Eucharist.  
Finally, on the right-hand side on the tablecloth, are a silver plate and some regional pottery beside the confectionery and fruit, these elements are symbolic of abundance, sensual desire, prosperity and immortality. The combinations of the four elements in each group are inked with the Four Seasons, the Four Elements (Earth, Air, Water, Fire) and with the Four Principles of Human Existence (Mind, Body, Spirit and Soul).  
The vivid detail, seen in the realistic drops of water near the fish for example, draw attention to the magical *chiaroscuro* accentuated by thin, transparent layers of paint.
20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.short_description: This still-life depicting fish, birds, fruit, confectionery, silverware and pottery was probably painted by Baltazar Gomes Figueira. It reveals two opposing realities: the spiritual world symbolised by four fish and a bunch of grapes, and the earthly reality and its dangers embodied in four dead birds, fruit and confectionery.
20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.provenance: Has long been part of the permanent collection of Grão Vasco Museum
