2187568a-30fb-56b8-a477-3f4a26e1478c.name: *Saint Philip Benizi in Glory*
2187568a-30fb-56b8-a477-3f4a26e1478c.description: In 1697 Domenico Maria Viani was summoned to Imola by the Servite fathers in order to paint three pictures for their church. One of them, depicting “the Virgin Mary and the patron saints of Imola” is no more extant, however we still have the “Saint Philip Benizi in Glory” and “the Saint Pellegrino Laziosi Healed by the Crucifix.” Viani worked in Imola for a year and a half on these paintings. With his saint Philip Benizi, the Bolognese painter entered his mature phase, combining the style of Guido Reni learned in his father’s workshop with the baroque language of another Bolognese painter, Domenico Maria Canuti and employing a Venetian palette with warm colours. The group of the saint with the angels is seen from below and it gives the impression of the image continuing outside of the frame. The painting has always been mentioned by guides and art historians as very beautiful. The sumptuous gilded frame was carved in 1710 by the Imolese sculptor Giuseppe Giuliani.
2187568a-30fb-56b8-a477-3f4a26e1478c.short_description: The painting was made in 1697 by the Bolognese painter Domenico Maria Viani for the Servite fathers of Imola. It is a mixture of classical academic culture and a fully baroque style. The carved frame was made by the Imolese sculptor Giuseppe Giuliani.

221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.name: Subterranean Passage to Fountain of the Virgin, Jerusalem
221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.description: A local Silwani woman carries a water jug and candle down to the Fountain of the Virgin to collect water. Another figure in the background is emerging into the daylight, having completed a similar trip. The Fountain of the Virgin, or Gihon Spring, is a freshwater spring in the Kidron Valley that represents the only local water source for Jerusalem. Other pools, like the Bethesda pool in the north of the city, held water transported from the springs at Artas, near Bethlehem. It is part of a complex and ancient water management system dating back at least to the Middle Bronze Age (c 2,000 BCE) that continued to represent a major source of fresh water for the Silwani and Jerusalem community until recent years.

23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.name: *St. Augustine*
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.description:
The monumentally proportioned, diagonally placed figure of Bishop St. Augustine dominates the work taking up almost two-thirds of the canvas. St. Augustine is sitting back, with one leg stretched out and the other bent at the knee. The Bishop is dressed in luxurious vestments and holds a burning heart in one hand, while with the other, he is writing in an open book. His bishop's mitre is also on the table. Behind his back there is a bookshelf, while on the other side, like a vision, is a rendering of the Holy Trinity.  
St. Augustine, a Bishop and Doctor of the Church, one of the four Latin Doctors, played a very important iconographic role in the Pauline order. Although the Paulines existed in the Middle Ages, they were formerly organised as an order in the High Middle Ages, living under the rules of St. Augustine. The choice of saints in Pauline iconography are not random, each figure symbolises a particular Pauline characteristic.  
This painting is by one of the greatest Pauline painters, Ivan Ranger. Born in Tyrol he joined the Pauline order as a trained lay brother-painter.
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.short_description: In this painting by the Pauline painter, Ivan Ranger, the Bishop St. Augustine is shown with his attributes of a burning heart, a book and a mitre. *St. Augustine* was painted for the Pauline Monastery in Lepoglava.
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.holder: Diocese Museum of the Zagreb Archdiocese

Gifted to the museum in 1940, prior to this, the work was in the sacristy of Lepoglava Parish Church, formerly the church of the Pauline Monastery, until the abolition of the order by decree of the Habsburg Emperor Joseph II in 1786.

23d6b4ee-6380-5185-a38f-672a711e7d14.name:
Shaykh Safi al-Din asking his disciples to accept honey from the villagers but not meat  
From the manuscript of *Safvat al-Safa* (The Quintessence of Purity), the Hagiography of Shaykh Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili (1252/3–1334)
23d6b4ee-6380-5185-a38f-672a711e7d14.short_description: “Shaykh Safi al-Din asking his disciples to accept honey from the villagers but not meat” is one of fourteen paintings in the only known illustrated copy of *Safvat al-Safa* (The Quintessence of Purity), a tazkira and hagiography of Shaykh Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili (1252/3–1334). *Safvat al-Safa* gives detailed information about the life, sayings, virtues, and miracles of Shaykh Safi, the spiritual founder of the Safavid dynasty (1501–1736). *Safvat al-Safa* is a biography book with hagiographical accounts which falls under both genres. In Islamic literature, the term "tazkira" is used for biographical texts and "hagiography" is used for books on the lives of the mystics. *Safvat al-Safa* includes actual information on the life of Shaykh Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili as well as mystical and supernatural stories. It appears to have been the main source of the Safavid chroniclers for the early period of the dynasty, as there are numerous copies and translations. Safvat al-Safa has an introduction (*muqaddima*), twelve chapters (*bab*), and an epilogue (*khatima*). Each chapter has numerous sections (*fasl*) which include multiple short episodes (*hikayat*).
23d6b4ee-6380-5185-a38f-672a711e7d14.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.name: *Annunciation*
24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.description:
The painting, a *bozzetto* (study), was acquired by the Italian State in 1915 as the work of Giaquinto. Over the years, it was attributed variously to different artists in the Neapolitan area, but in 1958 the small canvas was deemed definitively to be the work of the Puglian artist. After a stay of several years in Naples, Giaquinto moved between Rome, Turin and Madrid, where he worked as the head painter to the court of Ferdinand VI, becoming an outstanding exponent of the European Rococo style. In Rome, the artist had developed the Baroque tradition, adopting the magnificence and refinery of its forms and the colours of that artistic language, using it to reveal the truth behind feelings.  
The study is generally dated between 1753 and 1762 (the years he was working in Spain) on account of his artistic characteristics of that period, when the artist was using rapid, highly fluid brushstrokes to paint luminous, elegant and at times iridescent colours. These forms and colours made the painter one of the best known in the world, and even had an influence on the young Goya.  
The artist builds a scene that resembles a theatre: in the background, beneath the dove of the Holy Spirit, the cherubs observe from on high, as if from a box. Beneath the clouds, a large green cloth forms one wing of the obliquely set architecture. Beneath the rays of divine light, the Virgin Mary lifts her face towards the Angel Gabriel who appears on high, wrapped in a soft swirl of yellow cape, clouds and cherubs.  
The few domestic objects elegantly arranged around the “stage” relate the divine intervention to a simple, recognisable scene from daily life, bringing the believer closer and making him more involved.  
The canvas was thought to be the study for the painting showing the Archangel Gabriel that is part of an *Annunciation* kept at the Szépmuűvészeti Múzeum in Budapest. It has also been linked with the altarpiece in the Annunciata Church in Todi, and with that in the Church of the Hospital of the Brothers of Mercy in Graz.
24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.short_description: This is a decorative *bozzetto* for the Royal Palace in Madrid (Giaquinto moved to Spain in 1753). The dramatic arrangement of the figures is typical of the Neapolitan school. Giaquinto moved to Rome in 1723 and stayed there for 30 years. During this time he was close contact with the Italian painters Sebastiano Conca, Pietro da Cortona and Giovanni Battistta Gaulli.
24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.obtention: Acquired by the Italian State in 1915.

2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.name: *Taking of Christ*
2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.description: The painting is one of a group of works confiscated from the workshops of the painter in 1607 on the orders of Paul V, and subsequently transferred to the collection of cardinal-nephew Scipione Borghese as a gift from the Pope. It is one of the most famous paintings of the Cavalier d'Arpino because of the chromatic quality and the complexity of the composition. It shows Christ being taken to the Garden of Gethsemane according to evangelical accounts, which also describe some peripheral episodes. At the centre of the scene is the figure of Christ, who stands out in the luminous glow of the torches and appears to emit his own light. In the bottom right, Peter holds his knife aloft, about to cut off the ear of the high priest's servant Malchus. On the left-hand side we see a perfect diagonal line traced between the figures running after the naked boy in the foreground. Notably, this latter was taken by the painter from a lost painting by Correggio (c. 1489–1534), which he may have seen first-hand during a trip to Parma. The composition and the attitudes of the figures express the taste of late Roman Mannerism, of which the artist was the best exponent during the 16th and 17th centuries. Beneficiary of the major commissions of the time, including primarily those placed by Pope Clement VIII Aldobrandini, Arpino headed the most important workshop in Rome, where a young Caravaggio worked having recently arrived from Lombardy. The high drama imparted by the sense of isolation around the figure of Christ, highlighted by flashes of light, was an essential focus of study and inspiration for Caravaggio's *Martyrdom of St. Matthew* produced a few years later for the Contarelli Chapel of the Church of San Luigi dei Francesi (1599–1602).
2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.short_description: This painting was considered “the most beautiful work by the Cavalier” (Bellori). Giuseppe Cesari was involved in some of the most important commissions of the time, including for Pope Clement VIII Aldobrandini. He owned the most important workshop in Rome in the late 16th century, where a young Caravaggio also worked soon after his arrival from Lombardy. Here he developed the still lives of his formative years, studying the issue of light in great depth. This work inspired Caravaggio's *Martyrdom of St. Matthew*.
2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

253606f2-42fd-5770-a8f6-cd970b12f2cb.name: Nubian Boy
253606f2-42fd-5770-a8f6-cd970b12f2cb.short_description:
The painting provides a glimpse of everyday street life, probably in Cairo. A tired water seller rests on a wall in front of a building entrance. The boy depicted is carrying on his back a large portable water jar similar to SM1996-219 whilst holding in his hand small drinking cups.  
Ferraris was a renowned Orientalist painter, pupil of Jean-Léon Gérôme, who encouraged him in 1885 to set off on a journey to Egypt with another famous Orientalist painter, Ludwig Deutsch.

27672751-bd77-5df0-ac0c-0c65f49bf798.name: A Persian noble
27672751-bd77-5df0-ac0c-0c65f49bf798.short_description:
The painting of a Persian man is traditionally associated with the painting of a richly dressed woman. Due to his attire, there is no shadow of a doubt that the man is not a Safavid nobleman. He is standing in front of a water basin in the courtyard of a stately Persian house.  
  
The way the paint is applied in multiple layers as well as the strong Chiaroscuro clearly reveal that the painter was trained in Europe. This is also indicated by the fact that the painter mixed the wet colours directly on the canvas and executed the highlights in thick lead white. Equally European is the sombre palette and a preference for shaded hues. They stand in stark contrast to the Persian predilection for pure, luminous colours.  
  
These two paintings are possibly two of the extremely rare, if not the only, known examples of pictures painted by European artists in Persia. We know from the sources that several painters from Europe, especially from the Netherlands, worked in the 17th century for the Shahs.

27a151e4-bd94-52f6-b538-2f4bcdf9c778.name: *Madonna and Child with St. Anne (dei Palafrenieri)*
27a151e4-bd94-52f6-b538-2f4bcdf9c778.description:
The painting was conceived as an altarpiece for the Chapel of the Confraternity of the Papal Grooms (who following the abolition of horseback retinues had the privilege of accompanying the Pope during ceremonies) located in Saint Peter's Basilica. Commissioned in 1605, it was delivered shortly afterward and placed on the altar, before being immediately removed and transferred to the nearby Church of St. Anne, protector of the Confraternity.  
Caravaggio was paid a meagre sum, which was increased by Cardinal Scipione Borghese, who purchased the canvas for his city residence. This masterpiece was famously refused by the Confraternity, which disapproved of the realism used in the portrayal of their patron, whose name (“Anne”) means “Grace” in Hebrew, her daughter Mary and the Baby Jesus, all in a simple background barely illuminated by a single ray of light.  
The painting highlights the role of Anne as the creator; she who destroys “evil” and the role of the Virgin Mary who, with Jesus, crushes the head of the serpent, the symbol of sin. The subject also touched on the debate of the Immaculate Conception, in relation to Mary as a person, conceived without original sin (the dogma was not settled until 8 December 1854) and was therefore central to the dispute that split Catholics and Protestants at the time. The combination of these elements, in particular the extreme humanisation with which Caravaggio depicted the Holy Family, resulted in the judgement that the work was not sufficiently decorous for a representation of holy subjects, particularly at the time of the Counter-Reformation.  
A recent restoration has thrown new light on the technique used by the artist, who did no preparatory drawings. Indeed, the analyses carried out have shown some limited traces of incisions around the figures.
27a151e4-bd94-52f6-b538-2f4bcdf9c778.short_description: This painting was commissioned by the Confraternity of the Papal Grooms for the Sant’Anna Chapel located in Saint Peter’s Basilica. Considered to be lacking in decorum, it was removed after a month to the nearby Church of St. Anne in the Vatican, and later displayed in Cardinal Scipione Borghese’s collection. The religious theme is dealt with in an innovative, strongly humanised way. Caravaggio’s use of light greatly influenced his contemporaries, even the more classical painters. This work is an example of the contrast between the artistic views of the Counter-Reformation and uninhibited taste of the collector.

27f25605-a0d6-5226-be64-b5c88fc6fc1c.name: *Fall of Stalać*
27f25605-a0d6-5226-be64-b5c88fc6fc1c.short_description:
Having mastered the cobbling trade and after studying theology, in 1873, the Serb Đorđe Krstić went to further his education at the Munich Art Academy thanks to a scholarship from the Knez that came after he had prepared for admission to an arts and crafts school. By 1920, there were approximately 50 Serbian students enrolled there. Though pieces from his Munich phase measure up to the best works of the time, a later painting by this historical and genre artist is better suited here. After the initial, strong influence of realism, on his return to Belgrade, in 1883, he endeavoured to present an open manner of painting, with strong and coloristic effects.  
Stalać was one of the largest fortified towns in Serbia in the Middle Ages, serving simultaneously as a checkpoint on the approaches to the then capital Kruševac and to strategically important valleys. At the same time as four other forts, Stalać was burned down and laid to waste in 1413, in initial raids by the Ottoman Turks, who subsequently conquered Serbia in 1459.  
This painting was commissioned by King Aleksandar Obrenović for the 1900 Paris Exposition. However, the committee rejected it before the Expo for an excessively extreme depiction of fighting. When the painting was exhibited in the National Museum in Belgrade in 1901, 1,000 visitors flocked to see it every day.
27f25605-a0d6-5226-be64-b5c88fc6fc1c.author: Petar Petrovic
keywords: Historical Painting

289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.name: *Aeneas’ Flight from Troy*
289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.description: A painting of the same subject, now sadly lost, was made for Emperor Rudolph II of Austria (1586–89). Given its immediate success, Barocci made a copy in 1589. According to tradition, it was Cardinal Giuliano Della Rovere of Urbino who later gave it to Scipione Borghese. Scipione was so pleased with the painting that in 1618 he commissioned Gian Lorenzo Bernini to produce a sculptural group (the first by the famous sculptor) showing the same subject. The work demonstrates the exceptional technique of the Urbino painter, who worked continuously on religious subjects and portraits, this being one of his few secular pieces. The scenery through which the protagonists move – bold imagery that did not escape Rubens – is highly dramatic: flames chase them, and the smoke and darkness of the night emphasise the imminent tragedy. The foreshortening of the stairway in the foreground, light reflecting off the balusters, creates a highly scenic element serving the theatricality of the episode, and presages future solutions employed in Baroque art. In the background, in addition to the Antonine column, there are clear references to the work of Raphael and Donato Bramante, who, like Barocci, came from Urbino. The monuments shown appear to compare Rome to Troy in flames, almost wishing to recall the terrible Sack of Rome by the Landsknechts in 1527.
289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.short_description: Barocci was a predecessor of Baroque art. The complex division of space, the spontaneity and naturalness of the figures' movements, the colours, all had a strong influence on 17th-century art, particularly that of Rubens. His anti-rhetorical figures were not appreciated in Rome and considered remote from classical art. Cardinal Scipione was inspired by this work when he commissioned Bernini to sculpt a statue of subject. This canvas is a replica of Rudolf II of Austria's painting (1586–89).

28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.name: *St. Jerome*
28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.description:
St. Jerome, Father of the Western Church, is shown translating the texts of the Old and New Testaments (*Vulgate*) into Latin. The scene is rendered suggestively with a neutral background from which the light-bathed figure emerges. On a table, near the books, there is a skull, signifying the penitential aspect of the saint, and his meditation on the Passion and death of Christ.  
The composition, executed with high realism, is synonymous with the artist's style, giving the subjects a very particular theatricality that focuses solely on the actions or expressions of the characters without using monumental scenery or artifice, typical of Baroque art. St. Jerome was one of the most commonly represented figures of the Counter-Reformation. His active and contemplative life was held up as a model for the faithful, who saw in him a route to salvation, in addition to the importance placed on studying and translating the scriptures from Greek and Hebrew. The *Vulgate* was in fact the first Latin transcription of the Bible and therefore became a key tool for the dissemination of the sacred texts. The painting, according to tradition, was carried out expressly for Scipione Borghese, having recently been elected cardinal with the help of his uncle Camillo, who had become Pope Paul V on 16 May 1605. The cardinal, who helped the artist escape a prison sentence related to problems involving women in 1605, the year the piece is dated, was one of Caravaggio's great admirers, and procured 12 of the artist's pieces for his collection.
28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.short_description: The artwork was given as a gift by the artist to Cardinal Scipione Borghese, who had helped him get out of a Roman prison. It represents St. Jerome, one of the Fathers of the Church, in the act of translating the *Vulgate*. For this reason, he is considered the patron saint of archaeologists, librarians, translators and students in general. The canvas dates from 1605, the year in which Borghese was made cardinal, making this painting even dearer to the newly appointed prince of the Church.

29092d3e-f7b7-5e75-a750-72b4e7e7bbd1.name: *Fugitives Of Herzegovina*
29092d3e-f7b7-5e75-a750-72b4e7e7bbd1.short_description: In response to events in the Serbo-Turkish war of 1875-78, Uroš Predić presents his extremely realistic treatment of a subject glorifying not the heroic struggle for liberation, but the hardships of innocent people forced to go into hiding. The artist was inspired by similar works with historical subjects, like those painted by Jaroslav Čermak (1831-1878), but painted his figures from live models, mostly close relatives who posed for him in a Belgrade studio. Thanks to the world-renowned scientist and benefactor Mihailo Pupin (1854-1935), *Fugitives of Herzegovina* became a part of the collection of the National Museum in Belgrade in 1923.

29756bc5-95e1-5d47-be16-67719e7ac820.name: *The Franco-Tuscan Expedition to Egypt*
29756bc5-95e1-5d47-be16-67719e7ac820.short_description:
In 1827 the artist Giuseppe Angelelli took part in the Franco-Tuscan campaign to Egypt (1828–1829) sponsored by the French Government and the Grand Duke of Tuscany and directed by the archaeologist Ippolito Rosellini. Once back in Florence, the Grand Duke of Tuscany commissioned him to create a painting of those who took part at the campaign in Thebes.  
The two directors are represented in the core of the scene, wearing the Nizam, the official clothing, which has recently been required by the pasha and willingly adopted by most of them. Champollion is seated and Ippolito Rosellini is standing at his right, holding a sheet depicting one of the Kadesh Battle's scenes, that of Pharaoh grabbing an enemy's arm. In the middle, between the two protagonists, is the engineer Gaetano Rosellini, Ippolito's uncle and architect in charge of the two missions. On the left, several members of the Commissions: the elder Raddi, dressed in European garb and holding a lotus flower in his hand; the illustrator Duchesne is shown in the foreground with the colours on one side and a painting of ruins on the other.

29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.name: *Allegory of the Fortunate Reign of Moravia*
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.alternate_name: *Homage of Olympus to the Moravian Land*
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.description:
The composition is executed in depth. Under a Zodiac indicating eternity at the top edge, flies Fame, trumpeting the glory of Moravia. The top section features the symbol of Moravia, an obelisk with a chequered eagle, towards which *putti* fly with a laurel wreath and a crown. On the left, a female figure with a palm frond symbolises monarchical virtue while on the other side sits *Potestas*, who personifies power, and to whom the *putti* hand the field emblems of the Roman legions. Next to monarchical virtue is Victoria, with a laurel wreath on her head and a statue of the goddess Nike in her hand. Below are Mercury, the god of trade, Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, and *Cognitio*, the personification of knowledge. Their opposite on the right is *Religio*, accompanied by the Old and New Testaments. The group is observed by Diana, goddess of hunting, and Fortune with a wheel. The central motif is *Abundantia* with a cornucopia. At the bottom are Hercules, the war gods Mars and Bellona, an allegory of eternal fame, a water god and a *putto* with weapons. Below the group is an allegorical female figure with a helmet and a palm frond, possibly symbolising strength and competence.  
In the early 1730s, the proprietors of the Moravian Estates decided to commission decorative artwork to finish off the reconstruction of the Provincial House in Brno. Provincial Governor Maxmilián Oldřich Count Kounic assigned the job to the academic painter Daniel Gran and the quadraturist Gaetano Fanti. *Allegory of the Fortunate Reign of Moravia* was executed above the assembly hall benches, while *Apotheosis of the Rule of Justice*, an allegory of a “good government”, was placed above the governor's seat. Three preparatory sketches (Albertina, Vienna; Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg) and two designs in oil (Akademie der bildenden Künste, Österreichische Galerie Belvedere) have survived for the first scene. A mirror image of Gran's painting from the Moravian Gallery was created as a template for a print.
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.short_description: This workshop image of Gran’s mural from the Assembly Hall of the Moravian Estates was created as a template for a print. The top section of the composition – a world of allegorical figures and ancient gods - features the symbol of Moravia, an obelisk with the country’s coat of arms.

2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.name: *The Bazaar at Athens*
2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.short_description: The well-known Irish topographer Edward Dodwell toured Greece twice: in 1801 and 1805–6 and he later produced several works on Greece’s scenery, its antiquities and the people’s life. He managed to cover a wide range of Greek subjects and to record faithfully-in both his drawings and his descriptions- various aspects of Greek life and customs. Dodwell’s folio *Views in Greece* (1821) includes an identical image entitled “Bazaar of Athens”, which is obviously based on this watercolour. According to the artist’s description in the text, on the right-hand side is seen a coffee-shop frequented by important people, such as the disdar (e.g. Governor of Athens) depicted in a scarlet gown.
2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.author: Tsigakou 1995, 114, fig. 6
keywords: travels; Dodwell; Athens

2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.name: *Nativity*
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.alternate_name: Sketch for the altarpiece of the Voss Orphanage, Sopron
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.description:
Dorffmaister was a student at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1751 to 1759. In 1762 he settled in Sopron and worked until his death almost exclusively for Hungarian patrons as a fresco and altarpiece painter. He took commissions from everyone – bishops, various monastic orders and town or village communities.  
Being childless Charles Voss von Ehrenfels (d.1761) and his wife, Anna Dorothea Lanius (d.1770), made a pact that following the death of either one of them the one that survived should found an orphanage. Having survived her husband Anna Dorothea bought the Kisfaludy house in Sopron seeing it as a suitable building for an orphanage. The foundation charter of the institution was signed in 1768 and confirmed in the same year by Empress Maria Theresia.  
Following the death of Anna Dorothea, György Primes the vicar of Sopron, finished the construction and decoration of the orphanage whose chapel was opened in 1772, and decorated with an altarpiece by Dorffmaister accomplished in the same year.  
To the right of the altar, which takes up the entire main wall, there is a contemporary sculpture of the Guardian Angel. The commission for the altarpiece painting went to Dorffmaister who made an oil sketch, which has remained in the town to this day, and is illustrated here. In the building with its chapel that was newly consecrated in 2009 after a restoration, there is a community centre for Christian communities, courses, lectures, and various charitable activities.  
For the composition of the altarpiece for the Holy Trinity Chapel, the artist chose an unusual depiction of the Holy Trinity: he painted the figure of God the Father and the dove of the Holy Spirit among a choir of angels over a scene of the Nativity, gazing down at the stable in Bethlehem. In this representation, Dorffmaister merges three different types of picture: the Nativity, the Adoration of the Shepherds and the Adoration of the Magi. The result is one of Dorffmaister's most balanced and harmonious altarpieces. Beyond the motif of Mary's raised, shining white kerchief taken from northern Italian painting, the artist appears to follow the example of a mature Adoration of the Magi. The figures unfold from a dark background emphasised by strongly coloured drapery, sharp light cast on their faces, and light patches of folds in some of the garments.  
With this altarpiece, Dorffmaister's first major ecclesiastical undertaking in the town of Sopron, the artist reveals not only the rigour of his training but also shows how accomplished he is regards composition as well as style, depicting his figures in a confident and elegant manner.
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.short_description: A member of a Viennese artistic dynasty working solely from the Transdanubian region, Dorffmaister was an accomplished fresco painter, living from 1762 until his death in Sopron. The Voss Orphanage altarpiece, influenced by Viennese academic style, is one of his best studies.

2c586151-177a-57bd-9616-76904bd42503.name: *Surre Procession*
2c586151-177a-57bd-9616-76904bd42503.short_description: The Italian Orientalist painter Stefano Ussi's painting *Surre Regiment* depicts the deva caravan carrying gifts from Cairo to Kaaba, the pilgrims and a regiment of the Ottoman army assigned to protect the caravan. *Surre Regiment* is the largest painting of the Painting Collection of the National Palaces. The composition reflects the emotions of Muslims during the pilgrimage to Mecca, whose ethnic structures, growing styles and points of view regarding Islam are different. The frame of the painting dated 1873 is surrounded by Arabic Kufic script, which is a part of the 126th verse in Surah Al-Imran that reads, “There is no help or victory except from Allah, the All-Mighty, the All-Wise”. *Surre Regiment* is presumed to be included in the Palace’s collection by being purchased or given by Mısır Hıdivi as a gift for Sultan Abdülaziz.

2d72d94d-e1c6-5a81-840c-a012724c9917.name: Loss
2d72d94d-e1c6-5a81-840c-a012724c9917.description: Ismail Shammout’s Loss can be used to discuss displacement, exile, and the emotional aftermath of the Nakba. Painted in 1955, the work shows displaced Palestinians in what appears to be a refugee camp, where survival, protection, and uncertainty define everyday life. The central image of a mother holding and covering her child transforms political rupture into an intimate scene of fear, care, and fragile hope. For this reason, the painting is especially useful for explaining how modern Palestinian art gave visual form to loss, forced migration, and the struggle to preserve identity after 1948.

2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.name: "The Story of the Princess of the Blue Pavillion: The Youth of Rum Is Entertained in a Garden by a Fairy and her Maidens"
2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.description: Approximately one century after the Persian poet Nizami wrote his Khamsa (Quintet), the Indian poet Amir Khusrau Dihlavi composed a response using Nizami’s structure but varying his stories slightly. 301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.name: *A watchman on a Constantinople street*
301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.short_description: This painting shows an old watchman, carrying his lantern around the old streets of Istanbul. By the times of sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 CE – 1327 H/1909 CE) the nature of urban life in the Ottoman empire began to change markedly. In Istanbul, Izmir, Edirne, Salonica and other major cities, streets were paved and lit with gas lamps, while horse drawn trams increasingly plied the streets. Political reforms and  new technologies introduced in the13th century H/ 19th century CE gradually transformed Istanbul into a modern international city. Innovative technological achievements such as electric lighting became more and more common, slowly replacing traditionally essential services like those provided by the watchmen of the city, guarding the city quarters with their hand-held lanterns during the hours of darkness.

30b613c8-c840-5eba-a2ea-3334a058e6c5.name: *The Temptations of Saint Antony*
30b613c8-c840-5eba-a2ea-3334a058e6c5.short_description:
The painting by Domenico Morelli shown at the Universal Exposition in Paris, it’s among the artist’s most complex artworks. Both realistic and symbolic elements characterise the painting, as well as a strong mystic, but at the same time erotic, tension. Inspired by *La Tentation de Saint-Antoine* by Gustave Flaubert from 1874, the painting shows realism in the imaginary setting influenced by oriental elements. The work was finished in 1878 and sent to the French merchant Goupil to be shown at the Universal Exposition in Paris. It was also presented at the National Exposition in Turin in 1880 and completely misunderstood by contemporaries who blamed Morelli for having resigned to make fashionable art.  
A smaller version of it was painted by the artist while making a lot of preparatory drawings in which Saint Anthony is standing next to the rock wall. In the final version the Saint is seated on the ground trying to resist the temptations embodied by the two half-naked women on the left.

30f5e9ae-837a-53a1-bbb9-25a8759da077.name: *David with the Head of Goliath*
30f5e9ae-837a-53a1-bbb9-25a8759da077.description: The painting shows the key moment in the Old Testament story of David depicting the head of the giant Goliath, killed with a slingshot by the young shepherd. The canvas belonged to Cardinal Scipione Borghese from at least 1613, in which year, following payment, it was framed. The work dates from the artist's second stay in Naples (1609–1610), when Caravaggio, fleeing Rome having been convicted of killing a man, nevertheless continued to maintain a relationship with Cardinal Scipione. The latter's influence on his uncle Pope Paul V, after the painting was sent by the painter as proof of penance, convinced the Pope to grant a pardon. During his return journey, Caravaggio was delayed on the Tuscan coast near Port'Ercole, and died of unknown causes in July 1610, never reaching Rome. The oldest sources already recognise the artist's self-portrait in Goliath's face, but opinion differs regarding the young hero. Some see a self-portrait of the artist as a young man. As usual, the composition, executed using dark colours, demonstrates a lively and acute drama simply through the expressiveness of the faces. On David's unsheathed sword we can see some letters that have been interpreted to represent the virtuous motto “*HumilitAS Occidit Superbiam*”.
30f5e9ae-837a-53a1-bbb9-25a8759da077.short_description: Caravaggio innovatively painted himself as Goliath and sent the painting to Pope Paul V seeking pardon for the murder he had committed. The canvas may in fact be a double self-portrait, as David could be a portrait of the painter as a young man. The use of artificial light by Caravaggio has a moral function, probably expressing divine grace. It was at this time that Caravaggio’s artistic influence began to spread around the world.
30f5e9ae-837a-53a1-bbb9-25a8759da077.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

31375bcb-5762-5e4c-858e-10020d55be9a.name: The Sealed Fountain
31375bcb-5762-5e4c-858e-10020d55be9a.description: One of the springs which feeds into Solomon's Pools at Artas. 31cb9d95-2ea5-5b0f-87f9-ad3c5b11a8f1.name: *St. Charles Borromeo Consoling the Plague-Stricken*
31cb9d95-2ea5-5b0f-87f9-ad3c5b11a8f1.description:
The picture derives from events that took place during a plague epidemic in Milan in 1576. The subject is a frequently depicted moment in the life of St. Charles Borromeo (1538–1584), an archbishop and cardinal of Milan. The promptness of his canonisation, in 1610, does much to confirm his popularity, the cult of which reached the Habsburg monarchy. Sambach also painted an identical subject in 1752–1753 for a side altar in the Pilgrimage Church of the Holy Virgin in Sloup, near Brno. The picture was inspired by a much-copied painting by Pierre Mignard (c. 1647, Musée des Beaux-Arts, Caen). Beyond doubt, Sambach also drew on the approach of Johann Michael Rottmayr employed from 1721 to paint a picture for the Chapter Church in Salzburg, which develops Mignard’s model and achieved considerable popularity in Central Europe.  
In the signature of his Brno picture, Sambach ascribes its composition to Daniel Gran, who had painted a fresco on the presbytery wall of the same church in 1746. The two versions by Sambach share only one compositional motif. This is the figure of a seated, sick woman towards whom the saint is bending and who, in both cases, is being supported in the same manner by an assisting figure. St. Charles Borromeo is shown at a realistically rendered moment, reciting a prayer, his look averted from the dying woman, openly reading from the book held by an acolyte who is even indicating the place in the text. He appears lifelike and much more spontaneous than the traditional approach employed in the Sloup picture. In the Brno painting, Charles’s face is also more precisely modelled on the saint’s genuine appearance as captured by his contemporaries and found, for example, in a print by Giovanni Ambrogio Figino (1548–1608). The figure of the man standing in the background is also probably a portrait, and may be František Alexandr Hartl of Hartenberg, architect of the church in Matějovce and the person behind Gran’s – and possibly Sambach’s – involvement.
31cb9d95-2ea5-5b0f-87f9-ad3c5b11a8f1.short_description: A picture from the Matějovce Church which shows the archbishop and cardinal of Milan tending to plague victims. In the signature, the composition is ascribed to D. Gran, who painted a fresco in the same church in 1746. The composition reflects similar approaches to the subject by P. Mignard and J. M. Rottmayr.

Gran's fresco in the presbytery is dated 1746. Its counterpart, the St. Charles Borromeo picture, was originally Sambach's painting of St. John of Nepomuk, mediator to the dying and the persecuted (whereabouts unknown). Both pictures were mentioned and attributed to Sambach by J. P. Cerroni.

333072e2-7b70-5d9f-885f-267dbbb500a9.name: Pair of lacquer book covers
333072e2-7b70-5d9f-885f-267dbbb500a9.short_description: This binding has been detached from the unknown manuscript it once covered. The front cover depicts Fath ʻAli Shah Qajar (second ruler of the Qajar dynasty, r. 1798–1834), reportedly a passionate and skilled falconer, astride a horse holding a falcon as he looks out at the viewer. The back cover depicts a conversation between a youth, possibly a prince, and a young wandering dervish (*qalandar*), an image associated with Sufism, the mystical branch of Islam. The absence of the original manuscript makes it is difficult to confirm the intended meaning of the images on these covers or the connection between them.

345dfb37-6c70-5521-8c13-8c1dd4eec83c.name: *St. Mary the Magdalene*
345dfb37-6c70-5521-8c13-8c1dd4eec83c.description:
St. Mary the Magdalene is kneeling in front of the crucifix, next to her are a skull and an open book. She looks at the angels holding a chalice and a crown of thorns, symbols of the Passion of Christ and pointing to heaven.  
The painting shows a skilled thecnique and brilliant colours both deriving from the deep knowledge of the local pictorial tradition (the Carraccis, Guido Reni) together with that of Venetian and Roman contemporary painting.  
The picture is still in the original stucco framing. The cartuche above mentions the date 1757, when the painting and its pendant were put in the oratory and the chaplain Biagi paid for them. The coat of arms above the painting says “INVENI QUEM DILIGIT ANIMA MEA = TENUI EUM”.
345dfb37-6c70-5521-8c13-8c1dd4eec83c.short_description: Saint Mary Magdalene kneels in front of the crucifix with her attributes next to her. She looks at the angels above, holding a chalice and a crown of thorns, the symbols of the Passion of Christ. The painter, Gaetano Gandolfi, looks at the Bolognese painting of the seventeenth-century and at the contemporary Roman and Venetian schools.

34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.name: Two dragons entwined on a spray of stylised foliage
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.short_description: Probably executed in the Ottoman court atelier (*naqqashkhana*) in Istanbul, the remarkable intricacy of line and detail of this drawing belies its minute size. It belongs to a distinct style of painting that developed separate from the highly conceptual tradition of manuscript illustration in the second half of the 10th/16th century. Known as the "saz style" after the reed pen employed in its creation, this style highlighted fantastic and dazzling imagery that incorporates chinoiserie motifs and feathery leaves. Here, concealed among the dense, bristly foliage, are two silently slithering dragons, barely visible at first glance. Rather than emphasising pure line, the anonymous artist was caught up with the textural qualities of the dragons' scaly, speckled bodies and the sinuous veins of the serrated leaves. Drawings such as this were evidently reproduced through the aid of pounces or stencils; the LACMA depiction seems to have been made with the identical pounced drawing as a sketch in the Louvre, which was likewise mounted as an album page.
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.method_for_datation: While there are no dated works in the “saz style” an album presented to Murad III (Heigra 982-1003 / AD 1574-95) in Hegira 980 / AD 1572-72, now in Vienna, Austrian National Library (Codex Mixtus 313) includes works that closely parallel the drawing in terms of subject and style.
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.method_for_provenance: The calligraphic structure of the drawing and the serrated edges of the leaves and bristly texture of the dragons’ hide are all typical of the Ottoman “saz style”.

351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.name: *Mosque of Sidi Bu Madyan, Tlemcen, Algeria*
351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.short_description: The mosque adjoins the shrine of Sidi Bu Madyan, a twelfth century holy-man, and was built by the Marinid dynasty in 1339. Fabrizi's view shows clearly the richly carved stucco decoration framing the simple horseshoe arches; through one of these is seen the tiled mihrab (niche indicating the direction of Mecca) and the wooden minbar (pulpit). Fabrizi has captured the moment after the formal prayers when each worshipper makes a personal supplication to Allah, holding his hands out in a gesture to receive His blessing.

keywords: Orientalism

35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.name: *Woman In Oriental Dress*
35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.short_description: In order to evoke and convey the spirit of the Balkans and the Orient as faithfully as possible, Paja Jovanović meticulously recorded each detail of the interior of a typical Balkan or Eastern house. He also collected props that made up a family’s inventory of furniture (e.g. the hexagonal decorative table to the left), and carefully studied the physiognomies and characters of the men and women he encountered in the southern Balkans, in Egypt, Constantinople, the Caucasus and elsewhere. The precision of draughtsmanship and freshness of colour in this painting by Paja Jovanović ranks it among his more successful works from the mid-1880s.

keywords: Orientalism

35836245-6e1f-5582-81e3-6a2e34a2f528.name: *St. John the Baptist*
35836245-6e1f-5582-81e3-6a2e34a2f528.description:
This painting is one of the last undertaken by Caravaggio, during his second stay in Naples in 1610. The canvas shows an adolescent John the Baptist, a subject particularly dear to the troubled artist, who treated it on several occasions. In addition to the theme of solitude, the minister, who lived and died preparing for the coming of Christ, personifies sacrifice, symbolised by the ram and the bright red cape. Light brings out shape and detail from the brown background: the boy's body and the animal's fleece. According to the historiography, this piece and two others (*Magdalene* and *St.* *John the Baptist at the Fountain*) were intended as gifts for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, following his intercession with his uncle Pope Paul V.  
Having been condemned to death in Rome following the murder of Ranuccio Tomassoni in 1606, the artist left Rome taking refuge in Naples with the help of his patron Costanza Colonna Marquis of Caravaggio. In 1610, returning to Rome in the hope of a pardon, he stopped in Palo (a small port to the north of the city) and, probably due to a case of mistaken identity, he was imprisoned for two days. Having secured his freedom, he realised that he had lost all of his baggage, which had been sent back to the Parthenopean city. In a desperate attempt to recover it, Caravaggio died, possibly of malaria, on a beach near Port'Ercole in July 1610. Being notified of the event, and evidently aware of the gift of three paintings, Cardinal Scipione took immediate action to secure them, demonstrating the high esteem in which he held Merisi's work. Nonetheless, the cardinal only managed to recover one of the three works (*St. John*). It was initially housed in the family's city residence in Campus Martius.
35836245-6e1f-5582-81e3-6a2e34a2f528.short_description: Caravaggio was bringing this painting back from Naples to Rome as a gift for Cardinal Scipione Borghese. He was most probably stopped at Palo (Lazio) owing to mistaken identity and the artwork came into Borghese’s collection only after the death of the artist in July 1610. The theme of St. John was particularly dear to the artist, who recognised himself in this Saint because, like him, he felt the need to isolate himself from reality.
35836245-6e1f-5582-81e3-6a2e34a2f528.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

3583d624-13fa-58e9-9d82-9ef1b2d476f5.name: *Beethoven at the Palace*
3583d624-13fa-58e9-9d82-9ef1b2d476f5.short_description: Caliph Abdulmecid was interested in art in addition to administration. He opened many art exhibitions. He was chosen as honorary president of the Society of Ottoman Painters, which was founded in 1909, and he gave considerable financial support to the monthly journal published by the society. He took part in the Galatasaray Art Exhibitions with his paintings. For example, one of his paintings was accepted for an exhibition held at Galatasaray during the first years of the First World War. His works reveal him as a colourist and an accomplished portrait painter. Caliph Abdulmecid showed his paintings at the Viyana Exhibition, which was the first exhibition opened by Turkish painters in Europe in 1918.

35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.name: The Archangel Gabriel
35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.description: This icon depicts the Archangel Gabriel turned to the left, indicating that it comes from the Deesis tier of an iconostasis. He wears the *alb* (tunic) of a deacon and the liturgical coat of a bishop. In his right hand, he holds a sphere of light and in his left hand, a rod. The Archangel Gabriel, whose name means “man of God” in Hebrew, has been called the leader of the heavenly hosts. He is associated with numerous biblical events, including the announcements of the births of Mary and John the Baptist, and most importantly, the Annunciation, in which Gabriel proclaimed to the Virgin Mary that she would conceive and bear a son named Jesus.
35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2010. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.

35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.name: *A Ferry Crossing the Gagos River*
35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.short_description:
This is one of the both unnecessary and revolutionary illustrations in Abdallah ibn al-Fadl’s copy of Dioscorides’s medical treatise.  
The text states that on the shores of the Gagos River, jet can be found effective against pain in the uterus, but the artist took the opportunity to depict a ferry with a helmsman, two rowers, and eight passengers looking out of a porthole.
35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.type: Miniature from a copy of *Kitab al-hashaish*, a translation of Dioscorides’s *De Materia Medica*, scientific manuscript, miniature

3603d007-07c7-5d43-ad14-c40d81e1d215.name: A Sinner’s Plea to God

3603d007-07c7-5d43-ad14-c40d81e1d215.description: Marked as page 177 in the manuscript, this is the 12th and final painting to appear in the Bustan. It depicts group of sages in the wilderness: two debating over books, one praying alone, and one washing in a stream. Below the painting is an inscription in red naming the painter Hiranand, who was assigned by the workshop master to complete this illustration.

364e700b-5360-57b0-8f8c-45b5b51896ba.name: *Lot and His Daughters*
364e700b-5360-57b0-8f8c-45b5b51896ba.description:
The subject of the painting is covered in the Old Testament (Genesis, 19, 30–38), telling the story of Lot fleeing the destruction of the town of Sodom with his family. Alone in a cave with his two daughters, they give Lot wine for two successive nights and in his drunkenness he does not realise that he lies first with one and then the other, thus guaranteeing the continuation of his line.  
The canvas is part of a series of works used as *supraporte* (“over-door”) in the Borghese's city residence in Campo Marzio. The painting, executed by Guerrieri between 1617 and 1618, was commissioned by Marcantonio, a relative of Cardinal Scipione.  
The work was long thought to be by Gerrit van Hontorst, and highlights the importance of northern painting for Guerrieri, although he was also strongly influenced by Caravaggesque light. The oil lamp, which appears in the bottom left-hand corner, brightening the nocturnal ambience of the episode and illuminating the faces of the three protagonists, highlights the headdresses and jewels of the two maidens. Again the contrast between light and dark reveals the evident movement of the hands of the three figures, demonstrating that the artist was open to innovation, anticipating by a short time the great period of candlelight art. This latter is linked to the artistic trend deriving from the luminism of Caravaggio and Bassano, whose paintings were already in Cardinal Scipione's collection at that time. The handle of the valuable jug used by the maiden to pour the wine is engraved with a dragon, which along with the eagle, are the heraldic beasts of the Borghese.
364e700b-5360-57b0-8f8c-45b5b51896ba.short_description: The humble yet monumental language of Caravaggio influenced Guerrieri. The elegance of the young woman’s clothes contrasts with Loth’s sober, brown mantle. The painter also took an interest in how his contemporaries in Rome used light. The canvas was probably commissioned by Marcantonio Borghese.
364e700b-5360-57b0-8f8c-45b5b51896ba.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

366838a9-73be-5d88-a818-531e4ee3e0d0.name: Genealogical chart of Jahangir
366838a9-73be-5d88-a818-531e4ee3e0d0.short_description: This is a painted genealogy of selected male figures from the house of Jahangir, the fourth emperor of Mughal India (r. 1605–1627). For the Mughals, history and genealogy played an important role in establishing their legitimacy to rule, as well as their prestigious pedigree and culture. In the portraits, Jahangir and his descendants display similar idealized facial features, robes and turbans, adorned with rich fabrics and precious jewellery, as if adhering to a specific dynastic standard.

3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.name: *L’escalier des lions* (painting)
3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.short_description: This important painting depicts the official entrance of the Palais du Bardo as it was originally, with the *escalier des lions* and Mohamed Sadok Bey exiting the palace in official uniform, accompanied by Tunisian dignitaries, preceded by protocol officers and surrounded by the beylical guard. It shows the monumental *escalier des lions* with its archways and columns on the façade. We can also see its glorious white marble columns, capitals and ceramic panels decorating the walls and mounted on plaster and stucco (*naqsh hadida*). Through the entrance doors the black and white archways in an Andalusian style can be seen on the first floor.

370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.name: *Feast of St. Anthony of Padua*
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.description:
The subject is a relatively scarcely represented scene from the life of St. Anthony of Padua, priest, preacher and disciple of St. Francis of Assisi. The Franciscan saint sits at the table in the house of a wealthy man, blessing goblets of wine. On the left, a *putto* brings a lily, symbol of purity and one of the saint's attributes. On the right, precious tableware is displayed, as was customary at feasts from the 16th century onwards. Although the scene is illuminated at the centre, the picture features two pictorial sections: the left symbolising austerity and humbleness and the right, luxury and superiority. The artist also draws attention to the two sections by use of character types: the face of St. Anthony with his halo reflecting spiritual delight, while the gross face of the rich man shows sensual pleasure, greed and a boorish approach to the situation. The listening man on the right points out his gluttony, one of the seven deadly sins. The painter highlights the scene with a contrasting motif of deep-red drapery, which sets the colour tone for the whole picture. The painting stands out among Kracker's altarpieces and ceiling frescos because of its genre-painting atmosphere and use of chiaroscuro. It also manifests the artist's bold monogram *JK*, but not as distinctively as on some of his more sizeable compositions.  
The picture was part of the decoration of the refectory in the Franciscan Monastery in Moravská Třebová, together with *The Feast of the Holy Family* and *The Feast of St. Wenceslas*.  
Kracker was a leading exponent of the Vienna Academy style represented by Paul Troger and Michelangelo Unterberger. After studying in Vienna Kracker was active in the workshop of Josef Tadeáš Rotter in Brno, and later settled in Znojmo. His best-known works include ceiling paintings and altarpieces in the Church of St. Nicholas in Prague and in Nová Říše. His later work was associated with Hungary, where he joined the service of Bishop K. Esterházy in Jager.
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.short_description: The subject is a relatively scarcely represented scene from the life of St. Anthony of Padua. The canvas formed part of the decoration in the refectory of the Franciscan Monastery in Moravská Třebová. It is an early piece by the artist, J. L. Kracker who was active in Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary.

37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.name: *Rustam at the Fort near Mount Sepand* (folio from a *Shahnama* manuscript)
37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.short_description: A folio from the manuscript of the *Shahnama* (Book of Kings) epic poem by Ferdowsi tells the story of Rustam's military campaign to Mount Sepand to destroy the impregnable fortress city. The painting illustrates an episode when Rustam and his army approached the walls of a fortress. The warriors resorted to treachery, pretending to be salt merchants. The fortress guards believed the “merchants” and opened the gates to them. According to the content of the episode, Rustam is portrayed as a merchant, without his traditional attributes of a hero: tiger skin, helmet and weapons. Shabby figures of people, types of their headdresses and Chinese-style clouds may suggest the painter’s affiliation with a Shiraz school of miniature.

3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.name:
The constellations Andromeda and Pisces  
Folio from a dispersed *Kitab Suwar al-Kawakib* (Images of the Fixed Stars)
3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.short_description: The lady in this saffron-coloured robe and crown-like helmet is a personification of the constellation Andromeda, which was identified by the second-century CE astronomer Ptolemy and continues to be considered a major constellation. With the translation of Ptolemy’s *Almagest* in the court of the ninth-century Caliph al-Ma’mun in Baghdad, astronomers working under the patronage of the Muslim rulers in modern-day Iraq and Iran adopted the Greco-Roman astronomical knowledge and expanded on it from the indigenous Arab (*Anwa’*) and Indian astronomical traditions, in this illustration combining Andromeda with Pisces. The most prominent example of this tradition is 'Images of the Fixed Stars' written by the Iranian astronomer ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi (died 986), which contained two representations of each constellation, one looking up at the constellation from Earth and the other looking down on it from above. Al-Sufi’s work continued to be in broad circulation, and various copies exist in major museum collections.

keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; figure; female-figure; constellations; science; space; astronomy; astronomical; stars

38745087-0b6a-5699-94f5-57d4e4dbd0f8.name: *Idolaters Before an Idol*
38745087-0b6a-5699-94f5-57d4e4dbd0f8.short_description: A *Fal-nama* is a kind of book of divination that can be consulted at random. Opposite each painting in an explanatory text. The text for the museum’s stylistically very unusual painting is found in the Los Angeles County Museum and explains that the scene is enacted in the “Azure monastery.” The omens associated with the miniature are highly inauspicious.

387a8cd6-9d72-5dac-9a2c-95552d3ac478.name: *The Adoration of the Shepherds*
387a8cd6-9d72-5dac-9a2c-95552d3ac478.description:
This painting was executed by the Neapolitan painter during his stay in Bologna, for the Chartusian church of San Gerolamo. It is part of a series of eight, commissioned to different local painters, narrating episodes of the life of Christ.  
There is a strong naturalism inspired by Caravaggio and Ribera, but combined with the features of Neapolitan baroque such as dynamic movement, vivid colours, quick brush strokes and a lively composition. Nunzio Rossi shows some of the characters of the art in Naples around 1630–1650, when the local masters were working together with famous foreigners such as Van Dyck and Rubens. A touch of the style of Guido Reni, an artist that Rossi met while working in Bologna, is evident in the group of the Madonna with Child, reminiscent two pictures of the same subject (Naples, the Chartreuse, and Feldsberg castle), painted by Reni when the young Neapolitan came to Bologna.  
The focal centre of the composition is Madonna adoring the Child. Surrounding them are the shepherds and peasants with their animals and humble presents for the new born baby. The upper part of the painting is full of lively singing angels.
387a8cd6-9d72-5dac-9a2c-95552d3ac478.short_description: This painting was painted in Bologna for the Carthusian church of San Gerolamo. The strong colours and swift movements are indebted to the city of Naples with its paintings by foreign artists like Rubens and Van Dick and those by the member of the local school. In the Madonna with Child, note the influence of Guido Reni, the master of Rossi during his stay in Bologna.

3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.name: Moods: Those Who Go
3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.short_description: Umberto Bocccioni moved to Rome in 1901 where he was interested in painting, journalism and literature. Through his friendship with Severini, Boccioni attended Balla’s atelier and, at the same time, the school of nude of the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome. In 1907 he moved to Milan and met Previati and Marinetti, who wrote the Manifest of Futurism. In 1910 he signed the Manifest of Futurist Painters, in 1912 he signed the Manifest of Futurist Sculpture. His studies of Munch and Previati influenced the cycle called Moods. He starts doing numerous preparatory studies for the triptych: *Farewell, Those Who Go, Those Who Stay*; in which he set a correspondence between, colours, lines and feelings, moods. The painting is one of the studies for the series *Those Who Go* that belong to the first of two trilogies about Moods created in 1911, before the artist moved to Paris.

39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.description:
This set of 12 icons, the only one of its kind in the United States, is believed to be from the Pskov region of Russia. The icons were originally hung on the festival tier of an iconostasis, the partition separating the nave from the sanctuary of an Orthodox church. The festival tier highlights the major holidays of the Orthodox liturgical calendar. This set includes the following images:  
  
1\. The Meeting of Anna and Joachim  
2\. The Nativity of the Virgin Mary  
3\. The Nativity of Christ  
4\. The Presentation of Christ  
5\. The Transfiguration  
6\. The Raising of Lazarus  
7\. The Crucifixion  
8\. The Three Marys at the Sepulchre  
9\. The Descent  
10\. The Ascension of Christ  
11\. The Holy Trinity  
12\. The Feast of Pentecost

3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.name: *The Seven Saints Founders of the Servite Order*
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.description:
The whole series consisted of ten oval pictures. Two smaller paintings which were hanging near the apse, were lost at the end of the eighteenth-century, when the high chapel was refurbished. They were originally in the church of the Servites in Budrio, a small town near Bologna.  
The seven saints which are the founders of the Servite order are represented in three-quarters and move with eloquent gestures. In the background are depicted episodes of their lives and the saints’ attributes.  
Antonio Gionima, born in Venice, was one of the favourite pupils of Giuseppe Maria Crespi. The art historian Luigi Crespi praises his simple and free style and the freshness of his palette. His main features are quick brush strokes, the use of light and rich colours. He worked for a long time for the Servites of Bologna as well. For them he painted a similar series of portraits which were unfortunately lost. He died of tuberculosis when he was 35 years old.
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.short_description: The eight oval pictures decorating the nave of the church of San Lorenzo in Budrio represent the founders’ saints of the Servite order. They were made by the Venetian painter Antonio Gionima, one of the favourite pupils of Giuseppe Maria Crespi. In Bologna he developed a personal style, mixing his master’s features with a sort of expressive movement possibly derived from Aureliano Milani.
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.method_for_datation: The Servite fathers of Budrio decided to order ten oval pictures to hang over the arches of the chapels. The prior of the convent was Giovanni Antonio Cavalli (1719-1720), and the State Archive of Bologna still retains the receipt of payment signed by Antonio Gionima, dated 29th December 1720.
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.obtention: Moved from the church of the Servite fathers to the church of San Lorenzo.

3b8f26e5-b410-5ae8-b48c-3504c0b4eefd.short_description: An oil painting from the Qajar epoch depicts the Virgin Mary with a crown of stars standing on the crescent moon. These are not simply copied, but are always adapted to their own religious and artistic concepts. Mary is the only woman mentioned by name in the Qur'an. Sura 19 carries her name.

3bb6eb2b-6679-54ad-a0be-56e5b6e51786.name: Persian miniature mounted as album leaf
3bb6eb2b-6679-54ad-a0be-56e5b6e51786.alternate_name: Shah ʿAbbas receiving an Indian ambassador
3bb6eb2b-6679-54ad-a0be-56e5b6e51786.short_description:
Dated Hegira 1065 (AD 1654/55), the painting commemorates a meeting between Shah ʿAbbas I (r. Hegira 996 - 1038 / AD 1587-1629) and an Indian ambassador in 1618. We know that later in this year the Safavid ruler received both the envoy Khan ʿAlam of the Mughal ruler Jahangir (r. Hegira 1014-1037 / AD 1605-1627) and that of Sultan Muhammad Qutb Shah of Golconda (r. Hegira 1020-1035 / AD 1612-1626), a principality in the Deccan.  
  
Shaykh ʿAbbasi based his composition, of which three other contemporary versions are known, on one of Bishandasʼs work (or one of the numerous copies). Bishandas accompanied the embassy and portrayed the shah and the ambassador together with their entourage seated in a forest clearing. Since Shah ʿAbbas II (r. Hegira 1052-1077 / AC 1642-1666) sent an ambassador to Golkonda in the year 1065 (1654/55), it cannot be ruled out that Shaykh ʿAbbasʼs miniature painting was intended as a diplomatic gift. If this assumption is correct, it must be a posthumous rendition of the meeting between ʿAbbas I and the ambassador from Golconda.  
  
In Shaykh ʿAbbasisʼs oeuvre, references to India play a prominent role. Almost half of his works depict Indian men or women. It can also be shown that he took up motifs from Indian iconography and was even familiar with Deccani painting techniques.

3c16e6a6-882d-588d-8f9d-b0309a8c41db.name: *The Empress' boulevard*
3c16e6a6-882d-588d-8f9d-b0309a8c41db.short_description: Painted in 1865, this canvas was one of many the artist created depicting "the new boulevard of Algiers". This boulevard, built by the opera house where Saint-Saëns was performing at the time, was the architect Frédéric Chassériau's (the painter's uncle) first significant work. It was inaugurated in 1839 by Napoléon III and the Empress Eugénie, after whom it it was named, and marked the beginning of Algiers' new, European-style urbanisation programme, which affected both the city and its surroundings. Although these changes did bring the city's inhabitants a number of comforts, they also resulted in the irrevocable destruction of a number of very important monuments from the Ottoman era.
3c16e6a6-882d-588d-8f9d-b0309a8c41db.author: Dalila Orfali

3c3428ad-e6d9-50dc-93c0-7e7ab1c900d2.name: *An Elephant*; *An indian Ox*; *An Antelope*
3c3428ad-e6d9-50dc-93c0-7e7ab1c900d2.short_description: In 1891 Filippo Palizzi donated more than 300 paintings to the National Gallery of Modern Art of Rome in order to describe his entire career through his artworks. All of them are cited in the Chronological List of 1853, which includes 12 studies depicting exotic animals done in The Jardin des Plantes in Paris. The series is considered the preparatory base for the amazing painting *Dopo il Diluvio. Uscita degli animali dall’Arca* (*After the Flood. The Animals Exiting the Ark*), commissioned by King Vittorio Emanuele II for the Museum of Capodimonte and presented in 1867 at the Universal Exposition in Paris. Other animals, like the Indian ox, the antelope and the dromedary were depicted in the Jardin des Plantes in Paris with the same aim.

3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.name: *Visitation*
3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.description:
After studying locally in Langenargen, Maulbertsch went to Vienna where he was a pupil of Peter van Roy at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and where, in 1750, he won first prize in the academic painting competition. In 1758, he became an ordinary member of the Academy and was later a counsellor. Although both his home and workshop were in Vienna, his activities covered the entire Habsburg empire extending beyond its boundaries. Primarily a fresco painter, he was constantly overburdened with commissions from churches and secular patrons. His oeuvre includes several altarpieces, sketches and panel paintings, historical-mythological pictures, genre paintings and portraits, but also graphic works and etchings. In the course of his rich career, he traced a great arch of development from Late Baroque through Rococo to Neo-Classicism. He died in Vienna on 8 August 1796, while preparing his last great work, the fresco for Szombathely Cathedral.  
János Szily, the Bishop of the newly founded Szombathely diocese, commissioned Maulbertsch to decorate the salon of his personal residence in 1782. Almost 10 years later in 1791, he turned to Maulbertsch again for the altarpieces of Szombathely Cathedral. For the high altar, the Bishop ordered a picture representing the Visitation of Mary by Elizabeth, on the side altars the patron saints of Szombathely, St. Martin and St. Quirinus. In accordance with the pictorial practice at the time, the painter made some sketches which reflected his employer's requests and concepts, and sent them to Szombathely for approval. Some of these sketches have survived. The composition of the Pannonhalma sketch shows differences from the final version. On the altarpiece – executed in 1792 and gravely damaged during the World War II – Mary stands on the left, while in this sketch she stands on the right at the top of a stairway. Maulbertsch mentioned this modification in a letter he wrote to Bishop Szily in April 1792.
3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.short_description: Maulbertsch's later works clearly show the influence of Neo-Classicism, as seen here and in several other of the painter's major works in Hungary (for example in Vác, Győr, Pozsony (Bratislava), Pápa, Eger and Szombathely). This sketch is a version of the recently restored, large-size, Szombathely High Altar painting, which was torn to pieces at the end of the Second World War.
3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.provenance: Commissioned by János Szily, Bishop of Szombathely

3c658c98-f2f0-52eb-abb1-a1e480cb3390.name: A composite elephant with rider and groom
3c658c98-f2f0-52eb-abb1-a1e480cb3390.short_description: The origins of composite animals may date back to early Buddhist manuscripts of Central Asia. Later, they were introduced into Persian painting and subsequently became infused with the artistic essence of Northern and Central India in the sixteenth century. Such images prominently depict humans, real and whimsical animals, *divs* (demons) or angels, combined into mosaics of intertwined yet recognized animals such as horses, camels, and oxen. In Hindu tradition, such compositions may have represented the mystical doctrine of the internal unity of all beings. Other interpretations suggest the sovereignty of the heavens over the natural world, mirroring the power of a king over his realm and its people.

3ccbbb1a-eca6-5ee7-becd-0a2da22c8309.name:
Gushtasp slays the dragon of mount Saqila  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
3ccbbb1a-eca6-5ee7-becd-0a2da22c8309.short_description: Completed in 1010, Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) recounts the history of all of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam. It inspired countless works of art, including the masterful *Shahnameh* produced for Shah Tahmasp (r. 1524–76), the second shah of the Safavid dynasty. This folio AKM163 (folio 402 recto) from the Shah Tahmasp *Shahnameh* highlights the exceptional bravery and strength of Gushtasp, son of Shah Luhrasp.

3e51e99d-8ff0-545e-95fc-52a15be8b042.name: *A Coffee House in Tophane*
3e51e99d-8ff0-545e-95fc-52a15be8b042.short_description: A Thomas Allom composition which appears in the first volume of Robert Walsh’s book *Constantinople and Scenery of Seven Churches of Asia Minor* is *The Coffee-House*. This is an oil copy of the composition by Civanyan. Written by Robert Walsh, who served as the private priest of British ambassador Lord Strangford after 1820, the book was published in two volumes in London in 1838. It includes engravings and the book, which was later published in French, acted as an important visual resource on Istanbul and its engravings were used as models by numerous artists. In the corresponding text, Robert Walsh provides information on the interior organisation and decoration of the coffeehouse and relates various details ranging from making music and smoking pipes to the plays of the *meddah* (storytellers).

3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.name:
The rocky lotus: Sumulutun  
Folio from the manuscript of *Khawass al-Ashjar* (The Characteristics of Trees)
3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.short_description:
Born around 40 AD in Anazarbus in Cilicia (today’s Turkey), Dioscorides exerted a great influence on scholarship and practice from the Middle Ages until the 16th century. His treatise *De Materia Medica* was first translated into Syriac, a language generally familiar to physicians in the Abbasid empire (750–1258).\[1\] The earliest Arabic translation directly translated from a Greek copy\[2\] was made by two scholars, Istafan ibn Basil and Hunayn ibn Ishaq, in the mid 9th century in Baghdad under the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil (r. 847–61).1 Ibn Ishaq was a physician, Arab scientist, and Nestorian Christian. Known as the “master of translators,” he was active in the Bayt al-Hikm (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad.  
According to sources, in 948, Byzantine Emperor Romanus I offered a Greek copy of *De Materia Medica* as a gift to the Umayyad caliph of Cordoba, ‘Abd al-Rahman III (912-961). There is no evidence to suggest a full Arabic translation of this copy was ever made in Cordoba.\[3\] In the intervening years, both the Greek text and accompanying illustrations continued to undergo revision as new copies were made.  
A famous Arabic copy made in the first quarter of the 13th century was widely recopied and distributed and is now dispersed throughout many private and public collections, including the Aga Khan Museum Collection. Known as the Khawass al-Ashjar, it describes the fabrication of medicines from some 500-600 plants; animals, like fish and shellfish; and minerals that serve as the basis for pharmacology in Near Eastern countries and beyond.

3fa7c158-f2ad-5e29-985d-61f528ba2a1e.name: *The Rape of Helen*
3fa7c158-f2ad-5e29-985d-61f528ba2a1e.description:
Paris's kidnap of Helen, the beautiful wife of the king of Sparta, opens Homer's *Iliad*, an epic of the Trojan War. For artists, it provided a frequent source of moral, historical and entertaining scenes from the renaissance onwards.  
The drama of the event that led to the destruction of Troy is conveyed in detailed rendering of multiple figures moving through the picture area. Brutal, gory scenes are omitted; the artist presents the event as a theatrical spectacle. The suspense of the scene is enhanced by the presence of the elements: the wind blowing the flags, Helen's vermilion-red attire and pushing the sails of fleeing ships, and the sea. The ancient architecture of the harbour, with Tuscan columns and obelisks, was standard in the repertoire of 18th-century decorative painting. The warrior with erect shield on the left paraphrases Lysippus's “Borghese Warrior”, a staple object of study at art academies. The counterpart picture of *The Rape of Helen* was *The Rape of the Sabines*, a legend associated with the foundation of Rome and, according to Virgil, the continuation of Troy.  
Detailed narrative cabinet pictures with a host of figures are typical of the oeuvre of this academic Viennese painter who, together with Franz Janneck, specialised in the kind of decorative paintings favoured by art collectors. Inspired by Dutch 17th-century painting and, in particular, by Rudolphine mannerism, Platzer coined an original style, highlighting the sensory qualities of surfaces and things with scattered light and contrasting colours.

4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.name: *The Annunciation*
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.alternate_name: *La Madonna del Bell’Angelo* (*The Madonna with the Beautiful Angel*)
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.description:
This altarpiece was originally commissioned for the Fioravanti chapel in the former St. Bartholomew church. It was inaugurated in 1632. In 1647 the Barnabites fathers commissioned the same painter to complete two smaller side paintings with episodes of the life of the Virgin (the *Adoration of the Child* and the *Dream of St. Joseph*) and asked for some retouches to the *Annunciation*. In 1685 the church was inaugurated and the three pictures were moved to the fourth chapel in the right side aisle, where they remain today.  
The altarpiece soon became renown as the *Madonna del Bell'Angelo* (the Madonna with the beautiful angel) for the beauty of the announcing angel.  
Albani builds the picture by juxtaposing the standing Madonna, nearly indifferent to the annunciation, against the Angel that is bursting from the dark closed room with luminous shades of yellow. Following the angel, a cloud of cherubs and putti rolls from heaven in a chaotic but lively invasion. The picture mixes the naturalistic lesson of the Carraccis with the round lines and the vivacious movement of full Baroque style.
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.short_description: This painting was made by Francesco Albani, one of the pupils of the celebrated Carraccis. These three cousins strongly contributed to the Baroque revolution in Bologna and throughout Europe. Albani is a very pleasant painter. He tells the story of the *Annunciation* in a captivating way, showing the Madonna as a princess full of grace and self-control and the heavenly court bursting with enthusiastic life.

4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.obtention: The object is still preserved in the original location.

436f4699-37fd-544f-bb71-8f51ac527b09.name: Beatrice elevated by love
436f4699-37fd-544f-bb71-8f51ac527b09.short_description:
Alexandre Cingria made this stained glass window, with a counterpart, for the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes held in Paris from April to October 1925.  
  
This leaded stained glass window depicts Love (angel) carrying Beatrice. Love, represented in the foreground with eyes closed, holds Beatrice by her left ankle and her head. The woman, lying down, draped in dark green and red, wears a bracelet on each wrist. On either side, a bluish figure observes the scene. In the centre below the figures there is an inscription engraved in grisaille “Amore/e'l cor gentil/ sono una Cosa”, taken from a sonnet by Dante Alighieri. To the right of the inscription are the artist’s signature and his monogram. The scene is distributed on seven panels (a central rhombus, two lateral triangles and four quadrilaterals) inserted in a metal frame, with supports for stabilisation.
