65d47d8e-ddfc-5e73-9b72-7398f5e3072b.name: Amorous couple observed by a wet nurse
65d47d8e-ddfc-5e73-9b72-7398f5e3072b.short_description:
The brush drawing of a pair of lovers in close embrace is by Muʿin Musavvir, one of the most famous and prolific Iranian painters of the 17th century. Young amorous couples were a fairly popular subject in his time and they exist in countless variations. The present version is erotically charged, portraying a young Georgian man (distinguished by his fur cap) embracing a young Persian woman. Self-confident, she stops the demanding gesture of his left hand. Further dating evidence is provided by the swelling calligraphic line, characteristic of 17th century drawings. About a dozen brush drawings by Muʿin are known to exist; quite often, they show a similar palette consisting of red, green and ochre in addition to black ink  
  
Muʿin is known for his rather conservative style, remaining true, during his entire 60 year career, to the style established by Riza ʿAbbasi at the beginning of the 17th century. Therefore, Europeanising motifs are very rare in his oeuvre. However, in this piece he not only integrated a set piece probably stemming from European portraits and prints - the symmetrically divided and high-bound curtain - but also an old woman peering in through the door. The theme of the uninvited observer was to enjoy great popularity in Iran, especially in the 19th century, making it one of the earliest representations of this specific iconography.

66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.name: *St. Mary Magdalene*
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.description:
The altarpiece has a semi-circular top edge and shows the figure of St. Mary Magdalene placed in a shallow diagonal in the mid-ground behind step-like stone blocks. She is wearing a dress with long, wide, slightly flattened and relaxed folds and with her head thrown back, she is casting a repentant look at the sky, her hands around a large Crucifix. The scene, which takes place in a forest with a cave, has Mary Magdalene kneeling upon and leaning against natural stone blocks. Her other attributes are a whip with five lashes, a pot of ointment, a skull and an open book. The colours are muted and in many places dark, with an accent of light only on Magdalene's breast, face and hands and on the two angels' heads that peep from the cloud above the rounded cave opening.  
*St. Mary Magdalene,* commissioned by the boot-makers' guild to hang above an altarpiece in St. Mary's Church in Zagreb, was the work of Anton Cebej, who besides Valentin Metzinger, Franjo Ilovšek and Fortunato Bergant was one of the most respected Slovenian painters of the time. Three years later, in 1773, the cobblers' guild commissioned a painting from him for an altarpiece, which depicts the Death of St. Joseph.  
Cebej was particularly distinguished in religious compositions and portraits, and among his contemporaries, his style is closest to the Italian model. The professional crafts guilds of the same or different professions had a very strong humanitarian and religious component, and to express their religious obligations some guilds had their own altars of which they took permanent care, such as the guilds of Zagreb's Gradec already mentioned.  
Removed during renovation of the church, the altars and paintings became the property of collector Solomon Berger, founder of the Ethnographic Museum in Zagreb. The Museum of Arts and Crafts on several occasions bought or was donated pieces from his collection.
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.short_description: *St. Mary Magdalene,* commissioned by the boot-makers' guild to hang above an altarpiece they had also commissioned for St. Mary's in Zagreb, was painted by Anton Cebej, one of the most influential Slovenian painters of his time, distinguished in religious compositions and portraits. Among his contemporaries, Cebej's style is closest to the Italian model.
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.initial_owner: The painting hung above the altarpiece in St. Mary’s Church, Zagreb until 1908.
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.method_for_datation: In the bottom right-hand corner, on the edge of the open page of the book is the signature “17 Antonius Zebey F.70.”

66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.name: *Zubdat al-Tawarikh* (‘Cream of Histories’).
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.description:
The work is written in Turkish with large *naskhi* script in black ink on 90 leaves of delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper. Within are 55 miniatures depicting subjects in the text, some of them one to a page and some two. On pages 1b–2a two round medallions carry an inscription stating the work's subject and saying that it was prepared for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95). The text is written 37 lines to a page; the titles and chapter headings are gilded. Their illumination features floral compositions with arabesques (*rumi*) and Chinese-inspired motifs (*hatayi*-style), while that of the first two pages' medallions includes large floral motifs (*halkar*\-style).  
  
The work's dark-green cover is lacquered using a technique known as *Edirnekari*. The outer covers are richly decorated with gold and silver in floral compositions, while the inner covers feature medallions, pendants and corner-pieces. The binding is not original.  
  
The work, which was written by the court panegyrist (*Şehnameci*) Sayyid Loqman Aşuri, consists of two main sections. The first begins with the universe and the signs of the zodiac and continues with stories taken from the Torah, the New Testament, and the Qur'an which tell of the lives of prophets and those who rendered service to the faith. These are illustrated with paintings. The first part ends with genealogical trees of the Prophet Muhammad, the Four Orthodox Caliphs, and the sultans and high officials of Muslim dynasties such as the Umayyads, the 'Abbasids, the early Islamic period, the Ghaznawids, the Ilkhanids, the Seljuqs and the Timurids. The second part opens with Sultan Osman, the founder of the Ottoman dynasty, and goes up to Sultan Murad III, with 12 portraits of Ottoman sultans. It ends with descriptions of the political events of these sultans' reigns.  
  
This work was made for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III, and the quality of its paintings, its binding and its calligraphy make it one of the greatest works of Ottoman art created for a sultan.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.short_description: This manuscript includes stories of the prophets, the birth of Islam and histories of Muslim states. It was written on the order of Sultan Murad III by the historian Sayyid Lokman and illuminated by famous *naqqash* (painters) Molla Kasım and Ustad Osman. It is a unique work of Ottoman art.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.type: Manuscript, miniature, paper, ink, leather binding, lacquered

66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.method_for_provenance: The work was almost certainly written in Istanbul by order of the Sultan.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.obtention: Transferred to the Museum in 1915 from the Library of the complex in Aksaray (Istanbul) founded by the wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdülaziz ('Abd al-'Aziz) I, Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. 1300 / 1883; queen mother from 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).

6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.name:
Isfandiyar’s second exploit: he kills two lions  
Folio from a dispersed copy of Firdausi’s *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.short_description: Recounting the story of Iran from mythical times through to the arrival of the Muslim Arabs in the mid-7th century AD, the epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) was originally completed in 1010 by the poet Firdausi. These dramatic scenes centering on Isfandiyar, son of King Gushtasp, were included in a 1341 Shahnameh that is now dispersed. The story of Isfandiyar’s exploits recalls the seven trials that the great hero Rustam underwent in his quest to liberate King Kay Kavus from captivity in a much earlier Shahnameh story. Isfandiyar endured his labours en route to rescuing his two sisters, who were captured during the ongoing war between Iran and Turan. Isfandiyar decided to take the shortest but most dangerous route to the Brazen Hold, the Turanian fortress made of brass where his sisters were imprisoned.
6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

Tauris Publishers, 2000: 217­–47. ISBN: 9781850436591.
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; Shahnama; Shahnameh
materials: Ink, coloured pigments and gold on paper

69045a19-bb48-5ecd-b0f9-4fcd7a4df298.name: Pair of still lives
69045a19-bb48-5ecd-b0f9-4fcd7a4df298.description: This pair of paintings are from the collection of the Counts Calderini from Imola. In 1878, they were bequest to the municipality along with other works of art by Count Vincenzo. They were clearly pendants. On the table in the foreground fruit, flowers and dead birds are displayed.  This follows the still life style of German and Flemish tables as human traces are practically absent. These two pictures by Codino depict objects showing the social status of the owner such as the highly valuable ceramics alongside symbols which allude to the fragility of human things.   Flowers for example with their short life invite a meditation on time passing. Codino’s style strongly mimics reality, with an objective and clear filing of artificial and natural objects. The two works can be connected with the German still life school, namely to the production of Soreau and Peter Binoit, for the repeated repertory of objects and for the representation of the picture plane from a very near point of view.
69045a19-bb48-5ecd-b0f9-4fcd7a4df298.short_description: Both paintings come from the Calderini collection of Imola. They are stylistically close to the German school of still life painting. Things allusive to the fragility of life (the flowers bound to wither soon) and precious objects (ceramics) which show off the owners’ social status, are combined in these two works and painted in a highly quality style.
69045a19-bb48-5ecd-b0f9-4fcd7a4df298.method_for_datation: The name Francesco Codino (Italian translation from the German Franz Godin) and the date are inscribed on the lower left in the painting bearing inventory n. 59: “F.o C.[no] 16[31]”.
69045a19-bb48-5ecd-b0f9-4fcd7a4df298.obtention: Both pictures come as bequests from the collection of the Counts Calderini, from Imola.
69045a19-bb48-5ecd-b0f9-4fcd7a4df298.bibliography: Pedrini, C. *Catalogo della Pinacoteca di Imola*, Bologna, 1988, pp. 172-173.

696eb90a-0ce9-5dba-973b-b54eeda3a5ad.name: Miniature Folding Iconostasis
696eb90a-0ce9-5dba-973b-b54eeda3a5ad.description: Miniature and folding iconostases were used starting in the 16th century, both by priests who traveled to rural areas and domestically by the Russian people. These icons, which vary in size and composition, are scaled-down versions of the partitions found in an Orthodox church and were largely used as a way to bring faith into the home. This icon consists of 15 parts and depicts the Deesis, festival and prophet tiers. The Mother of God is pictured in the center of the top row, flanked by unidentified saints.
696eb90a-0ce9-5dba-973b-b54eeda3a5ad.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Simon Morsink, Amsterdam, in 2008. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.name: *Noah’s Ark*
69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.short_description:
Timur’s son Shah Rukh (r. AH 808-851 / AD 1405-1447) ordered the historian Hafiz-i Abru to write a continuation of Rashid al-Din’s famous history of the world, Jami al-tawarikh. Like the Il-Khanids, the Timurids were concerned with legitimizing their right to rule, and Hafiz-i Abru’s “A Collection of Histories” covers a period that included the time of Shah Rukh himself.  
  
The style of the manuscript’s miniatures is slightly old-fashioned compared with the otherwise refined Timurid painting, but the scene on the stormy sea is quite dramatic, with the fluttering sail, the ark breaking out of the picture frame and the swollen bodies. The animals that are to populate the earth are rendered both humorously and fairly realistically.
69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.type: Miniature from Hafiz-i Abru’s *Majma' al-tawarikh*, manuscript

6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.name: *King Béla III founding the Cistercian Monastery at Szentgotthárd in 1183*
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.description:
Originally, the painting hung in the abbot's reception hall in the Cistercian Monastery of Szentgotthárd, as one of a representative series of six *panneaux*. The six paintings perpetuate important events in the history of the Szentgotthárd Abbey as well as two moments of Hungarian history – the battles of Mohács and Szentgotthárd – believed by many to have had a direct influence on the fate of the abbey. The large canvases covered the walls of the room like wall hangings, with the uncovered sections of wall painted with landscapes to complete the historical compositions. Both the *panneaux* and ceiling decoration are by István Dorffmaister, and were commissioned by Abbot Marian Reutter. The programme follows the work of the scholarly Cistercian monk, Theophil Heimb's history of the Szentgotthárd Abbey, published in 1764. The book contains detailed accounts of events that are faithfully translated into visual images by Dorffmaister. The main episodes from the history of the Cistercian order in Hungary provided the theme for the series, beginning with the foundation of the order. It captures the moment the French monks were received by the king and his escorts – who are wearing colourful Hungarian costumes – in front of an antique *porticus*. In the background there is a distant view of 18th-century Pest-Buda with a few medieval details added. Behind the monks there is an imaginary view of the Romanesque Church and Abbey of Szentgotthárd. The pure forms, simple light effects and the light-coloured palette – the stylistic marks of the Late Baroque mixed with the elements of Neo-Classicism so appropriate at the end of the 18th century – suggest an optimistic view of history, which is a rarity in Hungarian art.  
While Dorffmaister's historical paintings were born in ecclesiastical surroundings and according to the traditional artist-patron relationship, they still bore fresh, modern meaning and became representative works of the new European tendencies of the era.
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.short_description: The *panneaux* series from Szentgotthárd depicts Hungarian historical subjects; one section of it is kept in Heiligenkreuz. The *panneaux* is a very special Neo-Classical series of paintings, in this one a *veduta* of Buda Castle can be seen in the background.
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.method_for_datation: One painting of the series is signed. Origin and date verified by historical documents.
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.obtention: Cistercian Monastery in Szentgotthárd transferred from the former Cistercian Monastery in Szentgotthárd. Transferred to the Museum of Fine Arts in 1950–51 where it remained until 1974 before being transferred to the Hungarian National Gallery.

6c0ec863-e0e7-5b08-9c07-4fe22fc9d7ae.name: *Oriental perfumes*
6c0ec863-e0e7-5b08-9c07-4fe22fc9d7ae.description: This advertisement shows that the influence of Orientalism was telegraphed to the public as a synonym for exotic places, buildings and dresses. This advertisement also could be related to the Russian ballets of Sergéi Diágilev.

6c64959a-ef24-5b36-b22d-27aafad34901.name: *Adam with Seth and his Family*
6c64959a-ef24-5b36-b22d-27aafad34901.short_description:
Painted on highest-quality mirror glass, this gold glass painting reproduces, in reverse, a print by Johann Sadelers I of a lost drawing by Maerten de Vos. It represents the rarely depicted scene in which the 130-year-old Adam brings home the harvest and is greeted by his third son, Seth, while Eve is preparing a meal with her children.  
  
The provenance of this reverse glass painting is verified by the signature of the artist, copper engraver and court glass painter Gerhard Janssen, who worked in Vienna.  
  
On several occasions, Janssen produced reverse glass paintings for Prince Karl Eusebius of Lichtenstein. The latter’s inventories show that Janssen not only made images on gold, but also in “blue with silver” on glass. He did not introduce the *eglomisé* technique to Vienna as a novelty as it was already known in the region of Bohemia and Austria around 1600 and prized by the nobility.
6c64959a-ef24-5b36-b22d-27aafad34901.obtention: Donated by Ruth und Frieder Ryser in 2006

6ce145a9-1c2f-50bf-a811-ee97df9fc4d0.name: Musical gathering
6ce145a9-1c2f-50bf-a811-ee97df9fc4d0.short_description: This colourful ensemble of musicians and entertainers illustrates the royal taste for music and dance in the Ottoman world, an interest shared with other Islamic and European courts. While single-page paintings had been introduced to the artist’s repertoire over a century before, the formation of the figures and the fact that they appear to direct their performance to an audience at their right suggests that this image formed one half of a double-page manuscript painting. Falling in line with earlier princely images depicted in Persian illustrated manuscripts, the audience would probably have consisted of a king and his attendants or courtly lovers enjoying a musical interlude in the country (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 42). Three women stand next to the musicians, dressed in peach- and crimson-coloured robes, while a fourth sits on her knees to play the *ektar*, a one-stringed lute. Meanwhile, a young boy sits to the left of the lute player and taps his tambourine to the music. The painting, once mounted on an album, retains part of a margin that was decorated in gold vegetal scrolls. While illustrated Ottoman manuscripts first tended to emphasize history and geography - sieges and battles and maps of conquered territories - this painting seems to fit into a later interest in the more peaceful aspects of courtly life. It probably dates to the early eighteenth century, during the reign of Sultan Ahmad III (r. 1703-30 CE), when war was not at the forefront of the political agenda and the sultan could refine his artistic taste, inspired by seventeenth-century Persian painting. Yet Ottoman features also abound: the cypress trees and cherry blossoms surrounding the musicians are reminiscent of such depictions on Iznik tiles made for the Ottoman court in the mid-sixteenth century under Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520-66 CE).
6ce145a9-1c2f-50bf-a811-ee97df9fc4d0.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
6ce145a9-1c2f-50bf-a811-ee97df9fc4d0.bibliography: Welch, Anthony and Welch, Stuart Cary, *Arts of the Islamic Book: The Collection of Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan*, London / Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1982. ISBN: 9780801498824.

6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.name: *Lamentation of Christ*
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.description:
The canvas dates from the Flemish painter's first trip to Rome (1602), and is contemporaneous with his first Roman commission: the paintings for the Sant' Elena Chapel in the Church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.  
The work was probably done for Cardinal Montalto and did not become part of the Borghese collection until 1827.  
The scene shows the Lamentation of Christ according to the Gospels. In the centre of the picture, conforming to the dramatic style typical of Baroque art is the body of Christ in a bold foreshortened position, stretched out on an ancient sarcophagus and surrounded by different characters. Mary supports him with the shroud (in which he is wrapped) while looking to the heavens, where beams of light pierce dark clouds, accentuating the almost nocturnal setting of the subject. John the Evangelist, the young apostle loved by Jesus, stands opposite the elderly Joseph of Arimathea. The right side of the painting shows two female figures: one the pious woman, almost hidden, and Magdalene, in full light, in the act of drying her tears. The high drama of the composition and the richness of the colours perhaps come from the famous *Deposition* that Caravaggio completed for the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella (1602–1604). The painting nonetheless reveals clear references to Dutch Mannerism, combined in this case with classical models copied by the artist in Rome, with brilliant colours and diagonal compositions taken from Venetian and Emilian painting.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.short_description: This work was painted by Rubens during his first stay in Rome (1602). He matched Barocci's colours, the dense brushwork of the late Titian, and the roman statuary and the light and shadow of Caravaggio. The Baroque genius had blended, in an absolutely original way, this tradition with new experimentation.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.name: *The Suicide of Lucretia*
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.description:
The *Suicide of Lucretia* is the work of the Baroque artist, Carlo Francesco Nuvolone, or Nuvoloni (as he is known to some authors) whose work belongs to the Milanese Baroque school. The painting, done in the latter part of Nuvoloni's career when he achieved work of a higher quality, is less cloying and has less pathos than earlier works. Taught by the Mannerist painter, his father, Panfilo Nuvolone (1581–1651) at the Ambrosiana Academy in Milan, he went on to study there with the well-known painter G. B. Crespi aka *il Cerano* (1557–1632). Influenced by Guido Reni, Francesco was nicknamed Guido di Lombardia. His work is characterised by pleasing colour, expression, sensuality and composed pathos. Francesco painted portraits, religious compositions and historical subjects. Other works by him are found in Milan (the Pinacoteca Ambrosiana and the Pinacoteca Brera), in churches in Pavia and Varese, in Piacenza (Museo Civico), in the Dresden Alte Pinakothek and in some chapels in Lombardy.  
The subject of the painting is Lucretia, daughter of the Roman senator, Lucretius Tricipitinus, and wife of the Roman consul, Tarquinius Collatinus. Following her rape by Sestus Tarquinius, son of King Tarquinius Superbus, she committed suicide in 510 BC, which spurred Roman discontent with tyrannical rule and led them to proclaim a Republic.  
The dying Lucretia lies diagonally in the foreground. Her torso unclad, she has a mortal wound to her breast. Her greyish flesh colour is in contrast to the rich folds of red drapery that cover her knees, and in harmony with the white and green fabric of her clothing. An older woman bends over her curved body wrapped in a dark cloak, from which her lit face and the palm of one hand poke out. Lucretia and the older woman create a simple, closed composition with characteristic composed Baroque ardour and exaltation. Lucretia, symbol of chastity and of tragedy at the same time, is the victim of her own beauty. In the mid-ground on the left-hand side of the picture, from the deep shadow alongside a pillar, peer the faces of three old men. On the opposite side, the composition opens out to a landscape, bounded with clouds, within which are two Roman soldiers. The painting is composed of light and cold tones, with a silvery range.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.short_description:
*The Suicide of Lucretia* is the work of the Baroque painter from Lombardy C. F. Nuvoloni, known by some as Nuvolone, who was born in Cremona. Taught at the Ambrosiana Academy by his father, Panfilo, he went on to study with G. B. Crespi. Inspired by the painter Guido Reni, he was nicknamed Guido di Lombardia, living and working in Milan, painting portraits, religious and historical subjects.  
The theme of this painting is the suicide of Lucretia. Lucretia was the daughter of the senator, Tricipitinus, and the wife of the Roman consul, Tarquinius Collatinus. In 510 BC, following Lucretia's rape by Sestus Tarquinius, son of King Tarquinius Superbus, the Romans ousted the king and declared a Republic.  
The painting shows the half-naked body of Lucretia in her death throes. Leaning over her is an older woman, while in the background three old men peer out. In the background landscape, Roman soldiers are barely discernable. In this painting, the artist depicts the tragedy of a beautiful woman with a composed ardour characteristic of the Baroque. He painted Lucretia in a cold and light tonality, richly lit with a silvery light; in the dark mid-ground, in contrast, are barely discernable figures.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.method_for_datation: The attribution to Nuvoloni by Dr. Grgo Gamulin in 1961 was through stylistic analysis and comparative material, as well as by comparison with the other established works of the painter.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.

6f8d6482-6333-5e44-8f9e-903c41299c06.name: Der Eulenruf
6f8d6482-6333-5e44-8f9e-903c41299c06.short_description:
Abstract composition with two stylized owls in a forest landscape. According to the artist, owls, like ghosts and bats, populate the night, and their call is considered a harbinger of doom. Wirtl-Walser finds iconographic inspiration in the world of nature, fossils and archetypes. She prefers to use old, mouth-blown glass as a support for her work, because it has more texture and greater irregularities than industrially produced glass. Over many years, in several workshops and through long series of experiments in her own studio, she has learned various ways of working the surface of the glass – from binding agents to painting techniques to the uses of various glues, and from layering and cutting to engraving and mounting.  
  
The artist created the mirror surface of the reverse glass painting presented here after studying old recipes for silver mirroring. An almost extinct mirror-making skill, silver mirroring has become one of her consistently recurring means of expression over many years.

706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.name: Miniature 'Mi'raj (the Miraculous Ascension) of Prophet Muhammad'
706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.short_description: Mi'raj is the scene of the Ascension of the Great Prophet Muhammad to Heaven to the throne of Allah. The iconography of the scene has become established in the Iranian painting tradition since the late AD 15th century. The composition of Mi'raj, together with the poetic dedication of God and His Prophet, traditionally opened manuscripts of historical, biographical and poetic works of classical Persian literature. In the centre of the scene we see Prophet Muhammad riding the fantastic animal Boraq, a mare with a woman’s head. Muhammad is traditionally depicted with a large flaming halo around his head. His face is covered by a veil, probably added to the picture later. In front of the Prophet, we see the Archangel Jabriel showing the way. Above the Archangel there is a lion, the heavenly personification of Ali, the first righteous Imam of the Shiites. Angels with gifts fly around the Prophet. Between the figures against the blue sky, golden "Chinese" clouds abound. The miniature subject combines two important Islamic legends. The Qur'anic Al-Isra (Night Journey, Surah 17) recounts the Prophet's magical night flight from Mecca to Jerusalem. The Al-Mi'raj (Staircase), narrated in hadiths, is the story of Muhammad's miraculous ascent to Heaven to the throne of God.

70fdcb57-1eeb-5564-b13a-e80bde43f3ba.name: *Courtyard of Justice at the Alhambra Palace, Granada*
70fdcb57-1eeb-5564-b13a-e80bde43f3ba.description: Sorolla depicted the Alhambra palace often. In this painting he chose the entry to the golden room. The beauty and exoticism of the Alhambra Palace fascinated European painters during the 19th century. Sorolla painted this monument in successive trips in 1909, 1910 and again in 1917. He was interested in architecture and especially in the Arab gardens, the play of light and water in their pools, and not so much in other topics.

keywords: The Alhambra; Painting development

718b2755-b86b-5577-8fe4-dae39544ddbd.name: Scenes from the Life of John the Baptist
718b2755-b86b-5577-8fe4-dae39544ddbd.description:
John the Baptist was the cousin of Jesus Christ and preached in the Judean desert. He lived a life of self-denial by wearing camel hair clothing and eating only locusts and wild honey. The people of the region came to him to be baptized in the Jordan River. When Jesus asked to be baptized, John proclaimed that he was not worthy of such a task and that Christ should baptize him. Christ insisted, however, and during the baptism the Holy Spirit descended and a voice from heaven proclaimed, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). John got into trouble when he criticized King Herod’s marriage to Herodias, who had a child from her previous marriage to Herod’s brother. Herod’s stepdaughter, Salome, convinced him to arrest John and demanded his head on a silver platter. Granting her wish, Herod ordered John beheaded.  
This icon shows several scenes from John the Baptist’s life in a single frame. At the top left, John is depicted in the wilderness, surrounded by animals. He receives inspiration from God in the form of flames. At the bottom, John is seen baptizing followers in the Jordan River while more followers prepare for baptism or don the white clothes of the newly baptized. In the top right corner of the icon, people stream out from the city while members of the aristocracy look on from above. The three figures in the central arch could be King Herod, his wife and stepdaughter, all of whom were responsible for John’s martyrdom.
718b2755-b86b-5577-8fe4-dae39544ddbd.obtention: Purchased by the Museum of Russian Icons from a private collection in 2010.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.name: "How Rustam Found a Spring"
71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.alternate_name: Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.description: The two miniatures 69.74.8 and 69.74.9 illustrate the first and second of Rustam's seven ordeals. The first depicts the frequently illustrated scene of Rustam's gallant horse Rakhsh killing a lion while the hero sleeps. The subject of the second miniature is, on the other hand, rarely depicted. Rustam and Rakhsh nearly die of heat and thirst in the desert before, with the help of divine providence, they find a spring. Rustam bathes and grooms his faithful steed by the water's edge, as seen here. The painter is very sympathetic to the closeness between the hero and his trustworthy Rakhsh.

71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.name: *Susanna and the Old Men*
71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.description:
The painting, signed and dated, was acquired by Marcantonio IV Borghese in 1783 along with other works of the Flemish school. No details are known about the commissioning of the canvas, which, like the Rubens' example (inv.277), handles a subject common to painting of the Counter-Reformation. The account is taken from the Old Testament, specifically the Book of the Prophet Daniel (13, 1–64), and illustrates well the defeat of deception, expressed by the two old men – shown with lustful eyes and faces – and the victory of truth, represented by the naked Susanna.  
Van Honthorst, known in Italy as Gherardo delle Notti, manages to transmit the feelings of surprise, indignation and shame in the Biblical heroine by the fountain, through her open mouth and terrified look. The study of mood is related to experimentation of Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Guido Reni, who rendered it first in marble and then on canvas.  
Although the composition follows a diagonal arrangement, possibly inspired by Emilian painting that he encountered on his long trip to Italy in the 1620s, the canvas belongs to the final productive phase of the artist. He was better known as a painter of “genre scenes” particularly renowned for the extraordinary lighting effects inspired by the Caravaggesque school of Bartolomeo Manfredi, which he frequented when in Rome. Despite connections to a secular theme and culture, van Honthorst, the leader of the Dutch Caravaggists, captures the instrument of Divine Will in the figure of Susanna, who is entirely surrounded by light, and who triumphs only after suffering cruel injustices.
71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.short_description: The subject is connected to the representation of the emotions according to the experimentation of Bernini and Reni among others. The theme of the painting relates to the concept of deception being defeated by divine truth.
71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

727ea8ec-c6ff-5c30-91b3-9e087af62768.name: *Interior of a Harem*
727ea8ec-c6ff-5c30-91b3-9e087af62768.short_description: Preziosi probably used models to recreate this harem scene which as an infidel Frank he would not normally be allowed to witness. However, there is nothing in this decorous interior which is impossible or unlikely and it may be based on a visit to the house of one of his Turkish friends. The furniture and fittings show western European influence, particularly in the curious rococo wall bracket and the fringed sofa in place of the traditional raised wooden platform covered with carpets. By the middle of the 19th century French style in interior design was fashionable in Turkey, especially a degenerate form of the rococo. A version of this composition, dated 1852, is much less restrained, its details deliberately pandering to the popular western idea of a harem, based on Arabian Nights imagery.
727ea8ec-c6ff-5c30-91b3-9e087af62768.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: costume; coffee; tobacco; rococo; Ottoman Baroque; Orientalism; women; Ottoman interior decoration; fashion

72ae01c0-55bc-584b-8258-a81263d1edbd.name: *Hamzanama*: Emissaries bring news from the provinces of Khaybar and Chin to Anoshirvan
72ae01c0-55bc-584b-8258-a81263d1edbd.short_description: "Sergeants-at-arms hastened off to all parts of the realm and found two ancient bricks, one in Khaybar and one in Chin. They brought the two bricks to Anoshirvan and reported to the emperor of the seven climes. The king summoned the *khwaja* to his retinue and, in his presence, asked the sergeants why the two countries were in ruins. The sergeants reported that in Khaybar there was a guebre named Hisham who did everything he could by way of cruelty and injustice, while in Chin, although the Khaqan was very good, he had a son named Bahram Gur, who was extremely egotistical and unruly. The subjects of those two kingdoms were tormented by the injustice of those two, and on account of them the kingdoms were in ruins."

72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.name: *Surname-i Hümayun* (‘Book of the Imperial Circumcision Festival’).
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.description:
The *Surname-i Hümayun* ('Book of the Imperial Circumcision Festival') is a work dealing with the celebrations held for the circumcision festival of Prince Mehmed, son of Sultan Murad III, which lasted for 52 days and 52 nights in AH 990 / AD 1582. It documents, in both word and image, how during the festivities the craft guilds paraded their various products, how a variety of entertainments were organised, how banquets were held and food distributed to the public every day, how the sultan would scatter gold and silver among the people from time to time, how poor children were circumcised and given new clothes, how beggars were made happy, and how people who had been imprisoned for debt were granted their freedom by having their debts paid. For this reason the *Surname* is an important historical source providing for us a record of the AH 10th- / AD 16th-century Ottoman lifestyle; its economy, social life, culture, art and entertainment.  
  
The celebration was held in the Hippodrome, i.e. the 'Horse Square'. The Ibrahim Pasha Palace is depicted here, and the three-storey wooden spectators' gallery erected at one of its corners for the use of palace officials and representatives of foreign governments, is an indispensable element of the scenes in the *Surname*.  
  
One of these scenes represents the parade of the glassmakers' guild. Here the sultan, seated on the enclosed balcony of the audience hall in the Ibrahim Pasha Palace, watches the glassmakers' guild along with the assembled people and the guests sitting in the spectators' gallery. The glassmakers present the glass objects they have made, even showing the stages of glass production and the tools they use with the help of a furnace mounted on a wheeled wagon.  
  
Another painting in the *Surname* shows the procession of architects and engineers with a faithful replica of the Süleymaniye Mosque made of wood and ivory. This picture is noteworthy because it represents Ottoman art in all its splendour, celebrated in both the depiction of the architect Sinan, who was still alive in this period and probably participated in this parade, and, through his most monumental building: the Süleymaniye Mosque.  
  
The celebrations of the circumcision festival are transformed into a painted story through 250 double-page miniatures with compositions generally similar to the two seen here.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.short_description: *Surname* is a magnificent manuscript telling the story of the circumcision festival of Prince Mehmed, son of Sultan Murad III, held at the Hippodrome in front of the Ibrahim Pasha Palace in AH 990 / AD 1582. The setting, processions and events are depicted both in writing and in miniatures.

72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.method_for_datation: Since some pages of the manuscript are missing, including the colophon, it has been ascertained from the Kepeci Ruus register in the archives (3 Safar 997/1583 no. 250, 37) that it was completed in 997 / 1588.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.method_for_provenance: It is known that this manuscript was prepared by the team of artists in the Topkapi Palace atelier, and that it was therefore produced in Istanbul.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.obtention: The *Surname* was made for Sultan Murad III in the Topkapi Palace atelier and is still in the palace library.

In the Surname, the writer Intizami describes the preparation of the work in a section entitled ‘Description of the painter and his qualities’, stating that it was prepared by Naqqash Osman (who, like himself, was from the town of Foça in Herzegovina) and his team, although he does not give the names of the members of the team. A document dated 997 (AD 1588) written by the court panegyrist Sayyid Loqman on the subject of raising the salaries of the team working on the Hünername and the Surname, though, does list the names of the team members. Although it is impossible to determine from this document who was working on the Hünername and who on the Surname (or on both), the document is important because it gives a general idea of which painters (naqqash in Turkish) and other artists might have been working on Naqqash Osman’s team. The names that appear in this document are:  
Calligraphers: Seyyid Kasım; Mustafa; Feramruz?; Ali; Abdurrahman.  
Bookbinders: Abdi Şaban; Mehmet Haydar; Kara Mehmed; Mehmed …; Recep Abdullah.  
Painters (naqqash): Osman; Lütfi; Ali; Mehmed Haydar; Velican; Mehmed Musavvir; Molla … ; İbrahim; \[another\] Osman; Ahmed Abdullah; Hüseyin Zergub; Mahmud Müzehib?; … Abdullah …  
Illuminators: Musa Ahmed; Yahya; Seydi; Abdi Zergub; Şaban; Hızır Gazi; Mehmed Abdullah; Mehmed Mustafa; Nasuh bin Abdullah; Perviz Abdullah; Abd … Yakub; Davud Abdullah; Yusuf Abdullah.

74a255de-faae-533b-ad80-5e73500284f7.name: *The Perfect Pearls*
74a255de-faae-533b-ad80-5e73500284f7.description: Riki Salam’s *The Perfect Pearls* is a tribute to family, ancestry and cultural continuity. Dedicated by the artist to “those who came before us,” the work draws inspiration from his Uncle Seaman Dans’ song "Perfect Pearl". At its centre is Salam’s great-grandfather, Hardie Salaam Snr., depicted as a deep-sea diver. Born in Malaysia, Hardie migrated to Australia to work on a pearl lugger in the Torres Straits, embedding his story within the broader history of migration and maritime labour. Within the pearl shell are portraits of Salam’s grandparents, Hardie Salaam Jnr. and Maude Louise Savage, accompanied symbolically by their seven children, who are represented as pearls. The branching black coral evokes the artist’s immediate and extended family tree, which stretches from Mossman, on Kuku Yalanji Country, across Cape York, the Torres Straits and into the Northern Territory and Broome. The crayfish point to contemporary Torres Strait commerce, while the trochus shells and sea cucumber reference the historic trade networks linking Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples with the Makassans.

keywords: Riki Salam, Acrylic on canvas, pearl diver, pearl lugger, pearl, Australia, Indigenous, aboriginal, painting, AMH, Australian Muslim History, Australian Muslim, coral, family, malay

75647d49-efe8-541c-828b-b58acf35195a.name: God Rested on the Seventh Day
75647d49-efe8-541c-828b-b58acf35195a.description: In this icon, God reclines on a bed, illustrating the part of the creation story that reads, “On the seventh day He rested” (Genesis 2:2). Angels hold his bed and the temporarily vacant throne aloft while the Holy Spirit, represented by a dove, flies above them. All this takes place within a circle featuring the archangels, the evangelists, Christ and the Mother of God. Meanwhile, scenes from the rest of the creation story take place below. Labels on the back of this icon reveal that it was sold by Gimbels department store in the late 1930s, suggesting that it once belonged to William Randolph Hearst. Hearst was a newspaper entrepreneur who famously sold off large parts of his immense art collection during the Depression.
75647d49-efe8-541c-828b-b58acf35195a.obtention: Sold at "Exhibition of Russian Icons Arranged by Hammer Galleries", New York City, in 1937. Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2013. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography; Biblical stories; Jesus Christ; Angels

7573e18c-a60a-5e4f-926f-d8e3c737746a.name: *Masquarade I*
7573e18c-a60a-5e4f-926f-d8e3c737746a.description:
An unframed decorative scene with fantastic architecture and a masquerade of noble company indicates that the canvas was part of an interior decoration, location as yet unknown. The central motif is an impressive open construction, an oval colonnaded hall merging into a park. The architecture – marble grooved columns decorated with sculptures, garlands and draperies – evokes an air of nonchalance with noble ladies and their cavaliers passing the time accompanied by music. The detailed attention dedicated to the figures lends emphasis to the spectacular nature of a picturesque scene. The theatrical overstatement of central perspective draws the viewer into an imaginary space, among *comedia dell´arte* actors, gallant couples, servants and musicians. These types of *Schaustück* (eye-pleasing) pictures represented a popular trend in the decoration of reception interiors, absorbing the viewer in their relationship between reality and illusion, not only in composition but also in the metaphors intrinsic to the costumes and mysterious masks. The motifs encourage the idea of unity in all of the arts and draw attention to the relationship between artificial and natural spaces.  
In his masquerade pictures, Minderhout took up the tradition of morality scenes based on aristocratic society (banquets and gardens of love), probably inspired by the prints of Claude Gillot (1673–1722) featuring scenes from *comedia dell´arte,* and the work of Hendrick Govaerts (1669–1720) from Antwerp, active in Prague and Vienna in the period when theatre established itself as part of court life. *Comedia dell´arte*, originally considered a “low” genre, became very popular, inspiring a number of artists. The visual rendering of its scenes was essentially influenced by the Galli-Bibiena family, Vienna court decorators whose members and pupils worked for the Czech and Moravian nobility. Czech and Moravian aristocrats often went to performances in Vienna and cultivated theatre in their palaces.
7573e18c-a60a-5e4f-926f-d8e3c737746a.short_description: A decorative scene with fantastic architecture and a masquerade indicates that the canvas was part of an interior decoration. The picture merges the Flemish tradition with late-baroque Italian painting in a highly original manner.
7573e18c-a60a-5e4f-926f-d8e3c737746a.method_for_datation: The painting paraphrases pictures found in the Archiepiscopal Palace, Kroměříž. Willem Augustin Minderhout participated in the decoration of the palace halls under Cardinal Ferdinad Julius Troyer (1745–1758). The artist’s initials and the style of the painting place it as part of the relatively prolific work of this itinerant artist, frequently producing related pairs of pictures.
7573e18c-a60a-5e4f-926f-d8e3c737746a.obtention: The picture, origin unknown, was acquired in 1945.

75ecd1ca-690e-54ec-ae5c-583c92e90430.name: *Street Scene in Cairo*
75ecd1ca-690e-54ec-ae5c-583c92e90430.short_description: *Street Scene in Cairo* from the Austrian painter Alphons Mielich. Mielich specialized in Oriental scenes, which he sold to aristocratic Austrian tourists as mementos of their trips to Egypt.

76c48506-d9b5-58bd-92bd-fbff17f0f18e.name: *David with the Head of Goliath*
76c48506-d9b5-58bd-92bd-fbff17f0f18e.description:
This painting was probably part of the collection of Cardinal Scipione Borghese, and in fact there is a 1612 document making reference to the biblical subject, concerning the acquisition of a frame for the work.  
The picture is attributed to the Neapolitan Giovanni Battista Caracciolo, also known as Battistello, but over the centuries the inventories have attributed it to many different artists. Apart from one entry in 1650, where the canvas was ascribed to Giulio Romano, it has usually been attributed to Caravaggesque artists.  
The young David is central and isolated, holding the decapitated head of the giant, Goliath, which rests on a marble base decorated with floral motifs.  
The biblical hero stands out from the dark background, appearing in the foreground bathed in an almost violent light, in a relaxed pose, apparently detached from the bloody deed he has just committed. His crossed legs, austere but serene face, and feathered red hat, an ostentatious show of contemporaneousness: all of the details in the composition are constructed using a “masking” technique. Battistello uses a traditional dark preparation of the picture for the background and the shadows. The shapes are rendered using a few, mainly earth colours, with strong highlights for emphasis.  
The young Battistello was influenced by the style of Caravaggio, who, in 1607, fled Rome for Naples having been condemned to death. He expanded on the Lombard master's study of nature and light, something which is evident in the painting. His style evolved further after 1612 with his experience in Rome, which enabled him to see the paintings of Carracci and his followers. Later visits to Genoa and Florence also helped to mould his style.
76c48506-d9b5-58bd-92bd-fbff17f0f18e.short_description:
The Neapolitan painter was one of the greatest of Caravaggio's followers, and his powerful work was an important factor in making Naples a stronghold of the Caravaggesque style. In this painting David, wearing a red hat, triumphs beside the severed head of Goliath.  
His crossed legs, austere but serene face, and feathered red hat, an ostentatious show of contemporaneousness, contrast with the bloody aspect of the traditional iconography.
76c48506-d9b5-58bd-92bd-fbff17f0f18e.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

776becd1-b151-59c4-9e46-f120b2d7a354.name: *The Nightmare of Zahhak*. Miniature from the *Shahnama* of Shah Tahmasp
776becd1-b151-59c4-9e46-f120b2d7a354.short_description: This Safavid folio once belonged to the so-called *Shahnama* of Shah Tahmasp (r. AH 930-984 / AD 1524-1576). It is probably the most luxurious and celebrated Shahnama manuscript ever produced for a royal patron. This painting depicts the tyrant Zahhak as he wakes up terrified from a nightmare announcing his death by the hands of the Iranian hero Faridun. His scream has awakened the entire palace. The *Shahnama*, composed in the AH 5th century / AD early 11th century, remains a nation epic of Iran.

779c654a-aa90-53f1-a122-5dbb8e302070.name: *Interior of a school, Cairo*
779c654a-aa90-53f1-a122-5dbb8e302070.short_description: In this scene depicted by Lewis, the Hoja or teacher is listening to his assistant rhythmically reciting the Quran (while beating time), as some children pay attention and others not. Some commentators have regarded the presence of a young girl as inauthentic, but young girls were able to attend Quran schools, according to the artist Charles de Tournemine, the scholar Edward Lane and the translator Richard Burton. Certainly not all women were illiterate, and some female descendants of the prophet were noted for their ability to read and recite the scriptures.

keywords: education; school; teaching; children; childhood; kuttab

78bb25e6-fdd2-5c9d-af72-c30e121b175e.name:
Gushtasp puts Isfandiyar in chains  
Folio from a manuscript of *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
78bb25e6-fdd2-5c9d-af72-c30e121b175e.short_description: Isfandiyar, eldest son and crown prince of the legendary Iranian king Gushtasp, was falsely accused of planning to seize his father’s kingdom. Not knowing the truth, his father ordered Isfandiyar chained and imprisoned in a mountain fortress. In a later battle with enemies, the king regretted his act and had Isfandiyar released so that he could provide military assistance. Gushtasp is portrayed here enthroned, wearing a blue robe. Blue was frequently used in Persian painting to signify key figures, particularly kings.
78bb25e6-fdd2-5c9d-af72-c30e121b175e.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper
materials: Opaque watercolour, ink, and gold on paper

7935012a-92f2-5749-a878-3506ddbb8dc4.name: *The Temple of Venus*
7935012a-92f2-5749-a878-3506ddbb8dc4.short_description: Giuseppe Sciuti initially worked in his hometown as a decorator, then moved to Naples and Florence. In Florence, the artist works with the Macchiaioli painters upon subjects linked to the “Verismo”, or realist, movement, and while in Naples he worked on history paintings. In Rome he decorated public and private buildings with historical and allegorical themes, pagan rituals and scenes from the Greek and Roman tradition, highly valued by the international market. *The Temple of Venus* is an archeological reconstruction of a sacred interior showing an offering to the goddess Venus for the beginning of Spring. The painting is part of the group of works by the artist presented at the Exposition in Milan in 1871, Nice in 1884 and London in 1888.

795bacd6-ac66-5eca-9599-838de1b288ee.name: *Natürmort*
795bacd6-ac66-5eca-9599-838de1b288ee.short_description: The foundation of Turkish painting drawing influence from western tradition was laid when the Naval Academy opened in 1795. In the period of Selim II, painting lessons were given at the academy. And course attendees were sent abroad after to develop their painting techniques and skills. These painters, who were known as the soldier-painters, worked in Gerome’s, Cabanel’s and Boulanger’s workshops in Paris. Halil Paşa provided a unique distinction to the analysis of impressionist light and colour. Because of his qualified knowledge about anatomy and his interest in depicting the human figure, Halil Paşa has a unique place in Turkish Art History.
795bacd6-ac66-5eca-9599-838de1b288ee.holder: Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University, Painting and Sculpture Museum
keywords: Painting; Halil Paşa; orientalist Turkish painters; still life

79ec3799-6c99-5734-a810-73dca9b04725.name: *Bildnis der ältesten drei Kinder Karls I. von England (Portrait of the eldest three children of King Charles I of England)*
79ec3799-6c99-5734-a810-73dca9b04725.description: This painting depicts the three eldest children of King Charles I of England and his wife Henrietta Maria. The five-year-old Crown Prince Charles (Prince of Wales and later King Charles II) is on the left leaning against a pillar, imitating the pose of a court dignitary. Beside him, grasping his hand is his younger brother James (Duke of York and later King James II of Scotland). On the right stands the upright, demure figure of the four-year-old Princess Mary, the future wife of William of Orange. Van Dyck masterfully depicts the opulent costumes of the children posing, as befits a courtly portrait, in front of a pillar and a sumptuous curtain, standing on a valuable oriental carpet and framed by two dogs at their feet.
79ec3799-6c99-5734-a810-73dca9b04725.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
79ec3799-6c99-5734-a810-73dca9b04725.obtention: This painting was purchased for the Dresden collection by the art agent Le Leu in Paris in 1744.

7b315354-8d00-5a9b-9462-8f8f378759d3.name: Rustam Slaying the White Div
7b315354-8d00-5a9b-9462-8f8f378759d3.short_description:
The overall layout of this hanging is reminiscent of courtly manuscript illustrations with its figure-rich inner field and the border on which birds and game cavort in lush vegetation. The somewhat naïve style of the figures suggests that this embroidery in chain stitch technique must have been made at the beginning of the 20th century.  
  
The central field depicts scenes from the life of Rustam, the most popular hero from Ferdausi’s national epic *Shahnama*, the Book of Kings. The scene in the lower third is the easiest to recognise. It shows Rustam slaying the White Div, the ruler of Mazandaran. Above this we probably see Rustam’s fight with Suhrab, one of the most tragic moments in the *Shahnama*. During the duel, Rustam slays the young man, who shows him a talisman as he dies and it is at that moment that Rustam realises that he has just killed his very own son. Meanwhile, the top scene shows an unspecified battle scene.  
  
Wall hangings fulfilled many functions in Persian houses, be it as decoration for niches or as curtains. In this case, it is even conceivable that the hanging was used in one of the many coffee and tea houses, serving as a backdrop for professional storytellers to illustrate their stories.
7b315354-8d00-5a9b-9462-8f8f378759d3.dates: Hegira early 14th century / AD late 19th-early 20th century
7b315354-8d00-5a9b-9462-8f8f378759d3.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar dated works and due to visual characteristics of some of the colours.

7b36747d-dca7-598b-b985-ad4799a191fe.name: The Mother of God of the Burning Bush
7b36747d-dca7-598b-b985-ad4799a191fe.description:
The Mother of God is shown in the center of this icon surrounded by rays of light that extend outward to form an eight-pointed star. Angels, archangels and symbols of the evangelists are pictured both in and around the star. This icon is a reference to a passage from the book of Exodus in which Moses saw the burning bush unconsumed by fire. Moses and other prophets are often interpreted as foretelling the coming of Christ while the unburnt bush serves as a symbolic representation of the Virgin Mary.  
In this icon, the four evangelists are represented by four winged figures. The angel represents Saint Matthew, the lion stands for Saint John, the ox symbolizes Saint Luke and the eagle is associated with Saint Mark. These symbols are based on the biblical interpretations of Saint Irenaeus (130-202).
7b36747d-dca7-598b-b985-ad4799a191fe.obtention: Purchased by the Museum of Russian Icons from ArtVKG, New York City, in 2012.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography; Angels

7b456f9b-750b-56db-a86f-8e36eccf0b62.name: *Khusraw Hunting*, folio from *Khusraw and Shirin*
7b456f9b-750b-56db-a86f-8e36eccf0b62.short_description: This painting from a manuscript of *Khusraw and Shirin* by the poet Hatifi demonstrates the importance of Persian literature in the Ottoman world. The manuscript contains seven paintings, executed in a distinctive style related to western Iranian tradition from the Aq Quyunlu but also borrowing elements from European sources. This scene depicts Khusraw riding on his horse Shabdiz while hunting. A poem on the final page of the manuscript identifies the sole artist of the work, who completed the calligraphy, illumination, gilding, and painting, as Suzi (“the burning one”).

7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.name: "Alexander is Lowered into the Sea"
7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.description: The Khamsa of the Indian poet Amir Khusrau includes a section on the philosopher-king Alexander the Great, who in Khusrau’s telling of his life led expeditions to China, Russia, and the Western Isles. In this copy of the Khamsa made for the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605), Alexander is shown being lowered into the sea in a glass diving bell. 7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.name: *Sacrifice of Abraham*
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.description:
This relatively large, upright rectangular painting depicts Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac as told in the Old Testament story (Genesis 22: 1–19). Omitting the narrative details of the story, the painter shows the moment Abraham is stopped by an angel just as he is about to carry out the divine command to sacrifice his own son, Isaac.  
The prevailing deep, dusky and dark palette along with dense shadows contrast with the lit masses, the dynamic distribution of which reflect the dramatic charge of the moment. The illuminated accents concentrate attention on the diagonally placed body of the victim, Isaac, while Abraham's elderly, worn-out face reveals his inner turmoil and the difficulty he faced in making the decision. The divine intervention of the angel breaks into the composition from the left, in a foreshortened diagonal of the opposite course.  
The picture is one of four works by Benković that Count Franz Lothar von Schönborn, Elector and Archbishop of Mainz and Prince Bishop of Bamberg, commissioned in 1715 while he was refurbishing the family castle in Pommersfelden. A print by Salomon Kleiner of 1728 shows the interior of Castle Schönborn following its re-arrangement of 1715, which is useful to reconstruct the order of the paintings. On the window wall of the middle room were Benković's *Sacrifice of Abraham* and *Hagar and Ishmael*, and on the ceiling the *Sacrifice of Iphigeneia* and *Apollo and Marsius*. Two paintings – *Hagar and Ishmael* and *Iphigeneia* – are on display in Castle Schönborn to this day, but the French military removed *Apollo and Marsius* and the *Sacrifice of Abraham* from the castle in 1801. The *Sacrifice of Abraham* allegedly turned up in a private collection in Rome in 1868, and then in London in 1936; the Association of Friends of the Strossmayer Gallery bought it in 1936.
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.short_description: *Sacrifice of Abraham* is one of four compositions commissioned by Federico Benković for the Schönborn family's castle in Pommersfelden. The painter achieves dramatic tension by depicting the very moment at which an angel stops Abraham from sacrificing his son, Isaac, as told in the Old Testament story.

7d1dabeb-3a46-50a1-8a1e-90fa8b90fffa.name: *The Vision of Saints Augustine and Norbert*
7d1dabeb-3a46-50a1-8a1e-90fa8b90fffa.description:
The structure of the picture is based on the contrast between an intricately segmented, sacred architectural space and a figurative group within it. While the artist represented the architecture with a scale of subtly harmonised and graded neutral tones accentuated by light falling from the left, the figures are rendered in rich tones of red, blue, gold and dark green. St. Augustine, surrounded by the founders of orders observing his rules, is additionally illuminated by the light of God's eye, penetrating the Host (monstrance) carried by an angel. The Host is being worshipped by St. Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian order. The monstrance is also an attribute of St. Norbert. A *putto* points to a burning heart an attribute of St. Augustine. An angel on the left aims bolts of anger at heretics.  
This small format picture, appearing as an autonomous piece rather than a *modello*, is among the leading works of Winterhalder Jr., a student, assistant and follower of F. A. Maulbertsch, whose motifs from Klosterneuburg appear in the picture. The theatrical architecture is derived from stage designs by the Galli-Bibiena family in Bologna, also active in Vienna and known from prints. The dating indicates that Winterhalder painted the picture after a period of collaboration with Maulbertsch in Dyje. The presence of major Premonstratensian saints places the work among paintings for the Louka u Znojma Monastery. The illusionary architecture bears witness to the decorative skills that flourished towards the end of Winterhalder's career.  
Josef Winterhalder Jr. was born in Schwarzwald. He came to Moravia with his uncle, a sculptor. He was first apprenticed to J. Stern in Brno and later to F. A. Maulbertsch. He frequently collaborated with A. Schweigl, with whom he coined a specific style for a number of Moravian chateau and church interiors. Winterhalder Jr. wrote a book on South Moravian artists which also contained his autobiography.

Winterhalder Jr. was a student, assistant and follower of F. A. Maulbertsch. The illusionary architecture is derived from the stage designs of the Galli-Bibiena family in Bologna.

7fee46c7-2496-508c-978f-4c40ead375bd.name: *Fama*
7fee46c7-2496-508c-978f-4c40ead375bd.short_description:
This stained glass represents a winged female figure, blowing a trumpet held in her right hand. In her other hand, she holds a ribbon with the inscription “FAMA”. She is dressed in a golden robe and a blue-white cloak. Her wings are multicoloured. The figure is set in a landscape consisting of various plants, flower, trees and hills.  
  
The inscription identifies the figure as Fama, the personification of renown and rumor. As a figure from Roman mythology, she is described by Virgil in the “Aeneid” as a winged creature, covered in feathers all over her body and with multiple tongues, mouths and ears. She spreads evil tidings, not resting even at night. The 14th-century English poet Geoffrey Chaucer wrote that Fama announces renown, fame or notability (positive attributes) from a trumpet of gold and scandalous rumor and gossip (negative attributes) from a trumpet of black tin. The glass painting therefore shows Fama’s positive side, which does not appear fearsome or evil.  
  
Stylistic elements substantiate an attribution to the Swedish-born Carl Almquist, who spent almost his entire artistic life in England. Some of the details in the stained glass windows of the small church of Betws Bledrws in the county of Ceredigion, Wales (1886–87) exhibit an affinity with Fama, suggesting a proximate dating. Almquist’s stained glass paintings of this time demonstrate the influence of the pre-Raphaelite circle around Edward Burne-Jones; the impact of the English Arts and Crafts movement is also apparent.

81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.name: *Annunciation*
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.description: The scene takes place in a domestic interior. The composition, based on a neo-Renaissance perspective shows a nearly archaic poverty. The scene opens outward allowing the viewer to feel directly involved in the event. The employment of three different sources of light is very original: the main light source illuminates the figures coming from the foreground. A light is emanating from a dove that symbolizes the Holy Spirit shines from above. A third beam of light shines from a side door. Far from the spectacular luminosity of Tintoretto, this painting employs a poor, nearly severe palette anticipating a naturalism of feeling and research on the human form. It is a careful representation of life typical of the early Baroque period as depicted by artists such as Caravaggio. Keeping in contact with Raphael and Correggio's noble classicism, Ludovico Carracci portrays life in a quotidian tone with a humble, direct and moving religiosity. This seems to reflect the spirit that a great interpreter of the Catholic Reformation, Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti, Archbishop of Bologna from 1566, applied to the visual arts, in his book *Sacred and Profane Images*, published in 1582. The altarpiece stood on a predella, painted by Camillo Procaccini before his departure for Milan (1585–86), which was lost during the Second World War.
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.short_description: A symbol of the early Counter-reformation in Bologna (more appropriately of the Catholic Reformation) because of its authentic and direct religious feeling. Based on its humble naturalism and its original experiments with light it is one of the paintings from Lombardy and northern Italy which led to the style of Caravaggio.
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.method_for_datation: The date 1584, hypothesized by the critics on stylistic basis, has been recently confirmed by historical documents about the building of the oratory where the painting was held (Feigenbaum 1990).
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.provenance: Church of San Giorgio in Poggiale (Bologna), Oratory of the Holy Sacrament
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.obtention: Commissioned by Giulio Cesare Guerini, a member of the Company of the Holy Sacrament, the painting became property of the Italian Government in 1866. The painting was taken back to the church of San Giorgio in Poggiale.  It was moved to the Pinacoteca shortly before the beginning of Second World War and it is still on show in this museum.

8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.name: *Madonna in Glory with the Patron Saints of Bologna*
8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.description:
This painting was commissioned by the Government of Bologna to thank the Virgin of the Rosary after the end of the plague in 1630. Originally it was used as a standard and carried in an annual procession, commemorating the end of the epidemic. The procession moved from the Palazzo Comunale to the church of St. Dominic and once there the standard was exhibited in the church for three days.  
The great painting follows a strict order. In the middle of the painting are the patron saints of Bologna, Petronius, Dominic, Proculus and Florian with two Jesuits saints, Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier, gathered around Saint Francis. All the saints look thankfully in the direction of the Virgin. The greyish shade of the sky is broken by a rainbow introducing the Madonna, calm and regal, lit by the only warm beam of light in the whole painting. In the lower part the town of Bologna looks desolately grey, depopulated by the plague, with no shades and half tones, the only signs of life are the small figures of the “monatti” collecting the dead bodies.  
The patron saints and the two Jesuits saints are a significant iconographical change, usually the plague was associated with St. Roch and St. Sebastian: the first one because he had plague himself and the second one because the arrows in his body were compared to the plague wounds. The altarpiece has a strong votive meaning, it shows how the people of Bologna had committed themselves to the Virgin and the patron saints and how grateful they were to be alive.
8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.short_description: This is one of the most famous votive pictures of Seventeenth-century Italian painting. It is a model from which many figures have been copied and rearranged. Technically, it represents a new experiment by the painter. Reni painted on silk, a stronger and more durable material. The shining silk pervades the whole painting with silver luminosity.
8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.obtention: Moved to the Pinacoteca from the Palazzo Comunale in the Napoleonic age.

8416e828-5b8b-5b06-93d0-9f518e17c49a.name: The Emigrants
8416e828-5b8b-5b06-93d0-9f518e17c49a.short_description: Angelo Tommasi is a naturalistic painter, influenced by Courbet’s realism, and he played an active role spreading the technique employed by the Macchiaioli. The monumental painting *The Emigrants* shows a common situation in Italy after the unification process. The dramatic theme of overseas emigration is vividly depicted by the packed crowds at the Port of Livorno, of people who have resigned themselves to their fate and the expectation of embarkation. The painting's extraordinary dimensions contribute to an illustration of the theme of Italian emigration on an almost epic scale.

8479540f-abb9-5d15-8711-1c88a40879dc.name: A resting lion
8479540f-abb9-5d15-8711-1c88a40879dc.short_description: This single-page drawing depicts a resting lion seemingly squeezed between two golden-lined and gold-flecked borders. Positioned beneath the Chinese clouds and directly in front of the lion (as if being exhaled from the lion’s open mouth), an inscription dates the drawing. Illuminated borders, probably later additions, flank the lion; featuring white-backgrounded cartouches with golden inscriptions, they are presumably taken from a clutch of cartouches. [1] A Resting Lion is attributed to artist Mu’in Musavvir, who was famous for his draftsmanship and for showing acute attention to detail in his drawings of animals. Trained by Reza-e ‘Abbasi, Mu’in Musavvir had a long career and carried Reza-e ‘Abbasi’s artistic ideas and new styles into the 18th century. Drawing wild and exotic animals was in no way unusual at that time, since Safavid rulers showed great interest in them. [2]

8485bf89-aab8-53ff-a59e-03b0ed9c4935.name: The Last Judgment
8485bf89-aab8-53ff-a59e-03b0ed9c4935.description: The Last Judgment is a common topic in Christian art. It combines biblical and apocryphal stories into a unified account of the end of times, of Christ coming to judge the world and of the afterlife. Typically, Russian Orthodox icons that depict the Last Judgment show Christ enthroned with a scale and an open Gospel. He is often flanked by the Virgin and Saint John the Baptist, who intercede for humankind. Adam and Eve are frequently seen kneeling at Christ’s feet. In Russian Orthodox iconography, the “serpent of suffering” is often depicted as well. Originally, the serpent was viewed as the instigator of original sin, seducer of Adam and Eve and the embodiment of evil. In this icon, 20 sins are depicted along the body of the snake in order of severity. They are as follows: (1) lying, (2) greed, (3) tale-telling, (4) idle talk, (5) anger, (6) blasphemy, (7) gluttony, (8) drunkenness, (9) slander, (10) foul language, (11) adultery, (12) fornication, (13) rape, (14) vanity, (15) money-mongering, (16) self-love, (17) despair, (18) murder, (19) self-glorification and (20) pride.
8485bf89-aab8-53ff-a59e-03b0ed9c4935.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography; Biblical stories; Jesus Christ; Angels

84f5327f-428b-5355-b4b7-9d4e62a12ef9.name: *Bashi Bazouk*
84f5327f-428b-5355-b4b7-9d4e62a12ef9.short_description: This colourful watercolour, executed by the Istanbul-based, Maltese painter V. A. Preziosi, shows a Bashi Bazouk, a member of the irregular forces of the Ottoman army that came into use in the late 18th century. The bashi bazouk were mercenaries of great ethnic diversity, often from the Balkans, who fought for the Ottomans in hope of plunder, as they were not paid. An attempt by Husrev Pasha in Egypt to disband his Albanian bashi bazouks in favor of his regular forces began the rioting which led to the establishment of Muhammad Ali's rule. The bashi bazouk did not wear regular uniforms. In this case, the flamboyant character depicted here with his formidable moustache wears an astonishing array of clothing: a towering turban with tassles, an embroidered shirt and waistcoat with large open sleeves, a voluminous waistband and trousers. The outfit is finished off by elaborate footwear. A large yatagan dagger is secured in the waistband across the soldier's front, a gun slung across his chest.

84f69ff8-6c1a-5173-a0c7-4b706dba6ef1.name: Arabian Fantasy
84f69ff8-6c1a-5173-a0c7-4b706dba6ef1.short_description: Stefano Ussi lived between Florence and Rome, studied at the Academy of Fine Arts of Florence and then enrolled as a volunteer in the first Italian War of Independence, during which he was taken prisoner by the Austrian troops. He developed a model of historic painting characterized by a quick application of layers (almost a rough draft) and by a sharp chiaroscuro. In 1875 he followed a diplomatic delegation to Morocco, in which the painter Biseo and the writer De Amicis also took part. The Arabian Fantasy documents the "Lab-el-barode", a game with the dust played in honor of the Italian delegation. This episode was masterly described by the writer Edmondo De Amicis.

85859ee1-f41f-5403-935b-5caa9c428488.name:
Young men carried off by a Simurgh  
Possibly from a dispersed *Khamseh* (quintet) of Amir Khusrow (d. 1325)
85859ee1-f41f-5403-935b-5caa9c428488.short_description: A young man grips the feet of an enormous technicolour simurgh flying above choppy waters filled with giant turtles, fish and a crocodile which looks like a makara, the mythical sea creature with magic powers. This painting may depict the story by Bahram Gur’s Indian princess wife in the *Haft Paykar* of the Persian poet, Nizami. King Bahram Gur had seven wives who told him tales from their separate, coloured pavilions each day of the week. In the Indian princess’s story, the hero is dramatically rescued by holding onto the feet of a simurgh who brings him to a paradise-like land. Anthony Welch notes that the two figures in the beak of the simurgh may be the artist’s personal addition to the story (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 170). In any case the theme fits the Indian interest in adventure-romances featuring heroes who travel through (or above) strange lands and seas, as in Akbar’s Hamzanama. The painting has been attributed to Basawan, Akbar’s outstanding painter known for his sensitive observations, lush landscapes and use of perspective (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 170). In about 1635 CE the painting was mounted onto an album page decorated with magnificent gold-outlined flower paintings by the anonymous ‘Master of the Borders’ and bound in an album for Shah Jahan, Akbar’s grandson. The reverse of this page contains an Arabic prayer with Qur'anic expressions in black *nasta‘liq* script signed by Muhammad Husayn (d. 1020 H/1611-12 CE), the master calligrapher who was honoured by Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE) with the title, ‘Zarin Qalam’ (Golden Pen). There is a portrait of Muhammad Husayn as a teacher painted by Basawan’s son, the luminary Mughal painter Manohar. It must be one of Manohar’s earliest portraits since the artist included himself as a pupil in the composition and he looks to be no more than fifteen years old (Royal Asiatic Society; see Welch 1979, p. 179).

85c59150-e031-57be-b9c0-d8ea356538dc.name: *The Renaissance*
85c59150-e031-57be-b9c0-d8ea356538dc.description: This painting is inspired by the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said's effort to build a mosque in even the most remote villages in Oman as part of an architectural revitalisation program that sought to preserve old buildings while adding new civic structures. In this artwork, the mosque stands amid traditional architecture while the tree trunks and water symbolise the revival of a once-barren land.
