85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.name: Painting.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.description:
The painting shows a topographical view of Mecca with the Great Mosque in the centre surrounded by the houses of the city and the hills of the Meccan neighbourhood. In the middle of the large open court of the Mosque stands the nearly cubic, black veiled building of the Ka'ba, the holiest sanctuary of Islam. The simple structure of the Ka'ba has been little modified throughout the centuries although the building has been restored, in contrast to the Great Mosque which has been reconstructed several times. The painting depicts a view of it after the Ottoman rebuilding period of the AH 10th century / AD 16th century. Inspired by the imperial architecture of Istanbul, arcades with small domes arranged in a line surround the court on either side and the seven minarets were provided with two or three balconies. The painter has tried to show a town-planning measure of the Ottomans. The old Meccan districts were densely inhabited and the houses reached the exterior walls of the Great Mosque. It was decided to tear down houses that immediately bordered the walls in order to create a large area of open space before the Mosque and its façade, as was the rule within the mosque complexes in Istanbul, Bursa or Edirne.  
Representations of Mecca and the Ka'ba illustrate itineraries used by pilgrims for orientation during the *hajj* or appear on tiles and tile panels of the second half of the AH 11th / AD 17th century to the first half of the AH 12th / AD 18th century. They show detailed descriptions of the function of the different buildings. The dome in front of the Ka'ba on the left side of the *minbar* (pulpit), for example, covers the footprints of Abraham. The open building beside it houses the *Zamzam* well whose water the pilgrims drank and took home. The choice of the represented buildings, their arrangement and their execution resemble those of copperplate engravings in European descriptions of Mecca more than depictions of the same scene in contemporary prayer books or on the tiles mentioned above.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.short_description: Painting showing a topographical view of the city of Mecca with the Great Mosque in the centre surrounded by houses. In the middle of the large open courtyard is the black veiled building of the Ka’ba.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.dates: Hegira early 12th century / AD early 18th century.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.method_for_datation: The painting was acquired by the theologian and orientalist Michael Eneman (1676–1714), probably in Istanbul, where he was sent by the Swedish King Charles XII (1682–1718) as his envoy in 1709. After a journey through Syria, Palestine, Sinai, Egypt and Cyprus in 1711 and 1712 he came back once more to Istanbul before he returned to Sweden. It is assumed that the painting is a contemporary work because representations of Mecca and Medina were common at that time.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.method_for_provenance: The painting was purchased by the theologian and orientalist Michael Eneman during his stay in Turkey, probably in Istanbul, at the beginning of the 12th / 18th century. At that time, representations of Mecca and Medina were a common subject of Ottoman painting not only in oil but also on tiles or as illustrations of pilgrim and prayer books.

86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.name: *St. Augustine*
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.alternate_name: *St. Augustine Stepping On the Head of Heresy*
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.description:
*St. Augustine* furnished the entrance of the *Nossa Senhora* *da* *Graça* Convent in Lisbon ruled by the order of St. Augustine. Built around 1271, important reforms of 1565 followed by others in the 17th and 18th centuries, transformed the convent into one of the most sumptuous in Lisbon. After the earthquake of 1755 the convent collapsed and was rebuilt. The grand Italianate late Baroque painting, *St. Augustine,* was probably a gift from King José I to the friars, given that Lusitano was the king's first official court painter.  
The Saint, dressed in Episcopal robes, is writing while he steps on the head of Heresy. At his side a *putto* encourages some dogs to attack Heresy while another, in the lower part of the painting, is burning heretic books. An allegorical figure of The Church sits at the upper left-hand side as, rendered in dark ochre, it emerges statue-like out of the shadow. On the right-hand side a classical building in daylight sweeps into the background. Behind St. Augustine are ruined monumental columns. The realism, upheld by the depth of the landscape, contrasts with the crowded, chaotic interior of the St. Augustine's *scriptorium*.  
The painting, signed and dated by Vieira Lusitano, emphasises his nomination as *accademico di merito*, an honour bestowed on him in 1727 by the St. Lucas Academy in Rome. No other Portuguese artist had previously received this honour. Lusitano was influenced by Roman, late Baroque and Rococo art; his teachers included Benedetto Lutti (1666–1724) and Francesco Trevisani (1656–1746), a disciple of Carlo Maratta (1625–1713).  
*St. Augustine,* a large-scale geometric composition with calculated asymmetry and movement, has theatrical appeal. Its characters are set among solid architectural components and a naturalistic background. The *putti,* characteristics from the Roman tradition, enable the artist to play with symbolic elements while the sumptuous use of colour: ochre, red, various blues and white; the flesh tones and gold and silver details in the bishop's robes, is also notable. Vieira Lusitano had many sophisticated patrons. He often made use of allegory to introduce complex ideas into the works he was commissioned to paint.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.short_description: A late Baroque masterpiece influenced by Roman Painting. The scene, a contrast between the crowded, chaotic *scriptorium* of St. Augustine and the open classical cityscape, celebrates the author, bishop and Father of the Church St. Augustine stepping on the head of Heresy.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.initial_owner: Convent of Nossa Senhora da Graça, Lisbon
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.method_for_datation: Francisco Vieira Lusitano has signed and dated the picture.

86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.obtention: The convent and the order of St Augustine were extinguished and their assets confiscated by the Portuguese state in 1834. This painting was included among the objects that were confiscated and taken to the Fine Arts Academy Museum in Lisbon. When the museum closed, the collection transferred to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in Alvor Palace, Lisbon.

86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.name: *Death of St. Joseph*
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.description:
St. Joseph, the patron saint of a happy death and of Austria, became a principal subject of altarpieces around 1700. Many 18th-century artists embraced the subject, for instance Carlo Maratta in 1676, and it was adopted in around 1730 by Francesco Solimena, Giambattista Pittoni, Giambattista Piazzetta and Francesco Trevisani (Rome, S. Ignazio). Trevisani's work became a template for a number of pictures around the theme of St. Joseph, including Paul Troger's *Death of St. Joseph*. Korompay's Christ is very close to Troger's figure of Christ in the painting mentioned, especially in his mirror-image gesture. While in Troger's picture (and in the majority of the examples given) St. Joseph is lying on a bed, Korompay depicts him kneeling, supported by an angel. The motif was probably not the artist's own; he might have come across it in a reproduction print of an artwork from the Italian *Settecento*, a period that favoured motifs of drooping figures – whether they were saints or Christ himself – supported by angels. Pittoni employed this relationship between two figures in his *Ecstasy of St. Theresa*, Ricci in *Landscape with St. Mary Magdalene and an Angel*, and Trevisani in *Christ on the Mount of Olives*. The motif, however, can also be found in Troger's and Franz Anton Maulbertsch's early oeuvres.  
Korompay developed the composition of the main figures in a shallow foreground, placing them within a group of appealing gesticulating figures that provide a link with the second figurative layer represented by an angel and *putti*.  
The artist's segmented brushwork accentuates the illusion of the scene's ascending tendency. The palette features a rich scale of subtle warm shades blending into one another – from deep red to pale pink and mauve – making up the colour base of the picture. Korompay off-set this colour scheme with the pasty tones of lemon yellow and yellow-green seen in Joseph's gown, and the cold blue of Jesus' cloak, contrasting with his red undergarment.  
The painting was a template for the side altar altarpiece at the Parish Church of St. James, Brno, which is preserved there to this day.
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.short_description: St. Joseph, patron saint of a happy death, became a principal subject of altarpieces around 1700. The composition, based on paintings by F. Trevisiani and P. Troger, is the template for the side altar altarpiece at the Parish Church of St. James, Brno, preserved to this day.

8750b2ef-ed27-560f-a5b8-9740d8ab180c.name: 'A Palace Complex with Harem Gardens'
8750b2ef-ed27-560f-a5b8-9740d8ab180c.short_description:
The miniature, whose primary motif is a fantastic palace complex populated by a prince’s concubines along with their female servants and guards, in a way depicts the world as one great garden. In the distance we see the prince on the back of an elephant, and on the other side of the river all manner of activities are taking place that form a powerful contrast to the perhaps pleasant but enforced idleness of the women of the harem.  
  
The painting has been attributed to Faiz Allah, one of the many skilled artists who worked in the growing provincial courts at the time when the Mughals’ power was waning. He was familiar with the concept of European linear perspective, but he disregarded its laws, either deliberately or unintentionally.

888a6e61-03f6-52c9-9f55-414d518e18b8.name: Altar panel with Mary Magdalene and John the Baptist
888a6e61-03f6-52c9-9f55-414d518e18b8.description: In the Middle Ages, lepers were segregated from the rest of society in lazarettos. In Zurich, these were located outside the city walls, close to running water, and had a chapel of their own. The St. Moritz lazaretto, which was built on the Spanweid in 1364, housed destitute lepers. The chapel received a new altarpiece in 1506. The inside of the panels depicts St. Mary Magdalene in costly fashionable clothing with a pouch and a cutlery holder. She is holding an open pot of ointment and promising the lepers hope of healing.

88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.name: *Flügelaltar (Winged Altar)*
88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.description: The creator of this triptych, which was intended as a small travel altar for private prayer, was Jan van Eyck, the most important representative of Old Netherlandish painting. Characteristic features of his new artistic style are the miniature-like, extremely realistic rendering of details and the use of brilliant colours. Enthroned in the centre of the Basilica is the Madonna with her son, the infant Christ. Stretched out at her feet is a precious woven carpet. It has a rhombic pattern featuring eight-pointed stars set in circles. Its intense colours contrast with the muted hues of the ingeniously patterned floor tiles.

88ae5c68-848d-500a-a14d-08612e65ec15.name: *Traitor*
88ae5c68-848d-500a-a14d-08612e65ec15.short_description: During his frequent travels across the Balkans in the 1880s, Paja Jovanović acquainted himself with the ethnic makeup of the population, particularly in Lower Zeta (present-day Podgorica and the surrounding area), in the neighbourhood of Bar and in the border-lying area with Albania. It was here that Albanian, Serbian and Montenegrin inhabitants intermingled, so their characters, physiognomies, customs and vivid national costumes were entwined and fused into a whole in the paintings of Paja Jovanović. The image of capturing or trying a traitor, who, according to tribal custom, awaited sentencing, is certainly a noteworthy genre subject among those he selected to depict the life and customs of peoples in the Balkans. Unlike the first version, painted by Jovanović in 1885, this replica of The Traitor from the mid-1920s was painted in a more free-handed manner, in broad brush strokes and without insistence on details.

keywords: Genre Painting

890603fe-bd5e-5732-81cf-6842de790a60.name: *Der heilige Sebastian (Saint Sebastian)*
890603fe-bd5e-5732-81cf-6842de790a60.description: Antonello da Messina set the martyrdom of Saint Sebastian in Venice, as is evident from the waterways in the background or from the typical chimneys. As one of the largest European trading cities, Venice was a key hub for the exchange of exotic luxury goods. The two carpets depicted here would also have come to the lagoon city via trading routes. According to information provided by Stefano Carboni (2015), these were carpets from the Ottoman Empire. They were highly sought after as decorative items throughout Europe. Antonello da Messina painted this picture for the first altar of the Brotherhood of Saint Roch in the Church of San Giuliano in Venice. With its extremely steep perspective, the lifelike rendering of the flesh and the three-dimensional modelling of the nude figure, this work is a tour de force of early Renaissance painting.

89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.name: Dreams
89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.short_description: Vittorio Corcos is well known for his realistic paintings, especially his portraits of women. The woman depicted in the painting *Dreams* is Elena Vecchi, the daughter of a friend of the painter. Elena spent her adolescence at Corcos’ home. Presented in 1897 at the International Exposition Art of Florence, the portrait drew great attention and critical and public acclaim. Given the subject and its allusive title, it’s possible to see the image of a modern, proud and aware young woman that hitherto was represented only in literature: on the contrary, Corcos was able to masterfully represent it in painting. The scene was so admired that it was also reproduced on postcards. Corcos believed that while a portrait of a man has to show his social status, that of a woman always has to be appealing even if she is eighty years old.

89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.name: *All Saints*
89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.description:
A gathering of saints opens up into a view of the heavens, symbolising the Church Triumphant. The ancient festival of All Hallows dates to as early as 609. Saints of all nations glorify the Holy Trinity, together with angels. In the left foreground is St. Francis of Assisi, above him St. Anthony of Padua and St Florian with a flag. At the bottom in the centre is the patron saint of the country, St. John of Nepomuk, with a palm leaf, and two Moravian martyrs, Jan Sarkander and Jan Capistranus. At the bottom on the right is St. Norbert, a Premonstratensian saint, with a monstrance. Above him are St. Lawrence and St. Stephen holding stones, St. Andrew carrying a cross, St. Peter with a set of keys and St. John the Baptist with a cross and an inscribed ribbon. The central space is occupied by the Church Fathers St. Hieronymus, St. Augustine with a burning heart, and St. Gregory. Below Christ and God the Father on the left, are the Old Testament prophets, King David with a harp and Moses with the Decalogue. On the right is the Virgin Mary – model for the Church Triumphant – absorbed in prayer, and New Testament figures. Chains of figurative groups create several layers in infinite space, the illusion of which is enhanced by the contrasting foreground, the scale of colour and light effects, and the drapery by which the artist rhythmically joins the figures into a single spiral flow.  
This sketch-type painting was a study for a high altar painting in Milotice Parish Church near Kyjov. It is generally thought to be one of the best works of Josef Stern, an artist from Brno who came to Moravia from Graz having studied at the Vienna Academy and journeyed to Italy. He was court painter to the Dietrichsteins and was said to be among the most learned artists in Moravia. During his work in Kroměříž he met F. A. Maulbertsch, whose expressive style had a significant impact upon him.
89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.short_description: This sketch-type painting was a study for the high altar painting in Milotice Parish Church. The gathering of saints opens up into a view of the heavens, while chains of figurative groups make up several layers in infinite space to create an illusion that is enhanced by a contrasting foreground and the scale of colour and light.
89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.method_for_datation: Josef Stern’s authorship of the Milotice picture is upheld by 19th-century written sources; these references have been confirmed by modern style analysis.

8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.name: *1594 Burning of the Remains of St Sava*
8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.short_description:
The Serb Stevan Aleksić was a student of Nikolaos Gyzis at the Munich Academy of Fine Arts. The painting presented here shows him as a representative of academic realism, yet at the same time testifies to a significant gift for a striking play of light effects.  
In 1594, the Ottoman conquerors burned the remains of the Orthodox Christian saint Sava in Belgrade as a punitive deterrent against Serbian rebellion. St. Sava had played a pivotal role in the early 13th century. He was not just an Orthodox archbishop, but also the author of the first Serbian legal code. The foreign rulers thus asserted an important symbol of their power. In order to preserve the memory of the people's saint, a small church was first built on the site. Then, in 1935, the Serbian Orthodox Church prepared the ground for the St. Sava Cathedral, today one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world.  
It is no surprise that Aleksić made this choice of subject in 1912, considering the political backdrop of the time. It was the year when Serbia joined the Balkan League, which launched the First Balkan War against the Ottoman Empire.
8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.artist_deathplace: Modos, Kingdom of Serbians, Croats and Slovenians (nowadays in Serbia)
8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.author: Petar Petrovic
keywords: Historical Painting

8bd2685c-4d66-5da7-a343-412c67377856.name: *Birds in a Park*
8bd2685c-4d66-5da7-a343-412c67377856.short_description:
The source for this reverse glass painting has been identified as an oil painting of the same title by Flemish painter David de Coninck (or de Koninck), also known as Rammelaer. The glass painting was bought on the art market in 2016 as a work attributed to Anna Maria Franziska Pfyffer von Altishofen von Sonnenberg (1688–1757). However, the recently concluded restoration of this reverse glass painting uncovered a monogram and a date inscription previously obscured by the frame. Thanks to these elements, the work was re-attributed to her daughter, Maria Anna Pfyffer von Altishofen (1731).  
  
Mother and daughter came from a patrician family in Lucerne and were influenced by the painting style of Anna Maria Barbara Abesch (1706–73). Their reverse glass paintings have so far been little researched and were unknown to the public for a long time, as they remained in the private possession of the family.
8bd2685c-4d66-5da7-a343-412c67377856.obtention: Purchased from Stuker Auctions Bern in 2017

8d429717-91c1-58a8-8960-902c72d886d5.name: Fluidity
8d429717-91c1-58a8-8960-902c72d886d5.description: Mohammed Al Saleem’s Fluidity can be used to evoke the landscape experience of travel across the Arabian Peninsula. Although the work does not directly depict the Hijaz Railway or a specific railway journey, its abstract treatment of horizon, light, movement, and space can be connected to the visual impressions encountered by travellers moving through desert landscapes. The painting may help viewers imagine the atmospheric experience of journeys in the region, including those historically associated with the Hijaz Railway. Rather than functioning as a documentary image, the work offers a modern artistic reflection on landscape, distance, and the fluid perception of space in motion.

8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.name: *Patrona Hungariae sending St. Michael to Fight Against the Turks*
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.description:
In 1739, the Catholic convent in Sopron commissioned Martino Altomonte – a first-generation member of the Austrian High Baroque – to paint a picture for the high altar in St. Michael's Church. He passed the commission onto his son and collaborator, Bartolomeo. The Altomontes, who specialised in large church paintings, historical and triumphal compositions and frescoes, worked in the Italian Baroque tradition. Martino, although of Tyrolean stock, was born in Naples. He used an Italian version of his real name, Hohenberg, and first used his assumed name at the Polish court, where he painted compositions about the hereditary rulers. Later he was active in Vienna. His son, Bartolomeo, was a pupil of Solimena in Naples for two years.  
The vast altarpiece for Sopron echoes one of Francesco Solimena's (d. 1747) most popular creations, the fresco he painted in the San Domenico Maggiore in Naples in 1709. Bartolomeo continued to make use of details from Solimena's repertoire in his other works representing the Holy Trinity, St. Dominic with other saints, and the defeated heretics.  
In this picture, he adapted the subject to meet the wishes of his employers. The Virgin is represented as the patron saint of Hungary (indicated by the Hungarian coat of arms below her right hand), and the defeated are depicted as Turks wearing clothes and arms painted with pedantic accuracy. The impressive multi-coloured altarpiece, painted in the last years of the so-called Balkan campaign, illustrated for the faithful their release from Turkish rule – by then gradually becoming a reality – a notion suggested in the lower part of the picture by a battle scene, in the upper part by celestial rejoicing.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.short_description: In 1739, the Catholic convent in Sopron commissioned Martino Altomonte to paint a picture for the high altar in St. Michael's Church. He gave the commission to his son, Bartolomeo. Although this large altarpiece borrows motifs from Bartolomeo's teacher, Francesco Solimena's, painting in Naples the subject matter has a Hungarian actuality.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.method_for_datation: Through archive data, the signature and analysis of motifs.

8e7d84ba-9059-5c63-9b62-20ca88488664.name: *The Arrival of the Sclavonians in Venice*
8e7d84ba-9059-5c63-9b62-20ca88488664.short_description:
The veduta painted in reverse shows a sea harbour under a bright, open sky with galleys on the right being loaded by seamen. In the foreground, a pipe-smoking man sits on a pile of crates facing his fellow merchants. Next to gun barrels, rudders and anchors, two men in fashionable dress stand in conversation. A palace backdrop with strongly diminishing perspective rounds off the scene to the left.  
  
The source print for this work is drawn from Melchior Küssel’s (1622–83) *Iconographia* of 1671. The original picture, which carries no inscription indicating the location, is meant to show “the arrival of the Sclavonians in Venice with the prospect of the ships and galleys” after sketches by Johann Wilhelm Baurs (1607–42).  
  
In this interpretation, J.W. Baumgartner largely follows the template of the print, while simplifying the ornamentation of the galleys and palace friezes to improve the legibility of the reverse glass painting. Surprisingly, he also leaves out the dog sitting prominently in the foreground.

8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.name: *Nosocomium* \[Latin: Hospital\]
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.short_description: Silvio Rotta was introduced to painting by his father and, in his early years, produced mainly watercolours, genre compositions inspired by Venetian popular customs. In 1887, after an illness, the production of the artist underwent a radical change ad began to show social realism through the depiction of the insane. *Nosocomium* represents a psychiatric hospital where poor and sick were hosted and nursed. The scale of the canvas is accentuated by the diagonal of the benches and the path. The painting won awards at the 1895 Biennale of Venice and is now recognised as one of the most important works by Rotta. The scene’s realism offers a merciless analysis and public complaint about the patients’ living conditions. Caring of poor and sick was an important issue during the 19th century and a law to control hospitals and mental institution was discussed in those years.

8ff19610-7179-5f91-98b9-6a0065997c52.name: *Brieflesendes Mädchen am offenen Fenster (Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window)*
8ff19610-7179-5f91-98b9-6a0065997c52.description: This painting was the first in a series of quiet interior scenes incorporating only a few figures, which became characteristic of Vermeer's art from the late 1650s onwards. In particular, the theme of a woman writing or reading a letter is to be found in a number of his works; probably as a consequence of the vogue for letter-writing which had spread in Holland since the middle of the century. At the front of the scene is a carpet, decoratively crumpled so as to form a kind of barrier in front of the viewer. Similar Oriental carpets are to be found in many other paintings by Vermeer, suggesting that the Delft artist may have owned one himself.

908862b3-3d2c-5b16-93ce-f2a0873efd37.name: *Algiers port*
908862b3-3d2c-5b16-93ce-f2a0873efd37.short_description: Albert Marquet spent 1904 and 1907 in the company of Fauve, and in 1913 he lived in Tangier with Matisse and Camoin. Seven years later in 1920 he visited Algiers for the first time, and went on to spent a few months there every year henceforth. He also lived in Algiers for the duration of the Second World War. Marquet was friendly with most of the artists from the Algerian school, and exhibited his paintings in galleries in the centre of town. Many of his paintings were on the theme of Algiers' harbour. In 1939, his friends from the Salle Bordes organised his first solo exhibition. His style, which was characterised by the luminosity and clarity he saw in North Africa, was an important early influence on the Algerian painter Mohamed Temam.

keywords: Colonial city

90aa72df-4823-5e48-bcc0-2aa150e3f718.name: *The Suez Canal*
90aa72df-4823-5e48-bcc0-2aa150e3f718.short_description: Alberto Rieger studied at the Academy of Venice thanks to the patronage of the Baron Pasquale Revoltella, who commissioned him to create the painting showing the Suez Canal, which was presented at the Exposition of Fine Arts in 1864. The artwork is meant to celebrate the most important enterprise in Revoltella’s career; he personally travelled to Suez in 1861-62 to supervise the works for the construction of the channel that he promoted. The painting was executed by studying technical maps of the ground, sketches and photographs. The result is very close to the actual conditions of the city of Cairo, the pyramids and the delta of the Nile. The artist was commissioned also an open view of the city of Trieste by Pasquale Revoltella.

90f03bbd-926a-5169-8417-077f9aa6426e.name: Horse and Groom
90f03bbd-926a-5169-8417-077f9aa6426e.short_description: By the sixteenth century, a tradition existed in Iran for depicting royal horses either with or without their grooms for inclusion in albums. That these are prized horses is not only demonstrated by the fact that they have been singled out as the subject of a painting but because they are generally covered, as here, by decorative blankets and other elegant fittings. In addition, the well-dressed little groom in the painting wears the distinctive headdress associated with the early Safavid dynasty. The painting is ascribed in gold *nasta‘liq* to ‘Abd al-Samad, who produced several other works on the same theme in Iran and India. On the reverse are two calligraphies, one in white *nasta‘liq* signed by Sultan Muhammad Khandan and Hashim Mudhahhib (the gilder).
90f03bbd-926a-5169-8417-077f9aa6426e.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
90f03bbd-926a-5169-8417-077f9aa6426e.method_for_datation: As proposed by David Roxburgh, this painting along with several others, was once affixed to a page in an album complied for Bahram Mirza (Hegira 923-57 / AD 1517-49), brother of Shah Tahmasp (Hegira 930-84 / AD 1524-76), by the calligrapher Dust Muhammad in Hegira 951 / AD 1544-45. Some pages from the Bahram Mirza Album (in the Topkapi Palace Library) were removed and disassembled in the early 20th century.
90f03bbd-926a-5169-8417-077f9aa6426e.method_for_provenance: The style of the painting and the headdress of the groom are consonant with the early Safavid period when the capital was at Tabriz, where the court artist ‘Abd al-Samad, to whom the painting is ascribed, worked prior to joining the Mughal court in Hegira 957 / AD 1549.

914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.name: *St. Jerome*
914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.description:
The painting is signed (FED.BAROCIUS/URB. as PING. at) and first appears in the inventory of the Scipione Borghese collection in 1693. No details of the commissioning and dating of the work are known, but stylistic considerations allow us to place it in the final decades of the 16th century. This dating is close to his other painting in the Borghese Collection, *Aeneas' Flight from Troy* (inv.68) of 1598. Indeed the figure of the aged Anchises appears to be the same as the figure of St. Jerome, here intent on beating his chest with a stone.  
Federico Barocci, a renowned portraitist, was one of the most esteemed painters in Counter-Reformation Rome, and worked for the new religious congregations such as the Congregation of the Oratory founded by St. Philip Neri at the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella, and older orders such as the Dominicans at the Church of Santa Maria Sopra Minerva.  
This small painting, probably for popular worship, shows the saint in a cave, barely illuminated by the light of a candle in his lantern, cleverly placed along the right edge of the painting so as to direct the ray of light only on to the figure of the protagonist. His gaze, full of the spirituality that was a key feature of the great Urbino artist's paintings, is directed towards the face of Jesus nailed to the cross that he holds in his hand. Beside him lie objects of study and meditation: book, skull and hourglass, as well as the cardinal's hat that, along with the red cape around his body, recall the important role the saint played in the Church: translator of the Biblical texts (the *Vulgate*).  
The most recent restoration work carried out reveals a lion, from whose paw Jerome removed a thorn, sleeping like a cat in the background, indicating its absolute submission. Behind an opening in the rock, barely illuminated by the moonlight, is the Ducal Palace of Urbino, the artist's city of birth and probably where the work was painted.
914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.short_description: The painting, which in the background has the Ducal Palace of Urbino, the birthplace of the artist, shows St. Jerome a protagonist of the first cardinals of the church. He strikes his chest with a stone. The saint is in the dark, the only light coming from a small lamp. Lighting is part of the repertoire of the great Baroque era.
914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.name: *The Baptism of St. Augustine*
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.description:
The picture depicts the baptism of St. Augustine (354–430), together with his son Adeodat, by St. Ambrosius. Augustine, one of the Church Fathers and Bishop of Milan, influenced Christian doctrine from the Middle Ages to modern times with his writing.  
The base of the font is a beehive, a symbol of the church and an Augustine attribute. This picture was a template for a high altar painting in Jevíčko Church, commissioned by the Abbot of the Augustinian Monastery in Brno. It shares a number of motifs with *The Baptism of Prince Bořivoj* (Svatopluk?) by Josef Winterhalder Jr. (Silesian Provincial Museum, Opava). For example, drapery hangs in the foreground and columns form a vista into the temple space, with segmentation and illumination provided by a row of windows. The main light source in both pictures enters the scene through the vault to accentuate the central figurative motif, and although light is a unifying factor for both artists, for Havelka, it is assigned a different role. There are also similarities in the figurative aspects of both paintings, such as the standing and kneeling male figures in the foreground.  
These analogies may be explained either by a joint model (a print) from which both artists derived their motifs or by the fact that Havelka drew inspiration from J. Winterhalder Jr. The latter speculation is supported by the colour scheme of this design; silver-white and cold blue, colours that are not found in the rest of Havelka's oeuvre.  
The Museum of South Moravia in Znojmo holds another smaller version of Havelka's *Baptism of St. Augustine*. The Znojmo picture probably preceded the Brno design as its style appears more spontaneous and it is composed as a rectangle.  
Some of Havelka's pictures indicate that he was familiar with the work of F. A. Maulbertsch and J. W. Bergl, whose paintings were known in Havelka's native region. Similar compositions can be found in the work of C. Carlone and F. J. Spiegler (Merdingen).
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.short_description: St. Augustine, one of the Church Fathers, together with his son Adeodat, are baptised by St. Ambrosius. This is a template for a high altar piece in Jevíčko Church. Havelka’s style indicates that he was familiar with the work of both F.A. Maulbertsch and J.W. Bergl.
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.method_for_datation: J. I. Havelka’s authorship is illustrated by some of the figurative types, the light, sharp, segmented and vivid brushstrokes and the impasto application of white with a half-dry brush on the drapery crest. This attribution is confirmed by the transfer of the exhibited model into a larger format for the altar in the Jevíčko Church. The picture is ascribed to Havelka in both archive sources and in 19th-century literature.
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.obtention: The picture is on long-term loan from the Augustinian Abbey, Old Brno, which between 1956 and 1993 was administered by the Moravian Gallery, Brno.

91edb81f-fd53-5ef4-97f9-e53eac5c04c2.name: Saint Nicholas of Mozhaisk with Scenes from His Life
91edb81f-fd53-5ef4-97f9-e53eac5c04c2.description: Saint Nicholas, a 4th-century bishop from modern-day Turkey, is one of the most venerated saints in Russia. Stories of Saint Nicholas giving gifts to the needy and protecting children spread far and wide as people traveled or emigrated from Russia to other countries. In this icon, a full-length statue of Saint Nicholas is set in a *kiot* (wooden box). Painted panels with images of Christ and the Mother of God were once affixed to either side. In the center panel, Saint Nicholas originally held a sword in his right hand and a church in his left hand; both are now missing. The doors are illustrated with important scenes from the saint’s life.

9241049c-6cdf-5701-af96-c463f9661bf7.name: *Mosque Gate*
9241049c-6cdf-5701-af96-c463f9661bf7.short_description: Caliph Abdulmecid was interested in art in addition to administration. He opened many art exhibitions. He was chosen as honorary president of the Society of Ottoman Painters, which was founded in 1909, and he gave considerable financial support to the monthly journal published by the society. He took part in the Galatasaray Art Exhibitions with his paintings. For example, one of his paintings was accepted for an exhibition held at Galatasaray during the first years of the First World War. His works reveal him as a colourist and an accomplished portrait painter. Caliph Abdulmecid showed his paintings at the Viyana Exhibition, which was the first exhibition opened by Turkish painters in Europe in 1918.
keywords: Painting; orientalist Turkish painters

92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.name: *Still life with Fruits, Parrots and a White Cockatoo*
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.description: Jakab Bogdány left his native town, Eperjes (Prešov) in Upper Hungary, at a young age, going first to Vienna and then to Amsterdam where sources mention him in 1684, and where he may have pursued his studies. At any rate, Amsterdam, then the centre of middle-class genres, especially still life, was a perfect school for an artist just starting out. At first he painted flower and fruit pieces, which proved to be a lifelong experience for him, for the effect of the Dutch example remained discernible in this group of works throughout his life. Bogdány moved to London in 1688, and his technical expertise soon earned him fame among the English aristocracy. His most important clients were the royal family themselves. As a sign of both his artistic and social recognition, he gained English citizenship in 1700 and purchased an estate near London. He began to paint animal compositions, mainly exotic birds, designed for above doors or mantelpieces; most of these pictures are still in situ, found in their original settings in private collections in rural England. Influenced by the painter, Melchior de Hondecoeter, an outstanding Dutch master of bird paintings, Bogdány's are actually elegant genre pictures with exotic birds as actors against a background of elegant parks and classical buildings. He studied, and from the point of view of ornithology, accurately depicted, rare and colourful birds in the aviary at Windsor Park, which belonged to one of his main clients, Admiral George Churchill.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.short_description: Jakab Bogdány, born in Eperjes (Prešov), completed his studies in the Netherlands and became famous in England, becoming extremely popular with the English aristocracy. He was a master of the artistic form he practiced – still life paintings with birds – and worked for the royal family. The Hungarian state repurchased his splendid still life paintings with birds in the early 20th century.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and the date defined by stylistic analysis.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.obtention: Purchased from an English private collection in 1907; in the Museum of Fine Arts until 1974 and then transferred to the Hungarian National Gallery.

92b3efa7-036f-51ea-b0de-19ce7cc1ea97.name:
The Khaqan of Chin consults his advisors on the war with Iran  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Ismail II a
92b3efa7-036f-51ea-b0de-19ce7cc1ea97.short_description: The miniature painting “The Khaqan of Chin consults his advisors on the war with Iran” is from a dispersed illustrated manuscript of the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed by the Persian poet Firdausi ca. 1010. Shah Ismail II (r. 1576–77) commissioned the manuscript, following the examples of his grandfather, Ismail I, and father Shah Tahmasp, both of whom showed interest in Firdausi’s epic at one time during their reigns. Ismail II’s *Shahnameh* can be seen as a link in the chain of royal copies of the Book of Kings, after Shah Tahmasp’s spectacular manuscript and forming a bridge to the next period of royal patronage of the epic under Shah ‘Abbas (1587–1629). The manuscript was left unfinished upon Ismail II’s death. However, for a brief period, Ismail II’s atelier employed a number of artists who contributed to the illustration of the *Shahnameh*, including Siyavush, Sadiqi Beg, Naqdi, Murad Dailami and Mihrab. These artists did not sign their work, and attributions were probably made by the contemporary royal librarian. This painting is attributed to Siyavush, a Georgian slave at the court of Tahmasp who contributed an impressive total of 22 paintings to this manuscript. The scene shows the Khaqan and his advisors taking stock of the death of their champion Kamus-i Kashani in the recent battle with Rustam.

938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.name: *Remembrance*
938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.description:
A young woman in a coat lined with fur gazes out of the picture lost in thought while knitting a stocking and no longer listening to the sound of a violin. It appears that the music has reminded her of a past situation probably of a romantic nature. The violinist, sensing the woman's mental absence, remains in the background. A richly decorated mirror, glossy box, knitting basket, a broken string of pearls and precious sheet in the right-hand corner, make up a sentimental still life. The emotional air of the picture is accentuated by a landscape on the wall of an otherwise austere interior.  
Genre painting was once considered low and its subjects trivial if picturesque and amusing. With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century the subject of the actions and relationships between people, originating in 17th century Dutch burgher culture, became increasingly important. Pictures typically combined landscape, genre painting and narrative, with conversation often providing a vehicle for the “action”. Conversation scenes between men and women were particularly popular. They were largely based on the Dutch “fine style” promoted by Rembrandt's student Gérard Dou in Leyden, and shaped by the Scandinavian tradition of attention to detail and close observation of reality. While Rembrandt arrived at expressive internal visions, painters of the Leyden school mastered the techniques of representing different materials – later taken up by the Biedermeier. Pictures by the “*Fijnschilders*” were highly valued and sought after in their time. The word *fijn* encompasses more than the obvious notion of something fine, holding connotations including nice, refined, elegant, apt, precise and sensitive. In 18th-century Central Europe the style found admirers among both art collectors and painters. Braun, a member of the Vienna Academy, often transformed moralist paintings by the Dutch painters Frans van Mieris and Dou into pleasant pictures. He was also a competent portraitist, restorer and art dealer.
938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.short_description: With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century the subject of the relationships between people, originating in 17th-century Dutch burgher culture, became important. Braun, a member of the Vienna Academy, often transformed moralist paintings by the Dutch painters F. Mieris and G. Doue into pleasant pictures.

9409c213-6c6b-5cb6-a9b8-56b896a68058.name:
Two caracals and two deer  
Folio from a 1544–45 album assembled for Bahram Mirza
9409c213-6c6b-5cb6-a9b8-56b896a68058.short_description: This landscape shows two seemingly wild cats, or more precisely, caracals, observing two deer. The single-page drawing is attributed to Bihzad (ca. 1450–ca. 1535), who was one of the most famous artists of the Timurid period (1370–1507). It was once part of a folio mounted in the same *muraqqa’* (album) as Portrait of Hatifi the Poet (AKM160). Shah Tahmasp’s brother, Bahram Mirza, ordered the painter and calligrapher Dust Muhammad to complete this royal *muraqqa’* in 1544–45.\[1\] Although the second half of the inscription indicates Bihzad’s name, it is not a genuine signature. This was the traditional formula used to show respect for the master and to express modesty. Although these words and the surrounding illumination are a later addition, they may well reveal a close relationship between these two masters, Mawlana Wali and Bihzad, at the Herat court of Sultan Husayn Bayqara in the late 15th century.

963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.name: *Samson Imprisoned*
963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.description:
The painting is first mentioned as being part of the Scipione Borghese Collection in 1650, but no details of the date of its commission have survived. The date given (1590–1595) relates to the period in which Annibale, one of the founders of the *Accademia degli Incamminati*, was active in Bologna working on the decoration of the Palazzo Fava. It is possible that the naked figure of Samson is a draft, possibly a trial-run for one of the many monochrome nudes, often used as telamons, in the fresco decoration of noble Bolognese residences. Annibale continued his decorative work in Rome, where he worked on the famous Galleria di Palazzo Farnese. It was here, abandoned by his family, that he suffered from the depression that eventually killed him.  
The subject covers the biblical passage in the Old Testament (Judges 15, 12) in which Samson, imprisoned by Judas' men and about to be taken by the Philistines, is about to fulfil the Will of God. Invested with the Holy Spirit, he manages to free himself from his ropes and uses the jawbone of an ass to kill more than 1000 men. The painting does not show the action, but depicts the splendid, monumental muscular figure emerging from a dark background. We cannot even see his face, which thanks to its foreshortened position is hidden by shadow. All our attention is focused on the figure of the hero: the bent leg and the hands behind his back demonstrate the careful anatomical study undertaken by one of the greatest Baroque painters of the early 17th century.
963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.short_description: This work was probably painted in Bologna, a year before Annibale moved to Rome. It is actually more advanced than the decorations of Fava Palace in Bologna (the monochrome gods and frieze) and is closer to the classical forms of Palazzo Farnese. This painting is an example of the Carracci Academy.

964a5e5c-38f2-52e1-916c-5aa787fad913.name: "How a Braggart was Drowned in a Well"
964a5e5c-38f2-52e1-916c-5aa787fad913.alternate_name: Folio 33v from a Haft Paikar (Seven Portraits) of the Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami of Ganja
964a5e5c-38f2-52e1-916c-5aa787fad913.description: This miniature is an illustration of the most dramatic episode in the tale told by the Moorish princess in the Green Paviliion on Monday. While traversing the desert, Bashr, a good and pious man, and his bragging and evil-minded traveling companion come upon a jar filled with pure water sunk into the sand. After they have quenched their thirst, the selfish companion insists upon bathing in the water, in spite of Bashr's pleas against polluting it. The water turns out to be a deep well fed by a spring, and the heedless companion drowns. The tale ends happily for the deserving Bashr. The well is shown from two different perspectives to aid the viewer's comprehension of the scene.

97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.name: *Capture of Christ*
97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.description:
The canvas came to the Borghese collection due to the life annuity agreed in 1787 by Marcantonio Borghese with the sculptor Bartolomeo Cavaceppi, who gave a number of different pieces from his collection.  
The painting shows notable similarities to the *Capture of Christ* painted by Caravaggio (Dublin, National Gallery of Ireland), handling the same subject in a more balanced and composed manner. Bright armour that illuminates the scene contrasts with the central figure of Christ, dressed in red with his gaze lifted to the sky and his hands together, the only figure who is facing the viewer.  
The composition appears orchestrated with rhythm, suggesting a drama that is more theatrical than profound. The work shows the influence of the Caravaggesque language used by Bartolomeo Manfredi, focusing on a substantial simplification of the dramatic, artistic and moral implications of Merisi's painting. The Caravaggesque inventions thus became easier to spread and, reproduced in different contexts, they quickly became elements of “typical” painting, which in turn gave rise to the phenomenon of “Caravaggism”.  
This method, described as *Manfrediana methodus*, became widespread in Rome in the first decades of the 17th century, in particular among the ever-present colony of northern artists who came to new and prestigious commissions. Van Baburen, who worked with David de Haen on the decoration of a chapel in the Church of San Pietro in Montorio in Rome, was particularly able to mediate between the Caravaggesque lesson and the Baroque style of Rubens' work.
97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.short_description: The Dutch painter arrived in Rome around 1617 and assimilated the *chiaroscuro* of Caravaggio's style. He had an important role in establishing Utrecht as a stronghold of the Caravaggesque style.
97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

97c84e4d-b5db-513a-8e7d-cfa06d0b62ff.name: In Thee Rejoiceth
97c84e4d-b5db-513a-8e7d-cfa06d0b62ff.description:
This icon is based on a famous hymn written by 7th-century saint and theologian, John of Damascus, to the Mother of God. The hymn includes the following text:  
  
All of Creation rejoices in thee, O full of grace:  
the angels in heaven and the race of men,  
O sanctified temple and spiritual paradise,  
the glory of virgins, of whom God was incarnate  
and became a child, our God before the ages.  
He made thy body into a throne,  
and thy womb more spacious than the heavens.  
All of creation rejoices in thee, O full of grace:  
Glory be to thee  
  
In this icon, the images of the Mother of God and Christ are serene while the choir of saints and people depicted at the lower part of this icon are animated and immersed in song. The landscape, with green trees on a white background, is symbolic of paradise. The crowd at the bottom of the image represents humankind, and the domes signify the church.
97c84e4d-b5db-513a-8e7d-cfa06d0b62ff.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2013. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography; Angels

97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.name: *St. Joseph Calasanctius before the Virgin with Hungarian Pupils*
97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.description:
Felix Ivo Leicher arrived in Vienna from the Silesian town, Bílovec, with the support of the Piarist Fathers. He enrolled as a pupil at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna (his presence is documented from 1751) and won second prize in the academic competition of 1754, which made him a supported member of the Academy known as *Schutzverwandte*. He worked for a long time with Franz Anton Maulbertsch who remained a lifelong friend. His compositions, loose modelling, effective lighting and the ability to portray characteristic types undoubtedly betray the influences and ideas of Maulbertsch, although Leicher's approach is softer, weaker and without the expressive power, dramatic vitality or pictorial virtuosity of his master.  
Allegedly, a burgher of Tata commissioned this picture in Vienna for the Tata Piarists in 1767. Leicher worked in Vienna and was a pupil and protégé of the Piarists for whom he carried out a lot of work, undertaking several altarpieces on which he represented St. Joseph of Calasanctius (1556–1648) the founder of the Piarist order, who was canonised in 1767. In the main, these pictures refer to the educational activity of the order, depicting the saint with a circle of students as he recommends them to the patronage of Mary and the Infant Jesus whose figures appear among the clouds. This is the theme of the devout Tata painting *St. Joseph Calasanctius before the Virgin with Hungarian Pupils* depicting boys, dressed in contemporary Hungarian fashion, accompanied by St. Joseph and their guardian angel. The light, which draws the viewer's eye upwards, together with the expressive gestures and the sweet mild faces, call to mind the art of Leicher's master, Franz Anton Maulbertsch. The Tata picture is one of Leicher's most harmonious. He repeated this theme, in a larger format and different composition, in the Piarist Church of Brezno and paintings for altarpieces in the Piarist churches of Mikulov, Benešov and Nagykároly (Carei).
97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.short_description: A pupil of Franz Anton Maulbertsch, Felix Ivo Leicher worked on several altarpieces in Hungary (Vác, Martonvásár, and Besztercebánya (Banská Bystrica). The subject of this painting, commissioned by a burgher of Tata in Vienna for the Tata Piarists in 1767, is especially popular in Hungary because of its representation of children.
97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.holder: Hungarian National Gallery (on loan from the Kuny Domokos Museum, Tata)

9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.name: *Egyptian village scene*
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.short_description: Egyptian men and women are seen here in a town or village on the Nile. In the shade of an overhanging tree a market stall displays its wares, including paper lanterns and bread. At the stall behind, sugar cane is for sale. In the background is a mosque with a white minaret, though not distinctive enough to establish the scene's locality. Pilleau had visited Egypt in the winter of 1842-43 with Lieutenant Colonel George Everest (after whom Mount Everest was named) and two other companions, on their way home from India. On his return to England he published a set of twelve coloured lithographs, Sketches in Egypt (1845), which, like the better-known publications of Wilkie, Roberts and Owen Jones in the same decade, fuelled popular interest in Egypt and the Holy Land.
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: Economy; Market; sugar cane; Egypt; local product; rural life; eating; paintings

984e9648-99b0-5b96-b617-3bc4c6acf1fe.name:
The Night of Power (*Shab-i Qadr*)  
Folio from the *Khamsa* of Amir Khusraw Dihlavi (1253–1325)
984e9648-99b0-5b96-b617-3bc4c6acf1fe.short_description: This folio illustrates an episode from a five-part poem known as the *Khamseh* (Quintet), written in Persian between 1298 and 1305\[1\] by the prominent Indian poet Amir Khusraw Dihlavi. Known widely as Khusraw, he also wrote historical epics and romances, and worked under Turkish nobles in India in the late 13th century before entering the patronage of the royal court in Delhi, India.\[2\] Khusraw’s *Khamseh* (Quintet) evokes in its form and style a five-poem collection by the Persian poet Nizami (d. 1209). This copy of the *Khamseh* was produced near Delhi in the 15th century.\[3\] At some point in its history, its contents were dispersed. 'The Night of Power' (*Shab-i Qadr*) is the sole folio in the Aga Khan Museum Collection that originates from this dispersed manuscript.

986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.name: *St. Florian with a View of Jihlava*
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.description:
The picture is a typical example of a votive painting designed for a town environment. In their everyday prayers and pledges, people of the period turned to saints as protectors against the various perils of life. The promotion of saints in these roles was among the chief tools of re-Catholicisation in rural areas. St. Florian, protector from fire, was among the most worshipped. Here the saint is depicted as the protector of the town of Jihlava. Under Swedish siege during the Thirty Years' War the town suburbs were burnt down and the majority of the houses were destroyed. Only one-eighth of the Jihlava population survived.  
Jihlava is the oldest mining town of the Czech lands, renowned in the Middle Ages for its silver mines. Mining law was codified there for the first time in Central Europe, alongside municipal law. This formulary law became a template for a number of other mining towns. The economic development of Jihlava was facilitated by trade and crafts, especially weaving. In the mid-18th century, Jihlava was the second largest manufacturer of cloth in the Habsburg monarchy. This *veduta* is dominated by the Jesuit Church of St. Ignatius, with the parish Church of St. James in the background, on the right; the whole town is encircled by its walls. The square is lined with stone buildings, with arcades and a town hall that feature different types of vaulting. The regular ground plan of the right-angled network of streets with a square in the centre, the largest in Moravia, was defined by a building order made by King Přemysl Otakar II in 1270.  
The work of Václav Nosek has not yet been fully mapped as it has a relatively broad span. After settling in Jihlava in 1702, he worked for the town as well as for the Bishop of Olomouc (Kroměříž, 1711) and the Premonstratensian monastery in Louka u Znojma (*Education of the Virgin Mary*, side altar, 1712). In the 1720s, Nosek also produced templates for graphic illustrations of Episcopal prints.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.short_description: The picture is a typical example of a votive painting. The promotion of saints as protectors was among the chief tools of re-Catholicisation in rural areas. St. Florian, protector from fire, is represented here as the patron saint of Jihlava, one of the largest and wealthiest Moravian towns.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.initial_owner: Parish Church of St. James, Jihlava
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.method_for_datation: The archivist and historian Johann Peter Cerroni states that Nosek painted a picture of St. Florian with a *veduta* of Jihlava. By stylistic comparison the work may be associated with the painting in the Moravian Gallery.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.obtention: The painting from the Highlands Museum, Jihlava was transferred to the Moravian Gallery in Brno in 1962. It probably comes from the parish Church of St. James.

996c8cbc-b4e1-51f3-8b92-38f27863f839.name:
Bahram Gur hunts, slaying a lion and a lioness  
Folio from a dispersed copy of Firdausi’s *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
996c8cbc-b4e1-51f3-8b92-38f27863f839.short_description:
This folio from the dispersed copy of the “Freer” *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) depicts a classical Sasanian image of kingly power by illustrating an episode in the life of the Sasanian kings: Bahram Gur (r. 420­–38).  
Bahram V, “that great hunter”, is depicted in the midst of hunting lions (instead of the onagers—in Persian, gur—the source of his nickname). This adventure had begun with the king’s dispatching the male lion with an arrow to the heart; the beast roared mightily as it expired, alerting its mate. She herself lunged at Bahram, clawing him, but not preventing him from drawing his sword to slay her, too. As so often in Firdausi’s tales of Bahram, the hunt was followed by feasting and wine, and the inevitable inebriation. On this occasion, however, inebriation led to disaster and Bahram, aghast, prohibited the drinking of wine. But shortly thereafter, when wine also made possible the taming of an escaped lion, the king reversed his prohibition.
996c8cbc-b4e1-51f3-8b92-38f27863f839.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; Shahnama; Shahnameh; Freer; lions; hunting; animals
materials: Ink, opaque watercolour, gold, and silver on paper

999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.name: *The Prodigal Son*
999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.description:
The painting only became part of the Borghese collection in the 19th century, having earlier been mentioned in the collection of Prince Lancellotti, although the details of its commissioning are unknown. The canvas (1627–1628) reworks an earlier piece completed 10 years before for Cardinal Serra in Ferrara.  
The subject is taken from the parable of the prodigal son from the Gospel of St. Luke (15, 11–32). It tells of the forgiveness of a father who welcomes his youngest son after he has squandered his inheritance and been reduced to poverty and hunger. The scene in the canvas focuses on the moment when the aged father, shown in the centre of the composition, having found his son in such miserable conditions – rendered with marked realism in the rags tied around his waist – orders his servant to give him decent clothing. The boy is in fact busy putting on a clean shirt. The idea of a return to domestic intimacy is suggested by the closed window, in which the painter accurately renders the reflection of light.  
Guercino was able to portray this moment of family intimacy with great tenderness, in particular the detail of the dog resting his paws on the young man's lap, pleased that his master has returned home. The presence of the dog also enhances the symbolic idea of faithfulness often attributed to them, in accordance with allegorical custom in the Baroque tradition. This virtue is related to mercy according to the meaning given in the parable: the teaching that Christ imparted to his followers.  
Guercino, renowned as a painter of emotions, clearly shows here the father's forgiveness; he believed that his son was dead before he found him. From a stylistic point of view, we can see the influence of Venetian colourism, which Guercino had acquired on his trip to Venice in 1618, and which the artists blends together in a measured composition of classical inspiration.
999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.short_description:
In this painting, the colours are clearly influenced by Venetian art (Guercino stayed in Venice in 1618) combined with the more classical design of the figure.  
Guercino, renowned as a painter of “emotions” here clearly represents the forgiveness of a father who believing his son to be dead, is re-united with him.
999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

Prasad, S., *Guercino. Stylistc evolution in focus*, exhibition catalogue, San Diego, 2006, cat. n. 2, p. 11.

9a4260ca-f3e0-515c-9030-1c9a6bb50ae0.name: Oil Exploration
9a4260ca-f3e0-515c-9030-1c9a6bb50ae0.description: Abdullah Al Muharraqi’s Oil Exploration can be used to discuss Bahrain’s pioneering role in the oil history of the Gulf and the beginning of a wider regional transformation. Oil was discovered in Bahrain in 1932, making it the first country in the Arabian Gulf to enter the oil era. This discovery preceded similar turning points in neighbouring states, including Kuwait and Saudi Arabia in 1938, Qatar in 1939–1940, Abu Dhabi in 1958, and Oman in 1964. By showing workers around an oil well, the painting presents oil exploration not only as a technical or economic event, but also as a human and social process. The work is therefore useful for explaining how Bahrain’s early oil discovery marked the beginning of a new regional history, shifting Gulf societies from older economies based on pearling, maritime trade, and local labour toward oil-based modernisation, infrastructure, migration, and state formation.

9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.name: *St. Donatus*
9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.description: At the end of the 17th century, the Imperial General Count Donat Heissler commissioned an altarpiece painting for the church of the Holy Virgin in Buda to commemorate his release from prison. Heissler was commander-in-chief of the imperial army fighting in Transylvania and died in 1696 in a battle against the Turks. He commissioned and donated this altarpiece painting dedicated to the patron saint of prisoners and of the city of Buda from 1724, St. Donatus, who appears as a Roman soldier. Angels floating above the clouds hold the signs of his martyrdom:  a knife and a vessel full of his blood. Below, Castle Hill in Buda is depicted, its tempestuous landscape hints at St. Donatus' role in protecting it.
9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.short_description: A Baroque altarpiece painting of St. Donatus against the stormy landscape backdrop of Castle Hill in Buda.
9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.initial_owner: The Church of the Holy Virgin, Buda
9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.method_for_datation: By documents and the inscription on the painting

9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.name: Calligraphy mounted as album page
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.short_description:
The page with calligraphy and a floral border originally belonged to one of the albums compiled for the Mughal ruler Shahjahan (r. 1627-1658). The border consists of two overlapping tendrils with reduced foliage and a few stylised flower heads (peonies, lotuses and rosettes). With their golden contour lines and colours which allude to enamel, they are reminiscent of the pietra dura inlay work characteristic of the Shahjahan period. The tendril is enlivened by pairs of naturalistically rendered birds. It is this interplay of stylisation and naturalism that is important for the aesthetic appeal and visual pleasure.  
  
The four-line calligraphy is the work of Mir ʿAli Haravi. Born in Herat in 1476, he became a pupil of Sultan ʿAli Mashhadi after his basic education. After the capture of Herat in 1528 by the Uzbeks, Mir ʿAli Haravi, who had achieved renown, was brought to Bukhara, where he worked until his death in 1556.  
  
Among Mir ʿAli Haravi's great admirers was Shah Tahmasp's nephew Sultan Ibrahim Mirza (1540-1577), who owned several albums of the master scribe's calligraphy. Subsequently, the other great collector was Shahjahan and it is quite conceivable that some of his own Mir ʿAli calligraphies had formally been in the possession of Ibrahim Mirza.
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.initial_owner: Around 1987 Hashem Khorovani, Geneva, 1987-2004: art market, London
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.method_for_datation: The border is typicall for albums that once belonged to the Mughal ruler, Shajahan. Their dating was established by various scholars in the past decades.
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.method_for_provenance: Information from previous owner was provided by Christie's, where the object was bought in 2004.

9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.name: Persian miniature painting mounted as individual painting
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.alternate_name: Shepers and nobles greeting a prince and princess on horseback
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.short_description:
The miniature was executed with opaque watercolours and can most probably be attributed to the Safavid artist Muhammad Qasim. The rural scene is dominated by a princely couple on horseback being greeted by six men of different ages accompanied by four women. There are great stylistic and compositional parallels to the so-called Windsor-*Shahnama*, which was completed in 1648 and has been in the possession of the English Crown since 1839. It is suggested that the miniature was originally intended as an illustration for this manuscript of the *Book of Kings*.  
  
The border, richly decorated with arabesques, is quite probably the work of the Qajari illuminator Razi Taliqani. Such a conclusion has been drawn as it bares striking similarities to several comparable works by the artist that came onto the market in Paris and London at the end of the 19th/beginning of the 20th century. Such a proliferation of his work in Europe are the fruits born by his collaboration with Sidney Churchill (1862-1921) in the second half of the 1880s. As a civil servant of the British Empire, Churchill was then working in Iran. The mounting on thick cardboard speaks against its use as part of an album (pers. *muraqqaʿ*), which is corroborated by remnants of brownish paper on the reverse: a technique that was typically used to cover the back side of small Western picture frames, normally used for graphic art or photographs.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.dates: Hegira mid-11th century / AD mid-17th century (miniature); Hegira late 13th century / AD late 19th century (border)
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.method_for_datation: By comparision with similar dated works, esp. the so-called Windsor *Shahnama* of 1648 and its partly signed illustrations as well as similarly framed objects from collections in Paris and London.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.method_for_provenance: The object bears a stamp with the initials JR of the previous owner. There are similar objects with comparable borders in public collections in Paris and London which have been published and whose history is known.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.obtention: Purchased with funds of the Rietberg-Kreis
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.bibliography: Carey, Moya, *Persian Art: Collecting the Arts of Iran for the V&A*, London: V&A Publishing, 2017.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.artist: Attributed to Muhammad Qasim, died Hegira 1070 / AD 1659/60 (miniature); attributed to Razi Taliqani (border). Muhammad Qasim, active Hegira 1036-1070 / AD 1627-1659/60; Razi Taliqani, active Hegira before 1295-after 1327 / AD before 1878-after 1908/09.

9bc77e5d-4437-5fe8-99a0-82dd01f0d23c.name: He who Gives the Drink
9bc77e5d-4437-5fe8-99a0-82dd01f0d23c.description:
The artistic work entitled *He Who Gives the Drink* (1979) by the artist Mohanna Durra, which is currently on display at the Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts, is a prime example of Durra's unique combination of social realism and expressive modernism. The image portrays an elderly man attired in traditional Jordanian clothing, meticulously pouring a beverage (potentially water or tea) into a bowl. This unassuming, quotidian act evolves into a poignant meditation on human generosity, humility, and resilience. Durra's adept handling of light and shadow accentuates the man's weathered face and hands, lending spiritual gravity to an intimate, commonplace gesture.  
The warm colour scheme, characterised by ochres and browns, interspersed with soft blues, serves to evoke the arid yet luminous atmosphere of Jordan's landscape. The architectural background, which is not rendered with great precision, situates the figure within a traditional urban setting, reminiscent of the old quarters of Amman. The subdued brushstrokes and tonal gradations capture both the material texture of the scene and the emotional depth of the subject, characteristics that are indicative of Durra's mature style.  
This painting is indicative of the artist's sustained interest in the dignity of labour and the moral strength of ordinary people. Durra's depiction of such figures positions him within a broader movement in Middle Eastern modern art that seeks to honour local identity through everyday realism. His work *He Who Gives the Drink* engages in a profound visual dialogue on charity, endurance and the cultural ethos of giving that defines Jordanian and Arab life.
9bc77e5d-4437-5fe8-99a0-82dd01f0d23c.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts
keywords: drink; water; seller; man;

9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.name: *Paulines at Prayer*
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.description:
Their hands clasped in prayer, the Pauline brothers kneel on a paved balustraded terrace in a garden in front of a row of vases on pedestals with flowers in them, with palm trees behind them arranged in shortened perspective. The perspective of the composition, based on two intersecting linear scenes, shows the vision of the patron of the Paulines and St Paul the Hermit in a cave on the lawn. The vision of the Patron of the Paulines depicts the Virgin Mary, St. John the Baptist and the *Agnus Dei* with His leg curved around a flag with a cross.  
The use of perspective, accentuated by the row of classical pedestals, evokes an earlier style. The foreshortening decreases the depth of the scene and emphasises the initial pair of brothers and the first pedestal, which brings them closer to the front of the painting. The morphology and typology of the Pauline brother figures, St Paul the Hermit and the ornamental motifs on the vases together with the flowers in them, suggest a date of around 1740, being elements of the Baroque style. The work is in the style of the lay brother and painter, Ivan Ranger. Ranger, regarded as one of Croatia's greatest Baroque painters is most famous for his frescoes, which he painted in enormous numbers. Ranger was already a trained artist when he arrived at the Lepoglava monastery from Tyrol. The Pauline Order accommodated a number of lay brothers in their monasteries, comprising painters, sculptors, cabinet-makers and other masters of the arts and crafts. They produced works for the interiors of churches and monasteries in the monastery workshops.  
Lepoglava was the largest and most important Pauline monastery in Croatia. It was the main centre for educational and cultural learning, with a Latin grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates. The Paulines, together with the Jesuits, played a key role in promoting Baroque art and culture in Croatia.
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.short_description: The altarpiece, depicting the Pauline brothers in a garden praying in front of flower vases, is probably the work of the lay brother and painter Ivan Ranger, a trained artist who came from Tyrol. Ranger – who joined the Pauline Order in Lepoglava and remained there until he died – is regarded as one of Croatia’s greatest Baroque painters. He is especially famous for his frescoes, which decorate many Pauline interiors as well as other churches and monasteries. The Lepoglava monastery was the main centre of the Pauline Order. It had a grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates. Together with the Jesuits, the Paulines played a key role in advancing Baroque art and culture in Croatia.

9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.method_for_datation: From the Pauline Monastery estate, the attribution and date were established from the characteristics of morphology, style and typology.
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.obtention: The Diocesan Museum in Zagreb was founded in 1939 to safe-keep church artworks that for various reasons were in danger of devastation. This altarpiece was placed in the museum to preserve it.

9ca1f06f-1319-5325-a4ed-ef2842c72ef4.name: The Horse, the 50s spring
9ca1f06f-1319-5325-a4ed-ef2842c72ef4.description: Horses and camels were the traditional means of travel for nomadic and semi-nomadic groups in the Hijaz and Levant for generations. While the Hijaz Railway meant to industrialise the pilgrim travel from Damascus to Medina, quadrupeds remained an essential part of the pilgrimage route, as well as vital resources for the construction of the railway itself. While the railway served as a mechanised replacement for their labour, horses and camels remained vital to the path of the railway before, during and after its construction.

9d51960b-dfb8-57bd-aa72-d264926dc7d8.name: The Presentation of the Virgin Mary into the Temple
9d51960b-dfb8-57bd-aa72-d264926dc7d8.description: This icon shows the presentation, or entrance, of the Virgin Mary into the temple. The story derives from the apocryphal book of James and is one of the 12 major feasts of the liturgical year, celebrated on November 21. This icon shows the child Mary before the priest Zacharias, father of John the Baptist. Mary’s parents, Anna and Joachim, stand with a group of maidens who also serve in the temple. Mary is seen again in the sacristy being approached by an angel.
9d51960b-dfb8-57bd-aa72-d264926dc7d8.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2007. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Religious iconography; Biblical stories

9e1f46e4-2853-5545-a194-7e72c163548f.name: Concerning the punishment of an *Idolator* (one of the weak Muslims)
9e1f46e4-2853-5545-a194-7e72c163548f.short_description: This folio, along with two others in the Aga Khan Museum Collection (AKM89 and AKM40), comes from a manuscript assembled at the court of Shahrukh (d. 1447) and disassembled by the art dealer Émile Tabbagh in the 1920s and 30s. The manuscript’s content draws primarily from a world history prepared by Rashid al-Din (d. 1318) for the Mongol Ilkhan Oljeitu in 1307. It is not a simple copy of Rashid al-Din’s work, but rather a hybrid manuscript with a tangled history made even more complex by its dispersal. This folio reveals one of the abiding mysteries of the manuscript: here, similar to a group of other dispersed folios, an illustration appears in place of a block of missing text.
9e1f46e4-2853-5545-a194-7e72c163548f.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; Manuscript
materials: Ink, watercolour, and gold pigment on paper

9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.name: Miniature 'Wine-Server' ('Portrait of a Young Man')
9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.short_description: According to the inscription in the lower left corner of the composition, the author of the painting is Reza Abbasi, the most prominent Iranian artist of the AD 17th century. The founder of the new style of painting and the head of the famous Isfahan school, Reza Abbasi has departed from the bright decorative colours of the classic Persian miniature and turned to a more restrained and unusual palette. He chose a thin and sensitive calligraphic line as his main means of expression. Wine-server (Persian: *saqi*) - a young man who served at banquets, pouring wine to guests. A flask in a form of a gourd in his right hand testifies to his role. The man is dressed in a malachite green robe. An orange silk scarf is untied and carelessly thrown over his shoulders. His full face, dreamy staring eyes, curls falling down on cheeks, small gentle hands and graceful posture, the smooth curves of which seem to echo the flexible lines of plants - all correspond to the traditional type of an effeminate youth-*saqi*.
9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis and inscription reading by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1926, origin and date).
9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection.
