9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.name: *St. Peter Freed from Prison*
9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.description:
The work describes an episode in the life of Peter told in the Acts of the Apostles that took place during the unbridled persecution exercised by Herod. Imprisoned and guarded by two soldiers, the apostle is freed by an angel, who invites him to get up and guides him to safety outside the city walls without anyone seeing him. This miraculous feat is described using a basic but unusual composition, eliminating all characters other than the two protagonists. Foreshortening at the bottom of the painting brings the feet and the hand chained to the stump into the foreground, and the low viewpoint highlights the sudden appearance of the angel, who practically inspires in the viewer the same wonderment we see on the face of the saint, ragged and tired, on being woken so unexpectedly.  
In the 1790 inventory of the Borghese collection, the painting was described as the work of “Monsù Valentin”. The piece reworks some ideas typical of Caravaggism, such as realism based on a few details and the use of light as a tool for building the scene. The angel stretches out towards Peter and, rather than floating, appears to rest on a thick blanket of clouds, as if he is actually ready to lift up the old apostle. The Lombard artist's training was somewhat fragmented, taking him first to Rome, then to Venice, before joining Francesco Albani, one of the painters who best represents Bolognese classicism. Around the middle of the century, in 1656 and 1657, he also worked with Pietro da Cortona on the decoration of the Gallery of Alexander VII in the Quirinal Palace, becoming, along with Pietro Testa (“il Lucchesino”) and Nicolas Poussin, one of the main exponents of the Neo-Venetian styles of Roman Baroque painting.
9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.short_description: The painter – a follower of Caravaggio – was first influenced by Francesco Albani from Bologna and later by Pietro da Cortona. The lowered point of view highlights the sudden descent of the angel, inspiring in the viewer the same wonderment that can be seen on the face of the saint, who is ragged and exhausted in his sudden awakening.
9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.name: *Presentation of the Child in the Temple*
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.description:
The production of knotted carpets in Portugal has been documented since the 14th century, mostly in association with the Moorish community. With the expulsion of the Muslims and Jews in 1496 by King Manuel I (1469‒1521; r.1495‒1521), the Portuguese carpet workshops were inevitably abandoned and the manufacturing tradition was lost. Aside from local production, Portuguese consumers imported high-quality items as well. This ensured the supply of luxury goods to the wealthier clientele. Despite that Spanish carpets were esteemed throughout the 15th century, according to representations in paintings, by the second quarter of the 16th century, they were replaced by Ottoman carpets produced in the regions of Anatolia and Uşak.  
Although, surprisingly, there are no surviving examples of this type of carpet in Portugal, its presence in paintings, as well as in other documentary sources such as in inventories, confirms their presence in Portuguese interiors, thus enabling us to identify the patterns and original colours of the imported carpets. This is the case with this painting, where a Turkish carpet, placed on the floor near the altar, displays most probably a “small-pattern Holbein” design: it comprises a repeated pattern of alternating quatrefoils and octagonal medallions, with *kufic* script motifs represented in detail on the red border.
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.obtention: Transferred from the Convent of Santa Joana, Lisbon, Portugal, at an unknown date

a15b7e00-538c-5aa8-a826-c4febf856606.name: In the Desert
a15b7e00-538c-5aa8-a826-c4febf856606.short_description: Cesare Biseo was a decorator and a realistic painter. He was sent to Egypt in 1870 to decorate the Theatre of the Opera in Cairo, where the painter Stefano Ussi also was working. In 1877 Biseo took part in the diplomatic delegation in Morocco with Ussi and de Amicis. Biseo’s painting *In the Desert* shows an exotic Verismo style of painting and is an example of the high status oriental paintings had in those years with the rise of Italian interests in colonialisation. The painting was bought by the Italian state in 1890 and displayed in the National Gallery of Modern Art of Rome in 1907.

a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.name: *The Saints Mark, St. Anthony Abbot and St. Sebastian*
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.description: The painting was commissioned to Ubaldo for the church of St. Mark in Vigorso di Budrio (Bo). Saint Mark, clad in bright red is shown looking for inspiration for the Gospel, next to him is a lion, the emblem of the saint. In the foreground St. Sebastian is tied to a column, his body pierced by an arrow while an angel is handing him the palm of martyrdom. Nearby is St. Anthony Abbot with his classic attributes; the fire, the bell and the pig. The composition is very simple and clear. The light comes from one direction and symbolises the light of God to which the evangelist points. The painter is inspired by the great Bolognese school, in particular Guercino and Ludovico Carracci, and to the Venetian school.
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.short_description: The painting shows St. Mark writing the gospel, St. Sebastian tied to the column and St. Anthony the Abbot.
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.holder: Church of St. Gervasius and Protasius
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.method_for_datation: The step in the lower middle is inscribed “U.G.F. 1773” (Ubaldus Gandulfius fecit 1773).

a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.name: A richly dressed woman
a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.short_description:
This painting of a richly dressed woman is traditionally associated with the painting of a Persian noble. Contrary to him, it has not yet been possible to determine her ethnic origin.  
  
The way the paint is applied in multiple layers as well as the strong Chiaroscuro clearly reveal that the painter was trained in Europe. This is also indicated by the fact that the painter mixed the wet colours directly on the canvas and executed the highlights in thick lead white. Equally European is the sombre palette and a preference for shaded hues. They stand in stark contrast to the Persian predilection for pure, luminous colours.  
  
These two paintings are possibly two of the extremely rare, if not the only, known examples of pictures painted by European artists in Persia. We know from the sources that several painters from Europe, especially from the Netherlands, worked in the 17th century for the Shahs.
a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.dates: Hegira Late 11th century / AD Late 17th century
a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.method_for_datation: By comparison with European painting techniques.
a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.method_for_provenance: Information from previous owner was provided by Christie's, where the object was bought in 2013.
a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.obtention: Acquisition with funds from bequest of Gabriele Louise Aino Schnetzer

a17d79fa-1dd1-53bc-a161-d603dcc4f9c6.author: Axel Langer

a25c5878-db0c-5a19-af52-c86b77db879b.name: Pencase
a25c5878-db0c-5a19-af52-c86b77db879b.short_description:
Like Muhammad Baqir (active Hegira 1160s-1204 / 1750s-1790), Muhammad Sadiq is one of the best-known Persian artists of the 18th century. He was also a pupil of Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf (active Hegira ca. 1134-1190 / AD ca. 1722-1777). The pen box is signed with his typical formula “*ya sadiq al-vaʿd*” that alludes to the painter’s namesake, the sixth Shiʿi Imam Jaʿfar al-Sadiq.  
  
The lid and side wall of the pencase are painted with four figurative scenes starring three young women led by what appears to be a kind of princess. It is likely that the scenes tell a single story. It is not clear, however, whether they illustrate a literary work or whether they bear a philosophical meaning. It seems at least that the young women are on a kind of spiritual journey, leading from worldly pleasures to mystical fulfilment.  
  
Similar to Muhammad Baqir, Muhammad Sadiq quotes here from works by Muhammad Zaman (active Hegira ca. 1072-1105 / AD ca. 1662-1694) and ʿAliquli Jabadar (active Hegira 1059-1086 / AD 1649-1675) as well as Zaman’s brother Haji Muhammad (active Hegira 1084-1124 / AD 1673-1712).
a25c5878-db0c-5a19-af52-c86b77db879b.method_for_datation: The artist signed and dated his work.
a25c5878-db0c-5a19-af52-c86b77db879b.method_for_provenance: Information of previous owner was provided by Sotheby's where the object was bought in 2019.

a25c5878-db0c-5a19-af52-c86b77db879b.author: Axel Langer

a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.name: "Amr has the Infidels Thrown into the Sea"
a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.alternate_name: Folio from a Khavarannama (The Book of the East) of ibn Husam al-Din
a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.description: This painting, with its vibrant color palette and lively action, is taken from a manuscript of the Khavarannama (Book of the East), a gathering of tales relating the adventures of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. These mostly imaginary accounts of the exploits of 'Ali and his companions against demons, dragons, and kings were composed in emulation of the great Persian poet Firdausi’s Shahnama, but have the important religious figure of 'Ali as their main protagonist.

a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.name: Sufi assembly
a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.short_description: The miniature features a nocturnal landscape with a dervish surrounded by six male characters wearing costumes typical of the age of Shah Abbas I (1588-1629). The exquisite finesse of the drawing is enhanced by the subdued colour range, the gold highlights and the beautiful *nasta'liq* calligraphy of the Persian verses: ‘Don’t drink the wine-cup, for every drop is a king’s blood,/Don’t listen to the music, for every tune is just a tale of sorrow./The night has fallen; the drunken feast has neither lamp nor candle; /Join us, for the gathering of maids most fair is pleasant.’ (Translated into English from the Romanian version by Viorel Bageacu, 1987). The verses, as well as the image, are replete with Sufi symbolism.

a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.name: *The Coffee Shop*
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.short_description: Coffee shops in the Near and Middle East were regular meeting places for men, who could while away hours chatting, playing domino, smoking and – crucially if dangerously – talking politics. In early 20th century Cairo as elsewhere, spedific cafes became important hubs for social and political discourse.This painting shows a traditional Near Eastern street café. Customers are sitting on long benches in front of its wooden openwork facade, A waiter with a red fez carries a brass coffee pot (dallah) and a tray. Behind him, through the wooden screen, the preparation area, in which the coffee is made, can just be seen on the left. A man wearing a white turban and blue gown, perhaps the proprietor, looks out on the right. All present are captivated by a carpet seller, who is standing in front of the cafe, offering up his wares.

a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: dallah

a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.name: *Ecce Homo*
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.description:
The work may have been commissioned directly from the artist by Cardinal Scipione Borghese. It is first documented in his collection in 1613. In the canvas, the story of the Passion of Christ is transformed for the viewer into a subject of meditation. Light suffuses the body of Christ in a diagonal line high-lit by the hem of the red cloak held up by the executioner. We see the regal symbols that Christ was forced to wear, the crown of thorns, the reed sceptre and the red cloak as signs of mockery and derision, with which the Gospels tell us Pontius Pilate presented his prisoner to the crowd with the words “*Ecce homo*” (“Behold the man”). Along with the column (representing flagellation), and hammer and nails, which anticipate the crucifixion, the scene is transformed from a historical account into a meditative subject designed to inspire among the faithful feelings of compassion and shared pain with the martyr. The executioner, awkward and unrefined next to the beauty of Christ's face, is placed in the darkness – both literally and spiritually – as one who does not recognise the divinity of the Son of God. The capacity to inspire reflection on the dogma of faith while simultaneously engaging the viewer emotionally is the basis of the ethos of the Counter-Reformation. Communication of feelings and affections was also fundamental to the development of Baroque art.  
In this piece, Giovanni Baglione emphasises the dramatic sense of the scene through the use of *chiaroscuro* developed by Caravaggio and his followers from their experiments undertaken in Rome in the first years of the 17th century. On the other hand, Christ's face, gazing towards the heavens in a mood of total acceptance of divine will, reflects the more delicate and idealised style of the Carracci school, in particular Guido Reni.
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.short_description: The theme of derision is shown in comparison with those who don’t recognise Christ as the Son of God, sent to earth to save mankind. The scene sends a very clear message against the Reformation. Although the subject is intended for meditation, its theatrical style is a prelude to the drama expressed in Baroque art.
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

a5ace29e-e1bf-5a09-9df7-66c7741b63b4.name: *Odalisque*
a5ace29e-e1bf-5a09-9df7-66c7741b63b4.short_description: Sepia drawing representing odalisque, based on an epoch engraving. Painted by Joaquim José de Oliveira, Victor Rousseau’s disciple and master of painting and drawing of the Vista Alegre Factory, between 1869 and 1881.
keywords: Arts and Crafts; Daily utilitarian ware; Portugal; Vista Alegre; Factory; Orientalism

a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.name: *The Grand Bazaar*
a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.short_description: Amadeo Preziosi often presented genre scenes from Istanbul in his unique style. Specifically, he incorporated diverse scenes from the Bazaar in a number of his paintings. This venue, particular to Istanbul, has been of great interest to western artists, and in Edmondo De Amicis’s words “is not just a building but a town”. The Grand Bazaar, which housed shops for a wide range of commercial goods and catered to almost all of the needs of customers, offered an incredible visual richness and diversity to the western artist. A reflection of this opulence is also evident in Preziosi’s painting, which includes numerous details from daily life.
keywords: Amadeo Preziosi; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

a6e38d56-3857-5b4e-a7be-06bb9cacae78.name: *The Petition Writer*
a6e38d56-3857-5b4e-a7be-06bb9cacae78.short_description: Osman Hamdi focused on dilemmas such as East and West, love and hate, life and death. While stylistically reminiscent of western Orientalist painters, his works reflect a more nuanced appreciation of Ottoman society and culture. He also gave importance to details while reflecting the colourful scenes of Turkish culture, traditional architecture, Ottoman fashion and domestic and social life of the women in the Ottoman Empire. And it’s obvious that he is the first painter who used human figures in the western style.
keywords: Painting; Osman Hamdi Bey; orientalist Turkish painters

a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.name: *Mourning over the Dead Christ*
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.description:
In 1592 the Metropolitan Chapter of the Cathedral of Milan contracted with Federico Barocci for an altarpiece. The *Mourning over the Dead Christ* was officially commissioned for the altar of Saint Giovanni Buono in 1600. Unfortunately, the painter was already quite old, ill and had many personal problems. When he died, in 1612, the work was left unfinished.  
The great picture was carried to Milan in 1628 to be completed by a different artist. This project was blocked by the plague of 1630, and in 1739 the painting was finally exhibited on the altar without any further intervention. In 1763 it was moved and sold to the abbot Antonio Magnani who donated it the Municipality of Bologna.  
Many surviving drawings document the long and careful work in the creation of this painting. The figures are all gathered around the dead body of Christ, who is lying in the lower portion of the painting. The wide architecture above, which was planned to have been occupied by two flying angels, is empty and barely sketched. The dead body of Christ is sometimes compared to the *Pietà* painted by Annibale Carracci. Shining colours are reminiscent of the mannerist style and the figures express a strong emotional tension that was intended to be felt by the faithful watching the picture. This is following the rules of Counter-reformation art policy.
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.short_description: This great piece was commissioned in 1600 by the Chapter of the Cathedral of Milan to Federico Barocci. He is known as one of the most significant Italian painters working between the movements of Mannerism and Counter-reformation. When he died, in 1612, the work was not finished. The architecture in the background is barely sketched, the figures gather around the body of the dead Christ in full light, the focus is on strong emotional turmoil.
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.initial_owner: Chapter of the Cathedral of Milan
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.method_for_datation: The complex story of this patronage is documented by the annals of the Cathedral of Milan; we learn that the artist received 200 scudi on the 22nd April 1600. However, in 1608 he had only made a preparatory cartoon and some sketches. When he died the work was left unfinished.
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.obtention: The painting was bequest to the library of the Archigimnasium in 1811 by the abbot Antonio Magnani; deposited in the Pinacoteca Nazionale it was returned to the Municipality of Bologna in 2002. It is now exhibited in the Collezioni Comunali d'Arte.

a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.name: Rustam Slaying the White Div
a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.short_description:
Rustam is one of the most popular heroes of the *Shahnama*, the Book of Kings. In it, Ferdausi tells how Rustam must perform seven heroic deeds, the last of which is to kill the White Div and cut his liver out of his body to heal the blind Shah Kai Kavus. Rustam receives help from his hostage Olad, whom Rustam has tied to a tree, revealing to Rustam the appropriate time to defeat the White Div.  
  
The iconography of the scene has remained more or less the same over the centuries, it is also one of the most frequently illustrated episodes from the *Shahnama*.  
  
Several characteristic features of this page speak for its origin in Shiraz. Attributes, such as the extension of the illustration beyond the type area, the nebulous outline of the lines of text in interspersed flowers on gold, as well as the inclusion of other figures not mentioned in the text, all strongly indicate that its provenance was the Shiraz School.  
  
In the Safavid period, Shiraz could already look back on a long tradition of painting. This creative cultural heritage was reinforced in the late 1560's by a commercial boom in manuscript production, resulting in illustrations visibly gaining in quality and converging with courtly painting in Qazvin and Mashhad. The development of the Schiraz School specifically, which expanded so magnificently in the period from 1570 to 1590, is probably also connected with Prince Muhammad, who was governor of Shiraz from 1572 to 1578 before ascending to the Persian throne as Ismaʿil II.
a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar works from Shiraz whose time of production could be established through historical facts and stylistic features.
a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.method_for_provenance: Information obtained from previous owner was provided by the gallery where the object was sold in 2008.
a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.obtention: Acquisition with funds of the Rietberg Kreis
a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.bibliography: Lale, Uluç, “Selling to the Court: Late Sixteenth-Century Manuscript Production in Shiraz”, *Muqarnas*, 17 (2000): 73-96.
a909a05f-2311-5dcb-acdb-59719da1889b.author: Axel Langer
materials: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper

a9ca7e9d-4c7b-5b08-a2ab-9b56d4a9868f.name:
Isfandiyar kills the Simurgh  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Ismail II
a9ca7e9d-4c7b-5b08-a2ab-9b56d4a9868f.short_description: The miniature painting “Isfandiyar kills the Simurgh” is from a dispersed illustrated manuscript of the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed by the Persian poet Firdausi ca. 1010. Shah Ismail II (r. 1576–77) commissioned the manuscript, following the examples of his grandfather, Ismail I, and father Shah Tahmasp, both of whom showed interest in Firdausi’s epic at one time during their reigns. Ismail II’s *Shahnameh* can be seen as a link in the chain of royal copies of the Book of Kings, after Shah Tahmasp’s spectacular manuscript and forming a bridge to the next period of royal patronage of the epic under Shah ‘Abbas (1587–1629). The manuscript was left unfinished upon Ismail II’s death. However, for a brief period, Ismail II’s atelier employed a number of artists who contributed to the illustration of the *Shahnameh*, including Siyavush, Sadiqi Beg, Naqdi, Murad Dailami and Mihrab. These artists did not sign their work, and attributions were probably made by the contemporary royal librarian. In its bottom left-hand corner, this painting is attributed to Siyavush.
a9ca7e9d-4c7b-5b08-a2ab-9b56d4a9868f.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; miniature; painting; minature-painting; manuscript; shahnameh; Shahnama
materials: Opaque watercolour, gold, silver and ink on paper

a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.name: *Maria Varasdiniensis*
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.description:
The figures of the Virgin Mary and Child Jesus are hieratically positioned front-on. Beneath a textile canopy edged with labrequin, the ends of the drapes lifted and knotted, both wear conical cloaks, white wigs and crowns. At the top of the canopy is a gold ring with rays, upon which is the dove of the Holy Spirit with outspread wings. The ornamentation on the cloaks of both Mary and Jesus are motifs from the beginning of the 18th century, mostly acanthus and other foliate scrolls. In the middle of each of their cloaks is a painted gold heart within which are their individual monograms. On the other hand, the faces and wigs of both Mary and Jesus already show Rococo characteristics.  
The representation of Mary and Jesus in conical cloaks is a votive scene that first appeared during the Baroque period. More usually stiff cloaks scattered with floral motifs and adorned with jewellery such as chains and pendants hang over the cloaks like garlands.  
One of the foremost characteristics of the Pauline order was its veneration of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which resulted in her central place in their iconography. In 1672 there were 80 churches dedicated to the Virgin Mary.  
This votive painting of Mary, which hung above the pulpit in the nave of Lepoglava church, was probably intended for Varaždin as the Virgin Mary was its patron.
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.short_description:
A crowned Mary and Child Jesus stand front-on under a textile canopy. They both wear white wigs and conical cloaks richly decorated with gold hearts within which are their monograms. This votive-type Virgin and Child first appeared during the Baroque period.  
The Pauline Order especially revered the cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary and her portrayal had a central place in their iconography.
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.holder: Diocese Museum of the Zagreb Archdiocese
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.obtention: The painting came from the former Pauline Church in Lepoglava, Hrvatsko zagorje and gifted to the Diocesan Museum in Zagreb in 1940.
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.bibliography:
Baričević, D., *Bogorodice u zvonolikom plaštu* (Madonna in a Bell-Shaped Cloak), Zagreb, 1983.

a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.author: Nela Tarbuk
keywords: Lepoglava; Pauline Order; conical Madonna; floral decoration; vegetal decoration; jewellery; zoomorphic imagery; Christian themes

aa631f7f-3808-586d-b316-c8c2c17e2045.name: The Royal Doors
aa631f7f-3808-586d-b316-c8c2c17e2045.description:
In Russian Orthodox churches, the sanctuary, which contains the altar, is separated from the nave by a wall or screen called an iconostasis. A typical iconostasis has three doors. The “angel doors” are located on the right and left sides and sometimes depict the Archangels Michael and Gabriel. The “royal doors” are located in the center of the iconostasis and can only be entered at certain points during liturgical services by ordained clergy members. The use of the royal doors varies by local tradition, but they are typically opened during the reading of the Gospel and distribution of the Eucharist. The royal doors typically depict the Annunciation while the four evangelists are shown on four separate panels.  
This set includes the symbol for each evangelist: Saint John is shown with a lion, Saint Luke with an ox, Saint Matthew with a man and Saint Mark with an eagle, following the famous interpretation of Saint Irenaeus (c.120-202). The symbol for Saint Mark is different than the one depicted in The Mother of God of the Burning Bush icon in this collection, reflecting a difference in the interpretation of biblical texts by the iconographers for each image.
aa631f7f-3808-586d-b316-c8c2c17e2045.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2013. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Virgin Mary; Religious iconography; Angels; Allegorical and symbolical figures

aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.name: *Ecstasy of St. Catherine of Siena*
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.description:
The painting, which because of its small size was undoubtedly intended for private worship, is first listed in the Borghese Collection in 1790. The canvas shows St. Catherine of Siena, who belonged to the order founded by St. Dominic, who died in 1380 and was canonised in 1461.  
The saint is shown with her typical attributes: the crown of thorns, heart, crucifix and lily, plus a representation of the stigmata, which she received on 1 April 1375. The luminous background highlights the figure, which is arranged along a diagonal line inspired by the work of Correggio.  
The two angels that hold the saint emphasise the spirituality of her ecstasy, nonetheless returning her to reality. The work is rendered with great sensitivity by Agostino (who founded the renowned *Accademia degli Incamminati* in Bologna with his brother Annibale and cousin Ludovico).  
Agostino's work uses the natural world as a model. The canvas, usually dated to the final decade of the 16th century, is perfectly consistent with the dictates imposed on artistic production in the Counter-Reformation, stating that representations of saints must inspire compassion, the spirit of emulation and prayer among the faithful.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.short_description: The canvas shows the ecstasy of St. Catherine of Siena, who belonged to the Dominican order. Here the saint is shown with her usual attributes, similar to the Passion of Christ (crown of thorns, wounded heart, crucifix and – surprisingly – the stigmata that Catherine received in 1375). Agostino Carracci, who founded the renowned *Accademia degli Incamminati* in Bologna with his brother Annibale and cousin Ludovico, is one of the exponents of the naturalism movement, in place of the extreme realism of the art of Caravaggio and his followers.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.obtention: Acquired by the Italian State in 1902.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.bibliography: Della Pergola, P., *Galleria Borghese. I Dipinti*, I, Rome, 1955, n.11, pp. 18–19.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.copyright: Copyright image: Archivio fotografico Soprintendenza Speciale PSAE e Polo Museale della Città di Roma.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.author: Sofia Barchiesi
keywords: Religious orders; Dominicans; academy; religious object; Christian themes; Counter-Reformation; devotional painting

aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.name: Altarpiece: The Builder Shows King Ladislav (St. Ladislaus) the Drawings of the Cathedral
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.description:
The large wooden winged altarpiece of St. Ladislav (St. Ladislaus) held a cycle of 12 paintings depicting the Life of St Ladislav; 10 of them are extant today. The winged doors, painted on both sides with eight surfaces, closed off the main niche of the retable.  
Hungarian-Croatian King Ladislav I of the Arpad dynasty (c.1040–1095) founded the Zagreb diocese in 1094.  
The iconographic programme of the paintings is outstanding, mixing traditional scenes from the history of Ladislav, with a post-Trent interpretation, reinterpreted by the painter who depicts the king as a saint; a merciful saint who was canonised in 1192.  
According to the wishes of the bishop who commissioned it, most of the cycle refers to the domestic milieu – referring to its history – contemporary aspirations relating to the unification of the country and the establishment of the diocese of Zagreb.  
The painting, *The Builder Shows King Ladislav the Drawings of the Cathedral* depicts King Ladislav wearing a crown, and the builder showing the king a drawing of the cathedral roof as it is being built. Two barely visible male figures also take part. A large cathedral (later demolished) was built in the 12th century on the site of a smaller one from Ladislav's time. A similar scene, *St. Ladislav Shows a Cathedral with Two Towers to the Virgin*, embellishes the Chapter's oldest seal dating to the 13th century.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.short_description: A painted scene from the Life of St. Ladislav cycle, which links the legend of King Ladislav I of the Arpad Dynasty (around 1040–1095) with Croatian history, and accentuates the foundation of the diocese of Zagreb in about 1094.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.type: Painting, part of a cycle for the winged altarpiece of St. Ladislav
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.initial_owner: Zagreb Cathedral; the altarpiece was commissioned by Bishop Aleksandar Ignacij Mikulić (1688–1694). The side altarpiece of St. Ladislav was originally housed in the northern apse of the cathedral.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.method_for_datation: Bishop Mikulić ordered gilding and painting for the altarpiece In 1690. The painting and sculptural parts were already finished, so the cycle of paintings can thus be dated to this year. The historical documents include the testament of Bishop Martin Borković (1667–1687). Among the notes of the executor, capitular curator and canon Ivan Znika, there is an item about a payment made to the “*pictori Ioanni*” for the bishop's portrait. Stylistic analysis: eminently comparable are the portrait of the bishop (after 1687) and in 1690, the Life of St. Ladislav cycle altarpiece paintings.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.obtention: In 1882, following the earthquake of 1880, during the renovation and restoration of the cathedral in the Gothic-revival style by H. Bollé, the St. Ladislav (St. Ladislaus) altarpiece was removed from the cathedral. Parts of it were brought together for the Cultural and Historical Exhibition of Zagreb in 1925. After the exhibition closed on 31 December 1925, these pieces were given to the museum by the Committee of Zagreb Croatian Women for the Preparation of the Exhibition.

ab9dbdc1-5022-5a92-be31-a76cf3b05af7.name: Single-volume Qur’an with lacquer-painted binding signed by Lutf ‘Ali Shirazi
ab9dbdc1-5022-5a92-be31-a76cf3b05af7.short_description:
The first two of the three illuminated opening spreads bear an index of *sura* headings and a prayer. The main text begins on the third and is written in a fine, clear *naskhi* which compares well to that of Visal, the pen-name of one of the most highly esteemed calligraphers and poets of 19th-century Iran. The marginal commentaries are signed by Visal’s second son, Mirza Mahmud, pen-named *hakim* (’the physician’), who enjoyed a considerable reputation as a *nasta‘liq* scribe.  
The lacquer covers are the work of Lutf ‘Ali Shirazi, who had close associations with the Visal family. The outer covers are variations on the so-called *gul-u bulbul* (‘flower-and-bird’) theme, with two birds in a rose bush on a sparkling dark-brown ground. The doublures have a superb composition of an iris and other flowers on an imitation tortoise-shell ground. The borders have quotations from *sura* *al-Baqara*, II, verses 255–7 on the front and verse 201, with other religious phrases, on the back.

ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.name: *Departure of a Caravan to Mecca from Bab el-Nasr Gate, Cairo*
ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.short_description: Traditionally, most Muslim pilgrims went to Makkah on foot as part of a caravan. Cairo was one of the most important starting points for pilgrim caravans, particularly as it dispatched the ceremonial Mahmal, an ornamental litter containing a Qur’an manuscript and ritual hangings for the Holy Places. Traditionally, the Hajj caravan left the city from the Bab al Nasr gate. In order to ensure the caravan's smooth progression, the Amir al-Hajj organised each section and allocated it its correct place within the sequence. The caravan was headed up by bedouin guides, followed by water carriers and important officials. Next came the treasury and precious gifts intended for the Holy Places, carefully shielded by the ruler's special guards and soldiers. Another, well-protected treasury section - this one intended for the upkeep of the caravan itself - followed and, behind it, a numerous array of traders and merchants. The rest of the caravan was made up of the actual pilgrims from all over the region.

ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

ad19e46b-73be-59de-b600-34195f9350aa.name: *Crystal Palace in Oporto*
ad19e46b-73be-59de-b600-34195f9350aa.short_description: The Crystal Palace was built a decade after its counterpart in London, by Thomas Dillen Jones, to house the Oporto’s International Exhibition that congregated about 3 thousand stands from all over the world. By promoting such exhibition, Portugal sought not only to keep pace with progress but also to promote its own colonial empire.
ad19e46b-73be-59de-b600-34195f9350aa.author: DGPC
keywords: painting; iron architecture; international exhibition; Oporto

ad9f5054-4028-51c0-91cb-d8f1179760fa.name: *Two Figures*
ad9f5054-4028-51c0-91cb-d8f1179760fa.description: This little sketch of two female figures represents a typical orientalist-themed image. Sorolla could undertake studies abroad thanks to a grant. During that period he mainly produced two types of Oriental paintings, which were still very popular in that period: great scenes for the Academy where he studied and small works (as the one on display) to sell and augment his income.
ad9f5054-4028-51c0-91cb-d8f1179760fa.author: Covadonga Pitarch

ae42a45e-443f-5a1d-aaab-85cd72bce06d.name: *A Greek Mountaineer*
ae42a45e-443f-5a1d-aaab-85cd72bce06d.short_description: During the Ottoman occupation, Greek peasants who were dispossessed of their property often retreated to impregnable mountain regions, where they engaged in resistance against the Turks. These mountaineers, who both fascinated and frightened European travellers, were romanticised by artists and poets such as Lord Byron. The man depicted here clearly represents the type of mountaineer described by Byron. To emphasize his costume and his swift movement, he appears in full gear, the sleeves of his jacket falling freely to the back as if to underscore his impulsive gesture. Pistols and knives are tucked in his belt. His right hand rests on his musket; his left hand proudly touches the tip of his sword. Haag chose to place the figure in a grand mountainous landscape, complete with a ruined temple. This sacred monument may be identified as the temple of Apollo Epicurius in Arcadia in the central Peloponnese. This enhances the dignity of the figure, whose nobility and heroism are worthy of the principles of his legendary ancestors.
ae42a45e-443f-5a1d-aaab-85cd72bce06d.author: Washington, D.C., 1991, 80-81, no 28
keywords: travels; Greece; Haag

aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.name: *A Greek lady of Smyrna*
aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.short_description: The picture probably depicts a bride before being bedecked. Her outfit-one of the two customary types of urban bridal costume during the Ottoman period- consists of one or two pairs of pantaloons, a diaphanous selvedged chemise and a dress with tightly buttoned long sleeves and a sash worn low on the hips. Her overcoat is trimmed with fur, has wide pointed sleeves and the dress appears to have been hitched up, revealing the bottom of the pantaloons. Among the various testimonies bequeathed to us by the foreign artist-travelers who visited Greece in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries, the depictions of costumes are particularly important. The imaginative combination of the various garments and accessories that make up the Greek costume and the wealth of jewellery fascinated foreign travellers, who recorded them pictorially, often with a dubitable degree of accuracy.
aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.author: Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 503, fig. 888 (Elisabeth Karanopoulou)
keywords: travels; Athens

aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.name: *Pentecost*
aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.description:
Joseph Ignaz Mildorfer was born into a well-known Tyrolese painter-family and moved at an early date to the imperial city of Vienna to earn his living as did many of his contemporaries from Tyrol. Between 1740 and 1742 he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna where, in 1742, he won a competition and in 1751, following the example of his fellow painter, Paul Troger also from Tyrol, he became an academic professor. As a fresco and altarpiece painter, Mildorfer won fame and important commissions in Austria, Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary (Pápa, Sárvár, Fertőd, Holics (Holič) and Máriavölgy (Marianka). His skilfully executed early battle scenes bear witness to an almost unknown chapter in his oeuvre.  
Traditionally, the high altar painting in the Holy Spirit Church in Sopron along with the sketch made for it, were attributed to István Dorffmaister who was a graduate of the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and a resident of Sopron from 1782. However, recently, it has become clear that the execution of the high altar painting and the Pietà side-altarpiece are earlier: appearing to be the same age as the structure of the high altar, which together with its plastic decoration, dates to around 1750. The composition of the *Pentecost* altarpiece – the type of figures represented and their formation – are very close to the *Assumption* fresco painted by Mildorfer in the chapel of Castle Milotice in Moravia in the 1750s. Here similar character types swing into ecstasy; the same bearded characters, the use of very strong foreshortening close to caricature, and disproportioned, over-sized hands and feet. The strong light streaming into the picture from the dove of the Holy Spirit almost brightens the whole picture space: the figures of the apostles appearing before it almost as silhouettes.  
The Sopron altarpiece, along with the excellent *bozzetto* (sketch) both of which are attributed to Mildorfer, belong to a group of early Hungarian works from the generation of Viennese painters from the Paul Troger school.
aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.short_description: Recently attributed to the excellent Tyrolese painter, Joseph Ignaz Mildorfer, the high altarpiece in Sopron and its expressive *bozzetto* (sketch) belong to a group of early Hungarian works from the generation of Viennese painters from the Paul Troger school. Mildorfer was a master of several frescoes in Hungary (Pápa, Sárvár, Fertőd, Holics (Holič) and Máriavölgy (Marianka).
aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis of Mildorfer’s work

af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.name: *The Immaculate Conception with the Saints Petronius and Dionysius*
af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.description:
This altarpiece is one of the most celebrated works of the young Giovanni Antonio Burrini. It was commissioned by the noble Ratta family at the end of the seventeenth-century. Two saints are surrounding the Virgin. They are Petronius the bishop and patron of Bologna, and Dionysius the martyr and bishop of Paris who is often confused with the Areopagite. Saint Dionysius was probably painted by request of the patrons. It is believed that one of the members of the Ratta family was a diplomat sent by the pope to France to persuade Louis XIV to abolish the edit of Nantes and restart the prosecution of the Huguenots.  
The altarpiece is built on a pyramidal composition and is dedicated to the Carraccis and to Guido Reni. The delicate features and the brush strokes are reflective of Lorenzo Pasinelli and Sebastiano Ricci as both artists were working in Bologna at that time.
af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.short_description: This celebrated altarpiece is one of the masterpieces of the young Burrini. Depicted at the feet of the Virgin, Saint Petronius, the patron of Bologna, and Saint Dionysius, the patron of France. The lively figures are reminiscent of Lorenzo Pasinelli, while the luminous colours and the quick brush strokes are an homage to the Venetian artist Sebastiano Ricci.

af86cd22-a9d6-5bda-a51c-2d290fb277bb.name: *Infantry-attack during the occupation-campaign in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1878*
af86cd22-a9d6-5bda-a51c-2d290fb277bb.short_description: With an energetic stroke of the brush, Rudolph Konopa shows us an episode from the occupation campaign of the Austro-Hungarian Army in the Ottoman provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878. Konopa studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and was a co-founder of the *Hagenbund* in 1900. Konopa received many awards, including the gold medal of the Vienna *Künstlerhaus*. Later during World War I, he became member of the so called *k.u.k. Kriegspressequartier* (art division of the ministry of War) and worked as a war painter on the eastern and southern fronts.

aff0f573-5e91-5646-94a2-26bd51ba0e14.name: *Interior of a Harem*
aff0f573-5e91-5646-94a2-26bd51ba0e14.description: This painting was made around 1863 when the author travelled to Morocco with Mariano Fortuny. The reason for his travel was to paint the characters and picturesque garments as the way of life of the people from Morocco. The influence his experiences had on his works can be found in his paintings and drawings. During his travels he bought exotic artworks, such as Egyptian sarcophagi. Harem and markets are considered a genre painting in Orientalism.

aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.name: *Hajj Day*
aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.description:
Abdulhalim Radwi often evoked his hometown of Mecca, emphasising the importance of the Ka’ba as a source of universal energy and a religious symbol.  
In Hajj Day, the Ka’ba is surrounded by a central circle around which various elements of the composition revolve. The artist manipulates perspective so that near and far elements converge and intersect around the Ka’ba. Facial features are absent, and the artist has stripped the city of Mecca of all detail except for the main elements - the Ka’ba, the overlapping mountains and the pilgrims coming for the Hajj.  
  
In contrast to his colourful scenes, Radwi removes the vibrant colours in this work, opting for a monochrome palette to emphasise the unity of the elements under this universal energy. In his series depicting Mecca, the artist emphasises the importance of Mecca as a place of peace, where there is no difference between people, who are all there for the same reason regardless of their cultures or social status.  
  
Radwi often uses Arabic words and letterforms in his artwork, including religious expressions such as Allah; *bismillah*, or 'in the name of God'; *and la illah ila Allah*, or 'there is no god but God'), as well as other Arabic expressions. This demonstrates Radwi's commitment to incorporating an Arab and Muslim identity into his work. In addition, his continued use of visual symbols such as crescents and other motifs underlines the importance of these symbols as signs of cultural heritage.
aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art
keywords: Hajj; day; Mecca; Zam Zam; Zamzam

b25ced0a-8fbc-5812-85b3-eb1df7ad87a4.name: An Entertainment Scene (The third day of entertainment) from *Surname-i Vehbi*
b25ced0a-8fbc-5812-85b3-eb1df7ad87a4.short_description: The image at the left shows an earlier stage of the flotilla. A long raft in the foreground carries a huge structure shaped like a cypress tree from which strings of fireworks are suspended along with two Catherine wheels. Rockets and projectiles hurtle about. On the basis of Vehbi’s account, this is the float prepared by the artillerymen’s corps. A two-story structure set on a pair of caiques carries a troupe of dancers and musicians on the lower floor while pyrotechnicists are busy at work on the upper one.

b3ffe5a9-b94e-57b4-815b-88dcdb526256.name: *Tomb of Sultan Selim II*
b3ffe5a9-b94e-57b4-815b-88dcdb526256.short_description: Although essentially a realist painter, Şevket Dağ worked with free brush stokes in the style of Corot. He is celebrated for his paintings of the interiors of mosques. He took lessons from Osman Hamdi Bey, and followed his master in painting genre pictures reflecting various aspects of Ottoman life. In addition to mosque interiors he would also paint scenes in market places, still-life compositions and the interiors of houses. Over time, Şevket Dağ's work began to be appreciated abroad following exhibitions in European art centres such as Munich and Paris, and he was awarded a gold medal in the Munich International Exhibition of 1909. He later came under the influence of the impressionists.

b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.name: *Gallery of Paintings*
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.description:
The *Gallery of Paintings* shows a large curtained hall, its walls covered with paintings and two mirrors. There are paintings everywhere, on the floor and table, leaning against chairs and resting on stands. There are groups of men and women, members of the nobility and the middle class talking together and viewing the exhibition. Shifted from the central axis of the composition, behind a group of women around an oval table, is a large open door through which there is a view of a garden with a round flowerbed, fountains and architecture. Bordering the *scotia* – the area above the cornice over which rises the half-circle moulding of the ceiling – hangs a cartouche with a two-headed eagle holding a sword and key in its talons.      
A companion painting shows another curtained hall with paintings and many viewers, with a large door opening into another exhibition hall. Bordering the *scotia* in this painting there is a cartouche with a family monogram in the centre, flanked by two allegorical female figures holding a ducal coronet with five tines.  
The Gallery of Paintings genre developed in the 16th and 17th centuries when the first private collectors, the French and Italian nobility, presented their paintings, sculptures and other artworks in their mansions. As the popularity of these “exhibitions” grew, paintings of this kind increasingly showed imaginary galleries that did not represent any particular collection, but a selection of the best-known paintings of the time. *Gallery of Paintings* is attributed to the Flemish painter, Balthasar van den Bossche, who played an extremely important role in the early 18th-century art world. Among other things, he was manager of the Antwerp art gallery. Strongly influenced by the Flemish painter, David Teniers the Younger (1610–1690), Bossche was born only years before Teniers' death. Teniers was court painter and keeper of the art collections in Brussels. He painted several versions of the *Gallery of Paintings* composition, showing Archduke Leopold Wilhelm's art collection. It was from these paintings that attribution of the works of Italian Renaissance painters Giorgione, Titian and Veronese was possible.         
In all probability, acquisition of the *Gallery of Paintings* was for the manor of a prominent noble Croatian family or maybe by an industrialist. This type of painting was characteristic of Flanders during the Baroque period.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.short_description:
The *Gallery of Paintings* shows a large curtained hall, its walls covered with paintings and two mirrors. Individuals and groups of people are viewing the artworks and talking to one another.  
The interior scene is typical of a humanist's or wealthy merchant's home, turned, as was the fashion, into a gallery for artworks and other treasures.  
The *Gallery of Paintings* and its companion are attributed to the Flemish painter, Balthasar van den Bossche, whose work was influenced by David Teniers the Younger. Teniers depicted several variants of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm's collection as a *Gallery* painting. Bossche probably found inspiration in Teniers' *Gallery* paintings for his own, painted almost 20 years after Teniers' death.    
In all probability, acquisition of the *Gallery of Paintings* was for the manor of a prominent noble Croatian family or maybe by an industrialist.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.method_for_datation: The attribution was made by Miroslav Gašparović, Director of the Museum of Arts and Crafts.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.obtention: A gift of the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb in 1909: when the Museum of Arts and Crafts was founded in 1880, suitable material for the newly founded museum was taken from the National Museum's archaeological department. Thus, the Archaeological Museum donated the above *Galleries* because it had nothing in common with archaeology.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.bibliography: *Muzej za umjetnost i obrt, 1880–1970. Katalog izabranih djela* (Museum of Arts and Crafts, 1880–1970: catalogue of selected works), Zagreb, 1970.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.author: Nela Tarbuk, Miroslav Gašparović
keywords: Gallery of Paintings; Flanders; Balthasar van den Bossche; collection; collector; eagles

b4f75aa6-644c-5905-aa3f-64df7691791f.name: *Le retour de la guerre de Crimée* (painting)
b4f75aa6-644c-5905-aa3f-64df7691791f.short_description: This oil on canvas by B. de Boynier shows a Tunisian military parade returning from war in the Crimea, headed by the current bey, Mohamed Pacha, at the gates of the Palais de la Marsa (1856). The Nichan al-Iftikhar can be seen on the bey's chest. Foot soldiers and horsemen, dressed in European style, carry the Tunisian flag. The General Osman is at the head of the horsemen, and the General Rashid, the commanding officer of the Tunisian military expedition to the Crimea, is to the bey's right. Tunisia sent about 14,000 men in support of the Ottomans and their allies during the Crimean war of 1854–1856).

b5774f3e-8016-55ca-9542-099e3ef271b9.name: Portrait of Akbar in old age
b5774f3e-8016-55ca-9542-099e3ef271b9.short_description: This posthumous portrait of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE) was probably commissioned by his grandson Shah Jahan (r. 1628-58 CE), who was thirteen when the emperor died. The aged Akbar is depicted in three-quarter profile, a view reserved for figures of lesser rank but perhaps accepted for posthumous emperor portraits. Mughal conventions such as the golden halo and the fact that the emperor stands upon the orb of the world signify Akbar’s power as a ruler. The intricate details of his embroidered robe and sash, the pearls around his neck, and the bejewelled dagger hilt emphasize his royal standing and are complemented by a scrolling vegetal border rendered in gold. On the border of the album page, believed to be contemporary with the portrait, three of the emperor’s attendants stand symbolically (and literally) behind him, respectively holding his umbrella, standard, and shield. Two puttis, winged angelic figures derived from European models, hold a golden canopy protectively over Akbar’s portrait, while the antelope and deer depicted below, also on the earthly orb, associate the reign of the late emperor with a peaceful era. This portrait is believed to come from Shah Jahan’s last album, the compilation of which began around 1650 CE, and may never have been completed. Its paintings include several single-figure portraits that acted as models for future albums (Canby 1998, p. 151). The numerous border paintings are extremely developed and skilful works of art in their own right. In the early twentieth century, the “Late Shah Jahan Album” was unfortunately dispersed, and the pages, often split into two, were sold separately.

b5cc449f-cc5f-55d6-ae15-398d9f80fb06.name: Indian Miniature
b5cc449f-cc5f-55d6-ae15-398d9f80fb06.short_description: This one-page miniature painting from 17th-century India shows a Mullah alongside his valet, teaching a wealthy student or a young prince. A similar painting is found in the ‘Ardeshir Album,’ (no longer intact), which was most likely made during the reign of Muhammad Shah (1719-1748). According to the signature, Prince Dara Shikoh (1615-59) is visiting Mian Mir, who was the prince’s instructor while during his teenage years.

b64a1bbb-e3ff-5209-9c78-7304ea9b3d7d.name: Water Well
b64a1bbb-e3ff-5209-9c78-7304ea9b3d7d.description:
This powerful and emotional drawing reflects everyday life, community and endurance. The artist uses a limited colour palette of dark, soft tones to create a haunting atmosphere. At the centre, a group of women stand close together around a dark well, while a solitary figure stands apart, carrying heavy containers. The scene is both quiet and heavy, conveying the physical and emotional weight of their daily labour.  
The well itself becomes more than just a source of water; it also symbolises life, connection and memory. The women's bent figures and joined forms suggest unity and cooperation, as if they rely on one another for strength and survival. Their faces are not clearly visible, giving the image a universal quality and turning the women into symbols of resilience and shared struggle rather than individuals.  
The artist’s use of shading and blurred lines gives the drawing a dreamlike and timeless quality, as if the moment exists in both the past and the present. The open space and faint background add to the sense of isolation and endurance in a harsh environment.  
Overall, *Water Well* powerfully and poetically captures the intersection of women’s labour, community and survival. The simple composition and muted tones draw attention to the emotional depth of the scene, reflecting not only daily life in rural Jordan, but also providing a broader commentary on strength and perseverance.
b64a1bbb-e3ff-5209-9c78-7304ea9b3d7d.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts
keywords: watercolor; well; water; art

b748882b-f53d-5b43-8ea6-79478b997e1b.name: A prince and a hermit
b748882b-f53d-5b43-8ea6-79478b997e1b.short_description: This colourful rocky landscape depicts a prince visiting a hermit at his cave. The prince is seated pensively before the hermit while his eight attendants wait on both sides of a small creek. His stately horse appears to be the focus of the painting, its grand and stocky figure occupying the major part of the lower half of the painting and emphasized by a natural halo formed by the sandy-coloured ground upon which it rests. As Anthony Welch has observed, the stallion was a symbol of authority and splendour but also one of “worldly impermanence” (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 160). Along with the brightly and colourfully dressed servants, the great horse stands in stark contrast to the hermit and his companion (perhaps a disciple), who sits before the cave at the water’s edge; their gaunt figures indicate their renouncement of worldly possessions in favour of following the path to enlightenment through mysticism. The top half of the painting evokes an air of meditation and sombreness that affects even the prince, who may have come here seeking the guidance of a spiritual advisor. The relationship between a Sufi master (*shaykh*, *murshid*, or *pir*) and his disciple (*murid* or *shagird*) was a popular theme in Persian poetry and painting. The master was charged with the task of leading his student along the challenging path (*tariqa*) towards enlightenment and the attainment of oneness with God. The transfer of knowledge between murid and murshid was seen as the transfer of light from the heart of the teacher to that of the student. The combination of a Persian painting style fused with the use of a more earth-toned palette and naturalistic rendering of figures and landscape, however, suggest that the present painting was produced in India under the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE), a period marked by the synthesis of a diverse foreign and indigenous artistic styles. This combined aesthetic was a reflection of the ruler’s great tolerance for different religions; Akbar created the *Din-i illahi* (“Divine Faith”), which borrowed ideas from Islam, Christianity, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, and Jainism (Canby 1998, p. 111). Welch has attributed the work on stylistic grounds to the Persian painter 'Abd al-Samad, an artist of the Safavid dynasty (1501-1732 CE) who left the court of Shah Tahmasp (r. 1524-76 CE) to work first for Akbar’s father, the emperor Humayun (r. 1530-39 CE and 1555-56 CE), and then for Akbar (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 160). Welch also believes that the prince represented in this image could be Akbar’s son Salim, the future emperor Jahangir (r. 1605-27 CE), based on the likeness of this figure to that of a seated prince in a tinted drawing identified as Prince Salim and signed by 'Abd al-Samad, also in the Museum's collection (ibid., p. 162; for an image of this work, see Canby 1998, p. 110, no. 80, although Canby identifies this figure as Akbar). Sheila Canby, however, has suggested that the princely figure may represent Akbar if it can be linked to a hunting event (*qamargha*) in the Punjab ordered by the emperor in April-May 1578 CE at the alleged site of one of Alexander the Great’s successful battles (Canby 1998, p. 111). According to Akbar’s historian Abu’l Fazl (d. 1602 CE), Akbar experienced an epiphany in the midst of the hunt, which led him to cancel the hunt and free all of the captured animals. Unaware of what had caused his change of heart, Akbar’s close friends imagined a few different theories, one of which involved the ruler’s meeting with an anchorite who inspired him to adopt a more ascetic lifestyle, something he did, in fact, do for a while after the incident (ibid., pp. 111 and 113).

b7735908-2a85-5159-97b8-d8499ee4ac07.name: *A Scene from the Turkish Harem*
b7735908-2a85-5159-97b8-d8499ee4ac07.short_description: Austrian artists, which were part of the retinue of the Embassy delegation led by Hans Ludwig von Kuefstein that Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II sent to Murad IV in 1628, depicted audiences of the delegation, the sultan and his family, various Ottoman garments and intriguing facets of daily life. This painting is possibly a part of such a series. The 1654 inscription over the painting reads, “As it is not customary for distinguished Turkish ladies to leave the house or meet strangers, they invite each other to their homes and amuse themselves with dance, comedy and similar forms of entertainment”. In the lower section of the painting, guests are greeted while women dance to the rhythm of the tambourine. In the upper section, two women are seen dancing with scarves on their heads and embroidered kerchiefs in their hands, accompanied by musicians playing traditional instruments, such as rebab, santur, and tambourine. The carpets, garments and instruments are depicted in elaborate detail.

b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.name: *Still Life with Fruit, Dead Birds and a Bowl of Morels*
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.description:
The area of the picture featuring a seasonal still life is packed with dead birds – coal tit, great tit, goldfinch, pigeon, woodpecker, woodcock – and fruit such as grapes, damsons and apples, the produce of the autumn harvest. As is common with similar decorative still life paintings, the fruits shown do not co-exist in nature: morels are among the earliest spring mushrooms. The composition axis is provided by a silver-plated gun in the diagonal. Attention is drawn to the centre of the painting by red tones, changing to olive-green towards the edges.  
Still life paintings made appealing decorations for chateau interiors as supraports, in dining halls, hunting rooms and studies. The Central European artists continued the tradition of Flemish still life established by Frans Snyders and Jan Fyt.  
This still life is the only known work by Coelestin Anctor Ximenes, a remarkable artist of Spanish origin. In 1698 he became a burgher of Brno and an active member of the painters' guild. He signed a proposal that painters and sculptors be articled, the first attempt to detach artists from the guild system, which was followed by efforts to establish an art academy in Brno by the artists Etgens and Eckstein. The majority of artworks to originate in Moravia in the second half of the 17th century were the work of foreign artists mainly Dutch and Italian, while work by Czech artists prevailed in the 18th century.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.short_description: The painting, reminiscent of 17th-century Dutch models, is the only known work by Coelestin Anctor Ximenes, an artist of Spanish origin who settled in Brno. The picture comes from the chateau of the High Steward of Archduchess Marie Isabela of Parma, in Brussels.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.method_for_datation: The picture is marked and dated *Ximenes fe. 1697*.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.provenance: Collection of Count Salm-Reifferscheidt at the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.obtention: The picture comes from the collection of Count Salm-Reifferscheidt at the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau, where it remains to this day. The origins of the collection, which is dominated by Dutch painting, was associated with Antonín Karl Salm-Reifferscheidt (1720–1769), High Steward of Archduchess Marie Isabela of Parma in Brussels. Salm-Reifferscheidt also built the Rájec chateau, designed by Isidore Canevale.

b8b74d6c-8bd5-5f15-9490-e1dfa1ca07b9.name: "Firdausi's Parable of the Ship of Shi'ism"
b8b74d6c-8bd5-5f15-9490-e1dfa1ca07b9.alternate_name: Folio 18v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
b8b74d6c-8bd5-5f15-9490-e1dfa1ca07b9.description: In the introduction to the Shahnama, God launched seventy ships, bearing adherents to the religions of mankind, into a stormy sea. Clearly depicted on the central ship are the Prophet and his son‑in‑law and successor 'Ali sitting beneath the red canopy, while 'Ali’s sons, Hasan and Husain, stand nearby. Details such as the inlaid stars and figures with very small elliptical pupils are characteristic of works attributed to Mirza 'Ali, the son of the master painter Sultan Muhammad.

b98b5c58-b52f-54a7-85fa-fdea8460caf3.short_description: Bright, folkloristically vivid, technically impeccable and with an abundance of ethnographic detail, this is one of Jovanović’s best paintings, both in this period and as a whole. ba42b954-f590-57ca-907e-01a3ca4dde77.name: *Servant*
ba42b954-f590-57ca-907e-01a3ca4dde77.short_description: The painting depicts a young girl in front of a wall, the lower part of which has been decorated with ceramic tiles with a floral design. The girl is wearing a white dress with embroidery down its front and a long embroidered belt, while her hair is partially covered with a light veil. On the young girl’s chestnut hair there is a gold crown, with gems at its centre. Around her neck she wears a necklace with large gems, a thin bracelet on her left wrist and an armlet on her right arm. The girl is holding a tray on which there is a decanter and cup of blue-and-white porcelain and fruits.
keywords: Ottoman fashion

baf82baf-93a9-5da4-b22c-8e5e634174fe.name: Miniature
baf82baf-93a9-5da4-b22c-8e5e634174fe.description:
This framed octagonal miniature shows a scene in a portico where men and women talk. A large blue curtain, two ribbed columns and a lobulated arch over another hidden column set the composition where a bearded Arab man with a turban, dressed in traditional Turkish costume in blue, red and white, is seated on a carpet, looking at a woman and a man who is introducing her. On the right and left sides, two couples of Circassian odalisques complete the scene and a standing armed man closes it on our right side.  
In the horizon beyond the harem we can see magnificent palaces by the water, probably the sea in Istanbul.
baf82baf-93a9-5da4-b22c-8e5e634174fe.author: Cristina Giménez
keywords: Orientalism; Harem paintings; Women

baf9e3e8-08a9-59e2-8c21-17ce2e3a24c6.name: *Moorish Parade*
baf9e3e8-08a9-59e2-8c21-17ce2e3a24c6.description:
This painting was made around 1863 when the author travelled to Morocco with Mariano Fortuny. The reason of his travel was to paint the characters and picturesque garments as the way of life of the people from Morocco.  
His experiences can be seen in his paintings and drawings.  
During his travels he bought exotic artworks as Egyptian sarcophagi.  
Harem and markets are considered a genre painting in Orientalism.
baf9e3e8-08a9-59e2-8c21-17ce2e3a24c6.author: Ámparo López
keywords: North Africa; Orientalism; Travelling

bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.name: *Expulsion from Eden*
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.description:
The painting was until recently ascribed to Giovanni Antoni Pellegrini (1675–1741) but further study of comparative material and references by Visnja Bralic, an art historian from Zagreb, has led to a new attribution of the Venetian painter, Girolamo Brusaferro. Although little biographical information exists about the painter, his work is well known, and this knowledge is supported by other extant pieces by him. Brusaferro, who painted altarpieces for churches in Venice, and historical and mythological scenes for private collections, was a member of the Venetian painters' guild (1702–1722).  
The Expulsion from Eden theme was a popular subject for painters during the Baroque period. Here, the artist expressively shows the drama of Adam and Eve driven out of Paradise for their disobedience to God by an angry angel. The busts of the three actors almost fill up the whole surface of the canvas. The angel stands accented with flaming sword in hand, and according to the iconographic principle, in front of the gates of paradise, thus stopping Adam and Eve returning to their haven. The angel, powerfully illuminated, stands with outspread wings brandishing his sword, while the naked bodies of Adam and the hardly visible Eve are in penumbra. Their faces and movements reveal their fear and despair. While Adam is running from the glare of the flaming sword, Eve raises her hands and face to the sky, begging for Divine forgiveness. The colours are warm with a light hue. The figures, emphatically voluminous and in motion, heighten the dynamic nature of the composition.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.short_description: *Expulsion from Eden* is the work of the Venetian master, Girolamo Brusaferro, who painted numerous altarpieces for Venetian churches, along with other historical and mythological compositions. The Expulsion from Eden theme was a popular subject for painters during the Baroque period. The picture shows the moment when the angry angel, fiery sword in hand, drives Adam and Eve from their earthly paradise. The terrified and despairing exiles have committed the original sin, the shadow of which has fallen over the whole of mankind. While the powerful, naked Adam in painful spasm is bending over, Eve turns to heaven and begs for Divine assistance. The angel, with robust body and wide outstretched wings, brandishes the fiery sword at Adam. The impressive dynamic composition, marked, bright tonality and emphatic voluminousness of the figures distinguish this painting.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.method_for_datation: The attribution, made by Visnja Bralic, made use of existing literature, other comparative material and stylistic analysis.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.bibliography: Bralić, V., “Doprinosi opusu Girolama Brusaferro”, *Radovi instituta za povijest umjetnosti,* 28, Zagreb, 2004, pp. 134–145.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.author: Vedrana Gjukić-Bender
keywords: Italian Baroque painting; movement; religious object

bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.name: *Madonna and Child with St. John Nepomuk*
bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.description:
The painting is a *bozzetto* (study) for the altar piece commissioned by Benedict XIII for the canonisation of John Nepomuk on 11 March 1729, and intended for the Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano. The canvas shows John Nepomuk (named after his place of birth: Pomuk, the ancient name for the city of Nepomuk) kneeling before the Madonna and Child, surrounded by *putti* and angels.  
One in the foreground is showing the palm leaf of the martyr and has raised his finger to his mouth, a gesture that alludes to the virtue of the saint, renowned not only as protector of Bohemia, but also as the patron saint of confessors. John, confessor of the queen, aligned himself with the Archbishop of Prague against the claims of King Wenceslaus IV who imprisoned him for refusing to divulge the secrets of the confessional. He was tortured by the King before being flung from the Charles Bridge and drowned in the Vltava.  
The martyrdom is reproduced in the background behind the saint, who is dressed in his priestly robes and canonical cape. Beside Mary, another angel is giving the martyr the crown of stars that, according to tradition, surrounded his head as he floated in the river. The study, usually dated to the 1720s, was acquired by the Italian State in 1921, and is therefore not a part of the Borghese family collection.  
The painting is from Conca's early period when he was one of Rome's most fashionable artists. His painting style of grandiose and exuberant lines, similar to the style of Carlo Maratta, is characteristic of a later phase of Baroque painting, by then infused with the appealing and exuberant language of Rococo culture. As proof of the altarpiece's renown and the devotion of the Bohemian saint, prints were made of it, one of which was engraved by Gottlib Heiss in 1735 and is part of the Borghese collection.
bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.short_description:
The *bozzetto* (study) was made by Sebastiano Conca for an altarpiece in St. Giovanni in Laterano (now lost). Conca, from Naples, arrived in Rome in 1706 at which time his style was similar to that of Carlo Maratta.  
This is a typical example of a Baroque altarpiece, the *sacrum* appearing in a monumental internal space providing a clear perspective.  
Conca's painting, with its exuberant, grandiose lines, is characteristic of late Baroque art and its captivating and magniloquent language is taken from Rococo culture.
bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.obtention: The work was acquired by the Italian State in 1921.

be16f668-8f93-5fa4-976a-635754278a7f.name: The Combat of Khusraw Parviz and Bahram Chubina (Page from a Manuscript of the Shahnama (Book of Kings))
be16f668-8f93-5fa4-976a-635754278a7f.short_description: The illustrated page from a manuscript of the Iranian national epic, the Shahnama, depicts a contest between the Sasanian monarch Shah Khusraw Parviz (Khusraw II, r. AD 590–628) and a would-be usurper, Bahram Chubina. The protagonists, who competed for the Iranian throne, are both crowned. Bahram, the superior warrior, advances on foot toward a group of archers directed by Khusraw. This depiction of an epic battle cheekily includes, at the center of the page, a figure who has fallen, leaving his buttocks exposed. The humiliated man perhaps can be understood as representing an out-of-favor courtier, thereby drawing the centuries-old battle into the contemporary world of the manuscript’s creation.
be16f668-8f93-5fa4-976a-635754278a7f.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
be16f668-8f93-5fa4-976a-635754278a7f.method_for_datation: The page is from manuscript of the Shahnama produced for Shah Isma‘il II (Hegira 984-985/ AD 1576-77), of which there are fifty-five known surviving paintings, including the present example. The painting bears an ascription to the artist ‘Ali Asghar, who began his career at the court of Shah Tahmasp, in Tabriz. He subsequently entered the service of Sultan Ibrahim Mirza, nephew of Tahmasp and governor of Mashhad. Ibrahim Mirza was executed by order of his cousin, the newly installed Shah Isma‘il, and ‘Ali Asghar went to work in the atelier of yet another royal patron, this time in Qazwin—the new capital.
be16f668-8f93-5fa4-976a-635754278a7f.method_for_provenance: The page is from manuscript of the Shahnama, the Iranian national epic. The large size of the painting and the lavish use of costly pigments suggest a royal patron. Stylistic considerations suggest a date of 983-987/1575-80. Shah Tahmasp died in 984/1576 and was succeeded by his son Isma’il, who ruled for less than two years. He was followed by his brother, the nearly blind Muhammad Khudabanda whose own inglorious reign came to an end in 996/1588 with the accession of Shah ‘Abbas the Great. Shah Isma‘il, who is in fact known to have employed a coterie of distinguished artists, is then the likely patron of the book, which can be dated with some confidence to Hegira 984-985/1576-77 AD.
be16f668-8f93-5fa4-976a-635754278a7f.obtention: The Isma’il II Shahnama was in Paris at the Musée des Arts Decoratifs in 1912. Sold by Georges Demotte (1877-1923), Paris, 1916 or 1918 (sold to). be3d15c9-0b3c-5c76-b571-476211bfa7ab.name: *Bei der Kupplerin (The Procuress)*
be3d15c9-0b3c-5c76-b571-476211bfa7ab.description: A large area of this painting is taken up by a carpet. Owing to the clearly recognisable pattern, it is possible to identify this carpet as coming from Uşak, a town in western Anatolia with a long and rich history of carpet production. On account of the dark blue ground and the red, onion-shaped central medallion, it is possible to date this carpet to the first half of the 16th century. Vermeer presents a seemingly light-hearted, quiet scene in which the objectionable aspect of the situation is not immediately apparent. Nevertheless, he leaves us in no doubt that this is a scene of procuration: the fashionably dressed suitor is paying money while with his left hand he touches the breast of the young woman.
be3d15c9-0b3c-5c76-b571-476211bfa7ab.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
be3d15c9-0b3c-5c76-b571-476211bfa7ab.obtention: This painting was purchased from the collection of Count Franz Josef von Waldstein Wallenstein/Dux in 1741.

be44b9c0-4045-581b-a6e2-85c0f3bcd137.short_description: Emperor Franz Joseph visited the Suez Canal on board the Austrian ship, *Elisabeth*. He reached the Egyptian port of Ismilia on 14 Nov 1869 and stayed in Egypt until the 26 Nov 1869. During this trip, he also visited Cairo and Alexandria.
