bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.name: Portrait of Sultan Selim II
bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.short_description: This large album portrait of Sultan Selim II (reigned 1566–74) reveals much about his reign. It was Selim’s father, Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (reigned 1520–66), who solidified the geographical borders of the Ottoman Empire and refined the central administration of his government, allowing his son and successor to pursue more sedentary pleasures such as literature, art and wine-drinking. Nicknamed “Selim the Sot” for his affection for wine, the sultan was nonetheless a great bibliophile and patron of architecture, music and the arts of the book. The painter, poet and naval commander Haydar Reis depicted Selim II as larger than life; the robust sultan in his luxurious fur-lined and brocaded gold garment dwarfs both the page boy and the interior in which he sits in a cross-legged position on a carpet. This composition was one of a number of conventions for Ottoman royal portraiture developed in the 1570s and is similar to portraits in Loqman’s *Kiyafetu’l Insaniye fi Semailu’l-Osmaniye*, a study to record the physiognomy of the Ottoman sultans.
bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; painting; portrait; sultan; ruler

bfab383a-8a92-580d-828e-595be606bc38.name: Painting.
bfab383a-8a92-580d-828e-595be606bc38.description:
A fragment of a battle scene painted in gouache on paper. To the left of the painting is part of a wall with a balustrade from which two archers are drawing their bows ready to fire arrows at the enemy. A bearded figure on horseback, his lower half obscured slightly by the wall, wields a sword in his right hand and shield in the left. He is either about to attack or has just killed his opponent, whose body is bent backwards as if he is wounded or ready to throw the lance. In the centre of the painting another figure aims his lance at a soldier with a round shield and wide sword.  
The majority of works on paper discovered at Fustat are Fatimid and when this painting was acquired by the British Museum it was assumed that the painting was a Fatimid work. However, certain details suggest a later date, such as the kite-shaped shields, a type introduced by the Normans that was not in use in Egypt until the end of the AH 7th/ AD 13th century.
bfab383a-8a92-580d-828e-595be606bc38.short_description: A fragment of a gouache painting of a battle scene, from Fustat, Cairo. One of a small number of surviving paintings from the medieval period. The date of this painting is not certain; it is either Fatimid, like many other works on paper excavated at Fustat, or Ayyubid from the AH 7th / AD 13th century.
bfab383a-8a92-580d-828e-595be606bc38.method_for_datation: This painting was previously thought by scholars to date to the Fatimid period, but recent research dates it later to the Ayyubid period, due to the headgear worn by the figures on the left that resembles 7th- / 13th-century illustrated manuscripts produced in Syria, and the figure on the upper right who has a kite-shaped shield, a Norman design not used in Egypt until the end of the 7th / 13th century.
bfab383a-8a92-580d-828e-595be606bc38.method_for_provenance: The painting was found in an excavation at Fustat, Cairo.

bfc4be6c-b4b1-53d5-bc99-cd1d4f8fad8a.name:
Jahangir hunting lions from an elephant  
From a dispersed album
bfc4be6c-b4b1-53d5-bc99-cd1d4f8fad8a.short_description: Babur, Humayun’s father, was a direct descendant of the 14th-century Turco-Mongol ruler Timur. Babur was the founder of the Mughal Empire (1526–1858) in the Indian subcontinent, known as Hindustan throughout the Persian-speaking world. He was the first ruler to foster the artistic connection between Central Asia, Iran, and India. He felt a particular reverence for the Timurid artistic and cultural heritage and invited some Iranian artists to join his court. Artists from Bukhara (in present-day Uzbekistan) followed suit.

c00a74d5-7adc-54fe-85fc-96f35232755e.description: This painting copied, almost literally, an engraving by David Roberts, published on the Tourist in Spain series by Roberts in 1835. Roberts travelled from Cordova to Granada in February 1883 and painted many sketches and drawings that were used afterwards, in engravings and paintings.

keywords: Travel books; Alhambra; Painting

c0dbe8f9-c861-5074-9fb8-b7dfcde583ed.name: *Al Azhar University, Cairo*
c0dbe8f9-c861-5074-9fb8-b7dfcde583ed.short_description: Ludwig Deutsch  (1855-1935) was an Austrian-Jewish Orientalist painter. Here he tries to capture the atmosphere within the courtyard of the Al-Azhar mosque, first built in the 10th century and a major religious, intellectual and political hub of activity ever since. One of the oldest and most revered universities in the Islamic world, it was from here that a revolt against French troops was launched in 1798.  The French general Kleber was assassinated by Suleiman al Halabi, an al Azhar student, and later, Al Azhar was a focal point of protest against the Ottoman occupation of Egypt. Despite Deutsch's near-photographic style, his depiction is not entirely accurate and contains several errors: the arcades under the wooden oriel - their arches in reality wider and squatter - were not blocked up in his time, and the colour of the stonework is exaggerated. The praying men in the background are facing in the wrong direction (the direction of prayer or qibla in fact being to their right), Finally, the tall dark figure in the centre of the painting clutches what appears to be a Holy Qur'an between his dirty shoes, an act any Muslim would consider an absolute sacrilege.
c0dbe8f9-c861-5074-9fb8-b7dfcde583ed.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
c0dbe8f9-c861-5074-9fb8-b7dfcde583ed.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Al-Azhar Mosque; qibla

c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.name: *Eine junge Frau beim Ankleiden (Young Woman at her Toilette)*
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.description: A young lady is seated at a table with a mirror in front of her; she is about to adjust her hair with the hairpin she has in her mouth. This seems to have been prompted by the open letter, which presumably announces the imminent arrival of a male visitor. The silver jewellery box, the bed with the heavy curtain and the dog on the woman's lap-which can be understood as a sleepy defender of virtue-would seem to indicate the amorous content of the letter. Van Mieris depicts the various textures in the painting with an impressive richness of detail and exceptional precision: the silvery gloss of the lady's satin dress, the honey coloured wood of the lute, the soft fur of the red velvet jacket and the heavy, deep-pile oriental carpet with its broad gold fringe. All these expensive items also indicate the wealth of the subject, although they can also be interpreted as symbols of vanity and extravagance.
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.method_for_datation: Artist signatures: "Mieris Anno 1667" and "Anno 1667. Juny. Lud. Bat. F. van Mieris fecit"
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.obtention: This painting was owned by Eleonore Erdmuthe Louise (1662–1696), wife of Elector Johann Georg IV of Saxony, and later came into the possession of Augustus the Strong. It was mentioned for the first time in the inventory drawn up between 1722 and 1728, where it was described as "in the manner of Metsu".

c23084d0-7207-5ba4-a8e2-7af70bf14ee7.name: *Kitchen Still Life with Snails, Fish and Eggs*
c23084d0-7207-5ba4-a8e2-7af70bf14ee7.description: *Kitchen Still Life with Snails, Fish and Eggs* is part of a series of three table-top still life paintings that may hint at the discipline of Lenten fasting. They each seem to display foods, the consumption or preparation of which was allowable during the period of self-denial. The empty copper dishes and the cucumbers near them on one of the tables may refer to the Good Friday menu; another table bears apples, snails, fish, eggs, cheese and onions, foods which are also acceptable during the fasting period. The pail in the background probably contains a dairy product. In the third ensemble, besides the greenery, there are cheese, offal and plucked quails on display, and even some wine bottles. The menu here is of a richer, more permissive diet. The white napkins, executed in a particularly clumsy manner, contrast with the dishes and wicker objects painted with almost a craftsman-like gusto. Dark details tending towards black make sterner the characteristic colours of off-white and greyish brown, with a few green and timed yellow patches. As if to limit the pleasure of the eye by some puritanical consideration, the domestic and parochial spirit of a prim and eagerly careful arrangement surrounds the unconsciously arranged kitchen articles. There is no doubt that these still life paintings support the aims of the burghers, possibly contrary to the spirit of the environment in which the painting was executed. Regards dating, it is difficult to identify the period as adequate Hungarian analogies lack, but in looking further, we might set the Eperjes (Prešov) still life paintings beside the works of Martin Dichtl (1639/40–1710). However, the fact that the Kramers – a painter family from Eperjes (Prešov) – produced portraits in the spirit of the 17th century, but a century later, demands the utmost caution, as the Kramers among others could have worked on occasional still life works as well. Nevertheless, mention of a member of the Kramer family, Peter, in a document of 1643 in Eperjes (Prešov) means that he should be included among the possible painters of these three pictures.
c23084d0-7207-5ba4-a8e2-7af70bf14ee7.short_description: *Kitchen Still Life with Snails, Fish and Eggs* originates from Upper Hungary and is part of a series of three tabletop still life paintings that may hint at the discipline of Lenten fasting in a provincial manner. This painting together with its companion pieces, represent rare Hungarian examples of a widespread European genre.
c23084d0-7207-5ba4-a8e2-7af70bf14ee7.obtention: Purchased for the Hungarian National Gallery from an art dealer.

c2ef4889-9f51-575f-8794-b1fe85502111.name: An Entertainment Scene (Evening entertainment in the Golden Horn) from *Surname-i Vehbi*
c2ef4889-9f51-575f-8794-b1fe85502111.short_description: In this miniature we see an evening of rafts and fireworks on the Golden Horn. The grand vizier is seated on the Aynalıkavak quayside in the right frame and the sultan on the palace balcony. On the first of the two rafts in this procession, dancers and musicians perform in a garden of blazing cypress tree and Solomon’s seal fireworks. On the second is a revolving fortress stuffed with fireworks that have been set off while the military band at the stern of the raft plays.
keywords: Levni; miniature; entertainment; Dance

c4203a5d-6cf2-5678-9798-9a8246c935fb.name: Painting with female figure
c4203a5d-6cf2-5678-9798-9a8246c935fb.short_description: The painting depicts a young noblewoman, elegantly dressed and richly embellished with a variety of jewels. While at first glance the work is pleasant and successful, many inconsistencies are apparent upon closer inspection. With a skilful choice of colours, a refined rendering of details and an effective decorative composition, we can more closely observe that the woman is placed in a type of pavilion, whose depth is only weakly indicated by a veil. The figure of the girl herself is rendered without depth. The three-quarter face is turned to the left, the body is seen from the front, while the feet are in profile, turned to the right. The image is constructed with its singular elements in an unnatural way, seemingly without any knowledge of anatomy or perspective. Through these dissonances the work reveals itself to be an object influenced by Western art, which the artist tried to orient himself (i.e., to Western art) without knowing it in depth. Both the technique (oil on canvas) and the subject (a portrait) refer to traditions that are foreign to the local culture.
c4203a5d-6cf2-5678-9798-9a8246c935fb.holder: Museum of Civilizations / Eastern Art Museum
c4203a5d-6cf2-5678-9798-9a8246c935fb.bibliography:

Torre, P., "Un dipinto Qajar tra Oriente e Occidente", in S. Balbi De Caro (ed), *Gioielli dell'Iran*, Rome: De Luca Editori d'arte, 2007: 83-87.
c4203a5d-6cf2-5678-9798-9a8246c935fb.author: Michael Jung

c4ba74ec-5d96-5dd1-9cc3-a2a1553b4630.name: The Solovetsky Monastery
c4ba74ec-5d96-5dd1-9cc3-a2a1553b4630.description: Savvaty, a monk from the Kirilov Monastery, founded a small commune on the island of Solovki near the White Sea in 1392. He left the inhospitable island in 1435 and died later the same year. The next year, the monk Zosimas moved to Solovki and built the first monastic cell, which eventually became a splendid and wealthy monastery thanks to a lucrative salt trade and plentiful gifts. Zosimas remained the abbot until his death in 1478.  The monastery, with its numerous towers and thick, fortified walls, is depicted in the lower half of this icon, and Saints Zosimas and Savvaty are depicted above the monastery, flanked by two angels. This icon’s large scale and thematic content suggest that the image was produced at the Solovetsky Monastery.
c4ba74ec-5d96-5dd1-9cc3-a2a1553b4630.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

c4fe88f8-b165-52e3-b23f-fce061f8c81f.name: A Prince Meeting a Muslim Holy Man
c4fe88f8-b165-52e3-b23f-fce061f8c81f.description:
The young man in princely attire seated in the presence of a mullah, a Muslim holy man, is thought to be one of the sons of Emperor Jahangir (1569–1627, reign 1605–1627). The facial features of the prince conform to portraits of Sultan Khurram (1592–1666) who became the emperor Shah Jahan (reign 1627–1658).  
The young prince appears to be around 18 years of age. Khurram had an early interest in art and even commissioned court paintings at the age of 14. This miniature may be seen as an illustration of the prince's interest in Islam. Unlike his forefathers, Shah Jahan was a practicing Sunni Muslim. He is best remembered for building the Taj Mahal, the stunning white marble memorial to his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal.  
  
The painting is unsigned, making the identity of the artist unclear, but a tentative attribution can be made on stylistic grounds to the gifted court painter Manôhar (active c.1580–1620) and his atelier. The artist worked at court for at least forty years during the successive reigns of Akbar (1542–1605), Jahangir, and Shah Jahan.
c4fe88f8-b165-52e3-b23f-fce061f8c81f.location: Saint Louis, United States of America

c60f81d1-fdf2-584b-9846-a4725108786e.name: Persian miniature mounted as album leaf
c60f81d1-fdf2-584b-9846-a4725108786e.short_description:
This single leaf miniature of a kneeling young woman is one of a group of works that all show the same motif. The original design dates from shortly after 1550 and is part of an album (*muraqqaʿ*) made in Hegira 968 (AD 1560/61) for Amir Husayn Beg, the treasurer of Shah Tahmasp (r. Hegira 930-984, AD 1524-1576). Our fully coloured kneeling woman can be related to a lightly tinted brush drawing now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.  
  
As noted later, most probably by an Ottoman librarian in the margin, whether Vali Jan is actually the creator is questionable. The Persian artist left his homeland in the early 1580s and subsequently worked in the painting workshop of the Ottoman court. There he became famous for his intricate drawings of large, serrated leaves, so-called *saz*\-leaves. It can be said with certainty, however, that this painting found its way to Istanbul before 1700. This is indicated by an Ottoman copy from the early 18th century, which depicts the young woman mirror-inverted. At the beginning of the 20th century, the Armenian-born art historian Armenag Bey Sakisian acquired the leaf in Istanbul and published it in 1929 in his standard work *La Miniature persane du XIIe au XVIIe siècle*.

c60f81d1-fdf2-584b-9846-a4725108786e.method_for_provenance: The first known owner published this miniature in 1929.

Denny, W.B. , "Dating ottoman Turkish Works in the Saz Style”, *Muqarnas*, 1 (1983): 103-121.

c671443a-8a37-5c35-975f-840074e8db8a.name: *Woman Playing a String Instrument*
c671443a-8a37-5c35-975f-840074e8db8a.short_description: In this painting there is an Ottoman woman in her daily attire with her hair covered by an embroidered and printed kerchief. She plays a string instrument. Music was one of the most popular kinds of amusement in Turkish harems. The lute in particular, and similar string instruments, have always occupied an important place in the lives of women. This picture was used on the cover of a special issue of *Le Figaro Illustré* dedicated to Zonara and published in 1908, and also appeared in *Der'i Se'adet*, a book written by Adolphe Thalasso and illustrated by Zonaro.
keywords: Music; harem; court music; musician; female musician; traditional entertainments

c6e8e098-9188-59cf-be1b-4970bdaade20.name: Nablous : Australian cavalry entering the ancient Shechem, the capital of Samaria
c6e8e098-9188-59cf-be1b-4970bdaade20.description: A column of Australian cavalry gallops along a road on the valley floor into the small town of Shechem. The rear of the column is in the foreground, with the front of it just entering the town, whose buildings are visible in the distance. The valley is bordered, to the left and right, by steep-sided hills.

c766ed2c-4a3f-5af1-a216-8416ad33c1ad.name:
The thorny plant that grows in mountains  
Folio from *Khawass al-Ashjar* (*De Materia Medica*)
c766ed2c-4a3f-5af1-a216-8416ad33c1ad.short_description: One of the earliest scientific manuscripts to be translated from Greek into Arabic was Dioscorides’s *De Materia Medica*, as it is called in Latin. Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician, wrote his treatise on medicinal plants in the first century CE. The manuscript was initially translated into Syriac and then into Arabic in Baghdad in the 9th century (Guesdon and Nouri 2001, p. 118). It became the foundation for Islamic pharmacology and was copied widely. The present folio is from a rare dispersed 13th-century Arabic copy of the text, in which are depicted various medicinal herbs and roots with an accuracy characteristic of Arab scientific texts produced during this period. The illustrations follow the Greek model closely. The paintings do not lack artistic sensibility and, for accuracy, each specimen is depicted in its entirety from tip to root against the plain paper ground. The recto side of this page depicts a large red bramble plant with five thorned branches arranged symmetrically. A mass of green shoots, topped with red flowers, clusters at the base of the plant, which has a red root. The text identifies the plant as rasiyun, “the thorny plant that grows in the mountains.” The verso side of the page shows a single-stemmed plant with red spiky blossoms, and the text states that this medicinal plant is used in the treatment of skin disorders, including pustules, itching and ulcers.
c766ed2c-4a3f-5af1-a216-8416ad33c1ad.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
c766ed2c-4a3f-5af1-a216-8416ad33c1ad.bibliography: Guesdon, Marie-Geneviève and Vernay-Nouri, Annie, *L’Art du livre arabe: Du manuscript au livre d’artiste*, Paris: Bibliothèque Nationale de France, 2001.
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; plants; science

c7c7015e-6302-5b17-8d29-534365062bab.name: View of Torre de los siete Picos, the Alhambra Palace
c7c7015e-6302-5b17-8d29-534365062bab.description: In his travels to Granada Joaquin Sorolla was fascinated by the monument of the Alhambra, the palace of Naridd kingdom of Granada. It is, along with the Mosque of Cordoba, the most important monument of Muslim Spain. Sorolla's paintings are far away from the Orientalism topics, and instead it recreates in the beauty of its nooks and gardens, capturing a more personal and intimate perspective of the monument. In this view from afar, highlights the beauty of the building and its surroundings.
c7c7015e-6302-5b17-8d29-534365062bab.author: Covadonga Pitarch
keywords: The Alhambra; Painting development

c869c0fc-13da-5c97-9a34-aeb4470de17e.name: *Top of the garden at Marengo, ancient Marabout*
c869c0fc-13da-5c97-9a34-aeb4470de17e.short_description: This part of Algiers has a particularly rich history. The painting depicts the famous mausoleum of Sidi Abderrahmane Ettaâlibi ('Abd al-Rahman al-Thalibi) who was a member of one of the most ancient families of Algiers. He was buried here in the 7th century and was made the Patron Saint of Algiers due to his reputation as a wise and knowledgeable man.

c8a7c58e-d37a-5d59-9506-320c260a750e.name: Saint Nicholas of Zaraisk with Various Scenes
c8a7c58e-d37a-5d59-9506-320c260a750e.description: Saint Nicholas, a 4th-century bishop from modern-day Turkey, is one of the most venerated saints in Russia. He is known as a protector of the weak and poor. Stories of Saint Nicholas giving gifts to the needy and protecting children spread far and wide as people traveled or emigrated from Russia to other countries. In this icon, Saint Nicholas is shown full-length, giving a blessing with his right hand while holding the Bible with his left. He is flanked by images of the Mother of God and Christ. The images in the border depict important moments from his life.

c9b1b21a-3afb-57cb-86e1-8e151adf4e75.name:
Haftvad and the Worm  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
c9b1b21a-3afb-57cb-86e1-8e151adf4e75.short_description: The vast historical scope, imaginative power, and national importance of the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), an epic poem completed by Firdausi in 1010, have inspired countless works of art in all media. This folio AKM164 (folio 521 verso) from the *Shahnameh* produced for Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp (r. 1524–76) centres around Haftvad, a modest man with seven sons and one daughter whose fate is entwined with the rise of the Sasanian dynasty (224–651).

c9db4ac7-c541-5c49-b622-0b3423e00d75.name: Mirror case with compartment for instruments
c9db4ac7-c541-5c49-b622-0b3423e00d75.short_description:
The case houses a mirror that is protected by a lid. In the lower part is a compartment that can be pulled out which originally held various instruments, including a pair of scissors. The lid bears the signature typical of Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf: *zi baʿd-i muḥammad ʿali ashraf ast*. On the one hand, this is a commitment to Shiite Islam: "After Muhammad \[the Prophet\], ʿAli \[ibn Abi Talib\] is the highest." On the other hand, it can also be interpreted as an indication of a teacher-disciple relationship: "After Muhammad \[ʿAli\] follows in rank ʿAli Ashraf." Most likely this refers to Muhammad ʿAli (active Hegira 1111-1133 / AD 1700-1721), the son of Muhammad Zaman (active Hegira ca. 1072-1105 / AD ca. 1662-1694) and nephew of Haji Muhammad (active Hegira 1084-1124 / AD 1673-1712). For his part, Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf was the teacher of Muhammad Baqir (active Hegira ca. 1160s-1204 / AD ca. 1750s-1790) and Muhammad Sadiq (active Hegira ca. 1163-1209 / AD ca. 1750-1795). They are among the most famous Persian artists of the 18th century.  
  
The link to the artistic circle around Muhammad Zaman resonates in the decoration of the case. It shows roses and nightingales, pers. *gul-u-bulbul*. The theme had been present in Persian love poetry for centuries and echoes back to more mystical times. It is assumed that the painting genre goes back to Chinese bird-and-flower painting, which had become known in Persia in the 15th century. In the 17th century, after a lengthy interruption, it was Shafiʿ ʿAbbasi (active Hegira 1040-1066 / AD 1631-1656) who concentrated entirely on flowers and birds, inspired by both European prints and Indian examples. Muhammad Zaman, his brother Haji Muhammad, and his sons Yusuf Muhammad and Muhammad ʿAli further pursued the genre. In the hands of Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf and his pupils, it received its final alterations and ultimate form.

ca166fd8-40d8-5568-b817-4999a1ea04de.name: "The Eavesdropper"
ca166fd8-40d8-5568-b817-4999a1ea04de.alternate_name: Folio 47r from a Haft Paikar (Seven Portraits) of the Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami of Ganja

The story of the Seven Portraits comprises a series of moralizing tales as told to the Persian hero Bahram Gur by seven princesses. This lively and lyrical scene illustrates a story in which a youth spies upon maidens swimming in a garden pool by moonlight. The voyeur is barely visible here, peering out of the shuttered window, unbeknownst to the playful bathers below.

ca9bb919-8384-510d-b5f3-6ce0848cba75.short_description: After the blockade of the Nile delta by the Royal Navy and the Austrian War Navy, and the conquest of Sidon, British and Austrian forces then attacked the city of Acre. cbe9cbbe-7273-52d1-8920-45ea27d852f8.name:
Rustam shooting Ashkabus and his horse  
Folio detached from a *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) by Abu’l-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1010)
cbe9cbbe-7273-52d1-8920-45ea27d852f8.short_description: Recounting the legendary history of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam, Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed in 1010, inspired many illustrated copies. The present folio, which depicts one of the hero Rustam’s more unusual victories in single combat, was detached from a copy that is known as the “Big Head” *Shahnameh*. This name refers to the characteristic feature of the majority of its paintings: the large heads of its human figures.

cc673275-b5d7-50ff-bc5e-1a4f9c06e998.name: The Celebration of the Prophet Muhammad in Tangier
cc673275-b5d7-50ff-bc5e-1a4f9c06e998.short_description: Stefano Ussi lived between Florence and Rome and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts of Florence before enrolling as a volunteer in the first Italian War of Independence, during which he was taken prisoner by the Austrian troops. In 1875 Italian King Vittorio Emanuele II sent an embassy to Morocco which included the writer Edmondo De Amicis and the painters Ussi and Cesare Biseo. The innovative international relations policy of the young Sultan Mulay al-Hassan fostered relations with the Italian King. During his trip, Ussi sketched drafts on Arab every-day life scenes which later inspired his larger paintings.

cceaf42f-eb5f-541e-a0f9-aad5efa6922d.name: *Dispute between St. Catherine of Alexandria and the Philosophers*
cceaf42f-eb5f-541e-a0f9-aad5efa6922d.description: Johann Lucas Kracker was born into a family of sculptors who had settled in Vienna but originated from Czechoslovakia. Completing his academic studies in Vienna, his career began in Ljubljana and continued in Znojmo, where he married and had children. From the 1750s he worked in Hungary, initially for the Premonstratensians in Jasov. His greatest achievement is the monumental ceiling fresco in the nave of the Church of St. Nicholas in Prague, Malá Straná (1760/61). After “commuting” to Moravia and Lower Austria for over a decade, he settled finally in Eger in 1768 where his patron, Bishop Károly Eszterházy, showered him with work. The most notable of these commissions was the fresco in the library of the Lyceum of Eger (*The Council of Trent*) painted with his assistant, Joseph Zach in 1778. The signed oil sketch of St. Catherine for the high altar of Egerbakta Parish Church in the Hungarian National Gallery is a masterpiece of a later date. The religious dispute of the young Christian woman, Catherine of Alexandria who lived in the early 4th century, adjusts itself to a Viennese model and Michelangelo Unterberger's composition *The Twelve-Year-Old Christ in the Temple*. The style of the sketch is rugged and restless; the figures elongated and with small heads. Golden yellow predominates among the vibrant colours of the *bozzetto*, while in the final, larger variant both the forms and the colours are calmer. As victorious Ecclesia, Catherine, who converted 50 sages and the empress in a religious debate, proclaimed the truth of the Church shaken by the Enlightenment.
cceaf42f-eb5f-541e-a0f9-aad5efa6922d.short_description: Johann Lucas Kracker, a Viennese artist whose family was of Czech origin, finally settled in Hungary having married and had children in Znojmo. Employed by the Bishop of Eger who showered him with work, he worked on a number of frescos and altarpieces later in his career. This small, signed oil *bozzetto* is a study for the high altar of Egerbakta Parish Church.

cd089341-0bb9-55f0-b578-8f53eb67a553.short_description: During the rule of the Zand and Qajar dynasties in Iran (1750–1925), artists created paintings that combined both Persian and Western sensibilities. From Europe came the tradition of large-scale oil painting, while the subject matter of youthful beauty, patterned textiles, and court life was quintessentially Persian. Many of these works were arched at the top because they were originally intended for display in arched niches of buildings.

cd5b9635-c13b-5dc6-8783-210593843bb9.name: *Madonna with Child and Saints* (Anthony of Padua, Martin, Roch and Sebastian)
cd5b9635-c13b-5dc6-8783-210593843bb9.description:
Painted in 1655, the «small picture with the Blessed Virgin, St. Martin, St. Sebastian, St. Roch and St. Anthony of Padua for the municipality of Trasasso», is still in its original location.  
Made for a peripheral area, the painting is an example of the style of a young woman artist at the beginning of her carrier, when she was still strictly dependent on her father and teacher, the painter Giovanni Andrea Sirani. The painting of the *Madonna and Child and Saints* painted by Giovanni Andrea in the same years for the church of Santi Luigi e Alessio(today, in Rome, church of San Petronio dei Bolognesi) was clearly a model for his daughter and pupil. Elisabetta, however, goes back to the roots of Bolognese classicism, imitating the more vibrant and rich results of Annibale Carracci in his celebrated *Madonna with Saint Louis* (Bologna, Pinacoteca Nazionale).  
The divine is interpreted in a more human way through the intimate and confidential dialogue between the Virgin in glory with the Child and the saints, nearly tangible, standing on the step in the foreground. Tenderness is glimpsed under the polished and soft surfaces, a sort of prelude of the artist’s future stylistic inclinations: Elisabetta starts to experiment with her own language with a prestigious and difficult genre: the altarpiece.
cd5b9635-c13b-5dc6-8783-210593843bb9.short_description: The painting, made for a peripheral area, is the first public commission of by a famous woman painter at a very young age, she was only seventeen years old. It shows her extremely precocious talent and underlines the still strong link with Bolognese Classicism through the influence of Annibale Carracci and Guido Reni, the master of Giovanni Andrea Sirani, father and master of Elisabetta.
cd5b9635-c13b-5dc6-8783-210593843bb9.method_for_datation: The date of the execution, 1655, and the original location (unchanged) are quoted in the *List of paintings* written by the painter herself and published by her biographer, count Carlo Cesare Malvasia (*Nota*, in Carlo Cesare Malvasia, *Felsina pittrice*, Bologna 1678, (ed. cons. 1841), p. 393).

cd8363f9-fa9a-5f8b-942e-3c9d931124ec.name: Saint Paraskeva
cd8363f9-fa9a-5f8b-942e-3c9d931124ec.description:
Saint Paraskeva was born to Christian parents during the reign of Emperor Hadrian. She was given the name Paraskeva (Greek for “Friday”) since Friday was the day of Christ’s crucifixion as well as the day of her birth. She was arrested during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius for preaching Christianity. He offered her great wealth and even proposed marriage if she renounced her faith, but she refused. The enraged emperor placed her in boiling oil, and when she did not show any pain, demanded to know whether she had used magic to cool the oil. She responded by throwing the hot liquid at the emperor, instantly blinding him. He asked Paraskeva for help and she healed him with water from a nearby stream. Antoninus Pius set her free, converted to Christianity and stopped persecuting Christians. The inscription on the scroll in this icon reads as follows:  
  
\[H\]ighly praised is thy name – of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, my Lord God – now and forever. For thou forgave me and did not reject my humility nor my prayer; and thy being pleased by me is incomprehensible.

cd9d11ca-ddd3-5d4d-b4c1-278248c60b07.name: *The Judgment of Solomon*
cd9d11ca-ddd3-5d4d-b4c1-278248c60b07.short_description:
The only Persian artists in the 17th century who were able to break with the overwhelming influence of Riza-i Abbasi were those who were inspired by the greater naturalism that characterized not only European but also Indian painting.  
Shaykh Abbasi was one of them, and in this signed and minutely detailed painting, he set the court of Solomon in 17th-century Iran.

ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.name: "The Concourse of the Birds"
ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.alternate_name: Folio 11r from a Mantiq al-Tayr (Language of the Birds)
ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.description: The illustration on this folio depicts a scene from a mystical poem, Mantiq al-tair (Language of the Birds), written by a twelfth-century Iranian, Farid al-Din 'Attar. The birds, which symbolize individual souls in search of the simurgh (a mystical bird representing ultimate spiritual unity), are assembled in an idyllic landscape to begin their pilgrimage under the leadership of a hoopoe (perched on a rock at center right). The careful, harmonious composition is consistent with that of the late fifteenth-century Timurid miniatures also in the manuscript, but three factors indicate that this image is later: the presence of the hunter, who has no place in the narrative; his firearm, a weapon that gained currency in Iran after the mid-sixteenth century; and the signature of the late sixteenth- to early seventeenth-century artist Habiballah.
ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.initial_owner: Shah Abbas I, Isfahan, Iran (ca. 1600–1609); Shrine of Shaikh Safi Al-Din, Ardabil, Iran(ca. 1609–sack of Ardebil, 1826); M. Farid Parbanta(until 1963)

ce8c6cf9-eba8-53fb-82b0-2eb939b70f74.name: *Combat of Dalmatian Imperial infantry at Livno, August 8th, 1878*
ce8c6cf9-eba8-53fb-82b0-2eb939b70f74.short_description: Julius von Blaas received many commissions from the court and mostly painted portraits of the imperial family. He also painted naturalistic battle scenes depicting victories of the Austrian Army both past and present, like this scene of the occupation campaign of 1878. Here, the Dalmatian Imperial Infantry is attacking in line formation at Livno. The soldiers in the vanguard are already falling. Contrary to the prognoses of the foreign minister, Count Gyula Andrássy (1823–1890), the occupation campaign in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878 was not just a short “Sunday walk with a concert band”; instead the Austro-Hungarian troops had to face hard military resistance and rugged defence.

d2153895-57ef-583f-b177-30f75fa578f2.short_description: Filippo Palizzi came from a large family and, along with his three brothers, all painters, introduced in Italy a realistic style of painting which breaks away from academic tradition of religious, mythological or history painting. d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.name: Mirror box
d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.short_description:
The mirror box is signed with the characteristic formula "*kamtarin muḥammad baqir*" (the most humble Muhammad Baqir) and dated Hegira 1174 (AD 1760/61). Muhammad Baqir is one of the most famous Persian artists in the 18th century. He was the pupil of Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf (active Hegira 1134-1190 / AD 1722-1777) and worked in the 1750s on the borders of the so-called St. Petersburg album. Without doubt, this mirror box is one of his early independent lacquer works.  
  
Muhammad Baqir's oeuvre comprises border paintings for albums, single-leaf drawings and lacquer works. A striking feature of his art is his fascination in works by such renowned late Safavid artists as Muhammad Zaman (active Hegira ca, 1072-1105 / AD ca. 1662-1694) and ʿAliquli Jabadar (active Hegira 1059-1086 / AD 1649-1675) whose work he either copied or used as inspiration for his own creations. This is also the case with the three figurative panels of this mirror box. Thus, the half-naked bathing woman with a red towel sitting on a small rock can be compared to Muhammad Zaman's illustration of the bathing Shirin in a *Khamsa* from 1674/75.
d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.method_for_datation: The artist signed and dated his work.

d27f7bc1-9e5e-581e-a7d7-9666172ce6a8.name: *The Cock Fight*
d27f7bc1-9e5e-581e-a7d7-9666172ce6a8.short_description: Among the best known of his Orientalist paintings from the Balkans are those of domestic life, such as *The Cock Fight*. In this painting Jovanović builds a credible, believable scene. The spectators are fully engaged, each one reacts in his or her own particular way, consistent with their age and appearance. The singularity of Jovanović’s approach is even more evident when contrasted to Western European Orientalist paintings such as Jean Léon Gérôme’s famous *The Cock Fight* of 1847 or Ferentz Eisenhut’s depiction of a cock fight in 1894. Awarded the first prize at the Wien Künstlerhaus exhibition 1898, and having a great success at the Paris Salon in 1906, it was widely reproduced in subsequent years and was surely known to Jovanović. It is evident that studies of the figures directly from nature inform this painting. Jovanović was not only providing a new and authentic category of genre paintings but speaking specifically to a culture that was his own. In the process, he was giving significance to an area and ethnic groups heretofore ignored.
d27f7bc1-9e5e-581e-a7d7-9666172ce6a8.author: Petar Petrovic
keywords: Orientalism

d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.name: *The Grand Bazaar Istanbul*
d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.short_description: This painting provides a fascinating insight into the activities within the Grand Bazaar of Istanbul during the 19th century CE. First built in the 15th century, its importance had declined somewhat in the 19th century, as non-Muslim merchants increasingly established independent shops in the European quarters of Istanbul rather than staying in the ‘outdated’ bazaar. Nevertheless, in 1890, there were still well over 4000 shops in the Bazaar. This image provides much detail about the appearance of traditional merchants and shops. Men, including some soldiers in European-style uniforms, and women in colourful local dress can be seen milling about the bazaar, their costume revealing important details about their ethnicity, profession and social status.
d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: bazaar

d450789d-d8de-5381-91d6-952696e07e5e.name: *St. Catherine*
d450789d-d8de-5381-91d6-952696e07e5e.description:
This altarpiece painting represents a young St. Catherine half-kneeling on clouds and wearing a yellow and white dress with a red cloak. She has a crown on her head and holds a lily in her right hand. Beside her are some books and in front of her left knee is a sword. While the clouds surround her, angel heads look out from behind the clouds above her. The composition follows the traditional iconography of the subject.  
Xaver Ferenc (Francis) Falconer was one of the best known members of the Falconer family of artists, which according to tradition, originated from Scotland and settled in Buda at the end of the 18th century. Xaver Ferenc Falconer studied with his grandfather and another painter named Schultz, and became an independent master in 1761. After the early death of his father, the painter Polykarp Falconer, he studied painting with his stepfather János (John) Schultz, a painter from Brandenburg. In 1761 Falconer enrolled at Vienna's Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture (Academy of Fine Arts, Vienna). He was made a citizen of Buda in 1761, and in 1765 – along with his spouse (whom he married in 1763) – he bought a modest bourgeois house in the castle district of Buda. In 1794, their heirs sold the house and established a shop on the ground floor. Today this house is in the possession of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and serves as a guesthouse. From the altarpieces Falconer executed, only one is still *in situ* in Hungary, Szécsény. In the 1770s Falconer produced some signed altarpiece paintings for the cloisters of the Franciscan order in Croatia.
d450789d-d8de-5381-91d6-952696e07e5e.short_description: A Baroque altarpiece painting of St. Catherine from the Parish Church of the Viziváros (Watertown) in the district of Buda.

d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.name: *Shipping at Constantinople*
d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.short_description: Istanbul’s geographic position between Europe and Asia and on the only sea route that connects the Black Sea with the Mediterranean gave Istanbul great strategic importance. The control of the Bosphorus, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara, was repeatedly at stake in the 19th and early 20th centuries. This 1910 watercolour gives a wonderful impression of the bustling shipping and trading activities on the waters surrounding the city of Constantinople at the time. The view is taken from the Galata side of the city, looking across the Golden Horn towards its historic heart, dominated by imperial Suleymaniye mosque on the right and Bayezid tower in the centre. The Galata bridge, in its third incarnation as completed by the British firm G. Wells in 1875, can be seen connecting the two shores. Sailing boats like those seen here brought in wheat, spices and wood. The emergence of the steamship later in the century lead to enormous increase in the speed and volume of commodities shipped to Constantinople.
d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

d549811b-c5d8-5fa3-9488-5db916492dba.name: *The Dinner held at Delphi in Honour of the Painter by the Elder of the Village at Chryso*
d549811b-c5d8-5fa3-9488-5db916492dba.short_description: This drawing is almost identical to the plate entitled “Dinner at Crisso in the house of the Bishop of Salona”, which is included in Dodwell’s folio *Views in Greece*, (1821). The accompanying text testifies to the artist’s antiquarianism and his attempt to identify classical customs in 19th century life. *“The Bishop of Salona gave us a favourable opportunity of observing some customs which merit commendation as instances in which classical usages have survived. Before sitting down to dinner and after we rose from table we performed the ancient ceremony of washing the hands. Atin bason is taken round to all the company, the servant holding it on his left arm, while with his right hand he pours water from a pewter vessel on the hands of the washer, having a towel thrown over his shoulder to dry them with. This ceremony is mentioned by Hesiod, by Homer, and other authors…”.*
d549811b-c5d8-5fa3-9488-5db916492dba.author: Tsigakou 1995, 116, fig. 7
keywords: travels; Dupre

d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.name: *The Concert*
d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.description:
The painting, which was probably kept by the painter's family, is one of a series of Flemish works acquired in 1783 by Marcantonio Borghese. Gerrit van Honthorst, better known in Italy as Gherardo delle Notti, fitted in perfectly with the followers of Caravaggio in Rome, who revisited and reworked Merisi's favourite subjects, especially the secular themes. This piece, which dates from 1626–1630, apparently shows a simple musical theme, although in fact the composition hides a moral meaning.  
Typical of the art of the Counter-Reformation and particularly esteemed in the culture of the Netherlands, the artist's homeland, are themes related to allegories intended to express moral meanings. In this case, music, an excellent, virtuous, but also ephemeral art, is represented by an old woman who, in pointing to her toothless mouth, appears to be warning the three youths playing a concert of the fleetingness of youth and beauty.  
The subject also reveals the trick being played on the young man who, intent on singing, fails to realise that the maiden is taking his earring, with the complicity of the old woman, who is ready to slip it into her pocket. The theme of the trick is related to the allegorical evocation of the five senses: hearing through music, sight in expressive looks, taste through wine and food, touch by the gesture of the seductress, and smell through the nose, which the old woman appears to be pointing to. Special attention is paid to the table, where a basket of fruit is clearly visible. This element combines with the others in a sort of pastiche, the figurative motifs borrowed from famous Caravaggesque works, which also influenced the neutral choice of background.
d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.short_description: Gerrit Van Honthorst, called Gherardo delle Notti, absorbed the influence of Caravaggio during his stay in Italy (1610–1620). The subject, the composition, the still life on the table, the light falling on the left, all are quotations from Caravaggio's works.

d62a8aad-7189-5f2c-a39f-c9a6febe7aa4.name: *Ancient Istanbul Houses*
d62a8aad-7189-5f2c-a39f-c9a6febe7aa4.short_description: Hoca Ali Rıza is known as the first painter who used landscapes in Turkish painting. A study of the artist’s works also readily reveals architectural structures which have changed since his time. Such structures included mosques, fountains, dervish monasteries and lodges, tombs, *sebils* (public fountains installed by charities), ruins, cemeteries, bridges, stately homes new and old, towers, old houses and other subjects which architecturally and historically speaking might have been considered ordinary in his day, but which he pursued with a passion. Riza is completely realistic in his works and he specialized in depicting landscapes using light and shadow.
d62a8aad-7189-5f2c-a39f-c9a6febe7aa4.holder: Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University, Painting and Sculpture Museum
keywords: Painting; Hoca Ali Rıza; orientalist Turkish painters

d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.name: Women by the Well
d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.description:
This painting elegantly encapsulates a quotidian moment imbued with the rural essence of Jordanian tradition. The scene under consideration depicts a group of figures, predominantly female, congregated around a stone well situated beneath a clear blue sky, with lush greenery and palm trees serving as a backdrop. The utilisation of vibrant hues and meticulous attention to detail serves to elicit a sense of concord between humans, architecture and nature.  
The composition is centred on the well structure, which is composed of warm, sandy stones and framed by an arched entrance that serves as both a practical and symbolic focal point. This concept encompasses not only the physical source of water but also serves as a nexus for community and social interaction. The women's actions, drawing, carrying and pouring water reflect cooperation and rhythm in everyday life, while their vibrant clothing, rich in blues, reds and greens, highlights cultural identity and regional craftsmanship.  
The artist's employment of colour and light engenders an atmosphere that is serene and almost celebratory. The distinct contours and vivid colour scheme bear resemblance to folk painting and naïve art, placing emphasis on storytelling and collective memory as opposed to strict realism. This approach encourages viewers to recognise the aesthetic value of simplicity and to acknowledge the dignity of routine activities.
d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts
d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.author: Dina Turkieh
keywords: women; well; water; oil

d69d5ebf-06df-5404-94a9-7a8bcef7bfac.name: Mahmal Print
d69d5ebf-06df-5404-94a9-7a8bcef7bfac.short_description:
This copper print depicts the ceremonial *mahmal* in the pilgrimage procession from Cairo to Mecca during the month of *hajj*. The *mahmal* is a tent-like cloth covering the camel litter and bearing the new *kiswa* to be bestowed upon the Kaaba.  
  
Dated 1729 in Leiden, the Dutch publisher Pieter van der Aa printed this illustration of the religious caravan traveling to Saudi Arabia with Muslim pilgrims. The picture brings the pilgrimage to life and labels indicate the individual elements, including the commander and his wife who are carried within the palanquin.  
  
As worshippers around the world apply for the *hajj* visa, this print may reflect the importance of the pilgrimage for Dutch Muslims today, while contemporary exhibitions in the Netherlands commemorate this pillar of Islam.

d6d69c7b-e931-5628-b682-41484e297c16.name: *Woman with a Branch of Dates*
d6d69c7b-e931-5628-b682-41484e297c16.description:
Faiq Hassan was among the pioneering artists in Iraq who obtained formal art education and was awarded a government scholarship to pursue studies in Paris. In AH 1356 / AD 1938, he assumed the directorship of the recently established *Ma’had al-Funun al-Jamila fi Baghdad* (Institute of Fine Arts in Baghdad), a role he held until AH 1382 / AD 1962.  
Hassan belonged to the cohort of *'al-Ruwwad'* (the Pioneers), a group of painters that integrated elements of everyday Iraqi life into their artwork and defied conventional studio methods. He followed the artistic principle of istilham al-turath, which focused on taking inspiration from heritage. This principle was developed by *Jama'at Baghdad lil-Fann al-Hadith* (Baghdad Group for Modern Art), which was founded in AH 1370 / AD 1951.  
  
'A Woman with a Branch of Dates' shows an Iraqi woman wearing a black traditional garment and holding a basket of dates , before an abstract, flattened village background. Hassan preferred to depict everyday life in rural areas. He merged the artistic traditions of ancient Mesopotamia with modernism to cultivate an awareness of Iraqi national identity.
d6d69c7b-e931-5628-b682-41484e297c16.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art
keywords: woman; dates; water

d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.name: *Ships in a Harbour*
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.description: A finely executed Baroque painting of a harbour with ships and throngs of people on the shore. The composition is a rare example of a small size genre piece, which may have been part of a series. The execution of the painting is finely detailed, and contrary to its small size, the work is of high quality. This is an unusual representation within the iconography of this type of picture. Scenes of everyday life became common in the 17th and 18th centuries, and depictions of the “low-life” of peasants and the “high-life” of the aristocracy, featuring fashionably dressed figures in different scenes were also common. The popularity of seascapes and maritime pictures spread to Hungary by way of Flemish and Dutch painting. Small seascapes (*zeekens*) were a very popular theme representing – like this painting – imaginary views of exotic ports.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.short_description: A finely executed Baroque genre painting of a harbour with ships and throngs of people on the shore. Because of these and other features, the painting represents a rare example among Baroque seascapes.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.obtention: From the bequest of Count Jenő Zichy in 1903.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.bibliography: *Budapest az Újkorban* (*Budapest in the Modern Times*), (ed. G. Szvoboda Dománszky), Budapest, 1995, p.29
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.author: Beatrix Basics
keywords: Oil painting; genre painting; Zichy family

d75fdd85-26c2-5bef-8d42-b7e7435167f5.name: The rulers of the Mughal dynasty from Babur to Awrangzeb, with their ancestor Timur
d75fdd85-26c2-5bef-8d42-b7e7435167f5.short_description:
Timur occupies the central position in this group portrait. From the front, and on the left are the emperors Shah Jahan, Akbar and Babur, with Abu Sa‘id, ruler of Samarkand, and Timur’s son, Miranshah. On the right are the emperors Awrangzeb, Jahangir and Humayun, and two of Timur’s other sons, ‘Umar Shaykh and Muhammad Sultan. The figures are identified by legends in gold.  
The setting is a terrace overlooking a garden with cypress trees. The figures kneel on a rich floral carpet on which are precious objects, including two unusual incense burners and an enamelled table with two Chinese porcelain vases. So meticulous are the details that smoke rising from the incense burners can be seen.  
Although the composition must date from the beginning of Awrangzeb’s reign, the style of the painting suggests that it is an 18th century work, and that it was painted by Bhawani Das. His signature appears on a virtually identical hexagonal table in a painting in the Binney Collection.

d75fdd85-26c2-5bef-8d42-b7e7435167f5.method_for_datation: Date, provenance and attribution based on stylistic grounds as ell as the subject matter depicted.

d7670c25-7540-57e5-9687-097d572b293a.name: *Moor with oranges*
d7670c25-7540-57e5-9687-097d572b293a.description: Sorolla painted this Moor with oranges in Italy (where he lived on a scholarship), at the end of 1885 or beginning of 1886, long before he travelled to Tiwan, Morocco, in 1919. This is a typical example of Oriental painting made for sale, as Orientalist painting was very fashionable at the time. Sorolla painted mostly Moors and concubines, which conformed to Western ideals of life in the East and not necessarily with reality. Like the main character of this painting, a Moor smoking, wearing the exotic hijab and barefoot, holding an orange in his hand.
d7670c25-7540-57e5-9687-097d572b293a.author: Covadonga Pitarch
keywords: Orientalist painting; Spain; Formation of painters

d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.name: *The Hunt of Diana*
d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.description:
The work was commissioned from Domenichino by his patron, Cardinal Pietro Aldrobrandini. However, it came into the possession of Cardinal Scipione Borghese when he took it by force from the artist's study, depriving the original client, a nephew of Clement VIII (1592–1605), his traditional rival. The subject is inspired by a passage from Virgil's *Aeneid* (canto V) that describes the archery competition between Aeneas' friends: aiming at a dove tied to a post, the first archer hits the post; the second cuts the ribbon holding the bird; the third misses and the fourth shoots regardless to demonstrate his skill, and his arrow bursts into flames and ends up in the clouds. The sequence is transposed into the domain of nymph disciples of Diana, the goddess of hunting, an idyllic and luminous environment that represents the mythical Arcadia. The literary metaphors derive from the cultured Domenichino's involvement with G. B. Agucchi, secretary to the cardinal and adviser to the painter in the conception of the work.  
In the representation of the nymphs' play, the painter is attempting to paint the poetic and chronological narration of the facts, lifting pictorial art above poetic art and, in general dissolving the limit traditionally placed on different art forms; a topic that was widely discussed in the Baroque period.  
The pose and the expression of the “affections” (feelings) on the faces help to explain the succession of events, while the unbridled play is contained in a classical equilibrium. The nymph holding the greyhound shows us what will happen to the two male figures hidden amongst the bushes on the right-hand side of the canvas.  
According to the myth, Diana's terrible rage was unleashed against the hunter Actaeon who, having seen her bathing, was turned into a stag and devoured by his own dogs. One of the nymphs immersed in the water, tender and sensual, gazes at the viewer and links the internal and external spaces of the painting; another attempt to overcome limitations, in this instance spatial, that is typical of Baroque art.
d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.short_description:
The canvas was painted for Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, nephew of the preceding Pope Clement VIII, who had a strong dislike for the Borghese family. However, Cardinal Scipione wanted the painting for himself and had it forcibly removed from the artist's studio, imprisoning the artist for several days.  
In this painting Domenichino synthesises the colour of Bolognese painting, Roman drawings and Leonardo's theories on aerial perspective.

d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.name: *Feast at the House of Simon the Pharisee*
d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.description:
The work was initially attributed to Veronese, a hypothesis that, although incorrect, successfully identifies the inspirations of the artist, who, in his early twenties trained in Venice.  
In the lagoon city, the painter was able to study the work of Tiziano, Veronese and Tintoretto, as well as Bassano and Schiavone, reworking the characters of Venetian painting through his strictly Ferraran training.  
The scene develops within an open loggia framed by columns, two of which appear to be inspired by the columns of Trajan and Antoninus. The representation shows a well known story from the Gospel of St. Luke (7, 36–50) which tells of a feast at the house of Simon, a Pharisee, who believed that he had fulfilled all his duties to God and that, therefore, he had the right to a tranquil, comfortable life. The feast is interrupted by the sinner Magdalene, who shocks those present by kissing Christ's feet, washing them with her tears and sprinkling them with precious scented oils.  
The episode highlights divine mercy for sinners who demonstrate humble and sincere penitence. Arranged diagonally around the table, the figures are grouped into small genre scenes characterised by lively expressions, inspired by the style of Bassano. The sky in the background, crossed by intense strips of green, fades into the distant landscape. The fulcrum of the scene has been shifted to the left-hand side of the painting where Magdalene, the jar of ointment at her feet and her hair untied, turns her head in a silent dialogue with Christ.  
The intense colours, lively gestures and unusual perspective are indicative of the taste that precluded the scenic representations of the Baroque period.
d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.short_description: The historical reference refers to the Gospel of St. Luke: Mary Magdalene who was in the house of Simon during a banquet. Kneeling at the feet of Christ with her usual attribute, a jar of ointment, she washes His feet and dries them with her long hair. The protagonists of the scene are not in the central part of the composition, but on the left-hand side that becomes the fulcrum for the narrative.
d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

d804899b-9769-5c70-a8ff-438b6dcac6e8.name: *Hamzanama*: Mahlaj shows his skill to Zumurrud Shah and runs a spear through a tree
d804899b-9769-5c70-a8ff-438b6dcac6e8.short_description: "Mahlaj mounted a horse and began to exhibit his skill in spear-throwing. A camel stuffed with sand was brought, and Mahlaj charged it and planted his spear into its side in such a way that it passed straight through. Then he picked up the camel and its load and hurled it over his head. A cheer arose from the people. Next he speared the tree so hard that it split in two. 'My Lord,' said Mahlaj, 'if anyone can pull this spear out of the tree, he will have performed a real feat.' This he said, and he dismounted."

d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.name: The *Annunciation*
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.description:
Initially composed of four panels, this piece was originally of a different size. Recent tests have proved that its lower section has been cut on both sides. Prior to this recent modification, the work underwent further changes. The Virgin Mary is represented in the second condition of the Angelic Colloquium of the Mystery of the Annunciation, by Friar Roberto Caracciolo de Lecce (1425‒1495). That is to say, this is the moment of *cogitatio* or reflection, in which the Virgin considers the Angel’s words and demonstrates her prudence.  
Similar to other paintings alluding to this theme, the work bears witness to symbolism characteristic of representations of the Annunciation: the book that lays opened before Mary; the vase with lilies; the Angel’s sceptre; the bed, topped by its canopy and with its prominent front curtains, upon which the knots are formed; the column between the two characters, and the mat on which Mary is found standing.  
In recent years, the study of textiles through paintings, in its manifold categories, has proved to be very useful. Aside from documental sources and extant objects, paintings provide important visual evidence concerning an object’s trade and usage throughout time. In this particular painting, representing a Portuguese domestic interior, the Virgin Mary stands on a mat. Following the Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula, which stretched well into the 16th century, floors were commonly covered with mats, mainly in the summer, when they replaced carpets.  
Although this mat could be of Portuguese manufacture (Lisbon, Oporto or the Algarve) it has been associated with the mats woven with palm fibre and decorated with geometric patterns from sub-Saharan Africa, particularly those from the Congo (and Benin and Niger).
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.holder: Museum of Portuguese Decorative Arts – Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva Foundation
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.method_for_datation: Authorship was attributed to the Lourinhã Master (active between 1500 and 1540) by Luís Reis Santos in his work dedicated to this artist and published in 1963. This attribution has been rejected in more recent studies, thus it is classified here as the work of a follower of the master.
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.obtention: This was one of Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva's first pieces towards his collection of primitive artworks; donated by Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva in 1953.

Saldanha, Nuno, *Tesouros das Imagens, colecção Museu-Escola de Artes Decorativas Portuguesas – Pintura*, Lisbon: FRESS, 1996.

d8f09c37-b8cb-56c1-917a-f069f4830ef2.name: *The Governess*
d8f09c37-b8cb-56c1-917a-f069f4830ef2.short_description: The position of governess was one of the few professions open to middle-class women of modest means, but it was often a lonely and difficult life because the social status of a governess was ambiguous. She was not a servant in the usual sense but nor was she on equal terms with the family who employed her. Here, the young woman holds a letter which has obviously stirred memories of home. It may be news of a death in her family - letters or cards with black borders were used to announce deaths. Redgrave had a personal interest in representing the life of a governess: his sister Jane was a governess and died young.
d8f09c37-b8cb-56c1-917a-f069f4830ef2.dimensions: Height: 71.1 cm estimate, Width: 91.5 cm estimate

d943747b-f71a-55eb-8ef6-d6beeeed2083.name: Salim Kills Rhinoceros and a Lion
d943747b-f71a-55eb-8ef6-d6beeeed2083.short_description: This painting was once part of a *Shikarnama*, an album of images of the hunt presumably compiled for the Mughal emperor Jahangir while he was still a prince (and thus still known by his birth name, Salim). The prince is shown having just killed a lioness, with a pile of dead rhinoceros nearby. In the background are several dead antelope and around them a group of *shikari*s (hunt attendants), some with antelope slung over their shoulders, one holding the prince’s sword (wrapped in a cloth casing), and one holding a quiver full of arrows, but almost every one of them is looking or gesturing towards the cheetah on the other side of the stream that has just brought down yet another antelope.
keywords: hunt; illustration; miniature painting; border decoration; floral decoration; flower; elephant; arms; weapons; hunting
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

d97e8889-9ee3-5eb8-9ea9-a6732fa73dbd.name: The Mother of God Smolenskaya
d97e8889-9ee3-5eb8-9ea9-a6732fa73dbd.description: This Mother of God icon is known as a *Hodegetria* icon (Greek for “one who shows the way”). It is recognizable by the solemn expression of the Mother of God and the frontal position of the Christ Child delivering a blessing. The Christ Child sits on his mother’s left knee and holds a tightly rolled scroll. A copy of the original *Hodegetria* icon was brought to the Assumption Cathedral in Smolensk from Byzantium in the 12th century. In the 15th century, it was transferred to Moscow before being returned to Smolensk. The icon has a silver *repoussé basma* (hammered metal ornamentation) nailed to its surface, as well as a Kremlin School *cloisonné* raised halo dating back to the 17th century.
d97e8889-9ee3-5eb8-9ea9-a6732fa73dbd.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2001. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography
materials: Egg tempera on wood with silver basma, enamel

d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.name: Reverse painting on glass: Tattoo template with Christian motifs
d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.short_description: In Cairo, the most famous saints have their weekly visiting day. For Imam Shafi’i it is Friday. The mausoleum of the legal scholar, who died in 820, is one of the most popular sites for Muslim pilgrimages in the city. In the mid-1970s a wandering tattoo artist set up his reverse glass paintings every week on the market place in front of the Shafi’i Mausoleum and waited for customers: Muslims as well as Copts. One of the reverse glass paintings acquired from him shows two images of the Virgin Mary, once as the *Mother of God*, and again as *Our Lady of Sorrows*. The latter image served as a model for the *Mater Dolorosa* of the Florentine 17th century master Carlo Dolci, as it attained cult status from Alexandria to Aswan among Christians. It is said that, in a church on the west bank of the Nile, a coloured print of Dolci's *Our Lady of Sorrows* "cried tears of blood" from her right eye for the persecuted Copts.
d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
d9bc604a-632e-5b67-a98e-6e1c1d0aea7f.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.

db39b375-c70e-50cc-84c8-684cd0ce707f.name: Pencase
db39b375-c70e-50cc-84c8-684cd0ce707f.short_description:
The pencase is adorned with a characteristic decoration consisting of amorphous, leaf-like structures that are entwined together. In their entirety, they are reminiscent of spiral tendrils. Three slightly raised, copper-coloured cartouches “float” on top of this greenish-yellow ground. They are filled with a wave decoration that resembles the guilloche pattern of European goldsmiths.  
  
As far as we know today, this decoration was developed by Rajab ʿAli in the first half of the 19th century, with Abu Talib later taking up the style and making it famous. The pencase exhibited here was probably made by a copyist.  
  
According to an inscription on the top, the work was ordered by a man named Hasan.

dc9bec02-eb7b-5be5-b697-9d2faab3da93.name: *La Mhalla* (painting)
dc9bec02-eb7b-5be5-b697-9d2faab3da93.short_description: This oil on canvas by Bertrand de Moynier depicts the disembarkment of the *mhalla*, the field army, in the mid-19th century for the collection of taxes. The *mhalla*, a military term, was made up of soldiers, *mamluks*, civil servants, merchants and artisans, which were split into three categories: infantry, cavalry and artillery. This army was supported by informal troops and horsemen from local tribes. The beylical tent has been erected in the centre of the mhalla, next to the service tents for the bey's personnel and the tents for the administrative and fiscal representatives. The future 'Ali Bey III (1882–1902) can be seen in the centre of the painting, in front of the red and green flags.

dd5bbbcb-30cc-5383-b362-bb72392b0cce.name: Nasser and the Nationalisation of the Canal
dd5bbbcb-30cc-5383-b362-bb72392b0cce.description: Hamed Owais’s Nasser and the Nationalisation of the Canal can be used to discuss the Cold War period and the rise of twentieth-century Arab nationalism. Painted in 1957, the work refers to Gamal Abdel Nasser’s nationalisation of the Suez Canal in 1956, a moment that became a powerful symbol of anti-imperialism, national sovereignty, and Arab political self-confidence. Owais presents Nasser as a heroic leader surrounded by the people, transforming a specific political event into an image of collective hope and revolutionary legitimacy. The painting is especially useful for explaining how art participated in the construction of Nasserist ideology, where modernisation, social justice, and independence from British and French control were visually linked to the figure of the leader. At the same time, the work opens a discussion about the double nature of political development in the Middle East: the promise of liberation and national dignity on one side, and the centralisation of power around a charismatic state authority on the other.

dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.name: Safi ibn Vali’s Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’)
dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.short_description:
Written during the year-long pilgrimage undertaken by the author, Safi ibn Vali, in 1676–77, the Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’) gives advice to prospective pilgrims on every aspect of the journey: which ships to choose, how to stay healthy, the places to visit, the rituals to be observed and the people one is likely to encounter. Safi ibn Vali’s own pilgrimage (he commenced his journey on 12 Rajab 1087/ 20 September 1676) was made possible through the financial help of Zib al-Nisa, a daughter of the Mughal emperor Awrangzeb, for whom he had written a commentary on the Qur’an.  
  
This manuscript belongs to a long-established tradition of guides to the Holy Places (see MSS 1038), although the illustrations here differ in that they combine the diagrammatic views normally found in such guides with vivid and colourful scenes of the pilgrims and their caravans. The illustrations are simple in their conception yet their attention to detail is acute. They provide a cogent picture of camp life of pilgrims in the late 17th century.  
  
The illustrations:  
  
View of the port of Surat and the ships carrying pilgrims (folio 2b). Surat, on the Western coast of India, north of Bombay, was one of the main points of departure to Arabia. The view is oriented to the south.  
The pilgrims’ ships crossing the Sea of Oman (folio 3b). The two larger ships carry pilgrims; one, on the right, appears to be casting (or raising) anchor. The smaller vessels may be fishing boats.  
The mish‘ar al-haram and the ritual of collecting pebbles (folio 10a). The painting shows the pilgrims in the region of Muzdalifa, in a state of ihram (ritual purity), collecting pebbles.  
The pilgrims in the town of Mina, being shaved, making sacrifices and casting pebbles at the Devil (folio 10b). This day corresponds to ‘Id al-Adha on 10 dhu’l-Hijjah, the feast commemorating the Sacrifice of Abraham. By this stage, the pilgrims, who are in a full state of ihram indicated by their white garments, have already completed their initial circumambulation of the Ka‘bah (the welcome tawaf); the ritual of running between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa‘iyy) recalling Hagar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma‘il; the day of prayer at ‘Arafat – a most holy time when every pilgrim stands alone with God; and the gathering of pebbles at Muzdalifa in preparation for the stoning of the Devil at Mina. This recalls yet another chapter in the Abrahamic narrative in which Isma‘il stones the Devil seven times (the ritual is illustrated in the upper right-hand corner of the painting). After this a sacrifice is made. The pilgrims are released from most of the restrictions imposed by the state of ihram; men shave their heads and beards; women have their hair clipped. Pilgrims can now wear their normal clothes and leave for Mecca, where they perform another essential rite, a further circumambulation of the Ka‘bah known as the tawaf al-ifadah, which takes place on the same day.  
The birthplaces of the Prophet Muhammad; Fatimah; Abu Bak al-Siddiq; as well as the Madrasah of Sultan Sulayman, and a Bektashi lodge (folio 11b). These are shrines to visit in the vicinity of Mecca, which are not part of the hajj rituals.  
Plan of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca with the Ka‘bah (folio 12a).  
The camp of North African caravan of pilgrims (folio 15a).  
The camp of Egyptian caravan of pilgrims (folio 15b).  
The camp of the Syrian caravan of pilgrims (folio 16a). Unlike the pilgrims from North Africa and Egypt, the Syrian pilgrims are richly dressed and carry swords and gold daggers. Ahmad Pasha, the Syrian Amir al-Hajj, is identified by a caption (top left).  
The camp of the desert Arabs and the people of Najd (folio 16b).  
The camp of the caravans of the Indian (top) and Iranian pilgrims (folio 17a).  
Officials, scribes and secretaries (folio 17b). This is a small illustration, which is not captioned.  
Sharif Barakat, hakim haramayn sharifayn (‘Governor of the two Holy Sanctuaries’), riding to meet the envoy of Sultan Mehmed \[IV\], the Emperor of Rum (folio 18a).  
‘Abdi Pasha, the Amir al-Hajj of the Egyptian caravan, on his way from Mecca to Medina (folio 18b).  
The port of Mucha, in the Yemen (folio 21a). The illustration shows the pilgrims’ ships departing from the port as well as Sayyid Husayn, the Governor of Mucha, riding his horse (bottom right).  
The port of Jeddah (folio 22b). This view is very similar to that of Mucha (folio 21a) in that it combines views of the city and the pilgrims’ ships with one of the Governor of the city, Sunjuq.  
Man attacked by a lion (folio 21b); Man saved from the jaws of a lion (folio 23a); A feast (folio 23b). The three small-scale paintings are illustrations to a parable about a very poor woman taking pity on some beggars passing by and feeding them; her act of generosity was rewarded when a stranger saved her son from being eaten by a lion. The feast is probably in celebration of the son’s safe return to his mother.  
Script:  
  
Persian text copied in nasta‘liq; with 23 lines to the page.

deea46be-8061-564e-a1de-c2f20389f8a7.name: *Ayasofya (Hagia Sophia)*
deea46be-8061-564e-a1de-c2f20389f8a7.short_description: The majority of Turkish painters in the 19th century were Ottoman officers who had studied abroad. Hüseyin Zekai Paşa was one of those painters who paints in the western style. In his first works, he followed the painting tradition of 19th century by including thin paint dough and light colours. He made changes in his painting techniques through the Galatasaray Exhibition and turned into an impressionist, his work dominated by thicker brush strokes. In his paintings he combined impressionist colour techniques and a totality of composition with dexterity. Şeker Ahmet Paşa, Osman Hamdi Bey and Hüseyin Zekai Paşa opened the way for other Turkish artists – and in particular impressionists – in Turkey.

keywords: Painting; Hüseyin Zekai Paşa; orientalist Turkish painters

df2d65a4-48bc-5ed0-b535-bf708ffef329.name: Set of Two-Sided Mineia Icons
df2d65a4-48bc-5ed0-b535-bf708ffef329.description: The *mineia* icons record important dates in the calendar year of the Orthodox church. Feast days and saints are arranged by date and labeled. The icons are usually painted in miniature, and a typical day can commemorate up to ten feasts and saints. This two-sided *mineia* was once part of a set of 12 with each tablet featuring one month. The Museum of Russian Icons has ten icons from the original set.
df2d65a4-48bc-5ed0-b535-bf708ffef329.obtention:
Collection of the late artist Petros Sasaki, who purchased the tablets in Finland in the 1960s to early 1970s. Sold by Christie's Auction in June 2008 to a private collection, USA. Sold by Macdougall's Auction in 2009 to a private collection, USA.  
Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Chelsea Auction (private sale) in 2014. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

e14b8a41-6006-512e-b29f-7b0b558fe602.name: *Moses with the Tablets of the Law*
e14b8a41-6006-512e-b29f-7b0b558fe602.description:
According to the Biblical story (Book of Exodus), Moses, returning from Mount Sinai where God had given him the commandments carved on stone tablets, found the Israelites worshipping a golden calf made with the consent of Aaron from all of the available precious metal. Angered by the infidelity of his people, Moses smashed the tablets of the law.  
The painting shows the patriarch in all his violent disdain, screaming mouth contorted and hands gripping with ire the tablets he is about to smash. The expressive force of the scene involves the viewer in the dark drama, inducing him to hear the power of the scream against idolatry and the lack of faith in God. Moses' black clothes, almost mournful, highlight the luminosity of the bright red of his cloak. The influence of similar stylistic and chromatic solutions used by Caravaggio is obvious. The light, coming from the left, emphasises the expressive lines and withered skin of his arms and hands, while conversely stressing the vigorous strength inspired by faith, motifs influenced by Carracci.  
Critics do not agree on the date of the painting, theories ranging from the first decade of the 17th century to 1624–25. Nevertheless it has been in the Borghese collection from at least 1657, as the artist was greatly admired by Cardinal Scipione. Reni painted another version of the same subject for the Barberini, dated around 1625.
e14b8a41-6006-512e-b29f-7b0b558fe602.short_description: Reni can be placed mid-way between the classical, serene harmony of the Carracesque tradition and the dramatic vision of Caravaggio. The painter was held in very high esteem by Cardinal Scipione.
e14b8a41-6006-512e-b29f-7b0b558fe602.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.
