e189b316-270d-52f6-bc71-843ad7287741.name: Bookcover
e189b316-270d-52f6-bc71-843ad7287741.short_description: A pair of Qajar lacquered binding depicts Fath ʽAli Shah (r. 1797–1834) on the front cover, in his famous majestic pose clad in elaborate jewelled regalia and wearing his grander imperial crown, the Taj-e Kiyani, commissioned upon his accession in 1798. The back cover depicts a court scene, landscape, court and decoration. The king shown here is Mohammad Shah Qajar (r. 1834–1848), son of Fath ‘Ali Shah. Few minor differences in number of people, their cloth design and the objects, can also be noticed. The inner cover is decorated in a reversed composition. The main panel is adorned with a central scalloped medallion, two small pendants above and below and corner-pieces containing red and yellow rose bushes on green ground. The parts of the central field between the centre and corner-pieces are filled with gold painted flower and leaf motifs. The panel is framed with three borders; the middle border has a red ground with red and yellow rose bushes arranged between two borders with gold flower and leaf motifs on black ground. Although the patron of the cover has not been identified, the painting suggests that it could be the cover of a *muraqqa’* (album) or royal documents which was either commissioned by the Shah himself or by a prince or wealthy court official. In addition, although the binding is unsigned and undated, the quality of workmanship suggests that it was painted by one of the fine painters in the court ateliers. The spine has been removed and the gap has been closed.

e1a252df-9eac-5352-962a-9d3fc2c41c8c.name: Hulagu Enthroned
e1a252df-9eac-5352-962a-9d3fc2c41c8c.short_description: Hulagu, the Ilkhanid ruler of Iran (r. 1256–1265) and an ancestor of the Mughal rulers of India, is shown seated cross-legged on a gold throne, the back of which encircles his head like a glowing halo. A man is seated in front of the throne and on the carpet before him are two books and an astrolabe, a scientific instrument used for computing various astronomical problems, such as telling time. This individual is thought to be the Persian theologian and astronomer Nasir al-Din Tusi (d. 1274). The painting is probably the surviving half of a double-page frontispiece to a now-lost manuscript made in the imperial Mughal atelier, perhaps an historical or scientific text. The painting is the work of the artist Manohar.
keywords: Il Khanid; astronomy; illustration; miniature painting; court; science
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.name: *Die Madonna des Basler Bürgermeisters Jakob Meyer zum Hasen (Madonna of the Burgomaster of Basle, Jakob Meyer zum Hasen)*
e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.description: Oriental carpets appeared on paintings from the early Renaissance period onward, first on works of Italian and later of Dutch provenance. In most cases they served to focus attention on saints and holy figures. In this case, these are the Madonna and Child, at whose feet is a valuable, probably Anatolian woven carpet. The donor-the Mayor Jacob Meyer zum Hasen-and his family also kneel on the carpet, so that they also share in the atmosphere of holiness. At the same time, the carpet can be interpreted as signifying the wealth and status of the prosperous, influential mayor. The purely geometric pattern on the carpet shown here is so characteristic that the term "Holbein carpet" has become established as an art historical term.
e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.obtention: This altarpiece came into the Dresden Gallery from the collection of Zuan Delfino in Venice in 1743, when it was purchased by Francesco Graf Algarotti as an original painting by Holbein. During the Dresden Holbein exhibition in 1871 and the subsequent "Holbein Dispute", it was established that this painting is a forgery after the original painting known as the Darmstadt Madonna (now held in the Würth Collection, Schwäbisch Hall). The Dresden Madonna was painted by Bartholomäus Sarburgh in the years 1635-37.

This scene, which occurs in both texts, depicts Alexander and the Prophet Khizr’s search for the Fountain of Life. Although they begin the journey together, they are separated and only Khizr is successful. Here, he appears with the Prophet Elias at the Fountain, while Alexander continues his search in the background.

e2bed9ed-caa1-5725-83f6-d3e744776900.name: Our Epic Tale
e2bed9ed-caa1-5725-83f6-d3e744776900.description: Jassim Al Zaini’s Our Epic Tale can be used to discuss regional development, cultural memory, and the construction of modern identity in the Gulf. Although the work emerges from a Qatari context, it also speaks to broader transformations across the region during the oil era, when societies were redefining their future while preserving links to local traditions. The figures’ traditional clothing suggests that development is not presented as something imposed from outside, but as a process rooted in local people, customs, and collective memory. In this sense, the painting can be read as a visual statement, almost a political manifesto, in which modernisation is linked to cultural continuity rather than cultural replacement. The work is also useful for discussing how Gulf modern art participated in shaping narratives of progress, identity, and locally grounded development.

e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.name: The *Annunciation*
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.description:
The beginning of the second quarter of the 16th century marks the emergence of the representation of “Lotto” knotted carpets in Portuguese painting. These carpets, their name derived from the Venetian artist Lorenzo Lotto, who represented them in his paintings, are characterised by their geometrical, angular aesthetics lined up in a repetitive scheme. The Lotto carpets of Turkish origin probably reached the high-end Portuguese market through the Venetian export trade.  
The presence of these carpets in Portuguese interiors is mostly evidenced through representations in paintings, in particular those of the court painter Gregório Lopes (active 1513‒† 1550). In this representation of the *Annunciation*, the Virgin Mary stands on a Turkish carpet with a yellow, meandering arabesque pattern on a red field and a pseudo-*kufic* border. It’s relevance in the painting is reinforced by the artist, for he captures the very moment when the Archangel, as if suspended in time, places one foot on the carpet, and thus enters the sacred domain of the Virgin Mother. As such, the carpet is used as a device in the painter’s masterful depiction to mark the passage from one space to another, as though through a gateway.  
Interestingly, the opposing end of the same carpet is represented in another of Gregorio Lopes’s paintings, the *Presentation of the Head of Saint John the Baptist*, of around 1539 to 1541, a painting encompassing a ceremonial banquet in an aristocratic setting. In the *Annunciation* the artist takes the contrary approach, emptying the space of the splendour of the banquet, and replacing pageantry with a bare, peaceful interior befitting of the unfolding scene.
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho

keywords: painting; Annunciation; Portugal; Gregório Lopes; Lotto carpet

e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.name: *The Three Ages of Woman*
e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.short_description: *The Three Ages of Woman* is one of the few works by Gustav Klimt, the main artist of the Vienna Secession movement, in Italy. The painting was exhibited in 1911 at the International Exhibition of Fine Arts in Rome inside the Austrian Pavilion built by the architect Josef Hoffman (1870-1956). An entire room was dedicated to Klimt (*The Three Ages of Woman*, *The Kiss*, *The Sisters* and several portraits). On this occasion the painting of *The Three Ages of Woman* won a prize and was subsequently bought by the Italian State along with other 51 paintings and seven sculptures in order to be displayed inside the newborn National Gallery of Modern Art in Rome. The canvas, painted in the artist’s maturity, shows an old woman in profile with her body carrying the signs caused by the passing of time. The young woman and mother next to her and frontally depicted, holds her sleeping daughter. The central theme of the canvas is the three steps of woman’s life marked by childhood, maturity and old age. The outstanding “verism”, or “truth” of the figures is in sharp contrast to the decorative background that, with its gold and geometric decorations, is reminiscent of the Byzantine mosaics the artist saw during his voyages to Ravenna in 1903. The use of metals, glaze, coloured glass, and gold show the vogue of orientalism that spread among the artists who wanted to free themselves from western art conventions.

e39d2fbb-2774-52a9-868e-e26f46c215f7.name: *Preparing Medicine from Honey*, folio from a dispersed manuscript of an Arabic translation of the *Materia Medica* of Dioscorides
e39d2fbb-2774-52a9-868e-e26f46c215f7.short_description: This scene from a translation of *De Materia Medica* by Dioscorides is typical of the Baghdad School of illustration, which employed bold colors and symmetrical compositions to depict urban life. The use of an architectural structure to divide the painting into six sections is typical of the period, as is the fact that the oatmeal-coloured paper remains visible. This folio, which comes from volume 5, chapter 9 of the work, depicts a pharmacist preparing a honey‑based medicine in a cauldron while an assistant upstairs distributes it into jars.

e3b0645a-dca5-537b-86d7-5a168c647274.name: Mineia, February
e3b0645a-dca5-537b-86d7-5a168c647274.description: The *mineia* icons record important dates in the calendar year of the Orthodox church. Feast days and saints are arranged by date and labeled. The icons are usually painted in miniature, and a typical day can commemorate up to ten feasts and saints. This February icon was once part of a set of 12 *mineia*, with each panel featuring one month in the church calendar.
e3b0645a-dca5-537b-86d7-5a168c647274.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from the Temple Gallery, London, in 2007. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

e3bca328-205b-530c-8cb6-99cd21d8c8dd.name: *Two Musician Girls*
e3bca328-205b-530c-8cb6-99cd21d8c8dd.short_description: As opposed to the Western Orientalists who emphasize sexuality in their female figures, in Osman Hamdi’s paintings the female figures are often conscious of the period of Westernization in the Ottoman Empire, as well as their individual identities and talents, and are thus open to learning and self-development. In a number of Osman Hamdi’s works, the Ottoman woman is portrayed playing an instrument or reading and she always appears fully clothed. In this painting, which incorporates architectural elements of the Bursa Green Mosque, apart from musical instruments like the *tambur* (lute) and the tambourine, Ottoman decorative elements such as rugs, woodwork, stone carving, and tiles complement the artist’s unique approach to the female identity.
keywords: Osman Hamdi Bey; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

e545d6d3-eec2-54ad-b900-150487ea7465.name: *Judith in the Tent of Holofernes*
e545d6d3-eec2-54ad-b900-150487ea7465.description:
The work may have been acquired by Cardinal Scipione Borghese during the years that the French artist was in Rome (1623–1634), but it is not documented in the collection until 1650. The delicate medium shows a night scene illuminated by the light of candelabra. The Biblical heroine is shown kneeling in the act of asking God for the strength she needs for the bloody murder she is about to commit, while the unknowing Holofernes sleeps in a luxurious canopy bed decorated with a heavy silk damask that reflects the light of the flame.  
According to the apocryphal texts of the Old Testament, the beautiful Judith, a widow living in the town of Bethulia, which was besieged by the Assyrians, successfully wooed General Holofernes, who organised a banquet in her honour to seduce her. He falls into a drunken sleep in his tent, allowing the implacable maiden to decapitate the oppressor of the Israelites. On the dressed table lies the warrior's elegant helmet, while his shield stands on the floor. Three *putti* are trying to draw the sword from its sheath, evidently to give it to Judith. The inspired pose of the protagonist relates to the elegance of the setting, the fine detailing and the playful tone of the *putti*, worthy of following a Venus. The style reveals the artist's knowledge of classical Bolognese painting, which was very common in Rome in the early decades of the 17th century and was associated with Elsheimer's study of light.  
The artist, who is known to have completed another version of the same subject (private collection) is a specialist in painting on stone (slate and black marble), which allowed him to achieve very refined colours and an almost miniaturist rendering of detail, combined with the use of the medium as a natural base for the candlelight effect, which was ubiquitous at the beginning of the 17th century.
e545d6d3-eec2-54ad-b900-150487ea7465.short_description:
This is an unusual representation of an iconographic theme. The gestural expressiveness of the protagonist and the phenomenal lighting reflect the divine assistance given to Judith. Through faith she finds the strength to accomplish the bloody act of decapitating Holofernes.  
The French artist painted this small, precious piece on slate during his stay in Rome from 1625 to 1634, during which time he mixed with the entourage of Cardinal Scipione Borghese.
e545d6d3-eec2-54ad-b900-150487ea7465.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

e76ff42a-8d69-50d8-ac1f-2bbd53a08547.name:
Bijan takes the reins of Gushtaham’s horse  
Folio detached from a *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) by Abu’l-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1010)
e76ff42a-8d69-50d8-ac1f-2bbd53a08547.short_description: Recounting the legendary history of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam, Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed in 1010, inspired many illustrated copies. The present folio was detached from a copy that is known as the “Big Head” *Shahnameh*. This name refers to the characteristic feature of the majority of its paintings: the large heads of its human figures.

e77d0bf1-58c8-5972-8f5a-b708fbd506b7.name: The Mother of God Umilenie
e77d0bf1-58c8-5972-8f5a-b708fbd506b7.description: The *Umilenie* (tenderness) Mother of God icons display touching images that depict the Virgin caressing her Child. The distinctive feature of this icon type is that the Christ Child has his face pressed against her cheek and one arm around her neck. Finely executed and balanced in line, color and composition, this icon, the earliest in the Museum of Russian Icons collection, is a particularly beautiful example of this motif.
e77d0bf1-58c8-5972-8f5a-b708fbd506b7.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2000. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.

e781ed99-0334-5a17-84a6-d65ff343a949.name: *Allegory of Sight* (Venus and Cupid in a Picture Gallery)
e781ed99-0334-5a17-84a6-d65ff343a949.description:
From a series of paintings called the “The Five Senses”, this painting by Jan Brueghel the Younger is known as *The Allegory of Sight*. It displays a virtual treasure trove of Paintings, Sculpture, Scientific tools and more. At the center of the piece is Venus examining herself in a handheld mirror. A beautiful Turkish Carpet is draped over the table to the left of Venus. The fact that such a carpet is displayed among such a treasure trove of expensive and exquisite objects shows its importance.  
This painting shows an imaginary collection of art, scientific instruments, and curiosities of nature. It belongs to a popular genre of pictures developed by Antwerp artists in the 1600s that portray the cabinets, or rooms, collectors filled with art and wonders. The inclusion of Venus examining herself in a mirror reveals that this scene also doubles as an allegory of sight, and was part of a series of works depicting the five senses.  
Though an allegory, the scene contains artwork and objects based on real examples, including paintings by famous Flemish artist Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640) and Jan Brueghel’s father, Jan Brueghel the Elder. The ancient and modern sculptures as well as the array of vessels, jewels, coins, measuring instruments, and shells strewn around the room can be matched with surviving items.  
The remarkable works depicted by Jan the Younger illustrate the types of objects the well to do collected in the 1600s to demonstrate their status and knowledge. Within the space around you are works of art and nature that represent the varied categories of collecting popular at this time.

e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.name: Portrait of emperor Shah Jahan, his three sons, and Asaf Khan
e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.short_description: In this royal family portrait, Emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1628–58), sitting in haloed profile upon a gold-footed throne under a high white canopy, accepts a jewelled gift from his father-in-law, Asaf Khan. At his right are his three eldest sons—Dara Shikoh (1615–59), Shah Shija (1616–59), and the ill-fated Awrangzeb (r. 1618–1707), whose death effectively marked the end of the great Mughal Empire. All figures are resplendent in turbans decorated with jewels, pearl necklaces, different types of daggers (*khilanum*, *katar*, and *kard*), lavishly embroidered sashes, and gilded swords. An illuminated carpet lies underfoot.
e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

e80dfa93-78f5-57ec-a258-0a31de9fef63.name: *The daughter of the English ambassador riding in a palanquin*
e80dfa93-78f5-57ec-a258-0a31de9fef63.short_description: Until he was appointed as the court painter in 1896, Zonaro was predominantly commissioned by European embassies in Istanbul. In his memoirs, the artist reveals that British Ambassador Sir Philip William Currie (1894-96), who was one of Zonaro’s clients, commissioned a painting depicting his stepdaughter on the palanquin on her way to the church to marry a diplomat. Sir Currie also requested the view of the Golden Horn – as seen from the garden of the embassy – to be included in the background of the painting. The palanquin carriers, two embassy officials smartly dressed in their uniforms and the young woman sitting on the palanquin in her bridal veil, posed for the artist for several days.
keywords: Fausto Zonaro; Guillemet; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

e89fcc11-c4b2-5e7a-bd67-d16f31276971.name: *The Holy Sanctuaries at Mecca and Medina*
e89fcc11-c4b2-5e7a-bd67-d16f31276971.short_description:
The two detached pages most probably come from a copy of al-Jazuli’s *Dala’il al-khayrat* (full title, *Dala’il al-khayrat wa shawariq al-anwar fi dhikr al-salat ‘ala al-nabi al-mukhtar*).  
One of the most popular works of prayer in the Islamic world, it was composed by a native of Sus, Abu ‘Abdallah Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn Abu Bakr al-Jazuli (d. 1645). The work consists of prayers for the Prophet, together with his epithets, and a description of his tomb.  
Digressing somewhat from the text, Ottoman and Indian copies of the work almost always included depictions of the Meccan sanctuary besides that in Medina. The depictions in Indian copies were often diagrammatic in nature, in contrast to the more realistic, three-dimentional representations in Ottoman copies.

e8e696de-51ce-5fc5-a006-778ed003c783.name: *Saint Francis Xavier Recommending the Argonauts to the Virgin*
e8e696de-51ce-5fc5-a006-778ed003c783.description:
This small altarpiece was originally commissioned by the Jesuits for the chapel of the Academy of the Argonauts. The sumptuous ship in the background is an allusion to this association of the pupils of the Jesuit College.  
The Virgin crowned with stars holds the child and leans towards the Jesuit Francis Xavier, patron saint of travellers. He points to the ship and designates her the “Argonauts”, members of the Academy of the same name and promising pupils of the Collegio dei Nobili. This is the school held by the Jesuits in Bologna, attended by the sons of the aristocracy in the eighteenth-century. Creti is an ideal follower and pupil of Guido Reni and his school. He looks at the perfection and beauty attained by the master. The colours, with their pre-eminence of blues and greys in the background are an homage to the great Bolognese predecessor.
e8e696de-51ce-5fc5-a006-778ed003c783.short_description: The altarpiece shows Saint Francis Xavier, a Jesuit missionary interceding with the Virgin towards the sailors, personified by the members of the Academy of the Argonauts, in whose chapel the painting was hanging. Donato Creti, a follower of the school of Guido Reni, is looking for refined elegance and formal perfection.
e8e696de-51ce-5fc5-a006-778ed003c783.method_for_datation: Possibly the first painting of Creti for a church; it can be dated around 1710 based on stylistic reasons.
e8e696de-51ce-5fc5-a006-778ed003c783.obtention: Gianpietro Zanotti, in his *Storia dell'Accademia Clementina di Bologna* (1739, p. 108), writes that the altarpiece was painted for the Academy of the Argonauts, in the Collegio dei Nobili which was held by the Jesuits. After the suppression of the Jesuits in 1773, the Barnabites ruled the college. With the unification of Italy, some of the property of the college passed to the Municipality of Bologna. In the 1930’s the altarpiece was in a municipal deposit and was later moved to the Collezioni Comunali d'Arte.

e99f19c5-2155-5385-857a-049be3d918d9.name: "Man's Fate or the Man Taking Refuge in a Well Inhabited by a Dragon"
e99f19c5-2155-5385-857a-049be3d918d9.alternate_name: Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
e99f19c5-2155-5385-857a-049be3d918d9.description: This manuscript contains seventy-eight paintings and many text folios telling the famous tales of the jackals Kalila and Dimna. Based on the book of ancient Indian animal fables, the Panchatantra written by Vidyapati (Bidpai), the stories spread all over the Middle East where they became wildly popular. This manuscript has a strong flavour of Mamluk Egypt in the figure styles and bold drawings, with hints of Ottoman tulips and Safavid turbans. However, the burnt orange palette and darkly-inked lines have led to an attribution to Sultanate Gujarat where it is suggested this manuscript was copied from an Egyptian original. Its life in India is also attested by a Devanagari inscription at the end, although the rest of the Arabic text is written in a strong, left-leaning naskh-like script.

e9cd5ed9-9868-52d2-b520-c5f830442609.name: The last of the Abbasid Caliphs, Mustaʿsim (r. 1242–58)
e9cd5ed9-9868-52d2-b520-c5f830442609.short_description: This folio, along with two others in the Aga Khan Museum Collection (AKM40 and AKM41), comes from a manuscript assembled at the court of Shahrukh (d. 1447) and disassembled by the art dealer Émile Tabbagh in the 1920s and 30s. The manuscript’s content draws primarily from a world history prepared by Rashid al-Din (d. 1318) for the Mongol Ilkhan Oljeitu in 1307. It is not a simple copy of Rashid al-Din’s work, but rather a hybrid manuscript with a tangled history made even more complex by its dispersal. This folio is one of a group of folios that were originally prepared under Rashid al-Din’s own supervision and later incorporated into the Timurid manuscript.
e9cd5ed9-9868-52d2-b520-c5f830442609.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper
materials: Ink, watercolour, and gold pigment on paper

e9d20fa0-c214-51e8-a022-980c7d31384c.name: Tekke panel
e9d20fa0-c214-51e8-a022-980c7d31384c.short_description: *Hüsn-i Hat* is a type of calligraphy. Turks probably started to get interested in calligraphy after their arrival to Anatolia. The brightest period was during the Ottoman era. Calligraphy developed well beyond its functional role; it almost played a similar role to the paintings in Western art in terms of the level of its aesthetics. The script *"Ya Hazreti Şeyh Sultan Yusuf Sümbül Sinan Kaddes Allahu sırrahu"* (religious text, untranslatable) is written on a black background with *Zerendud* (gilded) calligraphy and designed as the *sikke* (tall felt hat) of the Sünbüli order. It stands over a small table in Rococo style and there are hyacinth flowers on either corner of the upper part. The sides of the plate are surrounded by two borders that are Rococo in design.
e9d20fa0-c214-51e8-a022-980c7d31384c.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
keywords: Caligraphy; Hüsn-i Hat; plate

ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.name: *Turkish ladies buying jewellery*
ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.short_description: This watercolour, completed in 1873, shows three elegantly dressed society ladies, their faces concealed by a light veil, visiting the shop of a jeweller, his wares displayed in a small multi-tiered glass case placed on the low platform in front. While one of the ladies is seated on a carpet at the entrance to the shop to examine a pearl necklace that the old, bespectacled proprietor has offered her, her two companions wait outside and shield her to some extent from curious eyes. Vittorio Amadeo, 5th Count Preziosi (1816-1882) was an artist of Maltese origin, who left for the Middle East in the early 1840s. He settled in Istanbul as a diplomatic translator and artist, specialising in touristic scenes, vistas and types
ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

eaf5a4c2-fc34-59cc-85e1-5bfdbe4b17c3.name: *Falcon chase*
eaf5a4c2-fc34-59cc-85e1-5bfdbe4b17c3.short_description: Fromentin's inspiration for this painting came from the journey he made in 1853 from Médéa to Laghouat, crossing the great expanses of the halfa grass and wormwood deserts. On his way, he came across a spring where grey vultures were drinking.
eaf5a4c2-fc34-59cc-85e1-5bfdbe4b17c3.author: Dalila Orfali

eba85bbe-07ea-54e1-b12e-dd3f891151d0.name: *Woman taking an afternoon nap*
eba85bbe-07ea-54e1-b12e-dd3f891151d0.short_description: Women in Orientalist art were frequently idealised: the theme of the naked, languishing concubine dominated European art throughout the 19th century. Alfred Chataud's work, however, seems to approach the theme with less artificiality, and indeed this watercolour shows a great degree of authenticity in depicting a scene from Algerian women's daily lives in the late 19th century. The painting even seems to resemble Gustave Courbet's *Demoiselles au bords de la Seine*.
eba85bbe-07ea-54e1-b12e-dd3f891151d0.author: Dalila Orfali
keywords: Orientalism; women; women's condition; harem

ec7fd0d9-9cc8-500f-9c45-55773ae4604c.name: *The Tortoise Trainer*
ec7fd0d9-9cc8-500f-9c45-55773ae4604c.short_description: Rather than depicting the “other” as a number of foreign painters did, Osman Hamdi portrayed his own culture and propounded his own cultural perceptions. The architectural decor suggests that the scene takes place in one of the upper-story chambers of the Bursa Green Mosque. Dressed as a dervish and slightly bent over, a man is examining in a contemplative fashion the tortoises roaming the floor. He sports an *araqiyya*, a flattish skull cap commonly worn by dervishes with a *destar*, or sash wrapped around it. He wears a belted, long red robe the borders of which are embroidered; his feet are clad in *çedik*, or slippers for indoor wear, made of yellow *sahtiyan*, Moroccan (goatskin) leather. He holds a ney in one of the hands he has clasped behind; a *nakkare* or a small kettledrum hangs down from his back.
keywords: Osman Hamdi Bey; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.name: The Mother of God Smolenskaya with Oklad
ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.description:
This is a *Hodegetria* (Greek for “one who shows the way”) Mother of God icon, recognizable by the solemn expression of the Mother of God and the frontal position of the Christ Child delivering a blessing. The Christ Child sits on his Mother’s left knee and holds a tightly rolled scroll. The original icon was brought from Byzantium in the 12th century and kept in the Assumption Cathedral in the city of Smolensk. In the 15th century, the icon was transferred to Moscow before being returned to Smolensk.  
This icon has four additional figures, two on each border: a guardian angel and Venerable Basil the Confessor on the left, and Saint John the Baptist and Saint Anne the Prophet on the right. The *oklad* (covering) is solid silver under mercury gilding with no apparent hallmark. The *oklad* has a large nimbus containing sculpted angels with openings for their faces and hands, as well as many gems and a raised floral and fruit design. An inscription on the bottom border reads as follows:  
  
At the Alenskiy-Skete in the area of Kerzhenets, the Schemamonk Filaret the icon painter, had painted this icon for the Schemamonk Iosif. At the year 7250 \[1740\] this icon was given to the treasury of the Schemanun Irinarkha. The Abbess, the nun Anafoliya donated this icon in the year 7376 \[1868\], at the third day of February to the Archbishop Antonij of Moscow and Vladimir.
ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2011. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography

ed6f29d0-e940-51f2-b1c8-d10b8385933e.name: *St. Sebastian Tended by Pious Women*
ed6f29d0-e940-51f2-b1c8-d10b8385933e.description:
The painting is first documented in the Borghese collection in 1650 although it is possible Cardinal Scipione acquired it directly during the artist's short stay in Rome (1624–1625) shortly before his early death on his return home.  
The painting shows a subject particularly common in the early 12th century: a pious women removing the arrows that martyred St. Sebastian and tending his wounds. According to a hagiographic account, Sebastian, an officer in Emperor Diocletian's Praetorian Guard who had converted to Christianity, was executed by archers who left him for dead. Tended by Saint Irene and her assistant, he returned to the Emperor with a new profession of faith, and was beaten to death with a club and his body left in the Cloaca Maxima.  
The cult of this saint reached its height thanks to the writings of Cesare Baronio in the late 16th century, and his iconography included elements similar to that of Christ. In 1607, Scipione Borghese began the restoration of the old Paleo-Christian Basilica of St. Sebastian outside the town walls on the Via Appia as part of a building policy promoted by the Counter-Reformation that encouraged a revival of the cult of martyrdom. He entrusted the commission to Flaminio Ponzio, who was also the architect for the Villa Borghese.  
The painting shows sentimentality in the face of the saint that inspires compassion in the viewer. The pose of the body is inspired by statues, and the twisting motion resembles one of the most well known ancient sculptures in Rome at that time, the *Lacoonte*.  
Rustici handled this subject on several occasions. In his skilful modulation of light on the body of the martyr he demonstrates his knowledge of the innovations of Caravaggesque painting, although he did not adhere to them completely, accentuating the suggestion of the hagiographic account with the expressiveness of Bolognese painting.
ed6f29d0-e940-51f2-b1c8-d10b8385933e.short_description:
St. Sebastian’s iconography is often associated with that of Christ. At the beginning of the 17th century the martyr is frequently represented at the moment he is found by the noblewoman, Irene, who takes care of him, in this way arousing the spectator’s feelings of compassion.  
The martyr is said to be buried in the early Christian basilica of St. Sebastian on the Via Appia, which was restored by Cardinal Scipione Borghese.
ed6f29d0-e940-51f2-b1c8-d10b8385933e.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

efcc7ec3-36f8-59b0-a853-5e760fd7f0b1.name: An obituary listing eight victims of the Nizari Ismaʿili assassins
efcc7ec3-36f8-59b0-a853-5e760fd7f0b1.short_description: This folio, along with two others in the Aga Khan Museum Collection (AKM89 and AKM41), comes from a manuscript assembled at the court of Shahrukh (d. 1447) and disassembled by the art dealer Émile Tabbagh in the 1920s and 30s. f03672a7-5a8f-5216-8d53-07817c3aa415.name: *The Prayer in the Desert*
f03672a7-5a8f-5216-8d53-07817c3aa415.short_description: Stefano Ussi lived between Florence and Rome and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts of Florence before enrolling as a volunteer in the first Italian War of Independence, during which he was taken prisoner by the Austrian troops. He developed a model of history painting characterised by a quick application of layers (almost a rough draft) and by a sharp chiaroscuro. In 1875, along with the painter Cesare Biseo, and Edmondo De Amicis, he accompanied an Italian diplomatic delegation to Morocco. At the opening of the Suez Canal the artist went to Egypt and created his first version of *The Prayer in the Desert* which is exhibited at the Accademia di Belle Arti in Florence. From that moment on, Ussi made both history and oriental-themed paintings.

f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.name: Members of Court of Sultan Selim II Mounted as an Album Leaf
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.short_description: From the late sixteenth century until the formation of the Republic of Turkey in 1922, the Ottoman sultans maintained a strong tradition of imperial portraiture. Influenced by European oil painting and Persian miniatures, Ottoman portraits provide important information about court ceremonies, changing fashions, and members of the court. The right side of a double-page composition, this painting was created as a pendant to a portrait of Selim II (r. Hegira 974-982/1566-1574) on the left, now in the collection of the Aga Khan Museum, Toronto. The musicians, servants, and courtiers, who are identified by their inscriptions, face left, toward the sultan, in a show of deference to their ruler. Taken together the pair of paintings depict a *majlis* scene reflecting the pleasure-oriented atmosphere of Selim’s court. It is possible that the figure of the court jester at far right is a self-portrait of the artist.
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.method_for_datation: Less formal than official Ottoman royal depictions, this painting (and its pendant) was likely made prior to Selim’s ascension to the throne in 1566 and was probably produced during his time as a prince governing Kütahya. Several of the figures depicted with captions can be further identified as boon companions of Selim II, one of whom, Turak Çelabi, died in 1561-62, suggesting a terminus ante quem for the work.
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.method_for_provenance: It is signed “Nigari, slave of Sultan Selim Khan.” Nigari was the pseudonym used by the famed Turkish navigator Haydar Reis, who was also well-known as a portrait painting under Sultan Suleyman and his son and successor Selim II.

f0e2d598-8e69-5768-bd25-d9db967e1292.name: Painting Entitled ‘al-Rihlah al-Hijaziyyah/ Sacred Pilgrimage Journey’
f0e2d598-8e69-5768-bd25-d9db967e1292.description: According to a plaque below the images, the painting depicts the pilgrimage of ‘Abbas Hilmi II, the Khedive of Egypt, which he performed in 1909. His portrait is on the left; on the right is that of Mehmed V Rashad, the contemporary Ottoman sultan. To the left and right of the Ka‘bah, which occupies the centre of the painting, are depictions of the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Many of the remaining images are based on photographs of the hajj published in the July 1953 issue of National Geographic.

f1bd5519-89c6-5066-9f1f-c6679831ca28.name: *Glorification of Reason*
f1bd5519-89c6-5066-9f1f-c6679831ca28.description:
The layout indicates that the picture was a template for a ceiling painting. Several figures with their attributes personify the reigning Habsburgs and an allegorical personification of Austria. They are approached by figures from ancient mythology led by Reason. The figures are placed on bizarre formations of a mist-like substance. Opposite Austria are Jupiter and Juno. Hercules with a lion personifies the virtue of an active life. Mars, god of war, next to him, lays down his weapon in a submission to Reason, and is holding an olive branch – symbol of peace – giving his blessings to Moravia. The Moravian emblem, an eagle on a checkerboard field, is depicted on a flag. Above Mars hovers Fame (Glory).  
The symbolism is not limited to the iconographic level. Light is a major content-shaping element in the picture: it radiates from within and represents an attribute of Wisdom, embodiment of Reason and Thought. Light is delivered by the god Apollo and a spirit carrying a flame, symbol of enlightenment. Antiquity is presented as the Golden Age of mankind and the heyday of philosophy; if light embodied the truth during the Baroque period it was associated with reason in antiquity.  
The apotheosis of the “enlightened reign” of the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty was a unifying subject of the art of “pragmatic sanction”. The origin of the sketch from the property of Counts Mitrovský, suggests that it could be a *modello* for the Assembly Hall in the former refectory of the Augustinian Monastery in Brno. This was later converted into a state administration building, known as a dicastery. The design paraphrases a painting by F. A. Maulbertsch found in the Hofburg Assembly Hall in Innsbruck.
f1bd5519-89c6-5066-9f1f-c6679831ca28.short_description: A template for a ceiling painting presents the apotheosis of the reign of the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty. The symbolism is not limited to the iconographic level. Light is a major content-shaping element. The picture paraphrases a painting by F. A. Maulbertsch found in the Hofburg Assembly Hall in Innsbruck.

f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.name: Saint Christophorus with the Infant Jesus
f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.short_description:
According to Emperor Jahangir's (r. 1014-1037 / AD 1605-1627) inscription, the image of St. Christopher carrying the infant Jesus and accompanied by a dog was painted by the court painter Miskin (a pen name meaning "the humble one"). Miskin contributed to the codification of the Mughal style and played an increasingly important role in the illustration of the chronicles of the Mughal emperors. He is known for his keen observation of humans and animals. For this work, he probably drew inspiration from European engravings with Christian themes, which were brought to India by Jesuits at the end of the 16th century.  
  
The border with the prominent hazelnut branch was originally part of a larger album project completed under the Persian artist Muhammad Baqir (active Hegira late 1160s-1204 / AD late 1750s-1790) between Hegira 1178 / AD 1765 and Hegira 1183 / AD 1770. Parts of the album with Mughal and Safavid miniatures and calligraphies were rebound for the Qajar ruler Fath ʿAli Shah (r. Hegira 1211-1250 / AD 1797-1834) in the Hegira year 1237 (AD 1822). The individual leaves of this album were sold at auction by Drouot in Paris on 23 June 1982. Other leaves that originally belonged to this convolute known as the Drouot or Baqir album are currently scattered. The leaf seen here has another miniature pasted on the reverse.

f2c8c673-16bb-5d8a-a1d0-ef90c0a872b5.name: Drawing of Two Fish
f2c8c673-16bb-5d8a-a1d0-ef90c0a872b5.description: In spring 2015, the Swiss National Museum acquired a rare drawing by the Zurich artist Hans Asper (1499–1571). The famous portrait of the Protestant reformer Huldrich Zwingli is another work by him. Here Asper has drawn two species of fish, a trout and an allis shad, and has meticulously captured the detail of their heads. He has signed his work at the right-hand edge and dated it 1540. This realistic drawing is one of the earliest surviving examples of an interest in science that was evolving within the circle around Huldrich Zwingli and Conrad Gessner in Zurich; as such, it is unique in Swiss art history.
keywords: Drawing; Fish; Trout; Allis shad; Science; Graphite; Watercolour; Hans Asper; Zurich; Switzerland

f2e1525e-6b39-51de-8e19-c3cca74a4562.name: *A Turkish Coffee-House, Constantinople*
f2e1525e-6b39-51de-8e19-c3cca74a4562.short_description: Preziosi was of noble Maltese birth, but against the wishes of his family rejected their chosen profession of the law to become an artist. From 1842, until his death forty years later, he lived and worked in Istanbul, renowned for his vibrant and evocative images of all the different races and cultures of that most cosmopolitan of cities. He became for a time well-known in Western Europe because many travellers, (including in 1869 the Prince of Wales) took his pictures home as souvenirs of their visit. Demand for his work prompted the publication in Paris in 1858 of a series of lithographs, Stamboul Recollections of Eastern Life.This is a fine example of Preziosi’s keen observation of contemporary Ottoman life, rapidly sketched yet full of accurately depicted detail.
f2e1525e-6b39-51de-8e19-c3cca74a4562.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: coffee; music

f2f5d2c9-669c-5eb0-99b1-c90588e93519.name: History of Sultan Süleyman
f2f5d2c9-669c-5eb0-99b1-c90588e93519.short_description: The Ottomans were especially interested in the recording of historical events and at the behest of Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95), the court historian Luqman compiled this versified account of the reign of Murad’s grandfather, Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66). The text is largely concerned with Süleyman’s defeat of Hungary in the summer of 1566, and the illustrations included here depict his arrival before the city of Szigetvar, the destruction and fall of the city and the sultan’s death and funeral. (He died during the siege of the city.) The simple and direct style of these paintings is typical of Ottoman historical illustration.

materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

f3955418-aaed-57fc-96f9-18195a4d076b.name: *Atik Valide Mosque*
f3955418-aaed-57fc-96f9-18195a4d076b.short_description: The majority of Turkish painters in the 19th century were Ottoman officers who had studied abroad. Hüseyin Zekai Pasha was one of those painters. Following his education at the Kuleli Military High School, he continued his studies at the Military Academy (*Mektebi Harbiye*), where he had a chance to learn technical drawing and perspective. His first period was realistic and his pictorial representation includes scenes or events from everyday life. In his first works, Hüseyin Zekai Pasha followed the painting tradition of 19th century, including thin paint dough and light colours. He made changes in his techniques through the Galatasaray Exhibition and eventually he turned into an impressionist whose work was dominated by thicker brush strokes.
keywords: Painting; Hüseyin Zekai Pasha; orientalist Turkish painters

f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.name: The *Annunciation*
f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.description:
Aside from the *Annunciation*, the *Mass of St Gregory* is one of the most common and important painting subjects in which representations of carpets can be found. Into one of the crucial moments of Christian iconography, artists transposed aspects of the typical Portuguese feminine interior spaces of the 16th century, with the marked presence of the female dais (*estrado*). Its use appears associated with the context of Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages.  
In this painting, the Virgin Mary appears kneeling on a mat: this, along with other similar representations bear witness to the past presence in Portugal of these types of small carpets that are non-existent in collections today. Such is the case of these “mats”, used during the summer as an alternative to the dense knotted carpets of the winter months, as well as of the tapestries, which alternated in the summer period with the *guadamecis*.  
The artist’s decision to include a mat, rather than an Oriental carpet, may be down to the painting being commissioned for a convent of the Order of Saint Claire, where the strict rules called for austerity. This appears in opposition to Gregório Lopes’s painting intended for a wealthy clientele.  
In addition, it all goes to prove the absorption and influence of African artistic production in Portuguese contemporary life and art since the 15th century, when mats, but also other objects such as saltcellars and ivory spoons, began to be imported to Portugal from Benin.

f445365e-28d3-5b5f-869c-11cd87fe18f8.name: The *Circumcision*
f445365e-28d3-5b5f-869c-11cd87fe18f8.description:
We are witnessing the representation of one of the most important episodes of Jesus’ childhood, in which, according to Jewish law, the Child gains its identity.  
The scene has been re-created in the interior of a Renaissance-style temple where the Holy Family and several figures cluster around the table where a priest is about to carry out the circumcision.  
Covering the altar there is a white towel, in turn, this covers a carpet, of which only the border, filled with “vine scrolls”, palmettes and foliage, is visible. This variant in the use of carpets in a painting makes this a very interesting document.  
Alongside its use as a floor-cover in paintings, when its symbolism is associated with dignity and spatial boundaries, carpets were used widely as a cover for altars in churches as well as in civil settings as furniture covers, as several Portuguese inventories attest.  
In the *Circumcision*, a so-called knotted “Holbein” carpet can be seen. It is put to the same use here as the carpet represented by Hans Holbein, the Younger (1497/8‒1543), in his famous portrait *The Ambassadors*, which thereafter gave this specific compositional structure the name “Holbein”.

f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.name: *Martyrdom of St. Januarius* (?)
f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.description:
The canvas was acquired by Camillo Borghese in 1818. Critics do not agree on the attribution, although it is acknowledged as clearly belonging to the culture of Southern Italian Baroque. The painting has been attributed to Cesare Fracanzano, a Puglian artist who first trained with Ribera and was later influenced by the artistic currents inspired by Van Dyke. Other scholars have suggested that the work is by a follower of Francesco Fracanzano, the brother of Cesare.  
Even the identity of the subject, who is undoubtedly a martyr, is not known for certain. Some scholars see the bishop-saint, one of the Fathers of the Church, as Ignatius of Antioch, the third largest and important city in the Mediterranean. The martyr was imprisoned by Emperor Trajan (96–117), who took him to Rome and had him killed by wild animals. In his “Letters”, he was the first person to use the adjective “Catholic” or “Universal” regarding the Church.  
The iconography of the saint killed by wild animals is also consistent with the hagiographic account of St. Januarius, Bishop of Benevento, who during the reign of Diocletian (284–305) was condemned to death and tortured on several occasions. Although he escaped unharmed from the wild animals, he was finally decapitated at Solfatara.  
The work is characterised by very dramatic gestures, accompanied by the piteous face of the saint. The artist took care to render in minute detail the lines of the face, the hands marked with age, and the emaciated body rent by the teeth of the wild beasts. The dappled fur and facial features of the animals are picked out in an almost exotic style. The colour of the fine cape, now in shreds, is striking and the elegance of the cloth of blue silk and gold is sumptuously rendered.
f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.short_description: Ignatius of Antioch – who inspired another Ignatius, the founder of the Jesuits – is perhaps portrayed here at the time of his martyrdom, killed by wild animals. Ignatius, one of the Fathers of the Church wrote seven “Letters” for the first time in which appear the terms “Catholic Church” and “Christianity”. It could also be the iconography of St. Januarius who was similarly killed by wild animals. The painting is characterised by an extreme theatricality of gestures.
f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

f4b200cf-1a1b-5c49-9a62-cb9310e74f00.name: Coffee-house
f4b200cf-1a1b-5c49-9a62-cb9310e74f00.short_description: Traditionally, social life in the Islamic world revolved around the tea-house or coffee-house, where men would gather to drink tea and coffee, eat sweet pastries or savoury food, and to smoke flavoured tobacco in water pipes (*narghile* or *qalian*). There they would play board games, listen to music and poetry recitations or discuss current events. This scene of a Turkish coffee-house would originally have been part of an album of images.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; border decoration
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

f54a1f1a-89eb-53ec-92f4-4b04e01290a2.name: Street Language
f54a1f1a-89eb-53ec-92f4-4b04e01290a2.description: Faraj Daham’s Street Language (2011) can be used to address the social dimension of Doha’s rapid urban transformation by foregrounding the construction workers who made this development physically possible. The dominant yellow and orange tones evoke Qatar’s intense climate, while the workers’ covered faces and direct gaze draw attention to issues of labour, migration, visibility, and anonymity. Rather than presenting modernisation only through architecture and urban growth, the work invites viewers to consider the human bodies behind these processes. For this reason, Street Language is especially useful for discussing Gulf modernity as a social, economic, and human phenomenon, not merely as a visual narrative of progress.

f601bc27-5ed9-59a8-af04-fa14ffab1f30.name: *The sufi saint Mian Mir praying at Medina*
f601bc27-5ed9-59a8-af04-fa14ffab1f30.short_description:
Mian Mir belonged to the Qadiriyya order of Sufism and spent the majority of his lifetime in Lahore. He was known for his religious tolerance and was revered by both Muslims and Sikhs. Prince Dara Shikoh, who was a key follower, is said to have read the oration at Mian Mir's funeral.  
  
He is shown praying in the courtyard of the Prophet’s mosque, in front of the ‘Garden of Fatima’, with the *rawda* and the green dome above the Prophet’s tomb in the background.

f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.name: *Two Bookcase Doors Depicting Shelves with Music Books*
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.description: This extraordinary still life is formed by two paintings depicting the shelves of a bookcase. Music books are casually displayed vertically and horizontally. The books are depicted tidy and dense on the upper level and on the lower levels they are untidy, including books laying down. On the lower shelves there are several writing devices: two pen dryers, an inkstand, a bottle of ink, and a bunch of goose-quills. The original provenance of this painting is uncertain: the first documented information is in 1801 when it was moved from the monastery of St Francis to the Liceo Musicale. For a long time, Father Giovanni Battista Martini was thought to be the patron of this painting. He was a great scholar, specialist in contrappunto, and one of the most significant personalities of XVIII century music. Recent studies (A. Mazza in *Le stanze della Musica*) show that the paintings were probably intended as a present for Father Martini, who was younger than the painter. From a careful analysis the inscriptions on the book bindings appear to be posterior to the date attributed to the painting, perhaps to adapt it to the musical culture of a new owner.
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.short_description: This extraordinary still life is formed by two paintings depicting the shelves of a bookcase with music books casually displayed vertically and horizontally. The books are tidy and dense on the upper level, untidy, and in some cases lying down on the lower shelves. On the lower shelves there are several writing devices: two pen dryers, an inkstand, a bottle of ink, and a bunch of goose-quills.
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.holder: Museo Internazionale e Biblioteca della Musica
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.dimensions: Left door 165,5 x 78 cm; right door 165,5 x 75,5 cm
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.obtention: The painting was part of the collection of Father Martini. It was moved along with his books after the death of his successor, Father Mattei, who saved this precious heritage from the Napoleonic confiscations. In 1801 the collections – donated to the municipality of Bologna – were moved to the suppressed monastery of St. James the Great. From 1804, this was the new Liceo Musicale of Bologna.

f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.name: *Apotheosis of King Saint Ladislaus*
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.alternate_name: Oil sketch for the high altar in the Primatial Palace at Pozsony (Bratislava)
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.description:
This sketch (*bozzetto*) in oil on copperplate was made for the high altar in the chapel of the archbishop's palace in Pozsony (Bratislava), built by Melchior Hefele. The chapel constitutes the last remaining example of fine Late Baroque art associated with the cult of St. Ladislaus in Hungary. The dome fresco, painted in the same year by Franz Anton Maulbertsch, represents the king striking water out of rock. The artist's intention was to revive the memory of the ruler who alleviated the thirst of his people by performing a miracle. The fresco shows the king on horseback as he performs the miracle, while in the altarpiece painting he is ascending to heaven. According to a legend current at the time, the king arranged for a portrait of Our Lady of Hungary, the Virgin Mary, *Patrona Hungariae*, to be painted on his battle flags. Thus, the white flag unfurling above his head bears the inscription “*S. Maria Mater Patrona Regni*” with an image of the Virgin and the Infant Jesus, much as if the flag was intended as a substitute for a more traditional celestial appearance. In other parts of the painting, St. Ladislaus is offering his crown together with the coronation regalia and the battleaxe, the latter being the king's usual attribute.  
Adreas Zallinger worked in Pozsony (Bratislava) from the 1770s; he was a pupil and a follower of Maulbertsch, sometimes assisting him in the execution of his work. The sketch illustrated here shows the influence of the Master's late style, his clear colours, silvery light and realistic representation of historic costumes and objects, all of which gradually dominated his work as his earlier passion and artistic inspiration began to leave him.
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.short_description: Andreas Zallinger was a member of Franz Anton Maulbertsch’s studio and worked on the decoration of the high altar in the Primatial Palace, Pozsony (Bratislava). This painting of the Hungarian Holy King is devoid of the Baroque vision.

f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.name: *Moses Striking the Rock*
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.description:
*Moses Striking Water From the Rock* was a production of the workshop of the Neapolitan painter, Francesco Solimena. Solimena was taught painting initially by his father, the Mannerist painter, Angelo, and was later a pupil of Francesco di Mario of Naples. The well-known artists, Pietro da Cortona and Luca Giordano also influenced Solimena's style. Although he painted mainly decorative, religious and mythological subjects, he also undertook decorative frescos and portraits. His work, representative of the Late-Baroque painting of Naples, reveals Rococo elements, as seen in this religious composition. Solimena ran his own celebrated art school where numerous familiar names of Neapolitan painting were educated. He also designed his own villa and palace.  
This painting holds many features typical of Solimena: the dynamism of the composition, the multitude of intermingled bodies within which he manages to show the marked elegance of individual figures who are strikingly illuminated against their brownish shadows to come out of the depths of the composition. The painting depicts the Biblical story of Moses leading the people of Israel through the wilderness to the Promised Land. When they arrive at a high rock – which symbolises Christ – the prophet strikes the top of the rock with his staff, and water pours from it. The thirsty people climb the rock to drink the water, in fact, an allegory of the faith and mercy of God. The water here prefigures the “blood and water” that poured from the wounded side of Christ, and refers to the Baptism. In the centre of the composition, Moses stands alongside the rock, water running down to the base. Above, in the clouds, God the Father hovers surrounded by angels. Together they create the culmination of this dynamic composition. The individual figures of men and women of all ages climbing up the steep rock with vessels in their hands are, on the whole, painted from behind and from underneath. The remainder of a somewhat distant landscape is discernable; on the left, an oasis with palm trees and tents, while to the right a few figures running towards the rock against the sky. Although painted in the academic manner, the colours are lively and intense and the figures are individualised and well painted. Solimena spent the whole of his working life in Naples and was one of the most prolific painters of the Late Baroque. This painting, probably produced in his workshop, may be a prototype for a larger fresco or altarpiece.
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.short_description:
Francesco Solimena's work, representative of the late Neapolitan Baroque, reveals traces of the Rococo. His father, Angelo, gave him his first painting lessons, and he was later a pupil of Francesco di Mario of Naples. The well-known artists, Pietro da Cortona and Luca Giordano also influenced Solimena's style. He was a prolific painter, creating altarpieces, painting frescos in churches and palaces, mythological compositions and portraits. He designed his own villa and palace and had his own celebrated school of art in Naples.  
*Moses Striking Water From the Rock* takes a low angle, depicting the many figures climbing the high rock out of which Moses struck water. The Bible relates how Moses led his people through the desert to the Promised Land. On the way, they stopped alongside a high rock above which, in the clouds, God the Father hovered. Moses quenching the thirst of the people is symbolic of Christ and religion: the thirsty people climbing the rock are bearing vessels to fill with the water of life. This painting bears all the features typical of Solimena's work. Probably created in his workshop, it was perhaps a prototype for a larger composition.
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.method_for_datation: Study of the literature, stylistic analysis and comparative material and consultations with eminent art historians.
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.

f85a3c6e-5d92-5e2a-9503-9f763a9619cb.name: A set of two reverse-glass paintings
f85a3c6e-5d92-5e2a-9503-9f763a9619cb.short_description:
The technique of reverse-glass, or *églomisé*, painting became popular in Iran in the early 19th century, possibly as a result of imports from Europe. In this technique, the paint is applied behind the glass in reverse order, with the highlights and details applied before the background colours. The technique had also been practised in China since the 18th century.  
Both the prince and the courtesan are depicted in bejewelled Qajar costume against European-inspired landscapes which are typical of Qajar paintings of the period. The paintings are not signed but have been compared to paintings by Mirza Baba, who may have been responsible for a cycle of reverse-glass paintings in the Marble Throne Hall of the Gulistan Palace in Tehran.  
The carved and richly painted frames, with their bird-and-dragon openwork scroll borders, are contemporary.

f85a994c-93f5-5c2e-a133-5f14f1826395.name: Reverse painting on glass: Al-Malik az-Zahir Baibars
f85a994c-93f5-5c2e-a133-5f14f1826395.short_description: A famous heroic epic painted on glass is played out in Palestine in 1260. The great moment for the former slave, al-Malik az-Zahir Baibars, arrives when he inflicts the first defeat on the Mongols. In the same year, Baibars, by now Sultan of Egypt, begins to gradually shut down the final strongholds of the Christian crusaders in the Levant; not so much due to religious zeal, but rather to eradicate "the Franks" as a source of unrest. Essentially, this saviour of Islam would lend himself to religious warriors as an icon. In 2005 the television series *Az-Zahir Baybars* is broadcast in Syria. The programme avoids, however, any religious instrumentalisation of the material. Given the religious furore in the Arabic world and beyond, the television series transmits a remarkable message: Muslims and Christians, in spite of their chequered and difficult historical relationship, are supporters of the same civilisation; both are called upon to contribute together to its continued existence.

f88cd52e-27ec-5aee-beba-ea252bcda254.name: *Gunsmiths at the Palace of the Alhambra*
f88cd52e-27ec-5aee-beba-ea252bcda254.short_description: This painting, entitled 'Gunsmiths at the Palace of the Alhambra, Granada' is a romantic, Orientalist phantasy designed to pander to the taste of 19th-century Europeans fascinated by the palace complex in particular since the publication of Washington Irving's 'Tales of the Alhambra' after his stay in Granada in 1828, and that of the British artist and designer Owen Jones, entitled 'Plans, Elevantions, Sections and Details of the Alhambra',  published in twelve parts between 1836 and 1845. Owen's work in particular, with its numerous precise architectural drawings and detailed speculations regarding the Alhambra's original colour schemes, was to exert a revolutionary influence on the European artists of his time, and there is little doubt that the Italian artist Filippo Baratti, too, consulted Owen's work in elaborating his painting's colour scheme, depicting especially the stuccoed walls in hues familiar from Owen's reconstructions.
f88cd52e-27ec-5aee-beba-ea252bcda254.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
f88cd52e-27ec-5aee-beba-ea252bcda254.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.name: *Joseph and Potiphar’s Wife*
f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.description:
The painting is a variation of the fresco painted by the artist in the Palazzo Mattei in Rome in 1615. Unlike that work, the figure of Potiphar's Wife is naked and the colours are based on tones of red and ochre. The different hypotheses advanced by scholars include the possibility that it is an approximate replica of the Mettei fresco completed for Scipione Borghese. During the pontificate of Paul V, the artist received a series of extraordinary commissions, including the decoration of the Loggia delle Benedizioni in the Vatican Basilica, and part of the frescos in the Sala Regia in the Quirinal. These were followed by commissions from Cardinal Scipione himself, such as the decoration and fresco at Villa Mondragone in Frascati near Rome, and the vault of the loggia at Villa Borghese.  
The canvas shows a well-known episode from the Old Testament (Genesis, 39, 7–18) extolling the chastity of Joseph, courted by the wife of Potiphar, the head of the Pharaoh's guards. The woman, offended by Joseph's rejection, is left holding his tunic in her hands when he escapes; she accuses him unjustly and has him thrown into gaol. During his imprisonment, Joseph becomes known for his ability to interpret dreams and is freed immediately.  
The highly contrasting *chiaroscuro* and the Caravaggesque ascending layering of colour, associate the painting with the work of the painter Simon Vouet in the 1630s.  
Joseph's almost running pose and the foreshortening of the raised right hand are particularly noteworthy. A contrasting sense of movement is provided by the body of the woman, who will not release him and is pulling in the opposite direction. She is fully illuminated by a beam of light that leaves Joseph's face almost in shadow. Skilful compositional knowledge is evident in the essential nature of the elements, which emerge from the darkness in a notably theatrical style.
f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.short_description: It is Lanfranco who carries out one of the first examples of Baroque painting in Rome for Cardinal Scipione: *The Council of the Gods* in the loggia of Villa Borghese. The biblical theme represented in this painting celebrates the virtue of chastity. The canvas, a replica of the fresco in Palazzo Mattei in Rome, is a play of light with, clearly, theatrical inspiration.
f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

f9ed44c8-8799-58bf-be2f-32f20262a305.name: *The conquest of Sidon by Austrian troops, September 27th, 1840*
f9ed44c8-8799-58bf-be2f-32f20262a305.short_description: During the oriental crisis of 1840 – as a result of the conflict in the Eastern Mediterranean between Egypt and the Ottoman Empire – a mixed squadron of British, Turkish and Austrian ships under the command of British Admiral Sir Charles John Napier (1786–1860) bombarded the city of Sidon on September 26th. The next day, allied Austrian and British troops landed and conquered Sidon. Josef Schönbrunner, an Austrian illustrator and restorer who was an alumnus of the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, duplicated the original by Leander Russ (1809–1864) in a very dignified way.

fbf36d0e-1c98-5536-895f-1b9eff88b55c.name: *The Place du Gouvernement in Algiers*
fbf36d0e-1c98-5536-895f-1b9eff88b55c.short_description: Albert Marquet spent 1904 and 1907 in the company of Fauve, and in 1913 he lived in Tangier with Matisse and Camoin. Seven years later in 1920 he visited Algiers for the first time, and went on to spent a few months there every year henceforth. He also lived in Algiers for the duration of the Second World War. Marquet was friendly with most of the artists from the Algerian school, and exhibited his paintings in galleries in the centre of town. Many of his paintings were on the theme of Algiers' harbour. In 1939, his friends from the Salle Bordes organised his first solo exhibition. His style, which was characterised by the luminosity and clarity he saw in North Africa, was an important early influence on the Algerian painter Mohamed Temam.
fbf36d0e-1c98-5536-895f-1b9eff88b55c.author: Dalila Orfali

fc95a324-d1b6-5cb0-852e-73608ea38c07.name: *Marco Polo in front of the Khan of Tartars*
fc95a324-d1b6-5cb0-852e-73608ea38c07.short_description:
Tranquillo Cremona studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Venice and then at Brera Academy in Milan. He is considered the “grand bohémien of Italian painting”. This painting was the artist’s first public success. He was fascinated by history paintings and Hayez’s manner as shown in his placement of Marco Polo in front of the Khan of Tartars.  
The artist’s hope to join the Italian embassy – which never happened – was the reason for his interest in the oriental theme. In the ideal recreation, oriental ideas, which were internationally shared, are linked to neo-gothic themes which were fashionable in Italy from the beginning of the 19th century.

fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.name: *Triumphal Procession of Charles V Duke of Lorraine*
fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.description:
The signature on this work is of an unknown artist. The composition is similar to that on a series of tapestries in Nancy, France, depicting the recapture of Buda, which saw an end not only to 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary but also to a long period of anti-Ottoman fighting. The event was represented in a series of contemporary graphic works, tapestries and paintings, but the painting illustrated here is a lesser known work.  
This allegorical painting represents the fictitious triumphal entry into Buda of Charles Duke V of Lorraine (1643—1690). Set against representations of Hungarian towns that played an important role in the anti-Ottoman campaigns, the triumphal coach of the duke, who was held up as a hero for his recapture of Buda from the Turks in 1686, is surrounded by flags. Also around the coach are allegorical female figures, and on the triumphal arch are statues of the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I and Pope Innocent XI.
fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.short_description: This allegorical painting depicts a fictitious triumphal procession of Charles Duke V of Lorraine into Buda. Lorraine was held up as a hero for his recapture of Buda from the Turks in 1686. The painting makes use of antique imagery and iconography.

fcdce33b-73b5-5f44-b815-567a60b30ab7.name: The Welcome to the Italian Delegation in Morocco
fcdce33b-73b5-5f44-b815-567a60b30ab7.short_description: Stefano Ussi lived between Florence and Rome and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts of Florence before enrolling as a volunteer in the first Italian War of Independence, during which he was taken prisoner by the Austrian troops. In 1875 he, along with the painter Biseo and the writer De Amicis, followed a diplomatic delegation to Morocco. The painting represents the solemn meeting in Fez between the Alauita sovereign and the Italian delegation from the Consular Office in Tangier. The bright colours and the treatment of the young Sultan appealed to Italians viewers. This episode was masterly described by the writer De Amicis in his book “Marocco” published in 1876.

fd2a384c-3dc1-5711-b73d-c141912a1a62.name: Manuscript of *Gulshan-i Raz* (The Rose Garden of Mysteries)
fd2a384c-3dc1-5711-b73d-c141912a1a62.short_description: Made for Nasir al-Din Shah Qajar (r. 1264–1313 AH/1848–96), the manuscript *Gulshan-i Raz* (The Rose Garden of Mysteries) consists of one hundred and nineteen calligraphic pages, each with ten lines of gold-sprinkled *nasta‘liq* in the hand of Shukrallah Nameh-Nigar. The name of Nasir al-Din Shah Qajar is mentioned on the page preceding the last one in the manuscript, and his portrait is painted on the central medallions on the front and back exterior covers. The binding reflects the combination of tradition and modernity during the Qajar period. It features the customary composition of scrolling vegetal motif in gold on a dark background wedded to European-style portraits of the shah.

fd83d0b9-980c-5d81-b47c-74aa8931e4de.short_description: The miniature, cut from a manuscript, illustrates an episode of Ferdowsi’s epic *Shahnameh*, in which Iskandar kills a dragon through trickery, by making it swallow an ox hide stuffed with naphtha. fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.name: *Trompe l’œil* with Pious Pictures of *St. Philipp* and the *Virgin Mary*
fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.description:
Elias Mögel was active in Pozsony (Bratislava). His family background is unknown; the first piece of information about him is his wedding in 1751. His last will and testament was written in 1779 and announced on 12 June 1786. His earliest, signed, still life dates from 1760, the latest from 1784. Mögel would have known the Swiss branch of *trompe l'œil* painting through the circle of Johann Gaspar Füssli (1706–1782). The Quodlibets of the writer and professor of drawing in Zürich already carry an unmistakable intention of a popular and artistic education; all that might be of interest to one wanting to appreciate art seems to be present in this picture and its pair: etchings and engravings of all possible techniques, paintings, different types of paper and materials find their place on a trimmed piece of illusionistically painted wood.  
Mögel's paintings served in the improvement of general taste while also evoking a pious disposition. The illusory painting creates a milieu for the depiction of the saints and thus the printed pious paper-pictures, having been popular since the Middle Ages, were advanced here to works of art while at the same time they continue a century-long tradition of religious still life painting. The pair of this painting, conserved in the Bishop's Palace in Vác, is a *trompe l'œil* with engraved pictures of *St. Barbara* and *Salvator Mundi* (after Piazzetta) fixed with an iron nail, and accompanied by a paper with text referring to the Saint.  
Mögel also painted profane *trompe l'œil* pictures and imitated the Dutch genre painters as well. His signed picture kept in the Xantus János Museum in Győr was inspired by Rembrandt's pupil, Frans Bol; his two small genre scenes in Sopron were modelled on Gottfried Schalcken's works. The scenes of the Card players and Pipe smokers in Andrássy Castle in Krasznahorka (Krásna Hôrka) are reminiscent of Adriaen Brower's pictures. A series of six character-head studies, also kept there, may be attributed to him conditionally, as can the *trompe l'œil* of a collector's cabinet in the Museum of Červený Kameň.
fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.short_description: Mögel, who worked in Pozsony (Bratislava), was a master of *trompe l'œil*. This work together with its pair imitated engravings representing pious paper-pictures that had been popular since the Middle Ages.

fdae7b92-4bc6-5157-9b5e-a4cfe7c51307.name: *The Ambulance*
fdae7b92-4bc6-5157-9b5e-a4cfe7c51307.short_description: Sava Henţia was a Romanian painter who studied in Rome and Paris. During the Romanian Independence War (the Russian-Ottoman war of 1877–1878), he was one of the four Romanian painters who accompanied the Romanian army on the front with the purpose of depicting scenes from the war. However, he did not only dedicate himself to painting, but also worked as a volunteer for the Romanian Ambulance Service. In the foreground of the painting The Ambulance, some Romanian doctors are attending Ottoman soldiers, while in the background can be seen medical tents of the Red Cross.

fec8780a-ff2e-551c-aafa-af473f5f2afe.name: Untitled
fec8780a-ff2e-551c-aafa-af473f5f2afe.description: This work by Abdullah Hamas, a Palestinian painter, expresses the urban interconnectedness between the holy cities of Jerusalem, Medina and Mecca. By tying these sacred geographies together along a diagonal axis, Hamas recreates the intertwined  nature of those holy cities and the movement between them as expressed in the original purpose of the Hijaz Railway. The axis, in this sense, reconstitutes a new imagined railway connected centres  of urban sacrality in the Hijaz and Levant.

ffa8bb2b-6412-5238-b1e9-19ae24e65029.name: Parting scene
ffa8bb2b-6412-5238-b1e9-19ae24e65029.description: On St. Berchtold’s day in 1801, the family gathered around Johann Caspar Lavater’s deathbed and said their farewells to the famous pastor of St. Peter’s church in Zurich. He died on January 2, 1801 of a gunshot wound received from a French soldier in September 1799 whilst trying to help soldiers injured during the capture of Zurich by General Masséna. His wife Anna Schinz, his brother Diethelm, his two daughters Anna, (the elder) with her husband Georg Gessner, and Louise, and son Heinrich Lavater with his wife Anna Barbara Ott are all gathered by his deathbed.
